Surah al-Naml

It is also called, as in al-Durr al-Manthur, Surat Sulayman. It is Meccan, as narrated from Ibn Abbas and Ibn al-Zubayr, may Allah be pleased with them. Some scholars held that some of its verses are Medinan, as will come if Allah wills. The number of its verses is ninety-five according to the Hijazi count, four according to the Basri and Syrian counts, and three according to the Kufan count. The connection of this surah with what precedes it is that it is like a completion of it, in that Allah, glory be to Him, added in it the mention of Dawud and Sulayman, and expanded in it the story of Lut, peace be upon him, more than in what came before. In it occurs: ﴿When Musa said to his family, "Indeed, I have perceived a fire"﴾ etc., and this is like an elaboration of His saying, glory be to Him, earlier: ﴿So my Lord granted me judgment and made me among the messengers﴾. Both surahs include mention of the Qur'an and that it is from Allah, the Exalted, and consolation of the Prophet (ﷺ), among other things. It is narrated from Ibn Abbas and Jabir ibn Zayd that al-Shu'ara was revealed, then Ta-Sin, then al-Qasas.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Ta-Sin﴾ It is read with imala and without it. The discussion of it is like the discussion of its counterparts among the opening letters.

﴿Those﴾ is a demonstrative referring to the surah mentioned. The distal demonstrative is used to indicate the elevated rank in excellence and nobility, or to refer to the verses recited after it, like the demonstrative in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Alif-Lam-Mim. That is the Book﴾, or to the verses in general. It is in the nominative case as the subject, its predicate being His saying, the Exalted: ﴿the verses of the Qur'an﴾, and the sentence is resumptive; or it is a predicate of His saying, the Exalted: (Ta-Sin). The idafa of (verses) to (the Qur'an) is for the glorification of its status, for what is meant by it is the revealed, blessed one, confirming what is before it, described by perfections that have no end. It is also applied to all that was revealed to him (ﷺ) for the purpose of miraculousness, and to a part of it. It is permitted here to intend either of the two meanings. If the second is intended, then "part" means all that was revealed at the time of the revelation of the surah. His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and a clear Book﴾ is conjoined to (the Qur'an), and what is meant by it is the Qur'an. Its conjunction to it, despite their being identical in referent, is like the conjunction of one of two attributes to the other, as in the saying: "This is the act of the generous and the munificent, the noble." Its tanwin is for magnification. (Mubin, "clear") is either from abana in its transitive sense, meaning: making manifest what is within its contents of wisdoms and rulings, the conditions of earlier generations and the conditions of the Hereafter, among which are reward and punishment, or the path of guidance and error, or the like. The well-known view regarding such ellipsis is that it conveys generality.

Or it is from abana in its intransitive sense, meaning bana: manifestly miraculous, or manifestly sound as a miracle. On both possibilities it is a laudatory attribute of (Book), confirming what the tanwin conveys of grandeur.

Since indefiniteness carries one kind of grandeur and definiteness another, and since the aim was comprehensive totality, (the Qur'an) was made definite and (Book) indefinite, and the arrangement was reversed in al-Hijr, with the definite placed first in both places, to increase the emphasis. Since He, glory be to Him, followed it here with speech about the particular, the fact that it is a Qur'an was placed first, because it more clearly indicates the particularity of what was revealed to Muhammad (ﷺ) for the purpose of miraculousness; so says al-Kashshaf.

Some eminent scholars said: the first attribute was placed first here in view of the precedence of the state of Qur'anness over the state of bookness, and it was reversed there, because the intent is to magnify it in terms of its comprising the perfection of the whole genus of divine books, as though it were all of them, and in terms of its being distinguished from others, unique in its kind, singular in its domain. Indicating its distinction from all other books after alerting to its encompassing the perfections of other books is more fitting for praise, lest one suppose at first that its distinction from others lies in its independence with particular attributes without including the perfect qualities of all other noble books. In this view, the (al) in (the Book) is for the genus.

The apparent view is that the (al) in (the Qur'an) is for the known, so its meaning differs in the two places, and the apparent wording of al-Kashshaf indicates this, as has been said, and an excuse was made for it: if both meanings return to magnification, then there is no harm in such a difference. It is also permitted that in both places it be for the known, or for the genus in both; so consider. It was said: the particular connection of each of the two places with what is specific to it is the determination of the path.

It is permitted that Book refer to the Preserved Tablet, and its making-manifest is that what will exist until the Day of Resurrection has been inscribed in it, so it makes it clear to those who look into it. Its being mentioned here after the Qur'an is in view of the connection of our knowledge to it, and its being placed before it in al-Hijr is in view of external existence, for the Qur'an, in the sense of what is read by us, is posterior to the Preserved Tablet. It is not hidden that taking the Book as other than the Tablet is more apparent.

Some said: the Tablet interpretation is not supported here by the idafa of the verses to it, since there is no established covenant of its containing verses, nor by describing it with guidance and good tidings, since these are in view of its making things clear, so it must be taken relative to the people, among whom are the believers, and not relative to those who look into it.

Ibn Abi Abla read "wa-Kitabun mubin" with both in the nominative, and this was explained as an ellipsis of a modifier with the modified put in its place, i.e., "and verses of a Book." It was also said that it is permissible not to consider an ellipsis, and that "book," being originally a verbal noun, may be predicated of a feminine referent. It was also said: something may be permissible as a follower but not permissible independently; do you not see that they forbade "came to me Zayd" and permitted "came to me Hind and Zayd."

The phrase ﴿Guidance and good news﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from (*ayat*, "verses"). The verbal noun is placed in the position of the agent for emphasis (*mubalaghah*), as if the verses themselves were the guidance and the good news. The governing element is the sense of pointing (*ma'na al-isharah*), which the grammarians (*nuhat*) call an implied governing element (*'amil ma'nawi*).

Abu al-Baqa' permitted, on the reading with the nominative in (*kitab*, "a Book"), that the circumstantial clause could be from it. He then said: "It is weak for it to be from the genitive noun. It is permissible for it to be a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in (*mubin*, "clear") on both readings." Abu Hayyan permitted that the accusative is an absolute verbal noun (*masdariyyah*), meaning: it guides with guidance and gives good news with good news. Or the nominative may be in apposition (*badaliyyah*) to (*ayat*). The Kufan grammarians stipulated two conditions for substituting an indefinite noun for a definite one: that the wording be identical, and that the indefinite noun be qualified, as in the Qur'anic statement ﴿We will surely seize him by the forelock﴾ ﴿a lying, sinful forelock﴾. This is not sound, as stated in the commentary on *al-Tashil* (Ibn Malik's *Sharh al-Tashil*), because the attested usage contradicts it. Alternatively, it may be a predicate following another predicate (*khabar ba'd khabar*) for that (verses), or a predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: they are guidance and good news.

﴿for the believers﴾ may be a restriction (*qayd*) applying to both the guidance and the good news together. The meaning of the verses guiding them, while they are already guided, is that they increase them in guidance. He, glorified is He, said: ﴿As for those who believe, it has increased them in faith, and they rejoice﴾. The meaning of their giving good news to them is clear, because they give them good news of a mercy from Allah, the Most High, and of approval and gardens in which they will have lasting bliss. So it is said. In the Shihabi glosses (*Hawashi al-Shihabiyyah*) it is stated that the guidance, on this possibility, is either in the sense of being guided (*ihtida'*) or in its literal sense. The specification of the believers is because they are the ones who benefit from it, even though its guidance is general. Taking "the believers" to mean those who are becoming believers is a forced interpretation, like taking their guidance to mean an increase in it.

It is also possible that it is a restriction applying to the good news only. The guidance then remains general, meaning guidance in the sense of indication and direction: guidance for all the responsible people, and good news for the believers.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 27, verse 3:**

﴿Who establish the prayer and give the zakat﴾ is a laudatory attribute (*sifah madihah*, a description of praise) of the believers. The establishing of the prayer and the giving of the zakat (*zakah*, obligatory almsgiving) are used as a metonym (*kunniya*, a figure of speech in which one thing stands for a broader concept) for the performance of righteous deeds in general, and are singled out specifically because they are, as it has been said, either the physical and financial acts of worship. The apparent meaning is that the zakat is understood as the obligatory zakat.

It has been objected that the surah is Meccan, and the zakat was only made obligatory in Medina. It has been said that there was an obligatory zakat in Mecca, but it was not like the obligatory zakat in Medina, so the verse should be understood as referring to it. It has also been said that the zakat here means purity from defects and adherence to noble morals, but this is contrary to the well-known meaning of zakat when it is paired with prayer, and the linking of giving (*itha'*) to it makes this interpretation unlikely.

The words of the Exalted, ﴿And they, in the Hereafter, they are certain﴾, may be understood in three ways: that it is conjoined (*ma'tuf*) to the relative clause; that it is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*) referring back to the relative pronoun; or that it is a resumptive clause (*isti'naf*) brought in with the purpose of emphasizing what the believers were described with, since certainty concerning the Hereafter entails fear, and fear entails bearing the hardships of obligation, so there must be the establishing of prayer and the giving of zakat. The pronoun here has been placed in the position of a demonstrative (*ism al-isharah*), which indicates the attainment of succession (*khilafah*) through judgment based on precedence. It is as if it were said: "These are the ones who believe and do righteous deeds, such as establishing the prayer and giving the zakat, and they are the ones certain of the Hereafter." Al-Zamakhshari called this resumptive clause a parenthetical insertion (*i'tiraḍ*), but his view that it can only occur between two things connected to one another, such as a subject and predicate, is not accepted by others.

He chose this possibility and said: "It is the preferred view, and what supports it is that the statement is constructed as an independent nominal sentence, in which the subject *hum* (they) is repeated, so that its meaning becomes: 'None are certain of the Hereafter with true certainty except these, who combine faith and righteous deeds, because fear of the consequence moves them to bear hardships,' end of quote."

Ibn al-Munir denied that such a construction indicates exclusivity (*ikhtisas*), and claimed that the repetition of the pronoun is for the sake of theory (*nazariyyah*) because of the separation between the two pronouns by the prepositional phrase. The truth is that it does indicate that, as they have stated, in such expressions as *huwa 'urf* (he is the one who knows), and likewise it indicates emphasis because of the repetition of the pronoun in it.

Abu Hayyan claimed that in what al-Zamakhshari mentioned there is a trace of Mu'tazilism (*dasisat al-i'tizal*, a concealed doctrinal bias). It is not hidden that his statement contains no more than an indication that the sinful believer has not attained certainty of the Hereafter with true certainty. Perhaps the reason for considering this a concealed bias is that he built this upon his position regarding the people of major sins and his saying about them that they are in the intermediate position between the two positions (*al-manzilah bayn al-manzilatayn*).

You know that the view he chose in the verse does not depend on the aforementioned statement. The alteration of the noble arrangement in the first two possibilities is for reasons that are not hidden. The placing of *bil-akhirah* (in the Hereafter) first in all the possibilities is for the sake of observing the verse-ending (*fasilah*, the rhyming final word of a verse). It is also permissible that it is for restriction relative to something else (*al-hasr al-idafi*), as in the Shihabi glosses (*al-hawashi al-Shihabiyyah*).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 27, verse 4:

﴿Indeed, those who do not believe in the Hereafter – We have made their deeds appealing to them, so they wander blindly.﴾ This is an explanation of the states of the disbelievers after the states of the believers. That is, they do not believe in the Hereafter and what it contains of reward for righteous deeds and punishment for evil deeds, as the Qur'an states. ﴿We have made their deeds appealing to them﴾, the ugly deeds, by what We have placed in them of desires and wishful hopes, until they see them as good. ﴿So they wander blindly﴾, that is, they are bewildered and hesitant. Their persistence in occupying themselves with these deeds and their absorption in them, without considering what follows from them, is implied. The fa' (so) indicates the ordering of the effect upon the cause. According to the majority (al-jama'ah), attributing the adornment (tazyin) to Him, glorified and exalted is, in its literal sense, true, and so is the adornment itself. Al-Zamakhshari, however, held that tazyin is either a metaphor for providing enjoyment through long life and abundant provision, or it is literal, and its attribution to Him, glorified and exalted, is metaphorical, while it is literal when attributed to Satan, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Satan made their deeds appealing to them﴾.

What justifies this metaphor is His, exalted is He, granting Satan respite and leaving him free until he adorns [deeds] for them. The motive for Him, glorified and exalted, to choose one of the two options is the obligation upon Him to observe what is best. It is reported from al-Hasan that the intended meaning of "deeds" is good deeds, and their adornment is the making clear of their goodness in themselves in the present and their leading to various benefits in the future. That is: We made good deeds appealing to them, so they hesitate in error and turn away from them.

According to this view, the fa' indicates the ordering of the opposite of the effect upon the cause, as in your saying: "I admonished him, but he did not heed." It implies the completeness of their obstinacy, stubbornness, and their reversal of affairs. This view has been objected to on the ground that tazyin has occurred mostly in reference to what is not good, such as His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The love of desires has been made appealing to people﴾, ﴿The worldly life has been made appealing to those who disbelieved﴾, ﴿Made appealing to many of the polytheists﴾, etc. Its occurrence in reference to what is good is rare, such as His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But Allah has endeared to you the faith and made it appealing in your hearts﴾. Furthermore, taking "deeds" to mean good deeds is made distant by its being attributed to their pronoun, while they have done no good deed at all. That the attribution is to them in terms of their being commanded to do them and their being obligated to them does not remove this distance.

Al-Tibi mentioned that what supports the earlier view is that the pattern of the opening of this surah up to this point is the same as the pattern of the opening of al-Baqarah. Thus His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, those who do not believe in the Hereafter﴾ is like His saying, exalted is He, ( Indeed, those who disbelieved ), and His saying, glorified is He, ﴿We have made their deeds appealing to them﴾ is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah has set a seal upon their hearts﴾.

The manner in which this indicates the view of the majority was explained earlier there. The construction is one of affirming the report (tahqiq al-khabar), and the meaning is their persistence in disbelief, and that they are such that faith is not expected from them moment by moment, as a sign that the decree of wretchedness has been inscribed upon them from eternity, and the sealing upon their hearts. He, exalted is He, made their evil deeds appealing to them, so they wander in the wilderness of error and bewilderment in the desert of disbelief. This interpretation is indicated by the use of the present tense in the relative clause and the past tense in its predicate, by the placing of His saying, ﴿so they wander blindly﴾ after it with the fa', and by the restriction of the address to what indicates majesty and dominance, in the manner of affirming the report, as in the verse of the poet:

Indeed she who struck a tent, emigrating
to the city of Kufa of the soldiers, the ghoul has consumed her love.

In the sound reports there is also what supports this interpretation.

(Ūlā'ika) is a demonstrative referring to those mentioned, who were described as disbelievers and as wandering blindly (al-'amah), and it is the subject (mubtada') whose predicate (khabar) is ﴿those for whom is the evil of the punishment﴾. It is possible that the intended meaning is: for them this is in the world, by being killed, taken captive, or having the agonies of death made severe upon them, based on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and in the Hereafter they are the greatest losers﴾. It is also possible that the intended meaning is: for them this is in both abodes, and this is what Abu Hayyan preferred. In that case, His saying, exalted is He: (wa-hum) etc. ... serves to clarify that what is in the Hereafter is the greater of the two punishments, on the basis that "al-akhsarin" (the greatest losers) is an elative form (af'al al-tafdil), and the comparison is made with regard to their two states in the two abodes, i.e., they are in the Hereafter greater losers than they are in this world, and not others. This is indicated by the definiteness of the two components, in the sense that their loss in the Hereafter is greater than their loss in the world, insofar as their punishment in the Hereafter is not cut off at all, whereas their punishment in this world is cut off. This is not the case with others among the sinning believers, because their loss in the Hereafter is not greater than their loss in this world in this respect, since their punishment in the Hereafter ends and is followed by the eternal bliss, so that they almost do not think that they were ever punished. Thus it was said.

Some of them said: the comparison is made with regard to what is in the Hereafter, i.e., they are in the Hereafter the greatest of people in loss, and not others, because they are deprived of reward and remain in punishment, unlike the sinning believers. It follows from this that their punishment in the Hereafter is greater than their punishment in this world, and this suffices for the explanation.

Al-Kirmani said: the elative form here is for intensification (al-mubalaghah), not for sharing (al-shirkah). Abu Hayyan said: It is as if he is saying: the believer has no loss at all, such that the disbeliever would share it with him and exceed it. He did not perceive that the intended meaning is that the disbeliever's loss in the Hereafter is greater than his loss in the world, so the sharing indicated by (af'al) is only between what is in the Hereafter and what is in the world. End of his words.

It seems that he concedes that the believer has no loss at all, and in this there is a discussion that is not hidden. And the placing of (fi al-Akhirah) first is either for the sake of the closing rhyme (al-fasilah) or for restriction (al-hasr).

Al-Alusi, *Ruh al-Ma'ani*, on Surah 27, verse 6:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And indeed, you are receiving the Qur'an﴾ is a resumptive statement (*mustanaf*, a new sentence that is not grammatically tied to what precedes it), brought after explaining some aspects of the noble Qur'an. It serves as a preface to the stories that follow it. Its opening with the two emphasizing particles (*inna* and *lam*) shows the complete concern with its content. The verb is put in the passive and the agent is omitted, who is Jibril (peace be upon him), for indication of him in His saying: ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down﴾. The unaugmented form *laqa* takes one object, and the augmented form *laqqa* takes two. Here the two are the deputy of the subject and *al-Qur'an*. The meaning is: "Indeed you are being given the Qur'an, being taught it, ﴿from the presence of One who is All-Wise, All-Knowing﴾," meaning, what a Wise One and what a Knowing One. In magnifying the two of them there is a magnification of the status of the Qur'an, and an explicit statement of the high rank of the Prophet (peace be upon him) in knowing it and in comprehending what it contains of sublime and subtle matters. Wisdom (*hikmah*), as al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani) said, is from God, Mighty and Majestic, the knowledge of things and their creation in the utmost perfection, and from the human being it is knowledge of existing things and the doing of good deeds. It is combined with knowledge (*ilm*), although knowledge is included in its meaning linguistically as you have heard, because of its generality, since knowledge relates to non-existent things and can exist without action. Wisdom indicates the perfecting and mastery of action. This also signals that among the sciences in the Qur'an, some are wisdom, such as the laws, and some are not, such as the stories and the reports of the unseen.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 27, verse 7:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When Moses said to his family﴾ is in the accusative as an object of an implied verb, addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ), who was commanded to recite a portion of the Qur'an that he received from Him, mighty and majestic, as a confirmation and establishment of what precedes it. The meaning is: mention to them the time when Moses (peace be upon him) said to his family. It has also been permitted that (idh) be an adverbial (zarf) governed by ('alim, "all-knowing").

Abu Hayyan in al-Bahr objected to this, saying that it is not clear, since the attribute would then become restricted by its complement. In al-Kashshaf it is said: what might be imagined from the restriction to a specific time is dispelled, since it is not a concept (mafhum) considered valid by those who hold such views; and because it is the preface to the story, it is fitting that it be a qualifier of it, as if it were said: how knowing He is, when He did to Moses (peace be upon him) what He did. Since that is among the signs of knowledge and wisdom in general, the restriction does no harm; rather it benefits, as it ultimately returns to a kind of causation (ta'lil) and reminder. End of quote.

It is not hidden that the apparent reading, despite this, is the first aspect. Then, the saying of Moses (peace be upon him): ﴿Indeed I have perceived a fire; I will bring you from it some news﴾ was during his journey leaving Midian, near the valley of Tuwa. He (peace be upon him) had strayed from the road on a cold, dark night, so he struck a flint, and his tinder kindled, and a fire appeared to him from the side of the mountain. The news he would bring them from the fire is news about the state of the road, because whoever goes toward the light of a fire on the road will know it. He did not leave the verb free of the sin (the prefix sa-) either to indicate that the fire's distance is somewhat great, so that they would not feel lonely if he (peace be upon him) was delayed from them, or to emphasize the promise of coming; for it, as al-Zamakhshari mentioned, enters into a promise to emphasize it and to show that it is certain to occur though it may be delayed. As for what has been said, that the sin indicates the nearness of the period to dispel loneliness, it benefits, according to what has been said, only in preferring it to sawfa, not over the bare form, which conveys the present sense that is more complete in dispelling loneliness.

Perhaps the better course is to regard it as for emphasis. It may not be said that he (peace be upon him) did not speak in Arabic and the matters of its discussions; for we say: what prevents it from being in a language other than Arabic something that fulfills its function? Rather, the report of the saying from him (peace be upon him) with these words requires that he spoke in his own language what conveys that, necessarily. The plural of the pronoun, if it is correct that there was with him (peace be upon him) none but his wife, is for magnification; and this is the reason God, exalted is His glory, called the wife of Moses (peace be upon him) "family" (ahl), although it encompasses a group of followers.

﴿Or I will bring you a burning brand (qabas)﴾, that is, a lit flame of fire, that is, taken from its source. So "qabas" is an attribute of "shihab" or a substitute for it. This is the reading of the Kufans and Ya'qub. The rest of the Seven and al-Hasan read "bi-shihabi qabas" with the genitive construction, and Abu al-Hasan preferred it. It is an explanatory genitive (idafah bayaniyyah), due to the general and specific relation between them, as in "thawb kharr" (a garment of silk), for a shihab may be a qabas or not a qabas. The two promises are made as a matter of conjecture, and for this reason they are expressed in the form of hope (tarajji) in Surat Ta-Ha. Thus there is no contradiction between what occurs here and what occurs there. The disjunction serves to indicate that if he did not obtain either of them, he would not lose one of them, based on the apparent state of affairs and trust in the custom of God, mighty and majestic, that He does not usually combine two deprivations upon a servant.

It has been said: it is permissible to say that the disjunction is because his need was for one of them, not for both; for he was in a state of travel, and had lost his way, so his aim was to find someone who could guide him to the road so that he would continue his journey; and if he did not find that, he would kindle a fire and ward off the harm of the cold while staying.

This has been objected to: it is reported in the story that a son had been born to him near the mountain on a wintry night and in a snowy darkness, and he had lost the way and his flock had scattered, so he saw the fire and said to his family what he said. This indicates that he needed both together. But he (peace be upon him) sought the truth and therefore used "or" (aw).

﴿That perhaps you may warm yourselves﴾, that is, in hope, or so that you may be warmed by it. "Al-salu," with a kasra on the sad and a long vowel (as-sila), or with a fatha and short vowel, is drawing near the fire to warm the body, which is warmth; and it is also applied to the fire itself. Or it is, with the kasra, the warmth,

and with the fatha

﴿Then when he came to it﴾, that is, the fire about which he had said: ﴿I have perceived a fire﴾. It has been said that the pronoun refers to the tree, but that is as you see it, and what he took to be a summons is not a summons, for the reason we have indicated. ﴿He was called﴾, that is, Musa, peace be upon him, was called from the side of the Tur (Mount Sinai). ﴿That blessed is﴾: its meaning is, "blessed is," and the ﴿an﴾ (that) is explanatory (mufassirah, "explanatory an"), because the calling contains the sense of saying without its letters.

It has been permitted that the ﴿an﴾ be the lightened form (mukhaffafah) of the heavy ﴿anna﴾, with its noun being a pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-sha'n). Some have prohibited this because there is no separation between it and the verb by ﴿qad﴾, the ﴿sīn﴾, ﴿sawfa﴾, or a negative particle, and such separation is necessary when it is lightened. This is because, in Abu Ali al-Farisi's "al-Hujja," the lightened ﴿an﴾ is only followed by nouns, so they found it ugly for a verb to follow it without a separator.

It is answered that what has been mentioned is not absolute, for they have explicitly stated that separation is not a requirement in certain places, among them when the verb is a supplication (du'a'). Perhaps whoever permitted it being the lightened form here made ﴿būrika﴾ a supplication. On this basis, it is permissible to claim that separation by one of the mentioned particles, outside of what has been excepted, is the general rule, as in his saying:

They knew that they would hope, so they were generous before they were asked for the greatest request.

It has also been permitted that the ﴿an﴾ be the verbal-source particle (maṣdariyyah) that governs the verbs, and then ﴿būrika﴾ would be either a statement (khabar) or a performative utterance (inshā') of supplication.

Al-Radi claimed that if ﴿būrika﴾ is made a supplication, then the ﴿an﴾ is only explanatory, because the lightened form is not followed by a performative verb by consensus (ijma'), and likewise the verbal-source form. This contradicts what the grammarians have mentioned, and the claim of consensus is not correct. The view that the meaning of the demand would be lost after interpretation as a verbal noun has already been discussed.

In al-Kashf, preventing its being made a verbal-source particle is that the meaning does not hold together, because ﴿būrika﴾ in that case is not suitable as good tidings. They have said: the opening of the address with that is good tidings to Musa, peace be upon him, that a great matter has been decreed for him, from which blessing will spread throughout the whole land of al-Sham. This is different from when ﴿būrika﴾ is an explanation of the matter (sha'n). End of quote. There is room for debate in this.

On both views, the speech is on the basis of the omission of the preposition, that is, ﴿he was called with that...﴾, and the prepositional phrase is attached to what is before it. It is not the deputy of the subject; rather, the deputy of the subject is the pronoun of Musa, peace be upon him. It has also been said that it is the deputy of the subject and there is no pronoun.

Some have also said, regarding the first view: the pronoun standing in place of the subject is not for Musa, peace be upon him, but for the verbal source of the verb, that is, ﴿he was called — he﴾, that is, the calling, and the calling is explained by what follows it. The more apparent view is that the pronoun refers back to Musa; that the ﴿an﴾ is explanatory; and that ﴿būrika﴾ is a statement, and it derives from ﴿barakah﴾ (blessing), whose meaning has already been discussed. It has also been said here that the meaning is: sanctified, purified, and increased in goodness.

﴿Whoever is in the fire and whoever is around it﴾. A group of scholars held that there is an implied noun (muḍāf muqaddar) in two places in the speech, that is: whoever is in the place of the fire and whoever is around its place. They said: its place is the spot in which it occurred, and it is the blessed spot mentioned in the words of the Exalted: ﴿He was called from the right bank of the valley, in the blessed spot﴾. The reading of Ubayy supports this: "Blessed is the land and whoever is around it." It has been inferred that the generality of ﴿whoever﴾ applies to every person in that valley and around it, from the land of al-Sham, which is marked with blessings, because it was the place of the sending of the prophets, peace be upon them, and their gathering place, alive and dead, and especially that spot where Allah the Exalted spoke to Musa, peace be upon him.

It has been said: ﴿whoever is in the fire﴾ is Musa, peace be upon him, and ﴿whoever is around it﴾ is the angels present, peace be upon them. This is supported by the reading of Ubayy, as transmitted by Abu Amr al-Dani, and by Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, and Ikrimah: "and whoever is around it of the angels." According to many, this is an explanation (tafsir), not a reading (qira'ah), because it contradicts the consonantal text of the mushaf on which there is consensus.

It has been said: the first is the angels, and the second is Musa, peace be upon them. Some dispensed with the implied noun by making the locative sense a metaphor for complete nearness, and went to the second view regarding the intended meaning of the two relative pronouns.

Whichever view is taken, the intention of this is the good tidings to Musa, peace be upon him. And the intention of the Exalted's words, according to what has been said: ﴿Exalted is Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾, is an expression of wonder on his part at that, and a notice that this which comes to pass is willed and brought into being by the Lord of the worlds, drawing attention to the fact that what occurs is of the great matters and mighty affairs, and of the rulings of His nurturing of the worlds, the Exalted. Or it is a statement to him, peace be upon him, purifying Allah, the Glorified, lest it be supposed from hearing His speech that there is any resemblance to human attributes. Or it is a request from him, peace be upon him, for that.

It has been permitted that it be an expression of wonder issuing from him, peace be upon him, with the supposed verb of saying, that is: and he said, "Exalted is Allah...," etc. Al-Suddi said: it is from the speech of Musa, peace be upon him, which he said when he heard the call from the tree, to declare Allah, the Exalted, free from the marks of created things. It seems that this is also on the basis of a supposed verb of saying, and he made the supposed element a conjunction upon ﴿was called﴾.

Ibn Shajara said: it is from the speech of Allah the Exalted, and its meaning is: "And blessed is whoever glorifies Allah the Exalted, Lord of the worlds." This is very far from the indication of the wording. It has been said: it is an address to our Prophet ﷺ, intended as a declaration of Allah's transcendence, and it is placed as an interjection between what

And as for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿O Moses, indeed it is I, Allah, the Almighty, the Wise﴾. It is connected in meaning to that (preceding statement). The pronoun (in *innahu*) refers to the matter (*damir al-sha'n*, the "pronoun of the matter," an anaphoric pronoun referring to a subsequent clause). His saying, glorified is He, ﴿Ana Allah (It is I, Allah)﴾, is a subject and predicate. "The Almighty" and "the Wise" are two attributes of the Majestic Name, preparing for what He wished to manifest through the hand of (Moses) of the miracle. That is: "I am Allah, the Mighty, who is capable of what imaginations cannot reach of great matters, among which is the matter of the staff and the hand, who does all that I do with far-reaching wisdom and firm management." The clause is the predicate of *inna* (indeed), explaining the pronoun of the matter.

It has also been permitted that the pronoun refers to what the speech indicates, namely the One Who speaks and calls out, and that *ana* (I) is the predicate. That is: "Indeed, the One who speaks to you and calls to you is I." The Majestic Name is then an explicative apposition (*'atf bayan*) to *ana*. The substitution (*badaliyya*, as a apposition in the sense of a complete substitute) is also permitted according to those who allow substituting a noun for the first-person pronoun as a full substitute. It is also permitted that *ana* is an emphatic (*tawkid*) for the pronoun, and *Allah* is the predicate.

Abu Hayyan criticized the reference of the pronoun to the speaker who calls, saying: when the agent is omitted and its verb is put in the passive, it is not permissible for a pronoun to refer back to that omitted agent, because that defeats the purpose of omitting it, and the intention is that it should not be spoken of. In response: no one has said that it refers to the omitted agent; rather it refers to what the speech indicates. And even if it were granted, there is no prohibition in that when it is in another clause.

Also, his saying, "and the intention is that it should not be spoken of," is not correct, because it may be spoken of and then omitted, being known and there being no need to mention it. Furthermore, the (inference of) the "carrying" (*al-haml*, the sense of the message) is valid without seeing (the speaker), because he (peace be upon him) knew Him, glorified is He, with certain knowledge of what settled in his heart, so it is as if he saw Him, Mighty and Majestic.

Now, regarding His saying, the Exalted: ﴿That blessed is whoever is in the fire﴾ and so on, there are other opinions:

The first: that what is meant by "whoever is in the fire" is the light of Allah, the Exalted, and by "whoever is around it" are the angels, peace be upon them. This was narrated from Qatadah and al-Zajjaj.

The second: that what is meant by "whoever is in the fire" is the tree which Allah made a place for the speech, and by "whoever is around it" are also the angels, peace be upon them. This was reported from al-Jubba'i. In what was mentioned there is the use of *man* (whoever) for other than the rational.

The third: what Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: regarding His saying, the Exalted: ﴿That blessed is whoever is in the fire﴾, he means, Blessed and Exalted is He Himself; as if the light of the Lord of the worlds were in the tree, and "whoever is around it" means the angels, peace be upon them. It is well known from him that what is meant by "whoever is in the fire" is Himself, Exalted; and it is also reported from al-Hasan, Ibn Jubayr, and others, as in al-Bahr (*al-Bahr al-Muhit*). The Imam criticized that, saying: we are certain that this report from Ibn 'Abbas is fabricated and invented.

Abu Hayyan said: if that is established from Ibn 'Abbas and those mentioned, it is interpreted with an omission, that is: "blessed is the One whose power and authority are in the fire." Shaykh Ibrahim al-Kurani, in his treatise (*Tanbih al-'Uqul 'ala Tanzih al-Sufiyya 'an I'tiqad al-Tajsim wal-'Ayniyya wal-Ittihad wal-Hulul*, "Alerting the Intellects to the Sufis' Exemption from the Belief in Anthropomorphism, Identity, Unification and Indwelling"), went to the soundness of the report from the rabbi (*al-Habr*, i.e., Ibn 'Abbas), may Allah be pleased with him, and to the lack of need for the aforementioned interpretation. For what prompted the interpreters, or those who judged it fabricated, to interpret or judge it fabricated, was the supposition that it indicates the impossible indwelling in Him, exalted is He. This is not so; rather what it indicates is His manifestation, glorified is He, in the fire and His being revealed in it. That is not indwelling at all, for a thing's being a means of manifesting something is not its being a locus for it. The image in a mirror, for example, is certainly external to the mirror in its own essence, unlike that which inheres in a locus, for it is present in it. Furthermore, His manifestation, exalted is He, and His appearance in manifestations is compatible with transcendence (*tanzih*).

According to him, the meaning of the verse is: "So when he came to it, he was called: that blessed is—that is, sanctified or something similar—whoever manifested and appeared in the form of the fire, according to what wisdom required, since it was the thing sought by Moses, peace be upon him, and whoever is around it of the angels, or of them and Moses, peace be upon them."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And glory be to Allah﴾ is a rejection of what the manifestation in the aspect of fire might suggest of resemblance (*tashbih*, likening to creation). That is: "And glory be to Allah above being confined to form, place, or direction, even though He appeared in them according to the requirement of wisdom, because He is described by the attribute of the Lord of the worlds, the Vast, the Holy, the Independent of the worlds. Whoever is so does not become confined to anything of the attributes of created things. Rather, He, Majestic and Exalted, remains upon His absoluteness, even beyond the restriction of absoluteness in the state of His manifestation and appearance in whatever manifestations He wills."

For this reason, it is related in the authentic hadith: "Glory be to You wherever You are" (*subhanaka haythu kunta*). So He affirmed for Him, exalted is He, manifestation in a "where," and declared Him transcendent of being restricted by that. ﴿O Moses, indeed it is I﴾, that is, the One who calls, manifested in the fire: ﴿I am Allah, the Mighty﴾, so I am not confined to a manifestation of inherent might, ﴿but I am the Wise﴾, and the requirement of wisdom is manifestation in the form of what you seek. It has been mentioned that assuming an omitted noun (*taqdir al-mudaf*), as some exegetes did, is a departure from the apparent meaning out of supposing a prohibited implication in it; and it has become clear that there is no prohibition, so there is no need for departure. End of quotation.

And it seems to you that you will say: this is a level beyond the level of intellects. Furthermore, there is no obstacle, according to the principles of the Sufis, to their intending by "whoever is around it" Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, as well; for in the abode, according to them, there is none other than Him, glorified is He, "no dwelling" (*dayyar*). There is no distance in the verse, according to Ibn 'Abbas, if what was mentioned from him is sound, being among the ambiguous verses (*mutashabih*, those whose meaning is not clear on the surface), and the positions on it are known to you. The more suitable interpretation for the general public is to say: the meaning is "that blessed is whoever his light appeared in the fire," and perhaps the preceding report from the rabbi points to this.

The attribution of the light to Him, exalted is He, is for honoring the thing attributed, and it is a particular light which was a manifestation of His great power and majesty, exalted is He. I heard from some of the eminent shaykhs saying: this light was neither the same as Him nor other than Him, in the manner of al-Ash'ari's statement regarding His essential attributes, Mighty and Majestic. This too is a Sufi approach which ultimately returns to the discourse of manifestation and appearance, as is not hidden. So reflect.

[Page 163]

Its being conjoined (ʿaṭf) to "būrika" (be blessed) is part of the same string that explains the call (*nidāʾ*). That is, it was called out that "be blessed" and that "throw down your staff." This is supported by the words of the Exalted after His saying, "O Mūsā, indeed I am Allah," with the repetition of "that" (*an*): "And that throw down your staff." The Qur'an explains one part of itself by another. This is what al-Zamakhsharī chose. It was objected that the renewal of the call in the words "O Mūsā," and so on, prevents this. It was answered that this is not a renewal of the call, because it is part of the explanation of the call that was mentioned. It was also said that it does not prevent this, because it is a parenthetical clause (*jumla iʿtirāḍiyya*). There is discussion on this point. It was also objected that "būrika" is a declarative statement (*ikhbār*) and "alqi" is a performative/imperative statement (*inshāʾ*), and an imperative cannot be conjoined to a declarative. From here it was said that the conjunction is to that by the supposition "and it was said to him: throw down," or the conjunction is to an implied element, meaning "do what I command you, and throw down." In reply, in such a case it is permissible to conjoin an imperative to a declarative, because the call (*nidāʾ*) has the meaning of speech. Rather, Sībawayh permitted "Zayd came, and [behold] ʿAmr," with conjunction.

This objection does not arise at all for one who makes "būrika" an imperative. It does arise for one who makes the conjunction to an implied "afʿal" (do). In that case the apparent form would be "fa-alqi" with the *fāʾ*. Abū Ḥayyān chose that the conjunction is to the sentence "Indeed He is Allah, the Mighty, the Wise," and he was not concerned by the difference between the two sentences being nominal and verbal, or declarative and imperative, because it was mentioned that the sound view is that the two conjoined sentences need not be alike in this respect, in light of what you have just heard from Sībawayh.

The *fāʾ* in His saying, "Then when he saw it writhing," is *fāʾ faṣīḥa* (the *fāʾ* that reveals an omitted clause), revealing a clause that has been omitted, relying on its being clear, and indicating the speed with which its content occurred. As if it were said: "So he threw it down, and it became a serpent. Then when he saw it moving violently, he was agitated." The clause "tahtazzu" (writhing) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) from the object of "raʾā" (saw). This is because it is visual (*baṣariyya*), as we have indicated, not cognitive (*ʿilmiyya*), as has been said.

His saying, "as if it were a jānn," is in the position of another circumstantial clause from it, or it is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "tahtazzu," according to the method of interlocking (*tadākhul*). The *jānn* is a small serpent that moves quickly. He, glorified is He, likened it in the intensity of its movement and its agitation, despite the size of its body, to small serpents that move quickly. So this does not contradict His saying in another place: "Then it was a manifest serpent" (*thuʿbān mubīn*).

It was also said: it is permissible that the description of it is by different attributes, according to its changing states in it. Al-Ḥasan, al-Zuhrī and ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd read "jaʾn" with an open hamza, to flee from the meeting of two unvocalized letters, although it conforms to the rule, as it has been said: "daʾba" and "shaʾba."

"And he turned back fleeing" (*wallā mudbiran*): that is, he fled. "And he did not return" (*wa lam yuʿaqqib*): that is, he did not come back upon his heels. From "ʿaqqaba" (he returned), when a fighter charges again after fleeing. The poet said:

They did not return when it was said, "Is there one who returns?"
Nor did they halt at any place on the day of dread.

This is transmitted from Mujāhid. Close to it is the saying of Qatādah: "that is, he did not look back." This is what al-Rāghib mentioned. This happened to him, peace be upon him, because of a fear that seized him. It has been said: it was due to the requirement of human nature, for a human, when he sees something extremely terrifying, is naturally afraid. Or because he thought that this was for a matter whose occurrence was intended through him. What indicates this is His saying, glorified is He: "O Mūsā, do not fear" (*lā takhaf*): that is, do not fear from Me, any creature, whether a serpent or other, trusting in Me and relying on Me. Or: do not fear at all, the verb being treated as intransitive. This is either merely for reassurance, without intending the literal prohibition, or it is a prohibition against the source of the fear, which is the supposition you have heard.

His saying, "Indeed, the messengers do not fear in My presence" (*innī lā yakhāfu ladayya al-mursalūn*), is a reason for the prohibition against fear. According to what has been said, this supports that the fear was due to the mentioned supposition, and that what is meant is "do not fear at all." What is meant by "ladayya" (in My presence) is in the state of nearness to Me, and that is at the time of revelation.

The meaning is that it is not fitting for the messengers to fear at the time of revelation to them. Rather, fear does not occur to their minds, even if there is something to be feared, because of their complete absorption in receiving commands and the drawing of their spirits toward the world of the dominion (*malakūt*). The restriction by "ladayya" is because the messengers, at other times, are the most fearful of people of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. He, exalted is He, said: "Only those of His servants who have knowledge fear Allah" (*innamā yakhshā Allāha min ʿibādihi al-ʿulamāʾ*), and none is more knowing of Allah, exalted is His majesty, than them.

It has been said: the meaning is "do not fear from anyone other than Me," or "do not fear at all." This is because what should be feared by the likes of you, O messengers, is only the bad end (*sūʾ al-ʿāqiba*), and the matter is not that there would be a bad end for the messengers with Me, that they should fear from it.

What is meant by the bad end is that of the Hereafter, not that of this world, lest the killing of some messengers, peace and blessings be upon them, be objected to. What is meant by "ladayya," according to al-Khafājī, is "at My meeting," and according to Ibn al-Shaykh, "under My authority." In either case, it follows from what has been mentioned that the messengers, peace be upon them, do not fear a bad end, because Allah, exalted is He, has secured them from that. If they feared it, it would follow that they were not trusting in Him, Mighty and Majestic. This is the correct view, as in the Shihābī glosses according to al-Ashʿarī. But the apparent meaning of the reports indicates that they, peace be upon them, did fear that. It was narrated that he, peace and blessings be upon him, used to frequently say: "O Turner of the hearts, make my heart firm upon Your religion."

[Page 169]

ʿĀʾisha, may Allah be pleased with her, said to him one day: "O Messenger of Allah, you frequently make this supplication. Do you fear?" He, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, said: "What would make me secure, O ʿĀʾisha, when the hearts of the servants are between two of the fingers of the fingers of the Most Merciful? When He wills, He turns the heart of His servant."

The apparent meaning of some verses also indicates this, such as His saying: "So none feels secure from the plan of Allah except the losing people" (*fa-lā yaʾmanu makra Allāhi illā al-qawm al-khāsirūn*). As for Allah, exalted is He, having secured them from that: if what is meant is what came within the glad tidings of Paradise to them, then it is established that the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, who were given glad tidings of Paradise, used to fear a bad end, while knowing of His glad tiding to them of Paradise. From this it is known that fear coexists with glad tidings, and it does not follow from this that there is no certainty in Him, Mighty and Majestic, because this is on account of the possibility that there is a condition that Allah, exalted is He, did not make manifest to them, for trial and similar divine wisdoms. And if what is meant is what is explicitly in "I have secured you" from a bad end, this possibility also remains in it, and fear arises from that. And if what is meant is what is required by His making them protected from disbelief and the like, it was answered that the angels, peace be upon them, were also made protected from that by Allah, exalted is He, and they fear.

In a report: When Iblīs was tricked, Jibrīl and Mīkāʾīl, peace be upon them both, wept. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said to them: "What makes you weep?" They said: "O Lord, we do not feel secure from Your plan." He, exalted is He, said: "Thus be; do not feel secure from My plan."

Perhaps that is because infallibility (*ʿiṣma*), according to us, in accordance with what is required by the fundamental principle that all things are ultimately attributed to the Chooser, the Agent (*al-fāʿil al-mukhtār*), as in the *Mawāqif* and its commentary by al-Sharīf al-Jurjānī, is that Allah, exalted is He, does not create a sin in the person. And according to the philosophers, based on what they held concerning the doctrine of necessitation (*al-ījāb*) and considering the receptivity of recipients (*istiʿdād al-qawābil*), it is a disposition (*malaka*) that prevents immorality, which arises initially through knowledge of the defects of disobedience and the merits of obedience, and is strengthened by the successive continuity of revelation with commands and prohibitions. In both senses, it does not necessitate the impossibility of sin.

As for it not necessitating that in the first sense, this is because Allah's not creating it is not obligatory upon Him, glorified is He, such that His creating it would be impossible for Him. And whenever creating it is not impossible for Him, exalted is He, how can security from the plan be attained?

As for it not necessitating that in the second sense, this is because the removal of that disposition is also possible. And the knowledge of defects and merits necessitating that disposition initially, and its being strengthened by the successive continuity of revelation, is not among the rational necessities. And when the matter is so, security is not attained merely by the occurrence of the disposition. Yes, some people said: infallibility is a special property in the person himself or in his body, by which the commission of sin from him is impossible. One who holds that security is possible may rely on this. It is not hidden that even if the proof is granted to be complete for this claim, it is in itself not valid.

In the *Mawāqif* and its commentary: what refutes this view is that if the committing of sin were impossible, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, would not deserve praise for abandoning sin, since there is no praise for abandoning what is impossible, because it is not within capacity and is not under choice. Also, there is consensus that the prophets, peace be upon them, are obligated to abandon sins and are rewarded for it, and if the committing of sin were impossible for them, this would not be the case. Also, His saying: "Say: I am only a human like you, to whom it is revealed" (*qul innamā anā basharun mithlukum yūḥā ilayya*) indicates their likeness to all people in what pertains to humanity, and their distinction through revelation. So the committing of sin by them is not impossible, just as it is not impossible for all humans. End of quotation.

Al-Khafājī, in his commentary on *al-Shifāʾ*, mentioned from Ibn al-Humām that he said in *al-Taḥrīr*: "Infallibility is the inability to disobey, and a restraining disposition against it that is not compelling." Then he said: this is consistent with the saying of al-Māturīdī: "Infallibility does not remove the trial," that is, the testing that necessitates the remaining of choice. Its meaning, as in *al-Hidāya*, is that it does not compel him to obedience nor render him incapable of disobedience, but rather it is a grace (*luṭf*) from Allah, exalted is He, that moves him to act and restrains him from evil, while choice remains and the trial is realized. End of quotation.

[Page 165]

This is clear regarding the absence of an intrinsic impossibility of committing sin. Perhaps what occurred in the words of some eminent scholars about the impossibility of their committing sin, peace be upon them, is to be understood as legal impossibility (*al-istiḥāla al-sharʿiyya*), as the words of al-ʿAllāma Ibn Ḥajar in his commentary on *al-Hamziyya* indicate. In sum: what the apparent meanings require and what reason testifies to is that the prophets, peace be upon them, do fear and do not feel secure from the plan of Allah, exalted is He. This is because it—even though committing sin is legally impossible for them—is not rationally impossible. Rather, it is among the possibilities upon which the power of Allah, exalted is He, can be exercised. With consideration of its intrinsic possibility, and that Allah, exalted is He, has no obligation upon Him, and with the existence of the possibility of restricting the absolute by what has not been explicitly stated for a wisdom such as His will, no one protected can hardly feel secure from the plan of the Living, the Self-Subsisting King. So the prophets and the angels are all fearful, and out of fear of Him, glorified is He, Mighty and Majestic, they are apprehensive. You do not have the right to restrict their fear to the fear of reverence, since the apparent meaning is generality, and there is no evidence for specificity that the masters of scholarship would rely upon.

Yes, it may be said that security from the plan can be attained, by Allah, exalted is He, creating in the servant a necessary knowledge that what he fears does not occur at any time at all, because Allah, exalted is He, knows that it will not occur in that way, although it is intrinsically possible. Perhaps this occurs for the people of Paradise so that their pleasure is complete in it. It has been said:

If you wish to live a pleasant life,
then do not take to yourself anything whose loss you fear.

It is also not far-fetched that this occurs for whoever Allah, exalted is He, wills among His servants on the Day of Resurrection, even before entering it. But no sign has established for me that this occurs for anyone in this life. And Allah, exalted is He, knows best. So reflect on this. And Allah, exalted is He, guides you.

Al-Imām [al-Rāzī] transmitted from one of them that he said: the meaning of the verse is: when I command the messengers to manifest a miracle, they should not fear regarding the manifestation of that. Otherwise, the messenger may certainly fear.

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Except for one who wrongs and then substitutes good after evil, indeed I am Forgiving, Merciful﴾. The exception here is, according to many, *munqati'* (disjunct, not of the same category as what precedes). However, it is narrated from al-Farra' (a grammarian of Kufa) and al-Zajjaj (a grammarian of Baghdad) and others that what is meant by "one who wrongs" is one who sins among non-prophets, peace be upon them. The author of *al-Mat'a* (*al-Mat'a* by Ibn Bashir? [sic]) said: the meaning according to this is: "But whoever among the rest of the servants wrongs and then repents, I shall forgive him." A group said: what is meant by it is one from whom a minor lapse has proceeded, and there has issued from him what is contrary to the preferable course (*khilaf al-awla*) in relation to his station among the Messengers, peace be upon them. The purpose is to correct what may occur to the heart of negating fear from all of them, while among them there is one from whom that has issued. The meaning according to this is: "But whoever among them has done something that has the appearance of wronging, then repents, I shall forgive him, so he should not fear either." This, according to what has been said, includes whoever among them did any such thing before his mission. Some restricted it to one from whom something of that kind issued before prophethood, and said: the word *thumma* ("then") supports this, for it is clearly indicative of temporal succession. Perhaps the more apparent view is that it is specific to one from whom it issued after the mission, because the term "Messenger" applies most clearly to one who is actually engaged in the mission, not to one who will later engage in it, or the more general sense. It seems that in what was mentioned under the first two views there is an allusion to what occurred from Musa, peace be upon him, in his striking the Egyptian (Coptic) and seeking forgiveness, and calling it "wronging" is by way of *mushakala* (matching of expression) with his saying, peace be upon him: "I have wronged myself."

They did not make it, according to this, *muttasil* (connected), even though the excepted item is included in the excepted-from, I mean the Messengers in general; for if it were connected, it would necessitate affirming fear for one from whom some minor lapse had proceeded among them, since it is an exception from the ruling, which is the negation of fear from them, and the negation of a negation is an affirmation, and that is contrary to the intended meaning. Therefore it is not connected, but rather it is the beginning of another ruling.

Al-Tibi (a commentator) preferred what the group said, on the ground that the situation of receiving the message and the beginning of the conversation with the one who was addressed directly (*al-Kalim*, Musa) requires the complete removal of fear. This is evident according to what they said. It was narrated from al-Hasan, Muqatil, Ibn Jurayj and al-Dahhak what indicates that it is a *muttasil* exception.

[p. 166]

The apparent view is that they intended by "one who" the one the group intended. Regarding its being connected, as you have heard, there is some obscurity.

Perhaps it is said: whoever applies the term "connected" to it in the opinion of the group is content with the mere fact that the excepted item is of the same genus as the excepted-from. If that suffices, well and good; otherwise he must affirm fear and make *baddala* ("substituted") a conjunction (*'atf*) upon an omitted new sentence, as though it were said: "Except one from whom a minor lapse has proceeded, for he fears, so whoever fell short and then repented is forgiven, so he does not fear."

Its summary: "Except one who wronged, for he fears at first, and fear is removed from him at last by repentance."

And from al-Farra', in another narration from him, that it is a *muttasil* exception from an omitted clause, and the estimate is: "Only others fear, except one who wronged."

Al-Nahhas rejected this, saying: an exception from an omitted element is not permissible, and if this were permissible, it would be permissible to say: "Do not strike the people except Zayd," meaning: "Only strike others except Zayd." This is contrary to clarification and to bringing what has no known meaning. He ended. And it is as he said. The statement that it is by consideration of the concept (*mafhum*) of fear does not benefit either.

A group said: *illa* here has the meaning of *wa* ("and"), and the estimate is: "And not one who wronged..." etc.

Abu Hayyan in *al-Bahr* criticized this, saying: it is worthless, because of the complete difference between *illa* and *wa*, so that neither can take the place of the other. Good opinion allows that they did not explicitly state that *illa* means *wa*, and that what attributed it to them was from his own estimate of it; and it may be that it is an estimate of meaning, not of grammatical construction. So do not be heedless.

The apparent view is that the exception is disjunct. Perhaps the more fitting view regarding the station of the Messengers is that by "one who wronged" is meant one who committed a sin, great or small, from among others than them. And *thumma* ("then") may be for temporal succession, so the verse gives forgiveness to one who substitutes immediately, a fortiori. It may also be for successive rank (*tarakhi rutbi*), and that is apparent between the wronging and the mentioned substitution.

*Tabdil* (substitution) may be transitive to two objects directly, as in ﴿We shall substitute for them other skins﴾, and it may be transitive to one of them directly and to the other by *bi-* or *min*, which is the thing taken away and the thing substituted, as in: *baddalahu bi-khawfihi aw min khawfihi amnan* ("he substituted for his fear security"). And it may be transitive to one object, as in *baddaltu al-shay'* ("I changed the thing"), meaning I altered it, and from it: ﴿Whoever alters it after he has heard it﴾. The meaning here is according to the one transitive to two objects, and it is transitive to one of them, which is the thing substituted, by *bi-* or *min*, so it is as though it were said: "Then he substituted for his wrong-doing, or from his wrong-doing, good," and His saying: ﴿after evil﴾ points to it. Its summary: "Then he gave up wronging and brought good," and what is meant by it is repentance.

So the meaning in the final analysis is: "Except one who wronged, then repented and turned away from it to what is in the sublime composition, for it is more suited to the situation of reassurance," so it is said.

The apparent view according to this is that the attribution of the substitution to "one who wronged" is literal. It has been said: the meaning is: "Then He lifted the wronging and the evil, erased it from the record of his deeds, and placed in its stead good, by means of his repentance," analogous to what is in His saying: ﴿Allah will substitute their evil deeds with good deeds﴾. Attribution of the substitution to "one who wronged" according to this is metaphorical, because he is the cause for God's substitution for him by means of his repentance. It seems to me you prefer the first.

The position of *man* (who) according to each of the two estimates, disjunct or connected, is apparent, and the apparent view is that it is a relative pronoun in both estimates. It is not hidden that if it is considered in the accusative position as an exception, or in the nominative position as an apposition (*badal*), the clause *"fa-inni"* ... etc. is a new sentence (*musta'nafa*).

As for the one who posited an omitted element in the speech and made *baddala* a conjunction upon it, saying: the estimate is "whoever wronged, then substituted," he makes the clause the predicate of *man*. Some allowed that it may be a conditional, with the clause *"fa-inni"* ... etc. as its apodosis. So reflect and do not be heedless.

Abu Ja'far and Zayd ibn Aslam read *"ala man zalama"* with a fatha on the hamza and lightening of the lam, taking *ala* as an interjection of introduction (*harf istiftah*). Abu Hayyan made *man* in this reading conditional, and I do not consider this obligatory. Muhammad ibn 'Isa al-Isbahani read *husna* on the pattern *fu'la*, diptotic (*mamnu' al-sarf*). Ibn Miqsam read *husunan* with a damma on the ha' and the sin, nunated.

Mujahid, Abu Haywa, Ibn Abi 'Ali, al-A'mash, Abu 'Amr (in the narration of al-Ju'fi), 'Ismah, 'Abd al-Warith, Harun and 'Ayyash read *hasanan* with a fatha on the ha' and the sin, with tanwin.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 27, verse 12:

﴿And insert your hand into your bosom﴾, i.e., the bosom (jayb) of your shirt (qamis), which is the opening through which the head enters, leading down to the chest, not the pocket in which dirhams and the like are placed, as is known today, because that is a later (muwallad) usage. Exalted is He did not say "fi kummika" (in your sleeve), because he (peace be upon him) was then wearing a woolen coarse garment (mudarra'a) that had no sleeve. It has also been said that al-jayb is the shirt itself, because it is cut (yujab), i.e., it is cut open, so it is a fa'l in the sense of maf'ul. Al-Suddi said: "fi jaybika" means "under your armpit."

Perhaps his intention is that the meaning is: insert it into your bosom, place it under your armpit. His garment, peace be upon him, according to what is related from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, had no buttons. It has also come in some reports that our Prophet ﷺ at some times wore an open-fronted shirt.

In the Sunan of Abu Dawud there is a chapter on "untying the buttons," in which he narrates through the route of Mu'awiyah ibn Qurrah, who said: My father told me, saying: I came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ with a group from Muzayna, and we pledged allegiance to him, and his shirt was open - and in the narration of al-Baghawi in Mu'jam al-Sahaba (his shirt's buttons were open) - he said: So I pledged allegiance to him, then I inserted my hand into the bosom of his shirt and touched the seal. Urwah said: I never saw Mu'awiyah nor his father except that they left their buttons open, and they never fastened them ever.

It has also come that he, peace and blessings be upon him, commanded the fastening of buttons. Al-Tabarani narrated, "from Zayd ibn Abi Awfa that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ looked at Uthman ibn Affan, may Allah be pleased with him, and his buttons were undone, so the Messenger of Allah ﷺ fastened them with his hand, and said: 'Gather the two flaps of your cloak over your chest.'"

In these two reports there is clear evidence that the bosom of the shirt was then at the chest, as it is today among the Arabs. This refutes the claim that it was contrary to the Sunnah and a practice of the Jews. And His command to him, peace be upon him, to insert his hand into his bosom, even though He, glorified is He, is able to make it white without insertion, was for the sake of a test, and He, glorified is He, may test His servants with whatever He wills.

It is apparent that His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and it will come out﴾ is the response to the command, because its coming out is consequent upon its insertion. It has also been said: there is an omission in the speech, its estimate being: "And insert your hand into your bosom, it will enter; and take it out, it will come out," so what is mentioned in the first is omitted in correspondence with what is mentioned in the second, and what is mentioned in the second is omitted in correspondence with what is mentioned in the first, so there is in the speech the figure of ihtibak (mutual omission), which is an artifice for which there is no need.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿white﴾ is a circumstantial (hal), and likewise His saying: ﴿without harm﴾, which is a precautionary qualifier (ihtiras), and its discussion has already passed. Likewise His saying, glorified is He: ﴿among nine signs﴾, i.e., a sign counted among the nine signs, or a miracle that you have along with it. The nine are: the splitting (of the sea), the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, the blood, the effacing (tamsa), which is turning their possessions into stone, the drought in their deserts, and the shortfall in their crops. For one who counts the staff and the hand among the nine, he may count the drought and the shortfall in crops as one, and not count the splitting among them, because he (peace be upon him) was not sent with it to Pharaoh, even though it preceded it slightly. And one who counts it says: its witnessing suffices for being sent with it, or it is a sending with it to those among his people who believed and to those of the Copts who remained behind and did not believe. In al-Taqrib it is said that the effacing, the drought, and the shortfall return to one thing, so the nine are this one, the staff, the hand, and what remains of the mentioned items.

The author of al-Fara'id held that the locusts and the lice are one, and the drought and the shortfall are one. It is also permitted that "fi tis'" (among nine) be disconnected from what precedes it, attached to an omitted element, i.e., "go among nine signs," and this is supported by His saying, exalted is He, afterward: ﴿So when Our signs came to them﴾, with "fi" meaning "with." A parallel of this omission is what occurs in the verse:

They came to my fire, so I said: "Are you humans?" They said: "Jinn." I said: "Be blind to the darkness."

And I said: "Come to the food," so among them ∗∗∗ a group envied humans their food.

For the estimate is "come to the food." And attached to this omitted element is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿to Pharaoh and his people﴾. According to what preceded, it is attached to an omitted element that occurs as a circumstantial (hal), i.e., "sent to Pharaoh." In either case, His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed they were a corrupt people﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf bayani), as if it were said: "Why did You send to them with what was mentioned?" So it is said: "Indeed they..." etc. The meaning of corruption (fisq) is either departing from what the Law obligated them to, if we say that someone obligating them to follow him was sent before Moses, peace be upon him, namely Joseph, peace be upon him, or departing from what reason obligates and what natural disposition (fitrah) requires, if we say that no one was sent to them before him, peace be upon him.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 27, verse 13:

﴿When Our signs came to them﴾, i.e., they became manifest to them at the hand of Musa, peace be upon him. So the "coming" (al-majī') is metaphorical for "becoming manifest" (al-zuhur), and its attribution to the signs is real (haqiqi). Some of the eminent scholars said: the "coming" is real, and its attribution to the signs is metaphorical; it is real in relation to Musa, peace be upon him, and the attribution to the signs is permissible because of the connection between them, since they are a miracle (mu'jizah) for him, peace be upon him.

Perhaps the point of shifting from "When Musa came to them with Our signs" to what is in the sublime arrangement of the text is to indicate that those signs were beyond his power, peace be upon him, like the rest of the miracles, and that he had no control over any of them. That they were a miracle for him lies in his informing of them and their occurrence through his supplication and the like. This does not conflict with attributing them to him, since they took place at his hands, for the miracle in His, glorified be He, saying: ﴿When Musa came to them with Our signs﴾ in another place. Some have explained a reason for the specificity of each of the two expressions to its own context: that there is in that place a mention of his dialogue, peace be upon him, and their disputation with him, so attribution to him was appropriate; and here, since this was not the case, attribution to the signs was appropriate, because the aim is to show their denial of them. The addition of the signs to the definite (al-'ahd) and their addition to the pronoun of majesty (ḍamir al-'azamah) carries what is not hidden of glorifying their status. ﴿Mubsirah﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from "the signs," i.e., clear and evident. Making "seeing" (al-ibsar) belong to them, which is real for those who contemplate them, is due to the connection between them and the people; for they only see through their reflection upon them. So the attribution is metaphorical, of the type of attributing to the cause. It is also permissible that what is meant is "giving sight to" everyone among the sensible who looks at them, or to Pharaoh and his people, based on His, exalted be He, saying: ﴿and their souls were certain of them﴾, i.e., making him see clearly, from (abṣara-hu), the transitive form with the hamzah of transport from (baṣura), and the attribution is also metaphorical.

It is also permissible that the signs be made as if they see and so guide; for the blind cannot guide themselves, let alone guide others. Thus in the speech there is a metaphor (isti'arah) that is implicit (makniyyah) and imaginative (takhyiliyyah), with a supporting element (murashshahah). In al-Kashshaf it is said: this aspect is more eloquent. It has also been said: the form fa'il has been used in the sense of maf'ul, so the metaphor is either in the term or in the attribution, so reflect.

Qatadah and Ali ibn al-Husayn, may Allah be pleased with them both, read: (mabsarah) with a fatha on the mim and the sad, on the pattern of masba'ah. The original basis of this formation is that it is mostly derived for a place where the root meaning abounds; so one does not say "masba'ah" (a place of lions), for example, except for a place where lions abound, not for a place where there is a single lion. Then it is used figuratively for that which is the cause of the abundance and dominance of a thing, as in their saying: "The child is a source of cowardice and stinginess" (mujbanah wa mabkhalah), i.e., a cause of the abundance of the father's cowardice and the abundance of his stinginess. That is what is meant here, i.e., a cause of the abundance of the beholders' insight into them.

Abu Hayyan said: it is a verbal noun (masdar) placed in the position of a noun and in the accusative as a circumstantial clause also. ﴿They said: this﴾, i.e., what we see or the like, ﴿is clear magic﴾, i.e., its magical nature is evident; on the basis that (mubin) is from (abana).

﴿And they denied them﴾ — i.e., they rejected them — ﴿while their souls were convinced of them﴾ — i.e., they knew with certain knowledge that they were signs from Allah, Exalted is He. Al-istiyqan (certainty, conviction) is more emphatic than al-iyqan (conviction).

In al-Bahr it is stated that (istaf'ala) here carries the meaning of (tafa''ala), as istakbara means takabbara. The most eloquent reading is that the waw is for circumstance (hal), and the sentence after it is a circumstantial clause, either with qad implied or without it. ﴿Injustice﴾ — i.e., against the signs — as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿because they were wronging Our signs﴾. They did great injustice to them, for they lowered them from their lofty rank and called them sorcery. It has also been said that the injustice was against themselves, but this is not the correct view. ﴿And arrogance﴾ — i.e., haughtiness and pride in refusing to believe in them, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and those who denied Our signs and were arrogant towards them﴾. The accusative of both words is either as objects of purpose (ʿilliyyah) relating to ﴿they denied﴾, and this, as has been said, is according to the consequence and the claim, as in the line of poetry:

*Be born for death, and build for ruin.*

Or it is as a circumstantial accusative (hal) relating to their subject, meaning: they denied them while being unjust and haughty. The first was preferred, since it is more eloquent and more fitting with His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So see how was the end of the corrupters﴾ — i.e., what became of Pharaoh and his people of drowning in that awesome manner, which is a lesson for the wrongdoers. The Qur'an did not mention it explicitly as an alert that it is exposed to every observer, well known to every dweller and present. Some included in "the end" their state in the Hereafter of burning and painful punishment. Placing the apparent noun in place of the pronoun is a condemnation of them and a warning to those like them.

Abdullah, Ibn Wathhab, al-A'mash, Talhah, and Aban ibn Taghlib read ﴿ʿIliyyan﴾ with the waw changed to ya' and the ʿayn and lam kasred. Its original form is (fu'ul), but they kasrated the ʿayn for harmony (ittiba'). It is also narrated that its ʿayn was pronounced with a damma from Ibn Wathhab, al-A'mash, and Talhah.

﴿And We gave David and Solomon knowledge.﴾ This is a resumed statement (kalam mustani'af), brought to confirm what preceded it, namely that he (peace be upon him) received the Qur'an from One who is Wise and All-Knowing, like the story of Moses (peace be upon him). Its introduction with an oath serves to show the utmost concern for its content.
