The meaning is: We gave each of them a portion of knowledge suited to him, from the knowledge of the laws (shara'i') and rulings (ahkam) and other things that are specific to each of them, such as the craft of making coats of mail (lubus) and the language of the birds (mantiq al-tayr). Muqatil restricted it to the knowledge of judgeship (ilm al-qada'), and Ibn 'Ata' restricted it to the knowledge of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Perhaps the first, as mentioned, is the better view. Or (it means) a lofty and abundant knowledge. The tanwin on the first reading is for diminution (lil-taqlil), and this is more fitting with the speaker being Allah, Mighty and Majestic, for every knowledge with Him, glorified is He, is little. On the second reading it is for magnification and abundance (lil-ta'zim wa'l-takthir), and this is more fitting with His bestowing of favour, Majestic is His majesty, for He, glorified is He, is the Great King, so what befits His dignity is bestowing favour with what is great and abundant. Thus each has its direction. It may be preferred that the second is correct. And among what should not be given attention is that the tanwin is for specifying the type (lil-nau'iyya), meaning a kind of knowledge, and what is intended by it is the knowledge of alchemy (ilm al-kimya').

﴿And they both said﴾, that is, each of them said, in gratitude for the knowledge that had been given to him: ﴿Praise be to Allah, who has favoured us﴾ with what He has given us of knowledge ﴿over many of His believing servants.﴾ On the basis that each one's statement was "He favoured me," but when relating it the plural form was used for both of them, for brevity. The relating of multiple statements, whether they were issued by the speaker himself or by another, with an expression that encompasses all of them, is not rare. Among this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O Messengers, eat of the good things﴾. It has been said: with this the excellence of the placement of the conjunction with waw rather than fa' becomes apparent, since what is understood from conjunction with fa' is that each one's praise is consequent upon giving to each of them what each was given, and not upon giving to each only what was given to himself.

It has been objected: if what was mentioned is granted, then conjunction with waw also suggests that each one's praise is upon giving what each of them was given, so what is prevented with waw is prevented likewise with fa'. And the Allamah al-Zamakhshari said: it is conjoined with waw rather than fa', although the apparent case is the reverse, as in your saying, "I gave him and he thanked," to indicate that what they both said is part of what was produced in them by the giving of knowledge and some of its obligations. So that was omitted, and then praise was conjoined to it, as if He, glorified is He, had said: "And We indeed gave them both knowledge, so they acted upon it and taught it and recognised the true right of the blessing in it and its excellence, and said: Praise be to Allah who has favoured us." The sum of this is that the giving of knowledge is among the great blessings and abundant bounties, and it requires the generation of gratitude more than what has been mentioned. So waw was brought, because it requires an omission, and what the requirement of gratitude entails is omitted, from His saying: "they acted upon it and taught it," for that is active gratitude, and His saying: "and recognised the true right of the blessing in it and its excellence," for that is inward gratitude, and with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they said﴾ etc., all the kinds of gratitude are completed, since it is verbal gratitude. In the omission there is an indication that what was omitted exceeds the limit of enumeration. It is known from what has been mentioned that this explanation for choosing conjunction with waw is preferable to what al-Sakkaki went to, namely leaving the sequence to the intellect, since the situation requires abundant gratitude, which encompasses all the kinds, whereas on his view it would be only the verbal kind. It is also preferable to what has been said: that it was not conjoined with fa', because the praise is for great blessings of which knowledge is one; if it had been conjoined with fa', the praise would have been for it alone, since the context clearly indicates that praise is for it and not for what it is itself part of.

Is there, according to what the Allamah mentioned, an implied (taqdir) hakikah or not? There are two opinions. Among those who went to the first is one who names this waw the eloquent waw (al-waw al-fasiha). The apparent meaning is that what is intended by the many who are preferred over them is those who were not given knowledge like their knowledge, peace be upon them both. And it has been said: that includes them and those who were not given any knowledge at all.

It has been objected that this is refuted by specifying the "many" as His believing servants, for their being entirely devoid of knowledge is impossible. And in their specifying of the many by mention there is an indication that some are preferred over them, so it is said, while what is understood by "some" is the few. In al-Kashshaf it is said that in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿over many﴾ it means that they were favoured over many and that many were favoured over them. It has been objected that there is an issue with this, for it indicates by implication that they were not favoured over the few; as for whether the few are favoured over them or are equal to them, that is not indicated, rather both possibilities are open.

The author of al-Kashf rejected this, saying that in such a context the many is not opposed by the few, rather it indicates that the ruling for the majority is the opposite. And since equality with the majority is remote from custom, especially as the default is difference, the author of al-Kashshaf ruled that it indicates that many were also favoured over them. Moreover, custom disregards equality in such a context, and makes opposition between the favoured and the one favoured over. Do you not see that when they say, "There is no one more excellent than Zayd," it is understood that he is more excellent than everyone? End of quotation.

In the verse there is the clearest evidence of the excellence of knowledge and the nobility of its people, in that they gave thanks for knowledge and made it the foundation of excellence, and did not regard as more important what they had been given of great dominion. It is also an exhortation to scholars to praise Allah, exalted is He, for what He has given them of His bounty, and to be humble and to believe that among the servants of Allah, exalted is He, there is someone who surpasses them in knowledge. How well said was the Commander of the Believers, 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, when he forbade excess in dowries from the pulpit, and an old woman objected to him with the words of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿And you had given one of them a heap of gold﴾, the verse. He said: "Every person is more learned than 'Umar." In this there is much of consoling the old woman's heart and opening the door of ijtihad (independent reasoning). And the Shi'a's making this one of his faults is among the greatest faults and most astonishing marvels.

Perhaps in the verse there is an indication of the permissibility of a scholar saying, "I am a scholar," and a number of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, have said this, among them the Commander of the Believers 'Ali, may Allah honour his face, and 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. As for what has spread of the hadith, "Whoever says, 'I am a scholar,' is ignorant," it is only known from the words of Yahya ibn Abi Kathir as a mawquf (a statement ending with a Companion or follower), with weakness in its chain. And this Yahya was one of the junior Successors (tabi'un), for he saw only Anas ibn Malik. Some narrators have erred and raised it to the Prophet (ﷺ). Its verification is in A'dhab al-Manahil by al-Jalal al-Suyuti.

[p. 170]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 27, verse 16:

﴿And Sulayman inherited from Dawud﴾: that is, he took his place in prophethood and kingship, and became a prophet and king after the death of his father Dawud, peace be upon them both. His "inheritance" of him is therefore a metaphor for taking his place, as is said, after his death. It was also said that what is meant is the inheritance of prophethood only; and it was said: the inheritance of kingship only. It is narrated from al-Hasan, and al-Tabarsi attributed it to the Imams of the Ahl al-Bayt, that it is the inheritance of wealth. This was rebutted by the fact that it is authentically established: "We, the company of prophets, are not inherited from." Al-Siddiq and al-Faruq, may Allah be pleased with them both, mentioned it in the presence of a group of the Companions, who are those who do not fear the blame of any blamer in the cause of Allah, and none of them denied it against the two of them.

Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi related from Abu al-Darda', who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: "Indeed the scholars are the heirs of the prophets, and indeed the prophets did not bequeath a dinar or a dirham, but they bequeathed knowledge, so whoever takes it has taken a great portion."

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub al-Razi, in al-Kafi, related from Abu al-Bukhturi, from Abu 'Abd Allah Ja'far al-Sadiq, that he also said this.

Among what indicates that this inheritance is not the inheritance of wealth is what al-Kulayni related from Abu 'Abd Allah: that Sulayman inherited Dawud, and that Muhammad inherited Sulayman, ﷺ. Also, the inheritance of wealth is not specific to Sulayman, peace be upon him, for Dawud had a number of other children besides him, as al-Kulayni related from him as well, and others mentioned that he, peace be upon him, died leaving nineteen sons. So reporting it of Sulayman has little benefit. And if what is meant is to inform of what it entails of Sulayman's survival after Dawud, peace be upon them both, then what is the motive for deviating from what it conveys without any obscurity, such as: "And Sulayman said after the death of his father Dawud: 'O people...'" etc.

Also, the context and the surrounding verses both refuse that the meaning be the inheritance of wealth, as is not hidden from the fair-minded. The apparent view is that the report from al-Hasan is not established, and likewise the report from the Imams of the Ahl al-Bayt, may Allah be pleased with them; for you have heard in al-Kulayni's report from al-Sadiq, may Allah be pleased with him, what contradicts its establishment. The inheritance of other than wealth is common in the Noble Book, for the Mighty and Majestic One said: ﴿Then We caused the Book to be inherited﴾, and He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿Then there succeeded them a succession who inherited the Book﴾. The difference in indicators does no harm, so understand.

His age, when Dawud, peace be upon them both, died, was twelve years or thirteen years, and Dawud had bequeathed the kingship to him. When he died, he ruled, at the age mentioned. It was said: Dawud, peace be upon him, had appointed him over the Children of Israel during his lifetime; this is related by al-Bahr.

He said, to make known the blessing of Allah, the Exalted, and to magnify its worth, and to call people to believe in his prophethood by mentioning the dazzling miracles that he was given, not out of boasting: ﴿O people﴾. Its apparent generality is all the people whom it is customarily possible to address.

Some of the eminent scholars said: what is meant by it is the leaders of his kingdom and the great men of his state, from both jinn and humankind and others, and the expression of them by what has been mentioned is by way of prevalence (taghlib). Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Awza'i that he said: "The people, according to us, are the people of knowledge."

﴿We have been taught the speech of the birds﴾: that is, their speech. In common usage, it is every utterance by which what is in the mind is expressed, whether single or compound. It may also be applied to every sound made, by way of explicit metaphor (isti'arah musarrahah). It is permissible to consider the likening of the sound-maker to a human, and there would be a metaphor by implication (isti'arah bil-kinayah), with the attribution of speech being imaginative (takhyili). It was said: it is also permissible that by speech is meant the mere sound, as a loose metaphor (majaz mursal), but this is not so good.

The verse of the poet may bear all three meanings:

"It did not prevent them from drinking except that a dove spoke in the branches of a thorny tree."

It may also be applied to this for the sake of correspondence (mushakalah), as in their saying: "the speaking and the silent" for the animate and the inanimate. What he, peace be upon him, was taught of the speech of the birds is, as has been said, that by which some of their meanings and purposes are understood by one another.

It is related that he, peace be upon him, passed by a nightingale in a tree moving its head and inclining its tail, and he said to his companions: "Do you know what it says?" They said: "Allah and His Prophet know best." He said: "It says: I have eaten half a date, so let the world perish." A ring-dove called, and he informed that it was saying: "Would that these creatures had not been created." A peacock called, and he said: "It says: As you judge, so you will be judged." A hoopoe called, and he said: "It says: Seek forgiveness from Allah, the Exalted, O sinners." A "tituwa" called, and he said: "It says: Every living thing dies, and every new thing wears out." A swallow called, and he said: "It says: Send forward good, you will find it." A "rakhamah" called, and he said: "It says: Glory be to my Lord the Most High, filling His heavens and His earth." A turtle-dove called, and he informed that it says: "Glory be to my Lord the Most High." He said: The kite says: "Everything is perishing except Allah, the Exalted." The sand-grouse says: "Whoever keeps silent is safe." The parrot says: "Woe to him whose concern is the world." The rooster says: "Remember Allah, the Exalted, O heedless ones." The vulture says: "O son of Adam, live as you wish, your end is death." The eagle says: "In distance from people there is intimacy." The frog says: "Glory be to my Lord, the Holy." The lark says: "O Allah, curse the hater of Muhammad and the family of Muhammad." The zurzur says: "O Allah, I ask You for the sustenance of a day for its day, O Provider." The durraj says: "The Merciful is established upon the Throne." End of quotation.

The placing of the frog among those mentioned of the birds is not in its proper place. Despite this, Allah, the Exalted, knows best the soundness of this narration. It was said: the birds used to speak to him, peace be upon him, as a miracle for him, like what happened with the hoopoe in the story that follows.

It was said: he, peace be upon him, was taught what the birds intend by their sounds in all their conditions, so he understood their glorification and admonition, and what they address him with, peace be upon him, and what some of them address to others.

In sum, he was taught from their speech what a human is taught from the speech of his own kind. It is not improbable that birds have rational souls and particular languages by which they convey their intentions, as with the human species, except that human souls are stronger and more perfect; and it is not far-fetched that they vary in degree as human souls vary, as he who said so has held.

It is permissible that Allah, the Exalted, teach their speech to whomever of His servants He wills, and this is not restricted to the prophets, peace be upon them; and what we have mentioned applies to all other animals. Some people held that Sulayman, peace be upon him, was also taught their speech, but that the birds were specifically mentioned because they were among his troops, whom he needed for shade from the sun and for dispatch in affairs. It is not hidden that the verse does not indicate this, so the claim requires a sound transmission. Some claimed that he, peace be upon him, was also taught the speech of plants, so that he would pass by a tree and it would tell him its benefits and harms; but I have found no sound report of that.

Many of the wise know the properties of plants by their colour, form, taste and other things, and in knowing them they have no need for their speaking with the tongue of utterance.

The pronoun in "We have been taught" and "We have been given" is said to refer to him and his father, peace be upon them both, but this is contrary to the apparent sense; the better view is that it refers to him alone, peace be upon him. Since he was a king obeyed, he addressed his subjects, in the custom of kings, to observe the rules of statecraft, by way of preparing what is required of the subjects in obedience and submission to commands and prohibitions. This was not from him, peace be upon him, out of self-magnification or arrogance, but observing the rules of statecraft in order to reach by them what is pleasing to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, among important matters. Our Prophet ﷺ indeed ordered al-Abbas to detain Abu Sufyan on the day of the Conquest until the battalions passed before him, for this purpose.

And "kull" (all) originally denotes encompassing, and it occurs for multiplication often, as in your saying: "So-and-so is sought by everyone, and knows everything," and this is a figure of speech (kinayah) or a well-known metaphor. This meaning is what is intended here if "min" is taken as a supplement (silah). It is the fitting meaning for the context of recounting blessings. If "min" is not taken as a supplement, then it remains on its original sense, as it is said. You know that this is not possible except if the collective whole is intended, and that is as you see.

In al-Bahr: the words of the Exalted, "We have been taught the speech of the birds," are an allusion to prophethood, and His words, glory be to Him, "and we have been given of everything," are an allusion to kingship; and the two sentences are like an explanation of the inheritance.

It is related from Muqatil that what was given to him is meant to be prophethood and kingship, and the subjugation of the jinn, humankind, the devils and the wind.

It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that it is what concerns him, peace be upon him, of the affairs of this world and the Hereafter.

It may be said: it is what a king needs of instruments of war and other things.

﴿Indeed this﴾: an indication of what was mentioned of the teaching and the giving, ﴿is truly the bounty﴾ and favour from Allah, the Exalted, ﴿the manifest﴾: the clear one, which is hidden from no one; or that this bounty which I have been given is indeed the manifest bounty, in which case it is from his speech, peace be upon him, certainly, appended to what came before it, to show that he only said what he said by way of thanks, just as he, ﷺ, said: "I am the master of the children of Adam, and there is no boasting" (with the letter ra' at the end, as in the well-known narration), meaning: I say this statement as thanks, not as boasting. Close to this meaning is "wa la fakhz" (and no disgrace/no boasting) with the letter zayn, as in the less-known narration.

[Page 174]

﴿And his hosts were gathered for Solomon﴾: that is, his armies were assembled from various places. ﴿From the jinn and mankind and the birds﴾ is an explanation of "the hosts," (covering those) at sea and elsewhere. It does not follow from this that the hosts gathered for him, peace be upon him, were all the jinn, all of mankind, and all the birds. For that is rejected, setting aside reason, by the story of Bilqis that comes later, and likewise by the story of the hoopoe.

It has been related from some of them that, peace be upon him, there would come to him one bird from each species of birds. This is explicit that what was gathered was not all the birds. It is hardly possible to intend "all" within "all," as the Imam also stated concerning the verse. The meaning is: God, exalted is He, made all these categories his hosts. For although it does not require presence and assembly in one place, but mere submission, entry into the sphere of his command, and obedience to him wherever they are, is sufficient, since the story of Bilqis also rejects that (the assembly), it is fitting that the announcement of this "making" come after the announcement of her and those with her entering the sphere of his command.

The apparent meaning is that this gathering was nothing other than the assembling of the armies, so that he might take them to fight those who had not entered the yoke of his obedience, peace be upon him. That he took them to Mecca in gratitude for what he was enabled to do in building the Bayt al-Maqdis is contrary to the apparent meaning. However, if a report concerning it is authentic, it is accepted. And the total of the mentioned categories is what befits his station, splendour, and greatness, whether (min) is taken as explanatory (bayaniyya) or partitive (tab'idiyya).

As for his being one of the two believers who ruled the whole inhabited world (al-ma'mura bi-asriha), if we accept the soundness of the report indicating it, its freedom from contradiction, and that it is explicit regarding the claim, it requires nothing more than the inhabitants of the inhabited world entering among his subjects and within the sphere of his dominion. And that was not instantaneous; rather, it was, if it is sound, gradual.

Some historians have mentioned that Bilqis only came under his obedience in the twenty-fifth year of his reign. The duration of his reign, peace be upon him, was forty years, and likewise the duration of the reign of his father Dawud, peace be upon them both.

The apparent meaning is that the one who gathers each of the three kinds consists of individuals from among them. Thus, from each kind there are individuals commissioned for this and prepared for it. Do not find this strange regarding the birds if you believe in the story of the hoopoe. You are not obliged to accept what the Imam said, that God, exalted is He, gave the birds intellect in the days of Solomon, peace be upon him, and did not give them that in our days. There is no harm for you in saying that they are in one state today and in that day. We mean by their intellect only that by which they are guided to their purposes, and the existence of that in them, and likewise in the rest of the animals, is something none but a stubborn person denies. Nor is it incumbent upon us to say that their intellects, in themselves, are like the intellect of man, in itself.

Perhaps among them are some that are guided to what many of the children of Adam are not guided to, like the bee. By my life, if they were devoid of intellect, as is said, and the existence of intellect in them were assumed, I do not think they would, after its existence, make anything better than what they make today while devoid of it. And it is not necessary that every intelligent being be accountable (mukallaf). Let the birds then be like the other intelligent beings to whom no prophet was sent to command and forbid them. It is also possible that they know their Lord and believe in Him, exalted is He, without a prophet being sent to them, like one who grows up alone on the top of a high mountain and is a believer in his Lord, glorified is He. Indeed, their being believers in God, exalted is He, and glorifying Him, and likewise the rest of the animals, is attested by the apparent meanings of the verses and reports, and we have already mentioned some of that. We have nothing that requires interpretation.

[Page 175]

Some have exaggerated and claimed that they are accountable, and that among them, and likewise among the other animals, there are prophets who have specific laws, and he argued for it with what he argued. The well-known position is to declare disbelief (ikfar) in one who claims that, and a group of jurists has explicitly stated his disbelief. The singling out of the three categories for mention is apparent in indicating that the wild beasts were not subjected to him. In a report recorded by al-Hakim, from Muhammad ibn Ka'b, there is what is apparent in indicating that they were subjected to him as well, peace be upon him, and we will mention it shortly, God willing. However, it is not relied upon.

The mention of the jinn first is to hasten to announce the complete strength of his dominion, peace be upon him, and the might of his authority from the very beginning, because the jinn are a rebellious group, a transgressing and defiant tribe, far from being gathered and subjected. The birds were not placed before mankind, even though their subjugation is also more difficult and more indicative of the strength of dominion and the might of authority, so that the two opposites and partners in many rulings, the jinn and mankind, would not be separated.

It has been said regarding the placing of the jinn first that the situation of subjugation does not avoid some humiliation, and that this is fitting for them. But this is nothing; for subjugation is an honour for the prophets, peace be upon them, since in reality it belongs to God, mighty and majestic, who subjected everything. And if it is considered in itself, then the reasoning by that is not suitable to the context. This suffices for its non-acceptance.

﴿So they are marshalled in order﴾: that is, their first is held back so that the last may catch up, and they may be gathered together, none of them lagging behind. This is because of their great number. It is possible that this is for arranging the ranks, as is customary in armies. The first is preferable. And in it, along with indicating multitude and conveying their complete eagerness to proceed, is an indication that they were governed and not neglected, so that no one would be harmed by them. The root of (yuza'un) is restraint and prevention. From this is the saying of Uthman, may God be pleased with him: "The ruler restrains more than the Qur'an restrains." And the saying of al-Hasan: "The judge must have guards." And the poet's saying:

"He whom his intellect and his modesty do not restrain,
for him, from the greyness of his temples, there is no restrainer."

The singling out of the holding back of their first ones, rather than driving their last ones, although the joining up is also achieved by that, is because in it there is compassion for both groups. As for the first ones, it is so that they may rest in general by stopping from travel. As for the last ones, it is so that they do not exhaust themselves with rapid travel. It has also been said that this is because their last ones are not able to do what their first ones are able to do of swift travel.

Al-Tabarani and al-Tastiy in his Masa'il recorded, from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, that their first ones are held back for their last ones until the birds fall asleep. God, exalted is He, knows best the soundness of the report. The apparent meaning is that this restraint, if their travel was not by the wind carrying them through the air, is itself (to be understood thus). The reports about his story, peace be upon him, are numerous.

Ibn Abi Hatim recorded, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: "Three hundred thousand chairs would be placed for Solomon, and the believers among mankind would sit next to him, and the believers among the jinn behind them. Then he would command the birds, and they would shade him. Then he would command the wind, and it would carry him. They would pass over an ear of grain and not move it."

Al-Hakim recorded, from Muhammad ibn Ka'b, who said: "It has reached us that Solomon, peace be upon him, had an encampment of one hundred farsakhs: twenty-five for mankind, twenty-five for the jinn, twenty-five for the wild beasts, and twenty-five for the birds. He had a thousand tents of glass upon wood, in which were three hundred free wives and seven hundred concubines. He would command the violent wind and it would lift him, then he would command the gentle breeze and it would carry him."

God, mighty and majestic, revealed to him, while he was travelling between heaven and earth, that He had increased his dominion so that no creature would speak a word except that the wind would bring it to him and cast it into his hearing.

It is related that the jinn wove for him, peace be upon him, a carpet of gold and silk, a farsakh by a farsakh, with his pulpit in its middle of gold. He would ascend it, and around him were six hundred thousand chairs of gold and silver. The prophets, peace be upon them, would sit on the golden chairs, and the scholars on the silver chairs, and around them the people, and around the people the jinn and the devils. The birds would shade him with their wings, and the east wind would carry the carpet a month's journey.

'Abd Allah ibn Ahmad in his Zawa'id al-Zuhd, and Ibn al-Mundhir, recorded, from Wahb ibn Munabbih, who said: "Solomon, peace be upon him, passed by, while in his kingdom, and the wind had carried him, over a ploughman from the Children of Israel. When he saw him, he said: 'Glory be to God! The family of Dawud has been given a kingdom!' The wind carried his words and placed them in Solomon's ear. He said: 'Bring me the man.' He said: 'What did you say?' So he told him. Solomon said: 'I feared for you the trial. Indeed, the reward of (Glory be to God) with God on the Day of Resurrection is greater than what you saw the family of Dawud given.' The ploughman said: 'May God remove your worry as you have removed mine.'"

In some narrations, he, peace be upon him, descended and walked to the ploughman and said: "I only walked to you so that you would not wish for what you are unable to attain." Then he said: "A single glorification that God accepts is better than what the family of Dawud was given."

Most reports on this matter are not relied upon. So hold to belief in what the Qur'an has stated and what sound reports indicate. And beware of championing what has no soundness, from what many storytellers (qussas) and historians mention, in which there are shocking exaggerations merely because they are possible matters, the power of God, exalted and majestic, can be connected to them. Thereby the door of mockery of religion is opened, and we seek refuge in God, exalted is He. And it is not far-fetched that most of what contains such things is the fabrication of heretics (zanadiqa), who intend by it to repel people from the religion of Islam.

﴿Until, when they came upon the valley of the ants﴾. "Ḥattā" is the particle with which speech begins, yet it also marks an endpoint (ghāyah) of what precedes it. Here it marks an endpoint of what is implied by His words, ﴿so they were marshalled﴾, that is, of their marching. It is as if it had been said: "They marched until, when they came upon..." The valley of the ants is a valley in the land of Syria with many ants, according to what is narrated from Qatadah and Muqatil. Ka'b said: it is the Valley of al-Sadir in the land of al-Ta'if. It was also said: it is a valley at the far end of Yemen, which is known among the Arabs and mentioned in their poetry. It was also said: it is a valley inhabited by the jinn, with the ants as their mounts. In my view, this last opinion is not worth considering.

The verb's construction with the preposition "ʿalā" (on), rather than directly or with "ilā" (to), is either because their approach was from a high place, so the preposition was used to indicate this, as al-Mutanabbi said:

"How much you have overstepped your rank by rising, and how much the stars have come close to you!"

Here, the nearness of the stars, even if he meant by them the verses of his poetry, is from above.

Or it is because the intended meaning of "coming upon" it is crossing it and reaching its far end, from the expression "atā ʿalā al-shayʾ" when one finishes it and reaches its end. Then "coming upon it" in the sense of crossing it is a metaphor (majāz) for intending that. Otherwise the warning about the coming trampling would have no sense, since it would have no meaning after they had crossed the valley where the ants were and passed beyond it. Apparently, on both interpretations, they came upon it on foot. It is also possible that they were travelling through the air and wished to descend there, and the ant sensed their descending and warned the ants.

﴿A certain ant said﴾. This is the answer to "when" (idhā). Apparently it made a sound that Solomon, peace be upon him, understood as meaning: ﴿O ants, enter your dwellings, lest Solomon and his hosts crush you while they do not perceive﴾. This is like how he, peace be upon him, understood the meanings of the cries of birds. That he, peace be upon him, was taught only the speech of the birds does not undermine this, either because she was, as Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Sha'bi, and ʿAbd al-Razzaq, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, and Ibn al-Mundhir from Qatadah, one of the birds that had two wings. Indeed, we have seen an ant that has two wings with which it flies. Whether that requires counting it among the birds is open to question.

Or because the understanding of what was mentioned came to him, peace be upon him, only on this occasion and was not habitual, as with understanding the cries of birds. Neither the preceding verse nor the reports negate that others of the animals may understand what is intended without this being habitual.

Ibn Bahr said: she spoke this as a miracle for Solomon, peace be upon him, just as the lizard and the arm spoke to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Muqatil said: he, peace be upon him, heard her speech from three miles away. According to this, she would have sensed their descent from this distance, and Solomon's hearing from her would not be far-fetched, because the wind, as is reported in the traditions, carries the sound to him. Or because God, Exalted, granted him at that time a sacred faculty by which he heard. However, the ant's sensing from such a distance is remote. The thing proverbially known among the Arabs for sensing from afar is the tick, to the point that they coined a proverb about it. You know that there is no harm in denying the soundness of this report.

It was also said: he, peace be upon him, did not hear any sound at all, but understood what was in the ant's mind by inspiration from God, Exalted. al-Kalbi said: an angel informed him of that. To the view that he did not hear a sound, the verse of Jarir alludes:

"Had I been given the speech of the ḥukl, Solomon would have known the speech of the ants."

By "ḥukl" he meant that whose sound is not heard.

Some said: as if, when she saw them heading toward the valley, she fled from them out of fear of being crushed, and another followed her, and she cried out a cry by which the ants nearby were alerted, and they followed her. So this was compared to addressing rational beings and advising them. For this reason they were treated as such, since she was made the speaker and the rest of the ants were made those spoken to. Thus the statement comes out as an allegorical metaphor (istiʿārah tamthīliyyah), and it is possible that there is in it an implicit metaphor (istiʿārah makniyyah).

You know that there is no necessity that calls for this. Whoever examines the conditions of the ants will not find it strange that they have a rational soul (nafs nāṭiqah). For it stores in summer what it will live on in winter, and it splits the grains it stores into two halves, for fear that the dew will reach them and they will sprout. Except for coriander and lentils, for it cuts each one of them into four pieces, and does not content itself with splitting them in half, because they sprout just as they would if they had not been split.

This and similar things require a universal, inferential knowledge, and that requires a rational soul. The Sheikh al-Ashraf (Sharaf al-Din) has demonstrated the existence of a rational soul in all animals, and the apparent sense of the verses and the sound reports requires it, as you have heard, old and new. So there is no need for you to say: it is possible that God, Exalted, created in the ant at that time speech, and in the rest of the ants intellect and understanding. As for today, there is no such thing in ants.

Furthermore, it should be known that the apparent sense is that the ant's knowledge that the one approaching was Solomon, peace be upon him, and his hosts, was through inspiration from Him, Exalted and Majestic. That is like the lizard's knowledge of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, when it spoke with him and bore witness to his prophethood, peace be upon him. The apparent sense is also that she was like the rest of the ants in body. Today there is among them what is near to the size of a fly, called the Persian ant. Some storytellers exaggerated its size, but there is no sound basis for that.

In some reports it is said that she was lame, and her name was Ṭākhiyah. It was also said: Jarmā. In al-Baḥr it says: the proper name of her was disputed, the text of which is: "I wonder who it was that assigned her a name specific to her, the sons of Adam or the ants?!" End of quote.

Whoever holds that animals have rational souls does not thereby deny that they have names which some of them assigned to others, but not with words like our words, rather with sounds articulated in a particular manner. Perhaps this comprises various features, each of which serves as a letter of the letters familiar to us. When one who knows them, among those of sacred souls, wishes to translate them, he renders them in terms we know. What brings this closer to you is that much of the speech of the Franks and their like sounds to us only like the chirping of sparrows and the like; but when it is translated for us in what we know, it appears to consist of familiar letters.

The apparent sense is that the tāʾ in "namlah" is for singularity (waḥdah), so the feminine form of the verb is due to observing the apparent feminine. Therefore there is no proof in this that the ant was female. So said some.

[p. 177]

It is reported from Qatadah that he entered Kufa, and people crowded around him. He said: "Ask me about whatever you wish." Abu Hanifah, may God be pleased with him, was present, and he was a young lad. He said: "Ask him about Solomon's ant: was it male or female?" They asked him, and he was silenced. Abu Hanifah said: "It was female." He was asked: "How do you know?" He said: "From the Book of God, Exalted: ﴿She said, 'A certain ant'﴾. Had it been male, He, glorified, would have said: ﴿He said, 'A certain ant'﴾. That is because 'namlah' is like 'ḥamāmah' (dove) and 'shāh' (sheep) in applying to both male and female, so one distinguishes between them by a sign, as in the expression: ḥamāmah dhakar (male dove) and ḥamāmah unthā (female dove), and huwa and hiya." So it is in al-Kashshaf.

Ibn al-Munir criticized this, saying: "I do not know what is more wondrous, his statement or that of Abu Hanifah, if this is indeed reported from him. For the ant, like the dove and the sheep, applies to both male and female, since it is a noun of genus (ism jins). One says: namlah dhakar and namlah unthā, just as they say: ḥamāmah dhakar and ḥamāmah unthā, and shāh dhakar and shāh unthā. So its wording is feminine but its meaning is open. It is possible that it be made feminine for the sake of its wording, even if it applies to a male. Indeed, this is the eloquent and commonly used usage. Do you not see his, peace be upon him, saying: 'One does not sacrifice a one-eyed animal, nor a blind one, nor a lean one'? How he, peace be upon him, put these attributes in the feminine form according to the wording, though he did not mean only female animals. So in His words, (she said: a certain ant), the feminine of the wording was observed, while as for the meaning, it allows the masculine and feminine equally. How could Abu Hanifah, may God be pleased with him, ask this and silence Qatadah with it, despite the abundance of his knowledge? The more likely is that this is not authentically reported from either of them." End of quote.

Ibn al-Hajib, may God have mercy on him, said: "Lexical feminine (al-taʾnīth al-lafẓī) is that there is no corresponding masculine for it in animals, like ẓulmah (darkness) and ʿayn (eye). There is no difference between it being an animal or something else, like dajājah (hen) and ḥamāmah (dove), when a male is intended by it; for it is lexically feminine. Therefore the view of one who claims that 'namlah' in His words, ﴿she said, 'a certain ant'﴾, is feminine because the feminine marker appears in 'qālat' (she said) is a mistake, since it may be masculine in reality. The appearance of the feminine marker is like its appearance on a lexically feminine verb, as in 'jāʾat al-ẓulmah' (the darkness came)."

One of the learned men of Transoxiana answered and said: "By my life, Ibn al-Hajib has been far-fetched here and has neglected what is obligatory, in that he raised an objection against the Imam of the people of Islam. His objection, with his words, 'and the appearance of the feminine marker is like...' etc., is nothing. For if it were permissible to bring the feminine marker to the verb merely because of the feminine form of a real masculine subject, then it would be necessary to permit saying: 'jāʾatnī Ṭalḥah' (Ṭalḥah came to me), though it is not permitted. His answer to this in his commentary is: 'This is not like the feminization of proper nouns, for in them only the meaning is considered, not the wording, contrary to the Kufans. The secret of this is that they transferred them from their meanings to another referent, so they considered the second referent. Had they considered their feminine form, that would be considering the first referent, and the meaning would be corrupted. Therefore one does not say: a'jabatnī Ṭalḥah.'" He called this a pure contradiction, as if he had forgotten what he had set down at the beginning of his book, his words: "If a masculine is named by it, its condition is the addition beyond three letters." That is, if a feminine in meaning is named by it, its condition is the addition beyond three letters. It is not hidden from anyone with the slightest discernment that "ʿaqrab" (scorpion), even though its feminine marker is hidden due to its being a proper noun, does not prevent considering its feminine nature so that it is barred from diptotic inflection. How then would being a proper noun prevent considering the feminine in "Ṭalḥah", though its feminine marker is lexical? Therefore, dropping the tāʾ from the verb is only because the tāʾ is brought only as a sign of the feminine subject, and the subject here is a real masculine. So too the ant, if it were masculine, it would be exactly like "Ṭalḥah," step for step."

What supports Abu Hanifah's view, may God be pleased with him, is what is reported from Ibn al-Sikkit: "This is a male duck (baṭṭah dhakar), this is a male dove (ḥamāmah dhakar), this is a sheep (shāh) if you mean a ram, this is a cow (baqarah) if you mean a bull. But if you mean a female, you say: hādhihi baqarah." End of quote.

al-Tibi approved this, then said: "It has become clear that the statement is what Ḥadhām said, and the doctrine is what the Imam followed."

In al-Kashshaf [p. 178]: the tāʾ in "namlah" is for singularity, so it is in the position of the lexically feminine. It may be treated as such, like tamr and tamrah, as is stated in al-Mufassal. It is not problematic with the like of "Ṭalḥah," where its verb is not allowed to take the tāʾ, because proper nouns are considered in meaning, not wording, contrary to the Kufans, to the end of what Ibn al-Hajib mentioned. There is no contradiction in considering the feminine in ʿaqrab if a male is named by it, nor in Ṭalḥah itself with regard to diptotic inflection, as some learned men of Transoxiana supposed.

Our Sheikh al-Tibi affirmed this, because consideration of meaning applies to what pertains to meaning, not to what pertains to wording. Attaching the sign because of the subject is either for real femininity, or for quasi-femininity arising from singularity, collectivity, or the like. So when the meaning, I mean femininity and quasi-femininity, does not remain, there is no reason for attaching it.

Regarding the diptote (mamnu' al-sarf) status, it is not considered in terms of the meaning of femininity, but rather in terms of this extra letter, either pronounced or implied. This is not disputed between the transmitter and the one from whom it is transmitted. And sufficient as evidence for considering the wording alone in this ruling is their distinction in (Saqar) between naming a masculine with it and a feminine, unlike (‘Aqrab). Had the opponent reflected, what he cited against it would have been in its favor, not against it. Moreover, the Imam, may Allah be pleased with him, is a Kufan, and the rule according to his school is demolished. End of quote. And it is a solid statement.

The prudent position is to affirm that this report is not authentic. For Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, whom you know, and he was then a young boy, and Qatada ibn Di'ama al-Sadusi, by the consensus of those knowledgeable about the narrators, was skilled in Arabic. It is therefore extremely unlikely that what was mentioned from both of them occurred. And Allah knows best.

Al-hatm means breaking, and the intended meaning is destruction. The prohibition, outwardly, is addressed to Sulayman, peace be upon him, and his soldiers, but in reality it is a prohibition in the manner of metonymy addressed to the ants, against stopping until they are crushed, because being crushed is not within their power. It is like your saying: "Let me not see you here," which outwardly is a prohibition to the speaker from seeing the addressee, while the intended meaning is a prohibition to the addressee from being in a place where the speaker can see him. So the sentence is either a resumptive sentence (istinaf) or a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal) for the sentence ﴿Enter your dwellings﴾.

As for the statement of some of them: when the meaning is the prohibition against stopping until one is crushed, there results a unity between the two sentences, which requires that it be a substitute of the whole for the whole, based on the premise that a command to something is identical to a prohibition of its opposite. But according to what has been mentioned, there is no need for this. In sum, Abu Hayyan's objection to the substitution view, on the grounds that the two sentences differ in their indicated meanings, is not well placed. Al-Zamakhshari allowed that (la yahtimannakum) could be an answer to the command, namely (udkhulu), and then (la) is negating. It was objected that the entry of the nun into the answer of a conditional is restricted to poetic necessity, as in his saying:

Whatever Fazara wishes from him, he gives it, and whatever Fazara wishes from him, it withholds.

In the Kitab it is said: this is rare in poetry; they likened it to the prohibition, since it is jussive and not obligatory. The ant, according to what is in the Kashshaf, intended: "Let not the soldiers of Sulayman crush you," but she came with what is more eloquent. Similar to this is his saying: "I wondered at myself and at its compassion," where he intended "I wondered at the compassion of myself," but he came with what is more eloquent, for the sake of generality and detail.

This was challenged in al-Bahr on the grounds that it involves the claim of the addition of nouns, which is impermissible. Rather, the apparent reading is that the crushing is attributed to him, peace be upon him, and to his soldiers, and the speech is with an elided modifier, i.e., "the horses of Sulayman and his soldiers," or something similar that can be validly supposed. There is room for discussion on this. The clause ﴿and they do not perceive﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the whole of the two conjoined elements, with the pronoun referring to both.

It is also permitted that it be a circumstantial clause from the soldiers, with the pronoun referring to them. Either way, restricting the crushing by their not perceiving their location, which implies that had they perceived it they would not have crushed, indicates the utmost courtesy of the ant toward Sulayman, peace be upon him, and his soldiers. Would that whoever disparages the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ, may Allah be pleased with them, would take her as an example, refrain from that, and display good manners.

It is narrated that when Sulayman, peace be upon him, heard the ant's words, "O ants," etc., he said: "Bring her to me." They brought her, and he said: "Why did you warn the ants of my oppression? Do you not know that I am a just prophet? Why did you say: ﴿Let not Sulayman and his soldiers crush you﴾?" She said: "Did you not hear my words: ﴿while they do not perceive﴾? Moreover, I did not intend the crushing of souls, but only the crushing of hearts. I feared that they would see what Allah the Exalted has bestowed upon you of rank and great dominion, and so fall into ingratitude for blessings. At least they would be occupied with looking at you rather than glorifying." Then Sulayman said to her: "Advise me." She said: "Do you know why your father was named Dawud?" He said: "No." She said: "Because he healed the wound of his heart." "And do you know why you were named Sulayman?" He said: "No." She said: "Because you are sound (salim) of heart and breast." Then she said: "Do you know why Allah the Exalted subjected the wind to you?" He said: "No." She said: "Allah the Exalted informed you of this: that the whole world is wind, so whoever relies upon it is as though he relied upon the wind."

This is the apparent wording, as is not hidden, and it contains what resembles the speech of the Sufis. And Allah knows best regarding the authenticity of what is reported, that she presented him with a jujube (nabqa), and that he, peace be upon him, supplicated for the ants for blessing.

It is permitted that the clause ﴿they do not perceive﴾ be in the position of a circumstantial clause from the ant, with the pronoun referring to the soldiers, like the preceding pronouns in His saying: ﴿so they are held back﴾ and His saying: ﴿until, when they came﴾, and it is from His speech, Exalted is He; that is, she said that while the soldiers did not perceive it. This is not something of substance. Something close to it is what has been said: that the clause may be conjoined to an implied element, and it is from His speech, Glorified and Exalted is He, as if it were said: "Sulayman understood what she said while the soldiers did not perceive that."

Al-Hasan, Talha, Mu'tamir ibn Sulayman and Abu Sulayman al-Taymi read (namulatun) with a damma on the mim, like (samurah), and likewise (al-namul), as in al-rajl and al-rajul, which are two dialects. From Abu Sulayman al-Taymi (numulatun) and (numul) with a damma on the nun and the mim. Shahr ibn Hawshab read (maskanakum) in the singular. From Ubayy: "Enter your dwellings, O women (adkhulna masakinakunna), lest they crush you (la yahtimannakunna)," with the nun preceding the kaf lightened.

Al-Hasan, Abu Raja', Qatada, Isa ibn Umar al-Hamdani al-Kufi, and Nuh al-Qadi read with a damma on the yaa, a fatha on the ha, and a shadda on the ta and the nun, as the imperfect of (hattama) in the intensive form.

From al-Hasan, with a fatha on the yaa and a sukun on the ha and a shadda on the ta. And from him likewise with a kasra on the ha. Its original form is (yahtatimannakum), from al-ihtitam. Ibn Abi Ishaq, Talha, Ya'qub, and Abu 'Amr in the transmission of Ubayd read like the reading of the majority, except that they made the nun of emphasis sukun. Al-A'mash read with the deletion of the nun and the jazm of the mim, and there is no disagreement regarding this reading on the permissibility of the verb being jussive in answer to the command.

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 27, verse 19:

﴿So he smiled, laughing at her speech.﴾ This is a consequence (*tafri'*) of what came before, so there is no need to posit a conjoined element omitted before it. The meaning is: he heard her, and so he smiled. The *fa* is taken as an explanatory *fa* (*fa' fasiha*), as has been said.

Perhaps he, peace be upon him, smiled at this out of joy at what he had been inspired with of the good state of himself and his soldiers in matters of piety and compassion, and out of delight at what God the Exalted had singled him out with, namely perceiving what is a whisper relative to human beings, and understanding her intended meaning from it.

It is also permissible that this was out of wonder at her caution, her warning, and her guidance to the management of her own interests and the interests of her kind. The first is more apt in relation to what follows of the supplication.

The word *(dahikan)* ("laughing") is in the accusative as a circumstantial (*hal*), meaning: beginning to laugh, that is, he had gone beyond the limit of smiling to laughter; or, he was one who would laugh in the future, on the basis that it is a *hal muqaddara* (a circumstance anticipated), as al-Tibi transmitted from some of them.

Abu al-Baqa' said: it is a *hal mu'akkida* (an emphatic circumstantial). This requires that smiling and laughing have the same meaning, whereas the known position is that they differ. Ibn Hajar said: *tabassum* is the beginnings of laughter without sound, while *dahik* is the spreading of the face such that the teeth appear out of joy, with a faint sound. If there is a sound that can be heard from a distance, then it is *qahqaha* (loud laughter). It seems that whoever held that smiling and laughing are identical restricted that to what came from the prophets, peace be upon them, for their laughter is a smile. Al-Busiri has said in praise of our Prophet ﷺ:

*A master whose laughter is smiling, and whose walking is unhurried, and whose sleep is dozing.*

Al-Bukhari narrated from Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, that she said: "I never saw him ﷺ laughing with his whole being," meaning: fully given over to laughter; rather, he would only smile. What the totality of the hadiths indicates is that his smiling, peace and blessings be upon him, was more frequent than his laughter, and at times he laughed until his molars showed. That he laughed in this manner is mentioned in the hadith: "The last of the people of the Fire to leave it, and the last of the people of Paradise to enter Paradise..." It was transmitted by al-Bukhari, Muslim and al-Tirmidhi. Likewise in a report transmitted by al-Bukhari concerning his having relations with his family during Ramadan. The hadith of Aisha mentioned earlier contains no more than her negation of seeing him ﷺ laughing with his whole being, and this does not negate that laughter occurred from him at some times, when she did not see it.

Al-Zamakhshari interpreted what is reported, that he ﷺ laughed until his molars showed, as meaning that the purpose is to emphasise the extent of the prophetic laughter that came from him, peace and blessings be upon him; and that there was not literally the showing of the molars, which are the last teeth.

Perhaps the reason He, glorified be He, did not say "So he smiled at her speech" but instead said "laughing" in the accusative as a circumstantial, is that the intended benefit is going beyond smiling to laughter. This is based on the principle that the purpose of a statement containing a qualifier is to convey the qualifier's affirmation or negation. It also signals the strength of the effect of her words upon him, peace be upon him, in that what came over him caused him to go beyond the limit of smiling and begin laughing, whereas his state was not merely smiling.

It seems that since the phrase "so he laughed at her speech" does not convey what we have mentioned in the way that the sublime wording does, it was not used. In *al-Bahr* it is said: since smiling may occur from mockery or anger, as they say, "he smiled the smile of the angry one" and "he smiled the smile of the mocker", and laughter is only for gladness and joy, God, may He be exalted, brought His words "laughing" to make clear that the smile was not mockery nor anger. End of quote.

It is not hidden that the claim that laughter is only for gladness and joy is refuted by His words: ﴿Indeed, those who committed crimes used to laugh at those who believed.﴾ That laughter came from the polytheists of Quraysh in mockery of their poor, such as Ammar, Suhayb, Khabbab and others, as the exegetes have mentioned; it was not out of gladness and joy. Likewise His words: ﴿But today those who believed will laugh at the disbelievers.﴾ as is apparent.

If you rush to interpretation, we say: the reality refutes it. If you deny that the people of understanding laughed at you, there is also more than this in it, so reflect. And God the Exalted is the Guide to the right course.

Ibn al-Sumayqa read *"dahikan"* as a verbal noun (*masdar*) in the position of a circumstantial. It was also permitted that it is accusative as an absolute object (*maf'ul mutlaq*), like *shukran* in your saying "he praised [out of] gratitude" (*hamida shukran*).

﴿And he said: My Lord, inspire me to be grateful for Your favour which You have bestowed upon me.﴾ That is: make me inspire the gratitude of Your favour, that is, restrain it and bind it so that it does not slip away from me. This is a metaphor for constancy in gratitude and persistence in it, as though it were said: My Lord, make me persistent in thanking You for Your favour. The hamza of *(awzi')* is for transitivity, and there is no need to consider *tadmin* (implicit meaning of another verb), nor to take the sense as "My Lord, facilitate for me that I thank Your favour, [being] one who inspires it."

From Ibn Abbas: the meaning is "make me thank."

Ibn Zayd said: that is, urge me.

Abu Ubayda said: that is, make me fond of it.

Al-Zajjaj said, as has been said: that is, inspire me.

Its linguistic derivation: restrain me from the things that distance me from You.

Al-Tibi said: on this basis it is a *kinaya talwihiyya* (an allusive metonymy); for he asked that He restrain him from what leads to ingratitude for the favour, by inspiring him with what binds the favour through gratitude.

The idiom of the favour is for generality, that is, all Your favours.

It is read *"awzi'ani"* with a fatha on the yā'.

﴿which You have bestowed⦆ That is, which You have bestowed upon them. Originally it is "bestowed with it", but the omission and direct connection were considered because the condition for omitting an oblique returning pronoun was lacking, namely that it be governed by the same preposition as the relative pronoun, in form, meaning and dependency. Whoever does not hold this principle to be generally valid does not consider what has been mentioned, and I see no harm in it.

﴿upon me and upon my parents⦆ The mention of his parents was included to increase the favour, for bestowing favour upon them is a bestowal upon him from one aspect that calls for gratitude. Or it is for generalisation of the favour, since the favour upon him, peace be upon him, benefits them. The difference between the two aspects is clear. Al-Zamakhshari restricted himself to the second, and it is more suited to gratitude.

That the supplication mentioned occurred after the death of his parents, peace be upon them, is certain, but the first has been preferred because it is more suited to His words: ﴿Work, family of David, in gratitude﴾ following His words: ﴿And We had certainly given David favour from Us﴾ and His words: ﴿And to Solomon the wind﴾, and so reflect, for it is subtle.

﴿and that I may do righteousness⦆ is conjoined to *(an ashkura)* ("that I may thank"), so he, peace be upon him, asked that He make him persistent also in doing righteous deeds. It seems that by gratitude he meant gratitude by the tongue, which entails gratitude by the heart, and he followed it with what was mentioned to complete it, since righteous action is gratitude by the limbs. In *al-Bahr* it is said: he, peace be upon him, first asked for something specific, namely gratitude for the favour, and second for something general, namely righteous action.

His words, exalted be He: ﴿that You approve⦆. It is said that it is a qualifier, either emphasising or specifying, if by it is meant complete approval. The specifying qualifier was preferred. By approval is meant acceptance, and this is not in any way a necessary consequence of righteous action, neither rationally nor by law.

﴿and admit me by Your mercy among Your righteous servants⦆ That is: among their number.

The statement, as coming from al-Zamakhshari, is a metonymy for making him one of the people of Paradise. Some have supposed Paradise to be a second object of *(admitme)*. On the view that it is a metonymy, no supposition is needed. The motive for one of the two readings, according to what is said, is to avoid repetition with what came before, since when he does a righteous deed he is necessarily among the righteous, for "righteous" has no meaning except one who performs righteous deeds. He followed the request for constancy in righteous deeds with a request that he be admitted to Paradise, because performing righteous deeds by itself does not entail admission to Paradise.

In a report: "No one among you will enter Paradise by his deed." It was said: "Not even you, Messenger of Allah?" He said: "Not even I, unless Allah covers me with His mercy."

It seems that the mention of "by Your mercy" in this supplication is an allusion to that. What was mentioned does not contradict His words: ﴿And that is Paradise, which you have been made to inherit for what you used to do.﴾ because the causality of the deed for the inheritance is by the mercy of God the Exalted.

Al-Khafaji said: you may say that he, peace be upon him, counted himself not righteous out of humility. That is, there is then no need for supposition or for arranging the speech within the category of metonymy. It is not hidden that this does not answer the objection, since the supplication for constancy in righteous deeds does not dispense with it.

It has been said: what is meant is that He, glorified be He, should place him among the prophets, peace be upon them, and fix his name alongside their names, and not remove him from the office of prophethood, which is a divine gift not attained through deeds. For this reason He mentioned mercy in the midst. Al-Tabrisi transmitted from Ibn Abbas something that alludes to this meaning.

It has been said: what is meant is: admit me into the number of the righteous, and make me be mentioned with them when they are mentioned. Its essence is a request for a good remembrance, which righteous action does not necessarily entail, since a person may truly be righteous and yet people may not count him among the righteous.

In this supplication there is a trace of the supplication of Abraham, peace be upon him: ﴿And grant me a tongue of truthfulness among the later generations.﴾ The aims of the prophets in such matters are otherworldly. It has also been said: it is possible that he meant by righteous action the discharge of the rights of God, may He be glorified and exalted, and that by righteousness in His words "among Your righteous servants" he meant the discharge of His rights and the rights of His servants, so that it is a generalisation after a specification.

Determining which of these sayings is preferable is left to your reflection, and God the Exalted is the Guide.

His supplication, peace be upon him, was, according to some reports, after the ants had entered their dwellings.

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is reported that the ant perceived the sound of the armies, though she did not know that they were in the air. So Solomon, peace be upon him, commanded the wind, and it stopped, so that they would not be frightened, until they entered their dwellings. Then he made the supplication.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 27, verse 20:**

﴿And he inspected the birds﴾. That is, he wanted to know which of them was present and which was absent. The root of *tafaqqud* (inspection) is *ma'rifat al-faqd*, knowing what is missing. The apparent meaning is that he, peace be upon him, inspected all the birds, in keeping with what the care of governing and concern for his subjects require, especially the weak among them. It is said that from every kind there used to come to him one bird, and he did not see the hoopoe. It is also said that the birds would shade him from the sun, and the hoopoe would cover his right side, so the sun reached him. He looked at the place of the hoopoe and did not see it.

It is reported from ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam that Sulayman, peace be upon him, stopped in a desert wasteland with no water, and the hoopoe would see water beneath the earth and inform Sulayman of it. He would then order the jinn, and the earth would be stripped away from it in an hour, as a sheep is skinned. They needed water, so he inspected the birds for this purpose and did not see the hoopoe.

﴿So he said, "Why is it that I do not see the hoopoe?"﴾ The hoopoe is a well-known bird, foul-smelling, which, it is said, eats blood. It is given the kunyas (teknonyms) Abu al-Akhbar, Abu al-Rabi', Abu Thumamah and others, as al-Damiri mentioned. Its diminutive by analogy is *hudhayhid*. Some claimed that its diminutive is said to be *hudahid*, by converting the *ya'* into an *alif*, and they recited:

*Like a hudahid whose wing the archers broke.*

A parallel to this is *dawabbah* and *shawabbah* as diminutives of *dubbah* (a small creature).

Apparently his saying, peace be upon him, that is based on his supposition that the hoopoe was present but something prevented him from seeing it, meaning: "Why is it that I do not see it, though it is present, for some reason, whether it is concealment or something else?" Then it became clear to him that it was absent, so he turned away from that and began saying: ﴿Or is he among the absent?﴾ as though he were asking about the accuracy of what had occurred to him. Here *am* is the disjunctive *am* (*am al-munqati'ah*), as in the saying: "Is it camels, or sheep?"

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: the purpose of the speech is: the hoopoe is absent, but he took the necessary consequence of its absence, which is that he does not see it, and so he asked, in the form of a rebuke, about the necessary consequence. This is a kind of concision. The interrogative in his saying *"Mā liya"* (why is it that I...) stands in place of the interrogative hamzah that *am* requires.

Its apparent meaning is that *am* is connective (*muttasilah*), and the hamzah stands in place of the interrogative hamzah. The meaning according to him is: "Is it that he is now absent from me, so I did not see him at the time of inspection, or was he among those who had been absent earlier, and I did not notice his absence?" The truth is what has preceded. It has been said that there is an inversion (*qalb*) in the speech, and the original is: "What is the matter with the hoopoe, that I do not see it?" There is no need, however, to claim this.

Indeed, it has been said that this reading is more fitting to the inspection being for the sake of care. It is also mentioned that the name of this hoopoe was Yaʿfur. That the hoopoe sees water beneath the earth was transmitted by Ibn Abi Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Hakim, who declared it sound, from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Saʿid ibn Mansur also transmitted from Yusuf ibn Mahak that when Ibn ʿAbbas said this, Nafiʿ ibn al-Azraq objected to him, as was his habit, saying: "How can that be, when a trap is set for the hoopoe, and a grain is placed in it, and it is covered with dirt, and so it is caught?" Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Indeed, sight benefits only so long as the decree has not come; when the decree comes, it comes between a man and his sight." Ibn al-Azraq said: "I will not dispute with you about anything after this."

There is no barrier, however, to saying: it is possible that it sees the grain too, but it does not know that picking it up from the trap entails its being caught. Many birds and other animals are caught by what they see, through some kind of trickery. It is also possible that it sees them and knows the device in placing them, but the decree overpowers it, so it supposes that it will escape if it picks them up in one of the ways it imagines. This would be like one who plunges into ruin, supposing deliverance, despite witnessing the destruction of many who plunged into it before him. When Allah, exalted, wills a matter for a people, He takes away the intellects of those who possess them.

Indeed, his seeing water beneath the earth, even if it is permissible according to the principles of the Ash'arites (*al-Ash'ariyyah*, the followers of al-Ash'ari), is something the intellect finds very improbable. I have no certainty about the soundness of the preceding report. al-Hakim's authentication

Page 183

is, according to the hadith scholars, judged to be what you know. Similar to it is what preceded from Ibn Salam, and likewise other reports that I have come across on this matter. There is no indication in the verse of that. Rather, the apparent meaning, based on what the condition of Sulayman, peace be upon him, requires, is that the inspection came from him, peace be upon him, as care for the affairs of his kingdom and concern for the weak of his army. It seems that he, peace be upon him, expressed his speech, as the glorious text relates, because of his strong supposition that what had destroyed it had not reached it, and so that, together with the inspection, it would be a combination of the two attributes of beauty and majesty, which is the most perfect in the matter of kings. Perhaps what happened with the ant was like the situation that reminded him, peace be upon him, to inspect.

And according to what preceded from Ibn Salam, the reminding situation, or rather the motivating one, is the descent into the wasteland with no water, and the hoopoe being a *qunaqinah* (a bird that was a guide for water). They relate in this that when Sulayman, peace be upon him, completed the building of the Temple of Jerusalem, he prepared to perform the pilgrimage with his host. He reached the Sacred Precinct (*al-Haram*), stayed there as long as he willed, and during his whole stay he sacrificed each day five thousand cows, five thousand camels, and twenty thousand sheep. He said to the nobles who were with him: "This is a place from which an Arab prophet will emerge, whose description is such and such, who will be given victory over all who oppose him, and who will be aided by terror from a month's journey away. The near and the far are equal before him in truth, and the blame of no blamer will deter him in Allah, exalted." They said: "By what religion will he judge, O Prophet of Allah?" He said: "By the religion of the *Hanifiyyah* (the upright monotheistic faith). Blessed is whoever believes in him and reaches him." They said: "How long is it between us and his emergence?" He said: "The measure of a thousand years. Let the one present among you convey it to the absent, for he is the master of the prophets and the seal of the messengers, peace be upon them." Then he resolved to set out for Yemen. He left Mecca in the morning, aiming for Suhayl, and reached Sanaa at the time of noon, which is a month's journey. He saw a land that pleased him with its greenery, so he descended to take a meal and pray, but they did not find water, and so what happened happened.

In some reports there is something that contradicts the account of the pilgrimage. It is related from Kaʿb al-Ahbar that Sulayman, peace be upon him, travelled from Istakhr intending Yemen, and passed by the city of the Messenger, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him, and said: "This is the abode of the emigration (*hijrah*) of a prophet who will be at the end of time. Blessed is whoever follows him." When he reached Mecca, he saw idols being worshipped around the House, so he passed by it, and the House wept. Allah, exalted, revealed to it: "What makes you weep?" It said: "O Lord, what makes me weep is that this is a prophet from Your prophets, and with him is a people from Your friends. They passed by me and did not descend, and did not pray at me, while idols are worshipped around me, apart from You." Allah, exalted, revealed to it: "Do not weep, for I will make you weep with faces prostrating, and I will send down in you a new Qur'an, and I will raise from you a prophet at the end of time, the most beloved of My prophets to Me, and I will make in you builders from My creation who worship Me. I will impose upon them an obligation, and they will flutter toward you as the eagle flutters to its nest, and they will yearn toward you as the she-camel yearns for her young, and as the dove yearns for her eggs. And I will purify you from the idols and the worshippers of Satan,"

[p. 184]

Then Solomon went on until he came upon the Valley of the Ants. The two reports cannot be reconciled.

What appears to be the most reliable of the reports is that when he (peace be upon him) had completed the building of Bayt al-Maqdis (the Temple in Jerusalem), he performed the Hajj and offered many sacrifices, gave the good news of the Prophet (ﷺ), set out for Yemen, and inspected the birds. He did not see the hoopoe, so he threatened it, saying: ﴿I will surely punish it with a severe punishment﴾. It was said that the punishment was the plucking of its feathers. This was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, and Ibn Juraij.

The apparent meaning is that the intended sense is all of its feathers. Yazid ibn Ruman said: the plucking of the feathers of its two wings. Ibn Wahb said: the plucking of half of its feathers. Some added to the plucking that it was thrown to the ants. Another added that it was left in the sun. It was said that the punishment was smearing it with tar and exposing it to the sun. It was said that it was confining it in a cage. It was said that it was placing it together with a different kind of bird. It was said that it was removing it from serving Solomon (peace be upon him). It was said that it was separating it from its mate. It was said that it was obliging it to serve its peers.

In al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit, the work of Abu Hayyan), it is said: The best view is that each of these sayings be taken as a figurative illustration (tamthil), and that this punishment was for discipline. It is permissible that God Most High allowed him this, because He saw in it benefit and advantage, just as He, glorified be He, permitted the slaughter of animals and birds for food and other benefits. Since the birds were subjected to him, and he could not complete what they were subjected for except through discipline and correction, it was permissible for him to be allowed what would set things right.

In al-Iklil by al-Jalal al-Suyuti, it is said: The verse may be used as evidence for the permissibility of disciplining animals and beasts by striking them when they are slow in walking or hasten, or the like, and for the permissibility of plucking the feathers of an animal for a benefit, on the basis that the punishment mentioned refers to plucking its feathers.

It is mentioned in the same work that Ibn al-'Arabi used it as evidence that punishment is in proportion to the sin and not in proportion to the body, and that the birds were under obligation (mukallafun), since no one is punished for abandoning an act unless he was obliged to perform it. End of quote. So do not overlook this.

﴿Or I will surely slaughter it﴾: this is like an ascent from the severe to the more severe, for in slaughter is the drinking of the cup of death. It has been said: everything short of death is easy. ﴿Or it must bring me a clear authority﴾, that is, a proof that clarifies its excuse for its absence. How subtle is the expression "authority" rather than "proof" here, since the excuse it brought led to the bringing of Bilqis, who was a sovereign (sultan). Furthermore, this clause, though it is joined to the particle of oath, is not in reality what is sworn to. What is truly sworn to are the first two clauses, and this one was inserted into their string for the sake of contrast (tuqabul).

This, as in al-Kashshaf, is a kind of taghlib (the rhetorical device of giving precedence to one of two parts) of subtle method. The meaning of his (peace be upon him) words is: one of these matters will certainly occur, in the sense that: if the bringing of the authority happens, there will be no punishment or slaughter, and if it does not happen, one of the two will occur. Thus "or" in both places is for alternation (tarddid). It has also been said that in the first place it is for choice (takhyir) between punishment and slaughter, and in the second it is for alternation between these two and the bringing of the authority. But this, as you see, is weak.

Some claimed that in the first place it is for choice, and in the second it means "illa" (except). But this involves neglect of the oath particle. It has also been allowed that the three matters are truly what is sworn to. His (peace be upon him) oath regarding the mentioned bringing is valid because he knew by revelation that it would happen, or because his strong expectation of it was based on something that arose in his mind that gave him this conviction. Otherwise, an oath about the future action of another without knowledge or strong expectation of it hardly suits any religious law.

It has been objected that his words ﴿We will see whether you have told the truth or were among the liars﴾ contradict the attainment of knowledge and of what he was told. The removal of this contradiction by saying that it is possible for it to bring a proof about which Solomon (peace be upon him) neither knows nor believes whether it is true or false is not sound, since his words "clear" (mubin) reject it. In sum, the view mentioned first is the correct one, so reflect.

Isa ibn 'Umar read (la-ya'tiyannahu) with a doubled, fathah-vowelled nun and without a ya'. In the Imam (the standard codex of 'Uthman), "la adhbahuhu" was written with an added alif between the dhal and the alif joined to the lam. Its reason is not known, like most of what occurs in it that departs from the known orthography (rasm, the established written form). It has been said that it is to alert to the fact that the slaughter did not take place.

Ibn Khaldun said in the introduction to his history: Arabic writing was at the height of excellence and fineness among Himyar, and Mudar learned it from them. However, they were not skilled in it because of their distance from civilization. At the beginning of Islam the Arabic script had not reached the peak of perfection and refinement, nor a middle level, because of the Arabs' position of bedouin life and wildness and their distance from crafts.
