As for the deviations from the rules of the orthography that occur in the writing of the Qur'an by the Companions (may God be pleased with them all), departing from what the principles of script and its craft among its experts require, such as adding the alif in "la adhbahannahu", they arise from lack of skill in the craft of writing, and the following of the early generations in their orthography is for the sake of blessing.

The explanation of some ignorant persons for that deviation, by what they explained it with, is not correct. What drove them to it is the wish to exonerate the Companions from deficiency, because they supposed that good penmanship is a perfection. But they did not realize that writing is among the civil crafts of livelihood, and that this is not a perfection in their case, since perfection in crafts is relative and not absolute, for its deficiency does not reflect on the essence in religion and the like, but only on the means of livelihood.

The Prophet (may the blessings and peace of God be upon him) was unlettered (ummi), and that was a perfection in his case and in relation to his station (peace be upon him). Similarly, his (peace be upon him) exemption from practical crafts, which are the means of livelihood and civilization, is not considered a perfection in our case, since he was devoted to his Lord, glorified and exalted be He, while we cooperate for the life of this world. Hence he (peace be upon him) said: "You are more knowledgeable about the affairs of your world." End of the summary.

You know that the addition of the alif in "la adhbahannahu" being due to their (may God be pleased with them) lack of skill in the craft of writing is very far-fetched. And the justification of that by what was mentioned before, namely alerting to the non-occurrence of the slaughter in this way, is also unlikely. Otherwise they would have added it in "la-u'adhdhibannahu" as well, because the punishment did not occur either.

As for what he pointed out, that skill in writing is not a perfection in their case, if he means that beautifying the script and shaping it in harmonious forms that the viewer finds pleasing and that souls incline toward, like other admired designs, is not a perfection in their case and its lack does no harm to their standing, then this is granted. But this is one matter, and what we are discussing is another. If, however, he means that writing in the form known to its experts, joining what they join, separating what they separate, writing what they write, and omitting what they omit, is not a perfection, then this is a matter for investigation. Do you not see that a scholar is not criticized for an ugly script or for its departure from beautiful shapes and pleasing forms, but he is criticized for joining what should be separated, separating what should be joined, writing what should not be written, not writing what should be written, and the like, unless that was for a reason?

The apparent view is that the Companions who wrote the Qur'an were skilled in the orthography of writing, knowing what requires writing and what requires not writing, what requires joining and what requires not joining, and so on. Yet they departed from the rules in some places for a wisdom. This is supported by what Ibn al-Anbari reported in his book al-Takmila, from 'Abd Allah ibn Farrukh, who said: I said to Ibn 'Abbas: O company of Quraysh, tell me about this Arabic Book: did you use to write it before God Most High sent Muhammad (ﷺ), joining what was joined and separating what was separated, such as the alif, the lam, and the nun? He said: Yes. I said: From whom did you take it? He said: From Harb ibn Umayya. I said: From whom did Harb take it? He said: From 'Abd Allah ibn Jud'an. I said: From whom did 'Abd Allah ibn Jud'an take it? He said: From the people of al-Anbar. I said: From whom did the people of al-Anbar take it? He said: From a stranger (tari') who arrived among them from the people of Yemen. I said: From whom did that stranger take it? He said: From al-Khaljan ibn al-Qasm, the scribe of revelation for the Prophet Hud (peace be upon him), who is the one who says:

Every year you introduce a custom,
and an opinion off the path that is crossed over.

And death is better than a life in which Jurhum insults us
among those who are insulted, and Himyar.

End of quote.

In the book Muhadarat al-Awa'il wa Musamarat al-Awakhir, it is said that the first of the Companions famous for writing in Islam were Abu Bakr, 'Umar, 'Uthman, 'Ali, Ubayy ibn Ka'b, and Zayd ibn Thabit (may God be pleased with them all). The apparent view is that they became famous in this only because they were correct in it.

The claim that these great Companions, and all the other Companions, did not know of the departure from the rule of the alif here, according to what the laws of the experts of script require, and likewise the other deviations that occurred, is a claim that no one with even a little good manners and fairness would make.

Similar to this is the claim that it is possible that those among them who knew it knew, but left its change to the form that agrees with the rules, or agreed with the error for the sake of blessing. Some people allowed that the deviation from the orthography by the Companions was due to the scarce skill of those from whom they took the craft of writing, so that he is the one who departed in such matters, and they did not know that he departed. Then the deficiency, if there is any, is on the part of those from whom they took it, and there is no deficiency in them, for they did not violate the rules they had learned. Violating rules that had not reached them and that they did not know is not considered a deficiency. This is close to what was mentioned before, but it does not have the same offensiveness.

Furthermore, after every discussion, fairness requires acknowledging the strength of the claim that the deviation was due to the weakness of the craft of writing, since, if it is correct that it occurred also in non-Imam texts and other writings, then this would be evidence for it. Perhaps it was not established, for otherwise it would have been transmitted. So reflect. And God Most High guides you.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 27, verse 22:**

﴿So he tarried not long.﴾ The apparent reading is that the pronoun refers to the hoopoe, and (*baʿid*, "long") is an adjective of time. The statement explains an implied question, as if it were said: "How much time passed in his absence after the threat?" So it was said: "He tarried not long," meaning he tarried for a short while. The time of his tarrying was described in this way to indicate his haste, out of fear of Sulayman (peace be upon him), and so that it would be known how the birds were subjugated to him. It has also been said that the pronoun refers to Sulayman, but that is, as you see, weak.

It has also been said that (*baʿid*) is an adjective of place, meaning: the hoopoe tarried in a place not far from Sulayman. Making it an adjective of time is preferable. It is related that when Sulayman (peace be upon him) descended, the hoopoe circled above, and saw a hoopoe, named, it is said, Afir, perched. It swooped down to him, and described to him the kingdom of Sulayman and everything that had been subjugated to him. His companion mentioned to him the kingdom of Bilqis, and he went with him to look, and he did not return until after the afternoon.

In some reports, when he (peace be upon him) did not see him, he summoned the leader of the birds, who is the eagle (*al-nasr*), and asked him, but he did not find knowledge of it with him. Then he said to the chief of the birds, who is the falcon (*al-uqab*): "Bring him to me." So it rose up, looked, and saw him approaching, so it made for him. He (the hoopoe) adjured it by God Most High, and said: "By the right of God who gave you strength and empowered you over me, have mercy on me." So it left him, and said: "May your mother be bereaved! The Prophet of God Most High has sworn that he will surely punish you or slaughter you." He said: "Did he make an exception?" It said: "Yes." He said: ﴿or he must bring me a clear authority﴾. It said: "Then you are saved." When he drew near to Sulayman, he let down his tail and his wings, dragging them on the ground, out of humility before him. When he came near to him, he took hold of his head and pulled it toward him, and said: "O Prophet of God Most High, remember your standing before God, Mighty and Majestic." Sulayman trembled, and pardoned him.

It is related from Ikrimah that he only pardoned him because he was dutiful to his parents, bringing them food and feeding them by hand because of their old age. Then he questioned him:

﴿He said: I have encompassed what you have not encompassed﴾, that is, in knowledge and awareness, and I have comprehended it from all its aspects. The beginning of his speech with this was to make it appealing to him (peace be upon him), to encourage him to listen to his excuse, and to win his heart toward accepting it. For the soul is more inclined toward an excuse that announces a wondrous matter, and more inclined to receive what it does not know. This is supported by his words: ﴿and I have come to you from Saba' with certain news﴾, where he explained his earlier vagueness in a certain way, and showed him (peace be upon him) that he had been engaged in carrying out an important service for him. For he described what he had brought with the word "news" (*nabaʾ*), which is a weighty report and a matter of great importance, and he described it with what he described. Al-Zamakhshari said: God Most High inspired the hoopoe, so he confronted Sulayman with this speech, despite what he had been given of the excellence of prophethood, wisdom, abundant sciences, and comprehension of many things, as a trial for him in his knowledge, and as a reminder that in the lowest and weakest of His creatures there may be one who has encompassed knowledge of what he (Sulayman) did not encompass, so that he would feel small in himself, his knowledge would seem small to him, and it would be a kindness to him in avoiding self-admiration, which is the trial of scholars, and how great a trial it is. End of quote.

It is objected that the encompassing of such sensory matters is not counted as a virtue, nor is ignorance of them a deficiency, since grasping them requires nothing beyond mere perception, which is common to rational and non-rational beings alike. And what came from him (peace be upon him), along with what is related of praise, thanks and supplication, is such that it would be fitting for divine wisdom to draw his attention to abandoning it? 

It is also objected that his saying "I have encompassed" ... etc. is apparently a statement of one who takes pride in his knowledge and belittles what is with his companion, and that knowledge of sensory matters, though not a virtue, its absence in relation to Sulayman and his kingdom, and the wind's conveying news to his hearing, indicates what it indicates. In the aforementioned admonition there is God Most High's affirmation of him (peace be upon him) in praise and thanks, which fits his earlier supplication: ﴿My Lord, inspire me to be grateful for Your blessing﴾. Perhaps, nevertheless, the preferable and more apparent view is what was mentioned first.

(*Saba'*) is declinable, on the basis that it is the name of a tribe of people who were named after their forefather Saba' ibn Yashjub ibn Yaʿrub ibn Qahtan.

Page 187

In the hadith of Farwa and others, from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), Saba' is the name of a man who fathered ten children, six of whom went to the right and four to the left. The six are Himyar, Kindah, al-Azd, Ash'ar, Khath'am, and the four are Lakhm, Judham, ʿAmilah, and Ghassan.

It has also been said that Saba' is an epithet of the father of this tribe of Qahtan, whose name was ʿAbd Shams, and it has been said ʿAmir, and he was given this epithet because he was the first to take captives (*sabā*).

Ibn Kathir and Abu ʿAmr read "*min Saba'*" with a fatha on the hamza, not declined, on the basis that it is the name of a tribe; then the place Ma'rib of Saba' was named after it, and between it and Sana'a is a distance of three (days' journey). It is also permissible that it refers to a specific location when declined, and to a specific city when not declined. They cited as evidence for its declension the verse:

*The arrivals, and Taym, on the heights of Saba',*
*the hide of the buffaloes has bitten their necks.*

Qunbul, through the route of al-Nabbal, read it with a sukun on the hamza, which is explained as treating the connection as a pause. Makki said: sukun in connection is remote, not preferred and not strong.

Al-Aʿmash read "*min Saba'*" with a kasra on the hamza without tanwin, which Ibn Khalawayh and Ibn ʿAtiyyah transmitted from him. It is explained that the genitive is marked by the kasra in observance of what it was originally, for it was originally the name of a man or a specific place, and the tanwin was dropped in observance of what it was transferred to, for it was made the name of a tribe or a city. And this, as you see, is weak.

Ibn Kathir in one transmission read "*min Saba*" with tanwin on the *ba'*, on the pattern of *raha*, treating it as a diminished (*maqsur*) and declinable word. Abu Muʿadh mentioned that he read "*min Sabʾa*" with a sukun on the *ba'* and an open hamza, without tanwin, on the pattern of *fa'la*; so it is not declined because of the inherent feminine ending.

Ibn Habib transmitted from al-Yazidi "*min Saba*" with a quiescent alif, as in their saying: "they scattered in the hands of Saba." A group read "*bi-naba*" with an alif in place of the hamza, and perhaps this reading is that of the one who read "Saba" with the alif, so that the two words balance, just as they balance in the reading of the one who read both with a kasra hamza and tanwin. In *al-Tahrir* it is said that "*min Saba bi-naba*" is called *tajnis al-tasrif* (paronomasia by inflection), which is when each of the two words stands apart by a single letter, as in God Most High's words: ﴿That is because you exulted in the land without right, and because you used to be exultant﴾, and the hadith: "Good is bound to the forelocks of horses."

Al-Zamakhshari said: God Most High's words "*min Saba bi-naba*" are of the kind of speech that the scholars of rhetoric call *al-badiʿ* (rhetorical embellishment), and it is among the excellences of speech that relate to the wording, on condition that it comes spontaneously, or is shaped by one who knows the essence of speech, preserving with it the soundness and rightness of meaning. Here it has come exceeding soundness, so it was beautiful and wondrous in wording and meaning. Do you not see that if "*bi-khabar*" were put in place of "*bi-naba'*", the meaning would be sound, but it is, as it came, more correct, because of the extra quality in *naba'* which the description of the situation matches. End of quote.

This extra quality is that the report is of great importance, and that *naba'* means a report of great importance, which several lexicographers have stated explicitly. It is apparent that this is a conventional meaning of the word. Some claimed that it is not conventional, but this is not valid. The statement of the hadith scholars, "*anba'anā*" (he informed us) is lower in rank than "*akhbaranā*" (he informed us) is not relevant, since it is their own technical term.

Al-Jumhur read "*fa-makutha*" with a dammah on the *kaf*, while the fatha is the reading of ʿAsim and of Abu ʿAmr in the transmission of al-Ju'fi, Sahl and Rawh. Ubayy read "*fa-makatha thumma qala*" (he tarried, then said), and ʿAbd Allah read "*fa-makatha fa-qala*" (he tarried, and said). Both readings, in reality, according to what is in *al-Bahr*, are explanation and not recitation, because they contradict the consonantal text of the codex.

In the seven canonical readings, "*ahatu*" (I have encompassed) was recited with the assimilation of the *ta'* into the *ta'* (*ṭāʾ*) while retaining the emphatic quality, and it is not a true assimilation.

Ibn Muhaysin read it with a true assimilation. Ibn al-Hajib objected to the first reading that emphasis (*iṭbaq*), which is raising the tongue to the part of the palate opposite it in order to voice the sound of the letter articulated, does not hold except with the letter itself, which here is the *ṭāʾ*, and assimilation requires changing it to a *tāʾ*, which contradicts its existence, since that would require it to be both existent and non-existent, which is a contradiction. The verification is that forms like "*ahatu*" with emphasis do not involve assimilation, but since the second sound can be pronounced with the first without difficulty on the tongue, it is like pronouncing a like letter after a like letter, so the term assimilation was applied to it as a broadening of usage, as al-Tibi stated.

In *al-Nashr* it is said that the *tāʾ* is assimilated into the *ṭāʾ* in God Most High's words: ﴿And establish prayer at the two ends of the day﴾. In *al-Tashil* it is said that when an emphatic letter is assimilated, it is permissible to keep the emphasis or not.

Sibawayh said: "Every speech is Arabic." So says the *Hawashi al-Shihabiyya*. So reflect.

In God Most High's words "*ahatu*" etc. there is an indication, by way of the allusion of the text and incidental implication, of the invalidity of the claim of the Rafidah that the Imam must not be unaware of any of the particulars. It is clear that if they mean by this that the Imam must have detailed knowledge of the rulings on all particular incidents that may occur, and must be ready with the correct answer to everything he is asked about, then the invalidity of their claim is most evident.

ʿAli, may God ennoble his face, was asked a question while he was on the pulpit of Kufa, and he said: "I do not know." The questioner said: "This place of yours is not the place of one who says 'I do not know'." Imam ʿAli, may God ennoble his face, said: "Yes, by God, this is the place of one who says 'I do not know'; as for one who does not say that, he has no place." He meant by this God, Mighty and Majestic.

If they mean that he must be knowledgeable in all the legal principles and in many of the detailed branches of those principles, such that if an incident occurred whose ruling he did not know, he would be capable of deriving the ruling for it correctly, then that is true, and it has the same sense as the statement of the majority of scholars: the Imam must be a *mujtahid* (qualified jurist). The full discussion of this matter is to be sought in its proper place.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 27, verse 23:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, I found a woman ruling over them﴾ — meaning: she manages their affairs, and none of them opposes her — is a resumptive clause (istie'naf) explaining what the news he brought was, and a detailed elaboration of it after a summary. By this woman he means Bilqis, daughter of Sharahil ibn Malik ibn Rayyan, of the lineage of Ya'rub ibn Qahtan. It is also said that she was of the lineage of Tubba' al-Himyari.

Ibn 'Asakir narrated from al-Hasan that the name of this woman was Layla, though this is contrary to what is well known. It was also said that the name of her father was al-Sarj ibn al-Hudahid.

It is related that her father was king over the whole land of Yemen, and he inherited the kingship from forty fathers, and he had no child other than her. So after him she gained dominion over the kingdom, and the nation submitted to her.

In some reports it is said that when her father died she coveted the kingship and asked her people to pledge allegiance to her. Some of them obeyed her and others refused, so they made a man their king, said to be her paternal cousin. He was wicked and conducted himself badly among the people of his kingdom, to the extent that he would commit adultery with the women of his subjects. They wished to depose him but could not overcome him. When she saw this, jealousy overcame her, so she sent to him offering herself to him, and he accepted her. He said: "What prevented me from initiating the proposal to you was only my despair of you." She said: "I do not disdain you, for you are a noble equal. Gather the men of my family and propose to me." He gathered them and proposed to her, and they said: "We do not see her doing this." He said: "Indeed she desires me." They mentioned this to her, and she said: "Yes." So they married her to him. When she was escorted to him, she went out with many people of her retinue and servants. When she was alone with him she gave him wine until he became drunk, then she killed him, cut off his head, and returned to her residence. In the morning she sent for his ministers, summoned them, and rebuked them, saying: "Was there not among you one who would be too proud to tolerate debauchery with the noble women of his tribe?" Then she showed them him slain. She said: "Choose a man to make king over you." They said: "We will accept none but you." So they made her queen. They knew that the marriage had been a deceit and a trick from her, and it became well known that her mother was a jinn.

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn al-Mundhir related this from Mujahid, and al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Mardawayh from Uthman ibn Hadir, that her mother was a woman of the jinn called Balqama daughter of Shisa. And Ibn Abi Hatim related from Zuhayr ibn Muhammad that her mother was Fari'a the jinn.

In the Tafsir of al-Khazin it is said that her father Sharahil used to say to the kings of the regions: "None of you is a suitable match for me," and he refused to marry among them, so he proposed to the jinn, and they married him to a woman called Rayhana daughter of al-Sakan. The cause of his reaching the jinn so that he proposed to them, according to what is said, was that he was much given to hunting, and he would sometimes catch jinn who were in the form of gazelles, and he would release them. The king of the jinn appeared to him and thanked him for that, and took him as a friend, so he proposed for his daughter and he married her to him.

It was also said: he went out hunting and saw two snakes fighting, one white and one black, and the black one had prevailed over the white. He killed the black one, took up the white one, and poured water over it, and it revived, so he released it. When he returned to his house he sat alone by himself, and behold, a handsome youth was with him. He feared him, and the youth said: "Do not be afraid. I am the white snake whom you revived, and the black one you killed was a slave of ours who rebelled against us and killed a number of us." He offered him wealth, but he said: "I have no need of it, but if you have a daughter, marry her to me." So he married him his daughter, and she bore him Bilqis. End of quotation.

Ibn Jarir, Abu al-Shaykh in (al-'Azamah), Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn 'Asakir related from Abu Hurayrah who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "One of the two parents of Bilqis was a jinn." 

What should be relied upon is that this report is not authentic. In al-Bahr it says: They have elaborated greatly in her story, meaning Bilqis, with things that are not established in the Qur'an or in sound hadith, and that what has been mentioned of these narratives is most like fables. For the apparent position, even assuming that marriage between humans and jinn occurred, which it is said one who asks about it should be slapped for his foolishness and ignorance, is that there would be no offspring between them. It was mentioned from al-Hasan, in what Ibn 'Asakir related, that it was said in his presence: "The queen of Saba' has one of her parents a jinn," and he said: "They do not produce offspring," meaning: a woman of mankind does not give birth to [a child] from the jinn, and a woman of the jinn does not give birth to [a child] from mankind.

Yes, something has been related from Malik that implies the soundness of this. In al-Ashbah wa al-Naza'ir of Ibn Nujaym: Abu 'Uthman Sa'id ibn Dawud al-Zubaydi related that he said: A group of people from Yemen wrote to Malik asking him about marriage to the jinn, and they said: "Here there is a man from the jinn who claims that he wants what is lawful." He said: "I see no harm in the religion, but I dislike that when a pregnant woman is found, she is asked: 'Who is your husband?' and she says: 'From the jinn,' so corruption would increase in Islam because of that." End of quotation.

Perhaps this was not established from Malik, because of the evident objections to the reasoning for the disapproval. Then I wonder: if a jinn woman conceives from a human, does she remain in her subtlety so that she is not seen, while the fetus is in her corporeal state so that it is seen? Or is the fetus subtle like her so that neither is seen? If its affair is complete, it becomes dense and appears like other children of Adam. Or she takes on the shape of human women for as long as the fetus is in her womb, during which it is nourished and grows by what reaches it from her nourishment. Each of these divisions is not free from improbability, as is not hidden.

The choice of "I found" (wajadtu) over "I saw" (ra'aytu) is for what was pointed out earlier: the indication that, in his absence, he was in the position of serving him, peace be upon him, by presenting himself in the manner of one who inspects their conditions and becomes acquainted with them, as if she were his quarry and lost thing, so that he might present her to Sulayman, peace be upon him. It was also said: to indicate that what he obtained was something not known at first, for finding (wijdan) is after loss. And there is in it an allusion to the strangeness of the situation. The pronoun in (tamlikuhum) refers to Saba', either as a name for the tribe, or to its people implied by mention of their city, as it is a name for it. There is nothing in the verse indicating the permissibility of a woman being a ruler, and there is no proof in the practice of a disbelieving people for such a matter.

In Sahih al-Bukhari, from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas, that the Prophet (ﷺ), when it reached him that the people of Persia had made the daughter of Kisra their ruler, said: "A people will never prosper who entrust their affair to a woman."

It is transmitted from Muhammad ibn Jarir that it is permissible for a woman to be a judge, but this is not established from him. In al-Ashbah: she should not be appointed to judgeship, even if it is valid for her, except in matters of hudud and retaliation. Abu Hayyan mentioned that it was transmitted from Abu Hanifah, may mercy be upon him, that she judges in matters in which she gives testimony, not absolutely, nor that a decree be written for her stating that so-and-so is authorized to rule; rather that is by way of arbitration for her.

﴿And she has been given of every thing﴾ — meaning: of the things that kings need, by the indication of (tamlikuhum). It may be said: the purpose is only to convey the abundance of what she was given.

The clause may be coordinated with the clause (tamlikuhum), and it may be a circumstantial clause (hal) from the nominative pronoun in (tamlikuhum), with or without the implied (qad). ﴿And she has a mighty throne﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said, as Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from him: that is, a noble couch of gold, its legs of jewels and pearls, well-crafted and of high value. It is also related from him that it was thirty cubits by thirty cubits, and its height in the sky was also thirty cubits. It was also said: its length was eighty by eighty, and its height eighty.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Zuhayr ibn Muhammad that it was a couch of gold, its two sides inlaid with rubies and chrysolite, its length eighty cubits by a breadth of forty cubits. It was also said: it was of gold studded with pearls, red rubies and green chrysolite, its legs of ruby and emerald, and upon it were seven chambers, each chamber with a locked door. Other things have been said, and Allah Most High knows the reality of the matter best.

In sum, the apparent meaning of "throne" is a couch. Abu Muslim said: what is meant by it is kingship, and there is no reason for this.

The Hoopoe's magnifying of her throne, along with what he was witnessing of the kingdom of Sulayman, peace be upon him, is either in relation to her own condition or in relation to the thrones of women like her among kings. It is permitted that this is because there was not for Sulayman, peace be upon him, a like of it, even though he was of great kingdom, for it may be found that some regional rulers possess something that the king to whom they are subject does not have.

In any case, describing it thus in the presence of Sulayman, peace be upon him, is for what was mentioned earlier of his, peace be upon him, encouraging to listen to his account; and in it is a direction toward his, peace be upon him, resolve to subjugate her, and for this reason he follows it with what necessitates invading her, because of her disbelief and the disbelief of her people, where he said:

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 27, verse 24:

﴿I found her and her people prostrating to the sun instead of Allah﴾ That is: they worship it, transgressing the worship of Allah the Exalted.

Al-Hasan said: "They were Magians, worshipping the lights." It was also said: "They were zanadiqa (heretics)."

The apparent reading is that this sentence is a fresh statement, and that the pause should be made at (ʿaẓīm, "great"). The author of al-Murshid said: "One should not pause at (ʿarsh, "throne"). Some have claimed that it is permissible, saying its meaning is 'great in the eyes of the people.'"

Abu Hatim and others among the earlier scholars denied this pause, and they attributed the one who held it to ignorance. The saying of whoever said that its meaning is "great is their worship of the sun instead of Allah the Exalted" is a weak statement, not to be relied upon, and there is nothing in the speech that indicates it. In al-Kashshaf: "Among the fools of the storytellers is one who pauses at (ʿarsh, 'throne'), meaning: 'great is that I found her,' fleeing from the Hoopoe's magnifying of her throne, and so he fell into a great error, which is the abrogation of the Book of Allah the Exalted."

﴿And Satan made their deeds appealing to them﴾ — namely the worship of the sun and its like of kinds of disbelief and sins. The clause may be coordinated with the clause (they prostrate), or be a circumstantial clause from the pronoun, in the manner mentioned just before.

﴿So he barred them﴾ — that is, Satan. It is also permissible that the pronoun refers to the adornment understood from the verb, meaning: the adornment of Satan barred them ﴿from the way﴾ — that is, the way of truth and rightness. ﴿So they﴾ — because of that — ﴿are not guided﴾ to it.

[p. 191]

Regarding His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿that they should not prostrate to God﴾: meaning, "so that they would not prostrate." The lam here is the lam of causation (lam al-ta'lil), and it is connected either to (ṣaddahum, "He barred them") or to (zayyana, "He made attractive"). The fa' in (fa-ṣaddahum) does not have to be causal, since it may be resumptive (tafrī'iyya) or elaborative (tafṣīliyya). That is, "He barred them from that so that they would not prostrate to God, mighty and majestic," or "He made that attractive to them so that they would not prostrate to Him, may He be exalted." It has also been permitted that "an" and what follows it form a verbal noun in apposition (badal) to "their deeds," with what lies between them being a parenthetical insertion (i'tirāḍ), as if it were said: "Satan made attractive to them the not prostrating to God, may He be exalted." This has been criticised on the grounds that it clearly counts not prostrating among the deeds, and that is far-fetched. It has also been permitted that this is an apposition to (al-sabīl, "the way"), with (lā) being superfluous, as in His saying, ﴿so that the People of the Book would not know﴾. As if it were said: "He barred them from prostrating to God, may He be exalted." It has also been permitted that there is an implied (ilā, "to") with (lā) again superfluous, and that the prepositional phrase is connected to (yahtadūn, "they are guided"), as if it were said: "They are not guided to prostrating to Him, mighty and majestic." You know that the addition of (lā), even though it occurs in eloquent speech, goes against the apparent meaning. It has also been permitted that there is no implied element, and that the verbal noun is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "Their habit is not prostrating." It has also been said that the implied element is (hiya, "it"), meaning: "Their deeds are not prostrating," and the objection mentioned just above applies to this too.

Ibn ʿAbbās, Abū Jaʿfar, al-Zuhrī, al-Sulamī, al-Ḥasan, Ḥumayd and al-Kisāʾī read (alā) with the lightened pronunciation, taking it as the particle of opening (lil-istiftāḥ), with (yā) as a vocative particle, and the object of address omitted, meaning: "Alā yā qawm, uskudū" ("Oh, O people, prostrate!"), as in the line:

*Alā yā-islamī dhāt al-damālīj wal-ʿuqad*
("Oh, O you, greet the one with the bracelets and the knots")
and its many parallels.

The alif of (yā) and the alif of connection in (usjudū) are dropped, and it was written with a yā joined to the sīn, contrary to the usual rule.

Al-Kisāʾī, in this reading, paused on a yā and began with (usjudū), and this is a voluntary pause (waqf ikhtiyār). In al-Baḥr (al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ, by Abū Ḥayyān): "What I incline to is that in this kind of construction that is transmitted from the Arabs, yā is not a vocative particle with an omitted addressee; for, in my view, the addressee may not be omitted, because the verb governing the vocative has been omitted and its subject has been dropped with it. So if we omitted the addressee, that would involve omitting the vocative clause and omitting its complement, which is the addressee. And if we do not omit it, it is evidence for the governing element of it, which is the vocative clause. The particle of vocative is not a particle of response like naʿam, balā, lā and ajal, after which the clause may be omitted as it is after them, because the preceding question indicates the omitted clause." So in my view, in those constructions, yā is a particle of alerting (ḥarf tanbīh), which is used to emphasise alā, which is itself a particle of alerting. This is permitted because the two particles differ, and for the purpose of intensifying emphasis. If emphasis has been found in combining two differing particles, both governing, as in the line:

*Fa-aṣbaḥna lā yasʾalnanī ʿan bimā bihi*
("So they came to the morning and did not ask me about what is with me")
and also in combining two identical particles, both governing, as in the line:

*Fa-lā wallāhi lā yulfā limā bī*
*wa-lā lilmā bihim abadan dawāʾ*
("No, by God, there is never found a remedy for what is in me, nor for what is in them"),
and this is permitted, even though they count it as a poetic necessity or as rare, then combining two non-governing particles that differ in form is permissible. And in the line:

*Yā laʿnatu-llāhi wal-aqwāmi kulli-him*
("O curse of God and of all the peoples")
(yā) is in my view not a particle of vocative but a particle of alerting, after which came the subject (mubtadaʾ), and it is not one of those cases in which the addressee is omitted, for the reason we have mentioned. End of quotation. There is room for discussion on this.

According to this reading, the sentence may be a resumption (istiʾnāf) of the speech of the hoopoe, either addressed to the people of Sulayman, peace be upon him, to urge the worship of God, Most High, or to the people of Bilqis, treating them as those addressed.

It may also be a resumption from God, mighty and majestic, or from Sulayman, peace be upon him, as has been said, and in that case it is with an implied (qawl, "saying").

Perhaps the most apparent is that it is a resumption from Him, mighty and majestic, Who addressed this community with it, and the sentence is parenthetical (muʿtaraḍa). With this reading, one pauses (wuqūf) at (yahtadūn, "they are guided") as a matter of good style (istiḥsān). This would necessitate increasing the number of verses of this surah according to what some have said, but it has been said that it does not necessitate this, because verse divisions are a matter of revelation (tawqīfiyya), and they do not depend on whether one pauses or not. So reflect.

The difference in meaning between the two readings is that in the verse, on the first reading, there is a reproach for abandoning prostration, and on the second there is a command to prostrate. Whatever the case, prostration is obligatory when reciting the verse. Al-Zajjāj claimed it is obligatory on the second reading too, but this contradicts what the jurists have expressly stated; for this reason al-Zamakhsharī said that it is not to be relied upon.

Al-Aʿmash read (hallā yasjudūn) with the particle of urging (taḥḍīḍ) and the verb attributed to the third person plural. In Ubayy's reading (alā tasjudūn) with the particle of presentation (ʿarḍ) and the verb attributed to the second person plural. In the codex of ʿAbd Allāh (alā hal tasjudūn), with the opening particle alā and the interrogative hal, and the verb attributed to the second person plural. This was reported by Ibn ʿAṭiyya. In al-Kashshāf there is something that contradicts what is his own position, and the one who knows the reality of the situation is God, mighty and majestic.

﴿Who brings forth the hidden in the heavens and the earth﴾: meaning, "who makes manifest the thing hidden in them, whatever it is." Al-khabʾ is a verbal noun used in the sense of the passive participle (ism al-mafʿūl), and some have interpreted it here as rain and plants. This was transmitted from Ibn Zayd. Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab that he interpreted it as water. The better view is generality, as a group transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās, may God be pleased with them both.

(Fī al-samāwāt, "in the heavens") is connected to (al-khabʾ). It is reported from al-Farrāʾ that (fī) here means (min, "from"), so that the prepositional phrase is then connected to (yukhriju, "brings forth"). The apparent reading is what preceded.

This attribute was chosen because it better suits the story, since it contains what is most similar to bringing forth the hidden, namely making manifest the affair of Bilqis and what is connected to it. On this same basis, the attributes of God, mighty and majestic, mentioned after it were chosen. It has also been said that the mention of this attribute is specific because the hoopoe was more firmly established in knowing Him and in comprehending His rulings through observing His effects, among which is what God, Most High, placed in his nature of the power to know water beneath the earth.

You know that the hoopoe being endowed with the power over what has been mentioned is not something for which there is a report one can rely on. Also, the reason stated does not hold on the reading of Ibn ʿAbbās and the six who are with him, (alā yasjudū, "that they should not prostrate") with the lightened pronunciation, if the speech is taken as a resumption from Him, mighty and majestic, or from the side of Sulayman, peace be upon him.

Ubayy and ʿĪsā read (al-khabā) by transferring the vowel of the hamza to the bāʾ and dropping the hamza. Sībawayh reported this from some people of the tribes of Banū Tamīm and Banū Asad.

ʿIkrima read with an alif in place of the hamza, so the vowel before it had to be a fatḥa. This is the reading of ʿAbd Allāh and Mālik ibn Dīnār. It was explained as the dialect of those who say, when pausing: hādhā al-khabw ("this is the hidden"), marartu bi-l-khabī ("I passed by the hidden"), and raʾaytu al-khabā ("I saw the hidden"), with connected speech treated as pausal speech. The Kufans permitted saying al-marʾa and al-kamʾa as al-maraa and al-kamaa, replacing the hamza with an alif and making the vowel before it a fatḥa, and it was mentioned that this replacement is a dialect.

It has been permitted that (al-khabʾ) is from this, but al-Zamakhsharī refused it, claiming that this is a weak and disparaged dialect, and gave the reason that when the letter before the hamza is quiescent, the way to lighten it is by omission, not by conversion, as is said of al-kamʾ: kamah. Al-Kashf commented on him, saying: "Deriving it from pausal speech has two weaknesses, because pausing in that way is not the language of the eloquent, and treating connected speech as pausal speech, in what is not frequently used, is also so. As for that dialect, the Kufans held that it is analogical." End of quotation.

Abū Ḥātim claimed that al-khabā with the alif is not permissible at all, and this comes from a deficiency of knowledge. Al-Mubarrad said: "Abū Ḥātim was below his companions in grammar and did not reach their level, except that when he left their city, no one was found more knowledgeable than him."

By the conjunction of His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿and He knows what you conceal and what you disclose﴾ to (yukhriju, "brings forth"), it is indicated that He, may He be exalted, brings forth what is in the human world of hidden things just as He brings forth what is in the great world of hidden treasures, because the meaning is: He makes manifest what you conceal of states and then recompenses you for them. The mention of (what you disclose) is for broadening the scope of knowledge, or to draw attention to the equality of the two with respect to divine knowledge. So it has been said.

The words of some indicate that by what preceded, His perfect power, may He be exalted, is indicated, and by this, His perfect knowledge, mighty and majestic, and that the inner and the outer are equal in it.

(What you conceal) was placed first for this reason, along with its suitability to what precedes it, namely al-khabʾ. The attribute of bringing forth the hidden from the heavens was placed first because it is more fitting to the context. The address, as has been said, is either to humankind, or to the people of Sulayman, or to the people of Bilqis, and in the speech there is a shift of person (iltifāt).

The two Ḥaramīs and the majority read (mā yukhfūna wa-mā yuʿlinūn, "what they conceal and what they disclose") with the yāʾ of the third person. In al-Kashshāf, it is reported from Ubayy that he read: "Alā tasjudūna lillāhi alladhī yukhriju al-khabʾa min al-samāʾi wal-arḍi, wa-yaʿlamu sirrakum wa-mā tuʿlinūn" ("Will you not prostrate to God, who brings forth the hidden from the heaven and the earth, and knows your secret and what you disclose?").

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 27, verse 26:

﴿Allah—there is no deity except Him, Lord of the Great Throne.﴾ This is in the sense of giving the reason for His—Mighty and Majestic is He—being described with perfect power and perfect knowledge. And "al-'Azim" (the Great) in the genitive is an attribute of "al-'Arsh" (the Throne), and it is the extremity of bodies, so there is no body above it. In the reports there is a description of its greatness that dazzles the intellects. It suffices in this regard that the Kursi (the Footstool), which the Noble Book has stated encompasses the heavens and the earth, is in relation to it like a ring in a desert. According to the philosophers, it is the "limit of directions" (muhaddad al-jihat), and they held that it is a spherical body devoid of stars, encompassing all the celestial spheres, and moving them by compulsion from east to west. Hardly anyone knows the measure of its thickness except Allah, the Exalted. In the sound reports there is what, in its apparent meaning, rejects some of that. Whatever the case, between its greatness and the greatness of the throne of Bilqis there is a vast difference.

Ibn Muhaysin and a group read "al-'Azimu" with a nominative ending (ḍamma). This allows that it be an attribute of the Throne, cut off (from the preceding genitive) by an implied "huwa" (He is), so the two readings are equivalent in meaning; and it allows that it be an attribute of the Lord.

﴿Qāla﴾ (He said) is a explanatory resumptive clause (*isti'nāf bayānī*), as if it were asked: "What did Sulayman (peace be upon him) do upon hearing that statement?" So it was said: he said, ﴿We shall see﴾, that is, regarding what you have mentioned. Here "seeing" (*naẓar*) carries the sense of careful consideration and reflection, and the *sīn* (in *sananẓuru*) is for emphasis, meaning: we will certainly find out by testing.

﴿Have you spoken the truth, or have you been one of the liars?﴾ This is a clause in which the verb is suspended (*mu'allaq*) by the interrogative. The apparent expected form would have been "or have you lied" (*am kadhabta*). The choice of what the noble wording has instead indicates that his lying in this matter entails his inclusion among those known for lying and firmly established in it. For such fabricated statements, arranged with an elegant composition that wins the hearts of listeners toward accepting them without having any basis in reality at all, especially in the presence of a great prophet whose might is feared, can only come from someone whose foot is firmly planted in lying and falsehood, and for whom it has become a disposition, so that he cannot restrain himself from it in any situation whatsoever.

Some scholars claimed that this wording was for the sake of observing the *fāṣila* (verse-ending rhyme), but this is not valid at all. The verse also contains, according to what is in *al-Iklīl* (by al-Suyuti), the acceptance by a ruler of his subjects' excuse, the averting of punishment from them, and the testing of their truthfulness in what they have offered as an excuse.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 27, verse 28:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Take this letter of mine and cast it to them﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) explaining the manner of the observation that he (peace be upon him) had promised, after he had written his letter in that assembly or after it.

"This" is a reference to the one present, and his (peace be upon him) singling him out for the letter, rather than the rest of the strong jinn trustworthies under his authority in disposal and discernment, was because of the signs of knowledge and wisdom he observed in him, and so that no excuse would remain for him at all. The verse also contains evidence for the permissibility of sending letters from the leader to polytheists to convey the call and invite them to Islam. The Messenger of God (may God's peace and blessings be upon him) wrote to Chosroes, Caesar, and other kings of the Arabs.

In the seven canonical readings it was recited as "fa-alqihi" with a kasra on the ha' followed by a ya', with the kasra stolen (ikhtilas) and the ha' sukun, and Muslim ibn Jundub read it with a damma on the ha' followed by a waw.

﴿Then withdraw from them﴾: that is, move aside (tanahha). This was interpreted thus because turning away entirely would contradict His saying: ﴿and watch what they return⦆ unless it were taken as inverted (qalb), as Ibn Zayd and Abu 'Ali claimed, and that is unsuitable.

His (peace be upon him) command to him to withdraw is from the category of teaching good manners with kings, as narrated from Wahb.

"Observing" means reflecting and contemplating. "Mādhā" is either an interrogative word in the position of the object of "yarji'ūna," and "raja'a" is used transitively as well as intransitively, or it is a subject (mubtada') and the clause "yarji'ūna" is its predicate. Or "mā" is interrogative and a subject, and "dhā" is a relative pronoun meaning "alladhī," its predicate, and the clause "yarji'ūna" is the relative clause, with the returning pronoun omitted.

Whichever is the case, the clause is governed by a suspended verb of the heart (mu'allaq), so its position is accusative by dropping the preposition. It has been said: "observe" means "wait," as in His saying: ﴿Wait for us, that we may borrow some of your light﴾, so there is no suspension; rather "mādhā" is a relative pronoun in the position of the object, so it is said. The apparent meaning, however, is that it means reflection, and that the intent is: reflect and find out what some of them return in speech to others.

This is evident that God Most High gave the hoopoe a power by which he understands what he hears of their speech.
Page 194

The expression "casting" is used because delivering it is not possible without that, and the pronoun is plural because the aim is to convey what is in it to all the people, and to uncover their state after that.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 27, verse 29:

﴿She said﴾ That is: after the hoopoe had gone off with the letter, thrown it to them, and withdrawn from them as he had been commanded. The mention of him is omitted, to signal his complete haste in carrying out the service he had been ordered to perform, and to indicate that there is no need to state it explicitly, since it is so evident.

It is related that he (peace be upon him) wrote his letter, sealed it with musk, stamped it with his signet ring, and handed it to the hoopoe, who went off with it and found her (Bilqis) asleep in her palace at Ma'rib. Whenever she slept, she would lock the doors and place the keys under her head. So the hoopoe entered through a window and dropped the letter onto her chest while she lay on her back. In another report, it was "between her breasts." It was also said that he pecked her, and she woke up in alarm. It was also said that he came to her while her commanders and troops were around her, and he hovered for a while while the people watched, until she raised her head, and he dropped the letter into her lap. When she saw the signet, she trembled and submitted, and then she said what she said.

It was also said: there was a window in the room upon which the sun fell every day, and whenever she looked at it she would prostrate. The hoopoe came and blocked it with his wings. She saw this, got up toward him, and he dropped the letter to her. She was a reader and writer of Arabic, from the lineage of Ya'rub ibn Qahtan. It is well known that she was of the lineage of Tubba' al-Himyari. The Arabic script was at its height of precision, perfection, and excellence during the dynasty of the Tubba'. It is called the Himyaritic script. Among the Himyar there was a script called the Musnad, whose letters were distinct, and they used to forbid teaching it without their permission. Mudar learned from Himyar, and some discussion of this has already preceded.

Ibn Khaldun preferred the view that the people of al-Hira learned Arabic writing from the Tubba' and Himyar, and the people of the Hijaz learned it from them.

That Bilqis was clearly an Arab, and that she read the letter, implies that the letter was in Arabic. Perhaps Sulayman (peace be upon him) knew Arabic, even though he was not an Arab. One who was taught the speech of birds is not far from being taught the speech of the Arabs, which is the most noble speech. It is also possible that he had someone with him who knew it, and likewise someone who knew other languages, as is the custom of kings who keep people speaking several languages so that they may translate for them what they need. It is also possible that the letter was not in Arabic but in the language of Sulayman (peace be upon him) and his pen. His pen, as related from Imam Ahmad al-Buni, was made of cane (kahini). Bilqis had someone who translated it for her and informed her of its contents. She then gathered the nobles of her people, informed them of this, and consulted them, as the Exalted has related of her in His saying: She said, "O chiefs, indeed a noble letter has been delivered to me..." etc.

Sulayman (peace be upon him) went ahead with writing the letter to her in this manner. The hoopoe's words support this: "and she has been given of all things," and the translator is among the things a king needs. It is also fitting for his dignity and greatness that he should not abandon his own tongue and imitate hers. It is also possible that she herself knew that script, and so she read the letter for that reason. The possibility that the letter was not in Arabic was preferred on the grounds that writing to her in Arabic would require knowing her condition, and he (peace be upon him) had not yet come to know it.

It has been objected that the hoopoe's words indicate that it was Arabic: "And I have come to you from Saba' with certain news. Indeed, I found a woman ruling over them." He (peace be upon him) is one who would not be unaware that Saba' is among the Arabs, and it is apparent that their queen is one of them. She described the letter as "noble" because it was sealed. In a hadith: "The nobility of a letter is in its sealing."

In Sharh Adab al-Katib it is said: "I honored the letter" means it is "noble" when you seal it. Ibn al-Muqaffa' said: whoever writes to his brother a letter and does not seal it has shown it disrespect. Ibn Abbas, Qatadah, and Zuhayr ibn Muhammad interpreted "noble" here as "sealed." It implies, as has been said, the recommendation of sealing a letter because of the nobility of its content and its dignity, or because of the nobility of its sender and the loftiness of his rank. She knew this either by report, or from the fact that the letter was sealed with his name, following the custom of kings and nobles, or from the fact that its messenger was a bird, or because it began with the name of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, or because of the strangeness of its matter and its arrival to her by an unusual means. It was also said that she assumed it, because the one who delivered it was a bird, to be a heavenly book, and this is not so.

The passive form "was delivered (uliya)" is used because the agent is not of concern. It was also said: because she did not know who sent it, or because the one who sent it was insignificant.

Shaykh al-Akbar, may his secret be sanctified, said in the Fusus: Among the wisdom of Bilqis is that she did not mention who threw the letter to her. This was only so that she would make her companions aware that she has connections to matters whose path they do not know. In this there is a kind of statecraft from her, which produced caution toward her among the people of her kingdom and her close counselors, and by this she deserved to be placed ahead of them. End of quote.

The emphasis of the sentence is for the sake of giving attention to the matter of the ruling,

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 27, verse 30:

As for the emphasis in His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿Indeed it is from Solomon, and indeed it says: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾, it is for that reason too, or because it occurs in answer to an implied question, as if it were said: "From whom is this letter, and what is its content?" So it was said: "Indeed it is from Solomon," etc. The emphasis with (inna, indeed) is appropriate in answer to a question, and I see no difference in this between a question that has actually been asked and one that is implied. It is known from what has been mentioned that the first pronoun in (innahu, indeed it) refers to the letter, and the second pronoun in (innahu) refers to its content, even though it is not mentioned. There is nothing in the verse that indicates that he, peace be upon him, placed his own name before the name of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and her knowledge that it is from Solomon may be due to his name being written afterwards.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Yazid ibn Ruman that he said: Solomon wrote: "In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. From Solomon ibn Dawud to Bilqis, daughter of Dhu Sharh, and her people: (Do not exalt yourselves against me) ..." etc. It is also permitted that it refers to his writing it on the outside of the letter, while the inside of the letter was (In the name of Allah) ... etc.

It has been said: the first pronoun in (innahu) refers to the heading, and that he, peace be upon him, headed the letter with his name, placing it first, so he wrote: "From Solomon (In the name of Allah) ... etc." Abu Hayyan favoured this view, then said: He, peace be upon him, put his name first out of fear that something unbecoming might come from her, since she was an unbeliever, so that his name would be a shield for the name of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. But this, as you see, is weak.

Writing the basmalah at the beginning of letters is something that the Sunnah of our Prophet ﷺ followed after the revelation of this verse, without dispute. As for before it, it has been said that his letters, peace and blessings be upon him, did not begin with it. For ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ibn al-Mundhir and others related from al-Shaʿbi, who said: "The people of the Jahiliyyah used to write: (In Your name, O Allah). The Prophet ﷺ wrote first: (In Your name, O Allah), until there was revealed: ﴿In the name of Allah be its course and its anchorage﴾, so he wrote: (In the name of Allah). Then there was revealed: ﴿Call upon Allah or call upon the Most Gracious﴾, so he wrote: (In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious). Then the verse of An-Naml was revealed: ﴿Indeed it is from Solomon﴾ to the end of the verse, so he wrote: (In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful)."

Abu Dawud related in his Maraasil from Abu Malik, who said: "The Prophet ﷺ used to write: (In Your name, O Allah). When ﴿Indeed it is from Solomon﴾ was revealed, he wrote: (In the name of Allah) ..." etc. Something similar has been related from Maymun ibn Mihran and Qatadah. In my view, this is something that hardly fits with the view that the basmalah was revealed before this verse, and this view should not be opposed. Al-Jalal al-Suyuti said in his al-Itqan: There has been disagreement about the first thing revealed of the Qur'an, in several opinions:

The first of them, which is the correct one, is: ﴿Read in the name of your Lord﴾, and he argued for it with reports after it, among them the report of the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) concerning the beginning of revelation, which is well known.

The second: ﴿O you wrapped in garments﴾.

The third: Surat al-Fatihah.

The fourth: the basmalah.

Then he said: In my view, this is not counted as an independent opinion, for it is a necessary consequence of the revelation of a surah that the basmalah is revealed with it, so it is the first verse revealed absolutely. End of quote.

This strengthens what we have said, for if the basmalah was the first verse revealed, it was the opening of the Book of Allah, the Exalted, and if that is so, it was fitting for his dignity, ﷺ, to open his letters with it, just as Allah, the Exalted, opened His Book with it and made it the first of what was sent down from it.

As for the view that it was revealed earlier, but that he, peace and blessings be upon him, did not know its prescribed status at the beginning of letters and messages until this verse was revealed, which contains Solomon's writing it in his letter to the people of Sheba, is something that none would venture upon except one ignorant of his rank, peace and blessings be upon him.

Some of the eminent scholars mentioned that when it is written in letters and messages, it is better to write it on a line by itself.

In Adab al-Kuttab by al-Suli it is stated that they prefer that the writer begin with the basmalah from the margin of the paper, then write the supplication level with it, and they find it ugly for the text to extend beyond the basmalah by only a little, nor do they write it in the middle, and the supplication should extend further. End of quote.

What is mentioned about writing a supplication after it did not exist in the early period; rather, what was written then was "From so-and-so to so-and-so."

Placing the name of the writer before the name of the addressee is prescribed, even if the former is less excellent and the latter more excellent. In al-Bahr, from Anas: "No one was more honoured than the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and when his Companions wrote a letter to him, they began with themselves."

Abu al-Layth said in his al-Bustan: "If he began with the addressee, it would be permissible, for the community has agreed upon it and done it." End of quote.

The apparent meaning of the verse is that the basmalah is not one of the particularities (of the Prophet ﷺ). Some said: it is one of them, but with the Arabic wording and the specific order, and what was in the letter of Solomon, peace be upon him, was not in Arabic wording, and it was translated for us into it; and this is not far-fetched.

ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Masʿud) read: "And indeed it is from Solomon" with an added waw, and Abu Hayyan explained it as a conjunction joining the sentence after it to the sentence "Indeed I have been sent a noble letter" (inni ulqiya). It has been said: the waw is the waw of circumstance (waw al-hal), and the sentence is circumstantial. ʿIkrimah and Ibn Abi ʿAblah read "that it is from Solomon, and that it" with a fatha on the hamza of (anna) in both places. This was explained as a substitution (badal) for "a letter" (kitab), i.e., "It was conveyed to me that it..." etc., or as the assumed reading being: "because it..." etc., as if it gave the reason for the nobility of the letter by its being from Solomon and its being headed with the name of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

Ubayy read: "an min Sulayman wa-an bismi Allah" with a fatha on the hamza and a sukun on the nun, and this was explained as the (an) being the explanatory one, since a sentence containing the sense of speech has preceded it, or as the lightened form of the heavy (inna), with the pronoun omitted.

The 'an (أنْ) in His words ﴿that you do not exalt yourselves over me﴾ may be explanatory (mufassira), with the la (لا) being prohibitive (nahiya). It may also be a verbal particle (masdariyya) governing the verb (nasiba), with the la being negative (nafiya). It has been said that it is also permissible for the la to be prohibitive. The verbal phrase is in the nominative case, either as an apposition (badal) to "a letter (kitab)," or as the predicate (khabar) of an implied subject (mubtada') suited to the context, meaning: its content is "that you do not exalt yourselves over me," i.e., that you do not act arrogantly toward me, as the tyrannical kings do.

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, according to the transmission of Wahb ibn Munabbih, and al-Ashhab al-'Uqayli, read "that you do not transgress (taghlu)" with a ghayn, from ghuluw, which is exceeding the limit, meaning: "that you do not exceed your limits."

﴿And come to me in submission﴾ is coordinated (ma'tuf) with what precedes it. If the la in it is prohibitive, then coordinating the command with it is clear. If the la is negative and the 'an is verbal, then coordinating it with it is coordination of an imperative clause (insha') with a declarative clause (akhbar), and the discussion of this is well known. Most scholars permit this in such a case. By "submission (Islam)" is meant faith (iman), i.e., "and come to me as believers." It has also been said that it means compliance (inqiyad), i.e., "come to me compliant and submissive." The call (da'wa) according to the first meaning is the call of prophethood, and according to the second it is the call of a king. What is fitting to his station, peace be upon him, is the first.

Some reports, as you will learn, Allah willing, support this. It is not objected that this implies the command to faith came before establishing proof of his messengership, and so would be a request for blind acceptance (taqlid), because the call mentioned is the first call, which does not require displaying a miracle or establishing proof. The custom of the prophets, peace be upon them, is to call to faith first, and when they are opposed they establish evidence and display miracles. In the present case, no opposition had occurred. It has also been said that the call was only accompanied by the establishment of proof, because the delivery of the letter to her in that state mentioned earlier is a dazzling miracle clearly indicating his messengership, peace be upon him.

It was objected that the delivery mentioned being a miracle is not clear, especially since it did not accompany a challenge. The second view was preferred, on the grounds that her words "Indeed kings..." etc. are explicit in calling to kingship and sovereignty.

It was answered that this is because she was not yet certain of his messengership, peace be upon him, at that time, or that it is a matter of stratagem to draw the people to respond by instilling awe in them through his being a king. This, as you see, is weak.

It is apparent that the letter contained no more than what Allah the Most High related. This is one of two reports from Mujahid. The second is that it contained: "Peace be upon whoever follows guidance. To proceed: do not exalt yourselves over me, and come to me in submission."

Some reports state that the text of the letter was: "From the servant of Allah, Sulayman ibn Dawud, to Bilqis, queen of Saba': Peace be upon whoever follows guidance," until the end of what was mentioned. Perhaps she, as is apparent, understood from contextual indications that they were the ones addressed.

What Allah, glorified is He, related includes the basmala, which, in its indication of His attributes, explicitly and by implication is that same basmala; the prohibition of arrogance, which is the mother of vices; and the command to submission, which encompasses the foundations of virtues. How wondrous is this letter, extremely concise and supremely inimitable! Qatada reported: thus were the prophets, peace be upon them, writing sentences, neither lengthy nor verbose.

Now, I have not found in the reports anything indicating that he, peace be upon him, wrote that on paper (kaghid), parchment (raqq), or other materials. What is famous on the tongues of scribes is that the letter was of the well-known paper, and that the hoopoe (hudhhud) took it from its edge with its beak, so that edge became wet with its saliva and part of it was lost, and that this was the right-hand corner at the bottom of the letter. They claimed that their cutting a piece of the paper from that corner was in imitation of Sulayman's letter, peace be upon him. This is not to be relied upon. Other practitioners of crafts and trades also have stories of this kind, and to intelligent people these are fabricated tales.

Al-Alusi, *Ruh al-Ma'ani*, on surah 27, verse 32:

﴿She said: "O chiefs, advise me in my affair."﴾ She repeated the report of her words to signal the extent of her concern for what lay within her domain. *Ifta'* (giving a fatwa, meaning a considered opinion or ruling) is, as the author of *al-Matli'* stated, pointing the one who seeks counsel toward the course of action that the one giving counsel judges right, through his opinion and planning, concerning the incident that has befallen him. Its purpose is the removal of the difficulty that has arisen for him, just as *ishka'* (complaining to someone) is the removal of a grievance. In *al-Maghrib* it is said that *fatwa* is derived from *fata* (youth), because it is an answer to an incident, or the establishing of a ruling, or the strengthening of an explanation of a problem. Whatever the case, the meaning is: "Advise me with what you have of opinion and planning regarding what has befallen me, and I have stated its essence to you." By what she said, she intended to win their sympathy and to put them at ease, so that they would support her and stand with her. She reinforced this with her words: ﴿I have never decided a matter until you witness it.﴾ That is, I do not settle any affair connected with the kingdom except in your presence and in accordance with your views. The use of *kana* (was) signals that she had persisted in this practice, or that nothing else had occurred from her in past time, so likewise in this matter. And "until you witness" (*hatta tashhadun*) is the limit (*ghaya*) of the decision.

The verse has been cited as evidence for the recommendation (*istihbab*) of consultation and of seeking the opinions of others in important matters.

In the reading of ʿAbd Allah: "مَا كُنْتُ قاضِيَةً أمْرًا" ("I was never one who decides an affair").

Al-Alusi, *Ruh al-Ma'ani*, on surah 27, verse 33:

﴿They said﴾ is a resumptive clause (*isti'naf*, a new sentence that answers an implied question), built on a question that arises from the narration of her words. It is as if it were said: "What did they say in reply to her?" So it was said: They said: ﴿We are possessors of strength﴾ in body and number, ﴿and possessors of great might﴾, that is, of valour, extreme courage and proven prowess in war. It was said: The people of her counsel were three hundred and twelve men, each one over ten thousand. This was narrated from Qatada.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted, from Ibn Abbas, who said: The consort of Sulayman had twelve thousand *qayls* (tribal chieftains), under the hand of each *qayl* were a hundred thousand. It was also said: Under her hand were four hundred kings, each king over a district, and under the hand of each king were four hundred thousand fighting men. She had three hundred ministers who managed her kingdom, and she had twelve thousand commanders, each commander having under his hand twelve thousand fighting men. These reports are closer to falsehood than to truth. By my life, the land of Yemen would scarcely be able to contain the number contained in the last two reports. I wonder what the size of her remaining subjects was, who would need this army, these commanders and these ministers for governing them, for managing their affairs and for organising their conditions.

﴿And the command is yours﴾ is a surrender of the matter into her hand after mentioning what indicates strength and courage, so that it is not thought to stem from weakness. The word *al-amr* (the command) is taken in its familiar meaning, or in the sense of *al-sha'n* (the matter, affair). It is the subject (*mubtada'*), and (*ilayki*, "to you") is related to a deleted element that serves as its predicate. It is estimated as delayed, in order to convey the intended restriction, which is understood from the context. That is: "And the command is entrusted to you."

﴿So see what you will command﴾: of peace or fighting, we will obey you and follow your opinion. It was also said: They meant: "We are men of war, not men of counsel and deliberation, and the opinion and planning are yours, so see what you think, and we will be in service." When she sensed from them an inclination towards war and a deviation from the right course, she began to refute their statement, which revealed their heedlessness regarding the matter of Sulayman, peace be upon him, as she believed it. This is His Exalted saying:

[Page 198]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 27, verse 34:

﴿Said she: "Indeed, when kings enter a town﴾ of the towns, in the manner of warfare and fighting, ﴿they ruin it﴾ by destroying its buildings and wasting the wealth in it.

﴿And they make the honoured people of it humiliated﴾ by killing, taking captive, expelling, and other kinds of abasement and degradation. He did not say, "and they humiliate the honoured people of it," even though that is more concise, for the sake of emphasis on the act of making and rendering. ﴿And thus do they act.﴾ This is a confirmation of her words from Him - exalted and majestic is He - according to what Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas. Or it is from her own speech, brought as an affirmation of what she described of their condition, by way of parenthetical concluding insertion (i'tiraد tadhyiliyy, "concluding interjection"), and as a confirmation that this is their constant custom. So the pronoun refers to the kings. It has also been said that it refers to Solomon and those with him, in which case it is a new statement (ta'sis) and not an affirmation (ta'kid).

It has been objected that affirmation is necessary on this view as well, because of its falling under the general rule (al-kulliyyah). It is as though she meant - according to what has been said - that Solomon is a king, and kings are of this condition, and our overcoming him is not certain, and there is no reliance on numbers, equipment, courage, and valour; perhaps he will overcome us and then what will be will be, so reconciliation is better. It has also been said that she had come to believe he would prevail, since she saw that the birds were subjected to him and that he sent them with a specific command to a specific person, while the doors were locked upon him. So she pointed out to them that he would prevail over them if they fought him, and he would ruin the towns and humiliate the honoured people. By this she corrupted their opinion and what she perceived from them of an inclination to fight him - upon him be peace - and she confirmed her opinion with her saying:

[Page 199]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 27, verse 35:

﴿And indeed, I am going to send them a gift, and will wait to see with what the envoys return.﴾ "Until I act according to what the situation requires." This clearly shows that she did not trust that he, peace be upon him, would accept her gift.

It is narrated that she said to her people: "If he is a worldly king, wealth will satisfy him, and we will deal with him accordingly. But if he is a prophet, wealth will not satisfy him, and we should follow his religion." The hadiyyah (gift) is a noun for what is given as a gift, just as 'atiyyah (gift) is a noun for what is given. The tanwin (nunation) in it is for glorification. The word nāẓiratun (waiting to see) is in apposition (ʿaṭf, conjunction) to mursilatun (sending), and bi-mā (with what) is connected to yarji'u (returns). Al-Hawfi reported that it is connected to nāẓiratun, but this is a gross error, as al-Bahr (Abu Hayyan's al-Bahr al-Muhit) mentions. The verb naẓara (to wait and see) is suspended (mu'allaq), and the clause is in the position of the object of it. The nominal clause, which indicates firmness and begins with the harf al-tahqiq (the emphatic particle, inna), signals that she was resolved in her opinion, which nothing could turn her away from, and no inclination could divert her from it.

There is disagreement about her gift. According to Ibn 'Abbas, it was a hundred male servants and a hundred female servants. Wahb and others said: Bilqis chose five hundred boys and five hundred girls. She dressed the girls in boys' clothing, with tunics and belts, and dressed the boys in girls' clothing. She placed gold bracelets on their hands, gold necklaces on their necks, and earrings and ornaments set with various kinds of jewels in their ears. She mounted the girls on five hundred female mules and the boys on five hundred horses, each horse having a gold saddle set with jewels and covered with brocade. She sent him gold bricks, silver bricks, and a crown encrusted with pearls and rubies, and sent musk, ambergris, and aloes wood. She also took a box and placed in it a virgin pearl and a bead of jizʿ (onyx) with a crooked hole.

She summoned a man of the nobles of her people called al-Mundhir ibn 'Amr, and sent with him men of her people who were people of judgment and intellect. She wrote a letter with him mentioning the gift, and said in it: "If you are a prophet, distinguish between the boys and the girls, and tell what is in the box before you open it." Then she said to the messenger: "If he tells you, then say to him: pierce the pearl with a straight hole, and insert a thread into the bead without the work of humans or jinn." She also said to the boys: "When Sulayman speaks to you, speak to him in a manner with feminine softness and effeminacy, resembling the speech of women." And she ordered the girls to speak to him in a manner with harshness, resembling the speech of men. Then she said to the messenger: "Look at the man when you enter. If he looks at you with an angry glance, know that he is a king, and do not be overawed by his appearance, for I am more powerful than him. But if you see the man cheerful and gentle, know that he is a prophet, so understand his words and the reply he gives."

The man set out with the gifts, and al-Hudhud (the hoopoe) came swiftly to Sulayman and informed him of the news. He, peace be upon him, commanded the jinn to strike bricks of gold and silver, and they did so. He ordered them to build a courtyard nine farsakh (about 27 miles) in extent, to spread in it the gold and silver bricks, to leave a space equal to the number of those bricks they had with them, and to build around the courtyard a wall of gold and silver rising high. They did so. Then he said: "Which of the beasts of land and sea is the most beautiful?" They said: "O Prophet of God, we have not seen anything more beautiful than the animals of the sea called such-and-such, with varied colours, having wings, manes, and forelocks." He said: "Bring them to me at once." They brought them to him. He said: "Tie them on the right and left of the courtyard." He said to the jinn: "Bring me your children." A great multitude of them gathered, and he placed them on the right and left of the courtyard. He commanded the jinn, the humans, the devils, the wild beasts, the predators, and the birds. Then he sat in his assembly on his throne, and placed four thousand chairs on his right and left. He ordered all the humans, jinn, devils, wild beasts, predators, and birds to line up, extending for farsakhs on his right and left.

When the people drew near the courtyard, and looked at the kingdom of Sulayman, peace be upon him, and saw the animals the like of which they had never seen dunging on the bricks of gold and silver, their own selves seemed small to them, and they hid what gifts they had with them.

It was also said: when they saw that empty place free of bricks, they feared they would be accused of that, so they placed what bricks they had with them in it. And when they looked at the devils, what they saw terrified them, and they became frightened. The devils said to them: "Pass on, there is no harm upon you." They passed by the columns of the jinn, the wild beasts, and the birds, until they stood before Sulayman. He turned to them with a cheerful face, received them with a fine welcome, and asked them about their condition. The leader of the people informed him of what they had come about, and gave him the letter. He looked at it and said: "Where is the box?" It was brought to him, and he shook it. Jibril, peace be upon him, came and informed him of what was in it. He said to them: "In it is a pearl that is not pierced, and a bead with a crooked hole." The messenger said: "You have spoken the truth. So pierce the pearl and insert the thread into the bead."

Sulayman, peace be upon him, said: "Who will pierce it for me?" He asked the jinn and humans, but they did not have knowledge of that. Then he asked the devils, and they said: "We will send for the earthworm." When it came, it took a hair in its mouth and penetrated the pearl until it came out from the other side. He said to it: "What is your need?" It said: "Make my sustenance in the tree." He said: "That is yours." Then he said: "Who will take care of this bead?" A white worm said: "I will, O Prophet of God." It took the thread in its mouth, entered the hole, and came out from the other side. He said: "What is your need?"
