It said: "Let my sustenance be in the fruits." He said: "That is yours."

[Page 200]

Then he distinguished between the boys and the girls. He ordered them to wash their faces and hands. The girl took water in her hand and struck it against the other [hand] and washed her face, while the boy took water in both hands and struck his face with it. The girl poured the water on the inner part of her forearms, while the boy poured it on the outer part. Then Sulayman, peace be upon him, returned the gift, as God, may He be exalted, has related.

It was also said: she sent with her gifts a staff which the kings of Himyar had inherited, and said: "I want you to tell me its top from its bottom," and [sent] a cup of water, and said: "Fill it with water that is sufficient, not from the earth nor from the sky." So Sulayman, peace be upon him, sent the staff into the air and said: "Whichever end reaches the ground first is its root." He commanded that horses be run until they sweated, and filled the cup with their sweat, and said: "This is neither from the water of the earth nor from the water of the sky." End of quote.

All of these are reports whose authenticity is not known, nor their falsehood. Perhaps some of them are such that the heart inclines to the judgment that they are false. And God, may He be exalted, knows best.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 27, verse 36:

﴿Then when he (the messenger) came to Sulayman﴾ There is an ellipsis in the speech, i.e., "So she sent the gift, and when it came to Sulayman..." The pronoun in "came" (jā'a) refers to the messenger. It is also permissible that it refers to the one to whom she sent the gift, but the first is more preferable. Ibn Mas'ud (ʿAbd Allah) read "when they came" (jā'ū), i.e., the messengers.

﴿He said: Do you give me abundance in wealth?﴾ This is an address to the messenger and to the one who sent him, using the masculine plural form to give precedence to the present over the absent, and applying the plural to two persons. It is also permissible that it is addressed to the messenger and those with him, and this is more in accordance with the reading of ʿAbd Allah. The first was preferred because of the intensification of denunciation and rebuke that are derived from the interrogative particle (hamza), according to what has been said, and their generalization to Bilqis and her people. It is supported by the coming of the saying of the Exalted:

[Page 201 marker omitted in the translation: the page number shown in the source is "201".]

﴿Return to them﴾ in the singular (*ifrad*). The indefinite *mal* ("wealth") in "(mal)" is used for belittling (*tahqir*).

Most of the seven readers (*qurra' al-sab'a*) read *tumiddunanni* with two nuns. Some transmitted the reading with the *ya'* (*ithbat al-ya'*). Hamzah read with assimilation of the nun of the nominative (*nun al-raf'*) into the protective nun (*nun al-wiqayah*), with the *ya'* of the first person kept. Al-Museyyibi, on the authority of Nafi', read with one light nun, the omitted element being the protective nun. It has also been allowed that the omitted element is the first nun, in which case its nominative marking is by a presumed sign (*'alamah muqaddarah*), as it has been said regarding the line of verse:

*Abitu usarri wa-tabitti tudallikki*
*wajhaki bil-'anbari wal-miski dhakiyy*

(I spend the night conversing in secret, while you spend the night rubbing your face with ambergris and fragrant musk.)

﴿What Allah has given me﴾, that is, of prophethood and sovereignty, which has no limit beyond it, ﴿is better than what He has given you﴾, that is, of wealth, of which what you have brought is part. It has been said that by "what He has given him" is meant wealth, since that is what suits the one being preferred over. The first interpretation is better, because it is more eloquent. The sentence is a justification (*ta'lil*) for the denial, and the speech is a metonymy (*kinayah*) for not accepting their gift. It is not meant as boasting about what he has been given. It is as though it were said: "I deny your supplying me with wealth, because what I have is better than it, so I have no need of your gift, and it holds no importance for me." The apparent view is that the aforementioned address was the first thing they came with, as the words of Allah the Exalted indicate: ﴿So when he came to Sulayman﴾ ... and so on. Perhaps this was because of his great eagerness to guide them to the truth. It has also been said that he, peace be upon him, may have said to them what is mentioned after what took place between them and him, of the things mentioned in the report of Wahb and others. The verse has been cited as evidence for the recommendation of rejecting the gifts of polytheists.

The apparent view is that the ruling is so when rejecting them serves a religious interest, not in every case.

The reason he did not say "What Allah has given me is better than what He has given you" as a circumstantial clause (*hal*) is that such a circumstance, which is the one establishing the difficulty, must be known, unlike the reason (*'illah*), and here it is not so.

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Rather, it is you who rejoice in your gift﴾ are a turning away (*idrab*) from what was mentioned of denying the supply of wealth and its justification, to the explanation of what moved them to it, namely, measuring his condition by theirs, and the limitation of their resolve to this world and its increase. The meaning is: you rejoice in what is given to you because your resolve is limited to this world and you love to increase it. In this there is a belittling of them that is not hidden. The gift is attributed to the one to whom it is given, and it may be attributed to that as well as to the giver. Or it is a turning away from that to a rebuke for their rejoicing in their gift, which they sent to him, a rejoicing of boasting, favor-seeking, and self-regard. The benefit of the turning away is to alert to the fact that supplying him, peace be upon him, with wealth is a reprehensible and ugly thing. To count it so, although it has no value in his sight, peace be upon him, is of what competitors compete for, and that is uglier, and rebuke with it is more fitting.

It has been said that their rejoicing in that gift is indicated by the indefinite form in the words of Bilqis: ﴿And I am sending a gift to them﴾, after her description of him, peace be upon him, as a great king. Likewise is what preceded in the report of Wahb and others concerning the true gem and the jasper, and the changing of the dress of the boys and the maids, and other things.

It has also been said that their rejoicing at what they sent him, peace be upon him, comes from their expectation of something greater than it from him, for gifts to the great often bring something greater than themselves, whether wealth or otherwise, such as preventing the ruin of their homes here. It has been said that the speech is a metonymy for rejection, and the meaning is: it is your right to rejoice at taking the gift, not mine. So take it and rejoice. This is a subtle meaning, except that there is obscurity in it.

﴿Return﴾ is a command to the messenger. It did not use the plural pronoun as it did earlier in the words ﴿Do you supply me﴾ ... and so on, because the return is specific to him, unlike supplying and similar acts. It has also been said that it is a command to the hoopoe, carrying another letter. Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted this from Zuhayr ibn Zuhayr, and it has been criticized as weak both in transmission (*riwayah*) and in rational assessment (*dirayah*).

Abdullah [ibn Mas'ud] read *irji'u* ("return," plural), on the basis that it is a command to the envoys. The verb here is intransitive, meaning: turn back and withdraw. ﴿To them﴾, that is, to Bilqis and her people. ﴿Then we will surely come to them﴾, that is, by Allah we will surely come to them ﴿with armies they cannot withstand﴾, that is, they will have no power to oppose them and no ability to face them. The root of *qibal* is facing, so it was made a figurative usage (*majaz*) or a metonymy for the power and ability to face them. Abdullah read *bihim* ("against them").

﴿And we will surely expel them from it﴾ is coordinated (*'ataf*) on the answer of the oath, ﴿from it﴾, that is, from Saba', ﴿humbled﴾, that is, in a state of being humbled after they had been in honor and power. The use of the plural of paucity (*jam' al-qillah*) emphasizes their humiliation. The words of Allah the Exalted ﴿while they are disgraced﴾ are another circumstantial clause. Although *sighar* means humiliation, what is meant here is their falling into captivity and enslavement. So the speech indicates that their expulsion will be by way of capture, not by way of exile. The answer to the oath has not been stated because it was conditional on a condition that was omitted when the statement was reported, relying on the context to indicate it, as though it were said: "Return to them; if they come to me in submission, well; otherwise we will surely come to them..." and so on.

He said, "O assembly, which of you will bring me her throne before they come to me in submission?" ﴿قالَ يا أيُّها المَلأُ أيُّكم يَأْتِينِي بِعَرْشِها قَبْلَ أنْ يَأْتُونِي مُسْلِمِينَ﴾ There is an omission in the speech. The meaning is: the messenger returned to her and informed her of what Sulayman had sworn to, so she prepared to set out toward him, for she knew that he was a prophet and that she had no power to fight him. It is narrated that when she set out she gave an order, and her throne was placed at the end of seven enclosures, one inside another, at the far end of one of her palaces. She locked the doors and appointed guards to protect it. She then set out toward Sulayman with her chieftains (aqyal) and their followers, and she sent to Sulayman: "I am coming to you with the kings of my people, so that I may see what your command is and what you call to of your religion." 'Abd Allah ibn Shaddad said: When she was one farsakh (parasang) away from Sulayman, he said: "Which of you will bring me her throne?"

From Ibn 'Abbas: Sulayman was awe-inspiring; no one would begin speaking about anything until he himself asked about it. One day he saw a cloud of dust (rahj) near him and said, "What is this?" They said, "Bilqis." He then said, "Which of you ..." etc.

The meaning of "in submission" (muslimin), according to what is narrated from him, is "obedient," and some of them said it means "believers."

They differed concerning the purpose behind his, peace be upon him, request for her throne. According to Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Zayd, he, peace be upon him, requested it in order to show her the power that comes from Allah the Exalted, and to astonish her. For this reason al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: "Perhaps it had been revealed to him, peace be upon him, that her throne was secured, so he wished to astonish her and show her some of the wonders that Allah the Exalted had granted him to perform at his hand, together with her awareness of the great power of Allah the Exalted and of what bears witness to the prophethood of Sulayman, peace be upon him, and confirms it." End of quotation.

The restriction of the bringing by the phrase "before" etc. is because that is more wondrous, more strange and further from what usually occurs, and it more clearly indicates the great power of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and the truth of his prophethood, peace be upon him, and so that her awareness of the marvels of miracles would be at the beginning of her arrival.

Al-Tabari said: He, peace be upon him, wanted to test the truthfulness of the hoopoe in his statement, ﴿ولَها عَرْشٌ عَظِيمٌ﴾ "She has a great throne." This was considered unlikely, since he, peace be upon him, had no need for such a test, for the sign of truthfulness in that matter was entirely clear to him, especially if what is narrated from Wahb and others is sound. It was also said: he wanted her throne to be brought so that it would be altered and changed, and then he would see whether she would affirm it or deny it, as a test of her intellect.

Qatada and Ibn Jurayj said: He, peace be upon him, wanted to seize it before she and her people were protected by faith and before their wealth could be prevented from being taken. Al-Kashf said: In this there is the point that the lawfulness of spoils is among what was specific to our Prophet ﷺ. In al-Tahqiq it is said: This does not fit with the rejection of the gift and its justification by his saying, ﴿فَما آتانِيَ اللَّهُ خَيْرٌ مِمّا آتاكُمْ﴾ "What Allah has given me is better than what He has given you."

It is answered that this is not a matter of taking spoils; rather, it is a matter of taking the property of a combatant (harbi) and disposing of it without his consent. Moreover, the apparent meaning is that it was by revelation, so it is possible that it was among his particular privileges for a wisdom. And it was not a gift to her, so the earlier rejection does not conflict with it. This is open to discussion. Perhaps closer to the heart is that this was in order to alter it, so that he could test her, as a test of her intellect, together with showing her some of his extraordinary signs that indicate the truth of his prophethood and the great power of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Then, the apparent point is that this statement came after the rejection of the gift, and this is the view held by the majority (al-jumhur).

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he, peace be upon him, said this when he began to examine the truthfulness of the hoopoe versus its falsehood, when it said, ﴿ولَها عَرْشٌ عَظِيمٌ﴾. In that case there is a reversal of the order of the narratives. I think this is not authentic from Ibn 'Abbas.

[Page 202]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 27, verse 39:

﴿Said an ʿIfrit⁽¹⁾ of the jinn﴾: that is, a wicked, insolent one. [He is] an explanation of him, since the wicked, reprehensible man who subdues his peers is called ʿifrit.

Abu Haywa read "ʿafrit" with a fatha on the ʿayn. Abu Rajaʾ, Abu al-Sammal and ʿIsa read, and it is narrated from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him): "ʿifriyah" with a kasra on the ʿayn, a sukun on the fa, a kasra on the ra, followed by an open ya and then the feminine ta. Dhu al-Rummah said:

"As if it were a star in the wake of an ʿifriyah, hurled down, shooting through the blackness of the night."

A group read "ʿifr" without a ya or a ta. In the dialect of Tayyi' and Tamim it is said "ʿifraah" with an alif followed by the feminine ta. There is also a sixth dialect, "ʿufariyah."

The ta in "ʿifrit" is, according to the well-known view, an added letter for intensification (mubalaghah). In al-Nihayah: the ya in "ʿifriyah" and "ʿufariyah" serves to assimilate them to "shirdhimah" and "ʿudhafirah," and the ha in both is for intensification, while the ta in "ʿifrit" serves to assimilate it to "qindil." End of quote.

The name of this ʿIfrit, according to what Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas, is Sakhr.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Jarir transmitted from Shuʿayb al-Jubbaʾi that his name is Kawazn.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Yazid ibn Ruman that his name is Kuwza. It is also said that his name is Dhakwan.

﴿I will bring it to you⁽²⁾﴾: that is, its throne. "Ati" may be a present-tense verb or an active participle. It is said: this is the more fitting, given the context of claiming to bring it within the period mentioned in His words, ﴿before you rise from your place﴾: that is, from your seat of judgment where you sit to rule. He, peace be upon him, would sit from the morning until noon every day. This was said by Qatadah, Mujahid, Wahb and Zuhayr ibn Muhammad.

It is also said: that is, before you rise from your sitting to standing. ﴿And indeed I am strong enough for it﴾: its carrying does not weigh heavily upon me.

Strength (quwwah) is a quality from which difficult actions proceed, and by which one who possesses it is able to bear great bodies. Therefore "qawiyy" was chosen over "qadir" here. The apparent sense of some scholars' words is that the sentence contains an ellipsis: some said, "that is, for carrying it," and others said, "that is, for bringing it." The second was preferred on the basis of what is immediately evident from the beginning of the passage, and the first on the basis that it is more fitting to His words "qawiyy."

﴿Trustworthy⁽³⁾﴾: I will not take away any part of it nor alter it.

---

(1) *ʿIfrit*: a wicked, mighty jinn; the word denotes an insolent and formidable being.
(2) The phrase is the speech of the ʿIfrit, promising to bring the throne of the Queen of Sheba.
(3) *Amin*: trustworthy.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 27, verse 40 (part 1 of 2):

﴿He who had knowledge of the Book said﴾: its being separated from what precedes it (without a conjunction) is to signal the difference between the two speakers, their two statements, and the manner of their two powers to bring it about, a complete contrast; or it is to remove the first from the level of consideration.

There is disagreement about identifying this speaker. The majority, among them Ibn 'Abbas, Yazid ibn Ruman and al-Hasan, hold that he is Asaf ibn Barakhya ibn Sham'iya ibn Minkil, and the name of his mother is Basura, from the Children of Israel. He was the minister of Sulayman according to what is well known. In Majma' al-Bayan it is said that he was his minister and his nephew (son of his sister). He was a truthful man (siddiq) who knew the Greatest Name (al-ism al-a'zam). It is also said that he was his scribe.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Mujahid that he was a man named Asțum, and it is said: Asturus.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Zuhayr ibn Muhammad that he was a man called Dhu'l-Nur.

He also related from Ibn Lahi'a that he was al-Khadir (peace be upon him). From Qatada that his name was Malikha, and it is said: Malakh, and it is said: Tamlikha. It is said: he was Hud. A group said: he was Dabba ibn Ud, forefather of the Banu Dabba from the Arabs; he was an excellent man who served Sulayman, and he was over a part of his horses. Al-Nakha'i said: he was Jibril (peace be upon him). It is said: he was another angel whom God Most High strengthened Sulayman with. Al-Jubba'i said: he was Sulayman himself (peace be upon him).

The separation (without conjunction) on this view is clear, for the sentence is then a resumptive sentence of explanation (isti'naf bayani), as if it were said: "What did Sulayman say when the 'Ifrit said that?" So it was said: "He said..." etc. The expression about him through what is in the noble text is to indicate the nobility of knowledge and that this honour was by means of it. The address in His words, ﴿I will bring it to you before your gaze returns to you﴾, is to the 'Ifrit. Why he did not bring it first, but instead asked the people with His words, ﴿Which of you will bring me her throne?﴾ and then said what he said and brought it, was intentionally so that he might show them that what is not possible for the 'Ifrits of the jinn, let alone others, is possible for him.

Restricting the address to the 'Ifrit is because he is the one who presumed the power to bring it from among them; making it for everyone, as in His words, ﴿That is nearer to your not being unjust﴾, is not evident with regard to what has been mentioned.

The Imam preferred this view and said that it is closer for several reasons:

The first: the relative pronoun is in the language specified for a particular person by the content of the clause known to the addressee, and the person known to have the knowledge of the Book is Sulayman; something that suggests this has preceded in this surah, so it is necessary to take him as intended and to direct the word to him. Asaf, although he shares in the content of the clause, is in it more complete, because he is a prophet and he knows the Book more than his community.

The second: bringing the throne at that delicate moment is a lofty rank; if it had occurred to someone of his community other than him, it would entail preferring that person over him, peace be upon him, and that is not permissible.

The third: if its bringing had required any of his community, it would entail a diminishment of his standing in the eyes of the people.

The fourth: the apparent sense of his words, peace be upon him, afterward, ﴿This is of the bounty of my Lord﴾ ... etc., implies that this extraordinary act was manifested by God Most High through his supplication, peace be upon him. End quote. There is room for discussion regarding it.

Some have objected to this view, saying that the address in (ātīka, "I will bring you") rules it out, for the proper wording would be: "I bring it before the gaze returns to the person," for example. You have already learned its answer. And that it would be more fitting to say afterward: "So when he brought it" rather than "So when he saw it" ... etc.

It has been answered that his saying that is to indicate that he has no power or strength in it, and perhaps the more evident view is that the speaker was one of his followers. This does not entail that he, peace be upon him, was not able to bring it in the same way, for the custom of kings is to assign their followers to tasks for their benefit which they are not incapable of performing themselves. So let what we are dealing with follow this custom. It does no harm in this that the purpose is something accomplished by speech—namely supplication—and does not require bodily labour and exertion, as is not hidden.

In Fusus al-Hikam: That took place at the hand of one of the companions of Sulayman, peace be upon him, so that it would be greater for Sulayman in the souls of those present. Al-Qaysari said: Sulayman was the qutb of his time, one who disposes affairs, and vicegerent over the world, and Asaf was his minister, and he was perfect. Extraordinary acts of custom rarely proceed from the qutbs and the caliphs, but rather from their inheritors and successors, because of their standing in complete servitude and their attribute of total poverty, so they do not dispose of anything for themselves; and among the favours of God Most High upon them is that He grants them the companionship of trustworthy scholars, who carry their burdens from them and execute their rulings and words. End quote. What is in the Fusus is closer to the path of people like us, though what has been mentioned is not free from examination according to the path of those people as well.

In Majma' al-Bayan: al-Ayyashi related with his chain that he said: Musa ibn Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn Musa met Yahya ibn Aktham, and he asked him about questions, among them: Was Sulayman in need of the knowledge of Asaf? He did not answer until he asked his brother 'Ali ibn Muhammad, who said: Write to him: Sulayman was not unable to know what Asaf knew, but he, peace be upon him, wished to make his community of jinn and men know that he was the proof after him; and that is from the knowledge of Sulayman, which he entrusted to Asaf by the command of God, and God caused him to understand that, lest his imamate be disputed, just as He caused Sulayman to understand during the lifetime of Dawud so that his imamate after him would be known, to confirm the proof upon creation. End quote. And it is as you see.

By "the Book" is meant the genus comprising all revealed scriptures. It is said: the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz). That the intended meaning is that according to all the preceding views regarding the relative pronoun is very far-fetched. It is said: the intended meaning is that which was sent down to Bilqis. The "min" is initial (ibtida'iyya, "from"). The indefiniteness of ('ilm, "knowledge") is for magnification and to indicate that it is a knowledge not previously known. It is said: that knowledge was by the Greatest Name of God Most High, which when one asks by it, one is answered. That scholar supplicated with it and his purpose was achieved; it is (Ya Hayy Ya Qayyum, "O Living, O Self-Subsisting"). It is said: (Ya Dhal-Jalali wal-Ikram, "O Possessor of Majesty and Honour"). It is said: (Allahu al-Rahman, "God the Merciful"). It is said: (in Hebrew, Ahya Sharahya).

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Zuhri that he supplicated with the words: O our God and God of everything, a single God, there is no god but You, bring me her throne.

Al-taraf is the moving and opening of the eyelids to look at something; then it was used metaphorically for the gaze. Its return (irtidad) is its cessation by the closing of the eyelids. And because it is a natural matter not dependent on intention, "return" (irtidad) was preferred over "reversion" (radd). So the meaning is: "I will bring it to you before the lid of your eye closes after having opened." It is said: there is no need to consider metaphor in the gaze, since the intended meaning is before the return of the moving of the eyelids to their closure after their opening; and in this there is scrutiny. The speech is on its literal sense, not from the figure of speech for speed.

It has been related that Asaf said to Sulayman, peace be upon him: Extend your eyes until your gaze reaches its end. So he extended his gaze and looked toward Yemen, and before his gaze returned to him the throne was present with him.

It is said: it is from the figure of speech, so it may be that he brought it within the time of a degree or two degrees' rising or something like that.

From Ibn Jubayr and Qatada that al-taraf means the object looked at, i.e. whatever the gaze falls upon, and that the meaning is: before there reaches you whatever your gaze falls upon at the farthest point you see when you look ahead. And it is as you see.

﴿So when he saw it settled beside him﴾: i.e., when
صفحة 205
Sulayman, peace be upon him, saw the throne present beside him, remaining in the state in which it had been. ﴿He said﴾, receiving the blessing with thanks, following the way of his brother prophets, peace be upon them, and the sincere servants of God, Mighty and Majestic: "This" — i.e., the bringing of the throne or its presence before me in this short period; and it is said: i.e., the ability to bring it, by means or directly — ﴿is of the bounty of my Lord﴾, i.e., His favour, exalted is His glory, upon me, not by any intrinsic entitlement of mine to it, nor by any deed of mine that would oblige Him — glory be to Him and exalted — to it. In the speech there is an ellipsis, i.e.: so he brought it and he saw it; so when he saw it ... etc. That which is omitted is omitted to indicate the complete manifestness of the matter and its being independent of being reported, and to signify the complete speed of the bringing, as if nothing at all had occurred between the promise of it and his, peace be upon him, seeing it. In restricting his seeing to its being settled beside him there is emphasis on this meaning, for it gives the impression that not even the beginning of the bringing intervened between them, as if it had never ceased to be present beside him.

So "settled" (mustaqirran) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state, and "beside him" ('indahu) is attached to it. This is, as we have indicated, a specific (khass) location, and for this reason its mention is permissible. Some thought that it is a general (amm) location, and so they found its mention problematic in light of the view of the majority of grammarians that when the complement of an adverbial of place is a general location it must be deleted. So some of them were compelled to hold that the adverb is attached to "he saw" (ra'ahu), not to "settled."

Among them are those who went, like Ibn Malik, to the view that the deletion of this is the usual practice, and that it may appear, as in this verse, and in the line:

"To you is glory, if your Patron is glorified; and if he is humbled, you are still in the midst of the ease of humiliation."

And you know that what is in the line can be considered a specific location just like that in the verse.

Regarding the manner in which the throne reached him, peace be upon him, so that he saw it settled beside him, there is disagreement.

Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn 'Asakir related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: The throne of the queen of Saba' did not travel between heaven and earth, but the earth was split open by it, and it moved beneath the earth until it appeared before Sulayman. This was the view of Mujahid, Ibn Sabit and others.

It is said: it descended before Sulayman, peace be upon him, from the sky; and he, peace be upon him, was at that time in the land of Syria, according to what is said, having returned to it from Sana'a; and between it and Ma'rib, the location of the throne, was about a two-month journey.

According to the view that he was in Sana'a, the distance between his location and the location of the throne was about three days. In either case, covering the long distance in a short time is a possible matter, and the Truthful One has reported its occurrence, so it must be accepted. And the righteous and the wicked agree on the occurrence of something greater than that, namely the sun's traversal of thousands of parasangs in the blink of an eye, although the proportion of the throne of Bilqis to the sun's body is the proportion of a grain of dust to a mountain.

The Greatest Shaykh (al-Shaykh al-Akbar), may his secret be sanctified, said: Asaf acted upon the very substance of the throne, annihilating it in its place and bringing it into existence beside Sulayman, from a place where no one perceives it, except one who knows the new creation occurring at every instant; the time of its existence was identical with the time of its non-existence, and each of them was in a single instant; and the very speech of Asaf was identical with the act in time, for speech from a perfect one is in the position of "Be!" from God Most High. The question of the throne's arrival is among the most difficult questions except for one who knows what we have mentioned about bringing into existence and annihilation. So the throne did not traverse a distance, nor was land folded up for it, nor did it tear through it. End of summary; he has a continuation that will come, God willing.

What he mentioned, that it happened by annihilation and bringing into existence, is among what is permissible in my view, although I do not hold that the renewal of substances entails the renewal of accidents according to al-Ash'ari; however, it contradicts the apparent sense of the verse. It has been used as evidence for the reality of karamat (extraordinary favours granted to saints).

You know that possibility invalidates the use of a proof.

He, peace be upon him, gave the reason for God Most High's favour upon him with the words: ﴿That He may test me﴾, i.e., that He may deal with me as one tested, i.e., examined: ﴿whether I will be grateful﴾ for it, by seeing it as pure favour from God Most High without any power on my part.

...and [I have] the strength and I fulfill its right? ﴿Or am I ungrateful?﴾ — by finding for myself a place of intervention in the matter, or by falling short in performing its obligations, as is the case with all the favours that overflow upon the servants.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Jurayj that the meaning is: "that He may test me: Will I give thanks when the throne is brought to me, or will I be ungrateful when I see one who is lower than me in worldly status more knowledgeable than me?" A similar view is reported in al-Bahr from Ibn Abbas, but its soundness is doubtful. Even further from soundness is what Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Suddi, that he said: "When he saw it [the throne] settled in his presence, he was dismayed and said: 'Is there a man other than me more capable of [what is] with Allah, the Mighty and Majestic?!'" The truth is likely a categorical judgement that this report is false.

The clause ﴿Will I give thanks?﴾ ... etc. is in a position of accusative (naṣb) as a second object (maf'ul thani) of the verb of testing (al-balwa), and it is suspended by the interrogative particle (hamza) from it, treating it as if it were the verb of knowledge (al-'ilm), although it is not synonymous with it. It was also said that its position is accusative as a substitute (badal) for the pronoun "ya" (of "liyabluwani").

﴿And whoever is grateful, he is grateful only for his own self﴾, i.e., for its benefit; because by it he binds the blessing with a tether, draws more increase, relieves himself of the burden of obligation, and frees himself from the stain of ingratitude. ﴿And whoever is ungrateful﴾, i.e., does not give thanks, ﴿then indeed my Lord is Self-Sufficient﴾ above His thanks, ﴿Generous﴾ in not hastening punishment, and in bestowing favours even with the absence of thanks.

The apparent reading is that "man" (مَن) is conditional, and the clause linked with the fa' (فاء) is the response of the condition. It was also permitted that the response be elided, indicated by what precedes it of its counterpart, and the mentioned clause stands in its place, i.e., "And whoever is ungrateful, then upon himself [falls the harm]", i.e., the harm of his ingratitude falls upon himself. This has been objected to on the basis that it does not suit his saying "Generous." It was also permitted that "man" be a relative pronoun (mawsula), and the fa' entered the predicate because it implies the meaning of a condition.

"He said" — that is, Sulayman (peace be upon him). The narration is repeated, even though what is reported (both before and after it) is his own speech (peace be upon him), as an alert to the difference between the preceding and the following: the first is a matter of thanksgiving to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, while the second is a command to his servants: ﴿Disguise for her her throne﴾, that is: make it such that it is not recognized. This is only achieved by altering it from the form and shape it had, and perhaps what is meant is alteration in general.

It was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and al-Dahhak that it consisted of adding to it and subtracting from it. It was also said: by removing the jewels upon it. And it was said: by making its lower part its upper part and its front its back. The lam in (laha) ("for her") is for specification, as in ﴿Come, for you (hayta laka)﴾, and so it indicates that she alone is intended by the disguising. ﴿Let us see﴾ is in the jussive, as the answer to the command. Abu Haywa recited it in the nominative, as a resumptive clause. ﴿Will she be guided?﴾ — to recognizing it, or to the fitting reply appropriate to the occasion.

It was also said: to belief in Allah, the Exalted, and His Messenger (peace be upon him), when she sees the advance of her throne while she has left it behind, its doors locked upon it and guards and chamberlains posted over it. This was related by al-Tabarsi from al-Jubba'i. But it is objected that the relevance of the disguising to belief does not clearly appear. ﴿Or will she be among those who are not guided?﴾ — that is, with respect to Our knowledge, to what has been mentioned of recognizing her throne, or the fitting reply appropriate to the occasion. For although her being among them in reality is a continuing matter, her being among them in the eyes of Sulayman (peace be upon him) and his people is a newly arising matter that becomes manifest through testing.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 27, verse 42:

﴿So when she came﴾ This begins the narration of the test that Sulayman (peace be upon him) intended. That is, when Bilqis came to Sulayman, the throne had been made unfamiliar to her and placed before him. ﴿It was said﴾, i.e., by Sulayman himself or through an intermediary, ﴿"Is your throne like this?"﴾ i.e., is your throne like this throne you see, the one you left behind in your land? He did not say, "Is this your throne?" so that it would not be a suggestion to her, which would defeat the purpose of the command to make the throne unfamiliar, namely presenting it in a form that causes confusion and doubt, so that her condition might become clear to him (peace be upon him), especially since she had been described to him (peace be upon him) as having deficient intelligence.

صفحة 207
In some reports it is said that the jinn feared that he would marry her and have from her a child who would possess the shrewdness of humans and the agility of jinn, since she had a lineage connected to them, and so he would control them with strong control. Therefore they accused her before him of madness and said that her legs were like the hooves of animals. For this reason he tested her with this and with what would lead to uncovering her shins. As for those who do not hold that she was connected to the jinn, they say: perhaps an envious person had accused her of this, so he (peace be upon him) wanted to test her in order to establish the reality of the situation. Some of them say: it was only so that she would be met with the same treatment she had given, when she made the youths and maidens unfamiliar, and she tested him (peace be upon him) with the pearl that was untouched and the jasper with a crooked hole. That this was in her throne, whose bringing near is very far-fetched given the distance and her great care for it, is more complete and more powerful, and it also contains a manifestation of a miracle that is not hidden. This, in my view, is closer to the heart than other views.

﴿She said, "It is as if it were it"﴾ She answered with what revealed the completeness of her intellect, in that she did not state with certainty that it was it, since it could be something similar to it. Rather, she used "as if" (ka'anna), which indicates, as it has been said, a strong probability that it is the same, with doubt about the opposite. Here "ka'anna" is not used for comparison, as is usually the case with it.

Ibn al-Munir mentioned in al-Intisaf what indicates that it conveys the strength of resemblance. He said: the wisdom in Bilqis's turning away in her answer from "Is it like this?" (hakadha huwa), which would correspond to the question, to "It is as if it were it" (ka'annahu huwa) is that "ka'annahu huwa" is the expression of one in whom the resemblance has grown strong, to the point that he doubts himself about any difference between the two matters, and almost says, "It is it." That was Bilqis's state. As for "hakadha huwa," it is the expression of one who is certain of the difference between the two matters and judges only that a resemblance exists between them. So it does not match her state, and therefore she turned away from it to what is in the glorious wording.

﴿And we were given knowledge before her, and we had been Muslims﴾ This is part of her speech according to what a group of exegetes chose. It is as if she sensed from what she witnessed a test of her intellect and a manifestation of a miracle for her. Since the apparent purpose of the question was the first, she hastened to answer with what revealed the completeness of her sound intellect. And since the manifestation of the miracle was less evident than that, she mentioned what relates to it last, namely her saying, "And we were given" ... etc. This also indicates the completeness of her intellect. Its meaning: we were given knowledge of the complete power of God Most High and the truth of your prophethood before this miracle, or before this situation, through what we witnessed of the matter of the hoopoe and what we heard from your messengers to us of the signs that indicate this. "And we had been believers from that time," so there is no need for the manifestation of this miracle.

You may also take it as part of what relates to the testing, and its sum is: there is no need for the test, because I believed before, and this suffices to show the completeness of my intellect.

It is also permitted that it be to explain the source of the strong probability that it is her throne, and the motive for good manners in addressing him (peace be upon him). That is: we were given knowledge through your bringing the throne before the seeing, or before this situation, by indications or by report, and we had been believers from that time. The use of the "we" of majesty follows the usage of kings, and it contains an exaltation of the matter of her Islam. It is not meant to refer to herself and her people with her, since the verse that follows makes that unlikely, where God Most High says:

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 27, verse 43:

﴿And that which she used to worship besides Allah prevented her﴾. This is an explanation from Him, glorified and exalted be He, of what had been preventing her from openly displaying the Islam she had professed until now. That is, what prevented her from displaying it was the knowledge that her former worship of the sun necessitated the day she was given knowledge. Here *mā* is a verbal-source particle (*mā maṣdariyyah*), and the verbal noun is the subject of (*ṣadda*, "prevented"). It has also been permitted that *mā* be a relative pronoun (*mawṣūlah*) referring to the sun, which would then also be the subject. The attribution is figurative (*majāz*) in both cases.

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, she was among a people who were disbelievers﴾, is a causal explanation for the causality of her aforementioned worship in preventing her. That is, she was of a people firmly rooted in disbelief, and therefore she was not able to display her Islam while she was among them, until she came before Solomon, peace be upon him.

Page 208

Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Ibn Abi 'Abla read *annahā* with a fatḥah on the hamzah, taking it as an implied *lām* of causation, meaning "because she." Alternatively, the verbal noun is made a substitute for the subject of (*ṣadda*) by way of inclusive substitution (*badal al-ishtimāl*).

It has been said that His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And we were given﴾ ... etc., is from the speech of Solomon's people. It is as if, when they heard her, they answered her question by saying, "It is as if it is he," and they said, "She has answered correctly," and she grasped the detailed matter. She was intelligent and discerning, and she had been granted Islam, and she knew the power of Allah, exalted is He, and the truth of prophethood through the signs that preceded, and through this wondrous sign concerning her throne. They then followed that with their statement, "And we were given knowledge" of Allah, exalted is He, of His power, and of the truth of what came from Him, glorified is He, before her knowledge, and we have remained upon the religion of Islam. This was from them a thanks to Allah, exalted is He, for His favor upon them over her, and their precedence over her in knowledge of Allah, exalted is He, and in Islam before her. This implied elided matter is indicated by making their knowledge and their Islam prior to hers. According to this view, His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And she was prevented﴾ ... etc., may be a continuation of the people's speech, or it may be the beginning of a report from Him, exalted and glorified is He.

It is related from Mujahid and Zuhayr ibn Muhammad that (*wa-ūtīnā*, "and we were given") is from the speech of Solomon, peace be upon him, and in (*wa-ṣaddahā*) ... etc., there is also a possibility regarding him as well. There is no hiding what is in making (*wa-ūtīnā*) ... etc. part of the speech of the people or of the speech of Solomon, peace be upon him, of remoteness and forced interpretation. There is no good in this aspect except the consistency of the feminine pronouns.

It has been said that (*wa-ūtīnā*) ... etc. is a continuation of her speech, and His statement, exalted is He: (*wa-ṣaddahā*) ... etc. is the beginning of a report from Him, exalted is He, to explain the goodness of her condition and the soundness of her Islam, free from any taint of polytheism, by making the subject of (*ṣaddahā*) His pronoun, exalted and glorified is He, or the pronoun of Solomon, peace be upon him.

Here *mā* is either a verbal-source particle or a relative pronoun, and before it there is an elided preposition (*ḥarf al-jarr*) in meaning, that is: Allah, exalted is He, or Solomon, prevented her from her worship besides Allah, or from that which she worshipped besides Him, exalted is He. Abu Hayyan transmitted this from al-Tabari and critiqued it, saying: "It is weak and is not permissible except in poetry, like his statement:

*You pass by the abodes and do not turn aside*

and it is not among the places where a preposition is omitted."

You know that the meaning with this is among what the heart does not find comfortable. Some have gone to the extreme of remoteness and claimed that His statement, exalted is He: (*wa-ṣaddahā*) ... etc. is connected to His statement, glorified is He: ﴿Are you guided, or are you among those who are not guided?﴾, and that the *wāw* in it is for the circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*), with the verb implied. In al-Bahr it is said that this is an opinion to be avoided because of the long separation between them, and because inversion and postponement are not resorted to except in cases of necessity.

By my life, whoever is fair will see that what has been mentioned is not something by which the noble speech of Allah, exalted is He, should be interpreted. I say, after the statements and counter-statements: the manner in which these clauses are connected requires careful reflection, so let it be considered. And Allah, exalted is He, is the Granter of success.

[p. 208]

﴿It was said to her: "Enter the palace."﴾ This is a clarifying resumptive clause (*isti'naf bayani*, a clause that answers an implied question). It is as if it were asked: "What was said to her after the aforementioned test?" So it was said: "It was said to her, 'Enter...'" etc. It was not joined by a conjunction to His saying, ﴿"Is your throne like this?"﴾, so that this meaning would not be lost. The word *lahā* ("to her") is used here, rather than as in what preceded, because of her status as the one being addressed. *Al-ṣarḥ* means a palace and every tall building. From it comes ﴿"Build for me a tower (ṣarḥan)"﴾. It is derived from *al-taṣrīḥ*, which means explicit, thorough declaration. Mujahid said: *al-ṣarḥ* here means a pool of water. Ibn 'Isa said: it means a courtyard. And *ṣarhat al-dār* means the open yard of the house.

It is narrated that Sulayman (peace be upon him) ordered the jinn, before her arrival, and they built for him on her route a palace of white glass. He had water run beneath it and put in it sea creatures, fish and others.

In another narration, they built for him a palace (*ṣarḥan*) and made for it floors of glass, as if they were water. They placed under the floors every kind of sea creature, and then they covered it. This is more consistent with the apparent meaning of the verse. His throne was placed in the front of it, and he sat upon it. Birds, jinn and humans gathered around him. He did this as a test for her as well, according to some. It was also said that it was to increase her awe of his affair, to confirm his prophethood, and to strengthen her in her religion. It was also said that the jinn had told him (peace be upon him) that she had hairy shins and a leg like a donkey's hoof, so he wished to uncover the truth of the matter through this.

[p. 209]

The Greatest Shaykh (*al-Shaykh al-Akbar*, Ibn 'Arabi) — may God sanctify his secret — said, in summary: He intended to alert her by action that she had spoken truly when she said about the throne, "It is as if it were it," since it had disappeared in Sheba and an identical one was found before her. So he made for her a palace of the utmost delicacy and clarity, as if it were clear water while not being water. This is the utmost fairness on his part (peace be upon him). I do not think the matter is as he said, and God knows best.

The verse has been used as evidence, by those who hold that her being ordered to enter the palace was so that the truth of the matter might be uncovered, for the permissibility of looking at a woman before proposing. There is a detailed discussion of this in the books of jurisprudence.

﴿When she saw it﴾, i.e., she saw its surface, on the basis that *al-ṣarḥ* means a palace, ﴿she supposed it to be a deep water﴾, i.e., she thought it was a great quantity of water. ﴿And she uncovered her shins﴾ so that her skirts would not get wet, as is the custom of one who intends to wade into water. Ibn Kathir, in the narration of Qunbul, read *sa'qayhā* with a hamza on the alif of *sāq* ("shin"), analogizing it to its plural *su'q* and *as'uq*, since it is a regular rule that a *waw* that is pronounced with a *ḍamma* (or preceded by one) is changed into a hamza. This carried over, by extension, to the singular form contained within it.

In *al-Bahr*, Abu 'Ali related that Abu Ḥayya al-Numayri used to pronounce a hamza in place of every *waw* preceded by a *ḍamma*, and he recited:

*Aḥabbu l-mu'qadayni ilā Mūsā*

In *al-Kashf*: the apparent view is that the hamza is a dialectal form of (*sāq*), and this reading that is established among the Seven supports it. It was objected that derivation rules out this view. Whatever the case, the statement of whoever says that this reading is not sound is itself not sound.

﴿He said﴾, i.e., Sulayman (peace be upon him), when he saw the alarm and terror that had come over her. It was said: the speaker was the one who had ordered her to enter the palace, but this is contrary to the apparent meaning. ﴿Indeed, it﴾, i.e., what she supposed to be (deep water) ﴿is a palace made smooth﴾, i.e., polished. From it comes *al-amrad*, for a young man without facial hair, and *shajara marda'*, a tree without leaves, and *ramla marda'*, a sand dune that produces nothing. *Al-mārid* means one stripped of goodness. ﴿Of glass﴾, i.e., of crystal, and it is the plural of *qārūra* (a glass vessel).

﴿She said﴾ when she witnessed this great matter: ﴿"My Lord, I have wronged myself"﴾, i.e., by what I was upon of worshipping the sun. It was also said: by my evil assumption about Sulayman (peace be upon him), in that she thought he intended to drown her in the deep water, but this is far-fetched.

Similar to this is what was said: she meant, "I wronged myself by testing Sulayman, until he tested me in this manner, which required that my shins be uncovered before his eyes." ﴿"And I have submitted with Sulayman"﴾, following him and bound to him. The turn (*iltifāt*, a shift from speaking about someone to addressing God) to the Majestic Name in His saying ﴿"to God, Lord of the worlds"﴾ serves to show her knowledge of His divinity, His singularity in deserving worship, and His lordship over all existing things, of which is what she used to worship before, the sun. It seems that this statement was a renewal of her Islam in the most complete form, and she expressed it in a manner free of any self-regard or arrogance at all, as is not hidden.

There has been disagreement about her situation after Islam. It was said: he (peace be upon him) married her, loved her, and left her in her kingdom. He ordered the jinn, and they built for her Sayl'hin and Ghamdan. He would visit her once a month and stay with her for three days, and she bore him a child.

Ibn 'Asakir narrated, from Salama ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Ribi'i, that he (peace be upon him) gave her Ba'labakk as her dower.

Many have mentioned that when she uncovered her shins, he saw abundant hair on them, and he disliked marrying her in that state. So he summoned humans and said, "What removes this?" They said, "O Messenger of God, the razor." He said, "The razor cuts the shins of a woman."

[p. 210]

In another narration, it was said to her, and she said, "Iron has never touched me." So Sulayman disliked the razor and said, "It cuts her shins." Then he summoned the jinn, and they said the same. Then he summoned the devils, and they prepared for him the depilatory paste (*nūra*).

Ibn 'Abbas said: That day was the first day on which depilatory paste was seen. It is narrated from 'Ikrima that the first to prepare depilatory paste were the devils of humankind, who prepared it for Bilqis, and this is contrary to what is well known. It is also reported that the bathhouse (*ḥammām*) was established on that day.

In the *Tarikh* of al-Bukhari, from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, he said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The first for whom bathhouses were made was Sulayman."

Al-Tabarani, Ibn 'Adi in *al-Kamil*, and al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab al-Iman* narrated from him as well, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The first to enter the bathhouse was Sulayman. When he felt its heat, he said: 'Oh! From the punishment of God.'"

It was narrated from Wahb that he said: It is claimed that when Bilqis embraced Islam, Sulayman said to her: "Choose a man from your people, and I will marry him to you." She said: "A woman like me, O Prophet of God, marries men, when there was among my people such kingship and authority as there was?!" He said: "Yes, indeed, in Islam there is nothing but that, and it is not fitting for you to forbid what God has made lawful for you." She said: "Marry me, if there must be that, to Dhu Tubba', the king of Hamdan." So he married her to him, then returned her to Yemen, and he gave her husband Dhu Tubba' authority over Yemen. He summoned Zawba'a, the commander of the jinn of Yemen, and said: "Work for Dhu Tubba' in whatever he employs you for." So he remained a king there, with work done for him in it, until Sulayman died. When a year had passed and the jinn realized his death (peace be upon him), a man from among them came, traveled through Tihama until he was in the middle of Yemen, and shouted at the top of his voice: "O assembly of jinn! Indeed King Sulayman has died, so lift your hands." They lifted their hands and dispersed. Thus the kingdom of Dhu Tubba' and the kingdom of Bilqis ended along with the kingdom of Sulayman (peace be upon him).

'Awn ibn 'Abd Allah said: A man asked 'Abd Allah ibn 'Utba: "Did Sulayman marry Bilqis?" He said: "Her affair ended with her saying: ﴿'And I have submitted with Sulayman to God, Lord of the worlds.'﴾" It was said: meaning, we have no knowledge beyond that.

The well-known view is that he (peace be upon him) did marry her, and this is the view of a group of historians. Al-Bayhaqi narrated in *al-Zuhd*, from al-Awza'i, who said: A tower of the towers of Tadmur (Palmyra) collapsed, and they found in it a beautiful woman with large dark eyes, well-proportioned, as if the folds of her body were the folds of scrolls. Upon her was a turban eighty cubits long, and on the edge of the turban was written in gold: "In the name of God, the Compassionate, the Merciful. I am Bilqis, queen of Sheba, wife of Sulayman ibn Dawud, peace be upon both of them. I ruled over the world, as a disbeliever and as a believer, what no one ruled before me, and no one will rule after me. My destiny has become death, so be brief, O seekers of the world." God knows best the soundness of the report. How many reports are there in this story whose authentic portion God alone knows! The story itself is wondrous, and it contains matters that break the norm; indeed, the intellect almost rejects it at first thought.

Among the things that are surprising, and God has a hidden wisdom in it, is that Bilqis's affair remained hidden from Sulayman for several years, as many have said, even though the distance between him and her was not extreme. God had subjected to him jinn, devils, birds and wind, as He subjected them. This is far more remarkable than the concealment of Yusuf's affair from Ya'qub, peace be upon both of them, by many degrees. Glory be to Him, from whose knowledge not even the weight of an atom in the heavens and in the earth is hidden.

Now, the Sufis have a lengthy discussion in applying what is in this story to what is within the souls. Perhaps the matter is easy for one who has even a little taste, after becoming acquainted with some of what has passed of their applications, and of what is in some stories concerning that. God Most High is the Guide to the straight path.

﴿And We had certainly sent﴾ is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with His words, Exalted is He, ﴿And We had certainly given David and Solomon knowledge﴾. It follows the same line of discourse as what precedes it. The lam is attached to the answer of an omitted oath, meaning: "By God, We had certainly sent ﴿to Thamud their brother Ṣāliḥ﴾." He swore to this out of concern for the importance of the matter. (ṣāliḥan) is either a substitute (badal) for (akhāhum), or an explanatory apposition (ʿaṭf bayān). The clause ﴿that worship God﴾ in His words, Exalted is He, ﴿أنِ اعْبُدُوا اللَّهَ﴾, is explanatory (mufassira) of the meaning of "sending," which implies speech, though not its letters.

It is permitted that it be a verbal (maṣdariyya) clause, from which the preposition has been omitted, meaning "that" (bi-anna). It has also been said "because" (li-anna). Connecting it to the imperative is permissible, and there is no objection to it, as has already been explained.

[Page 211]

It is also read with a ḍammah on the nūn, following the bāʾ in its vowel.

﴿Then behold, they became two factions disputing﴾: that is, Our sending suddenly coincided with their division and their disputing, so one faction believed and another faction disbelieved. This is what God, Exalted is He, related in another place in His words: ﴿The chiefs of his people who were arrogant said to those who were deemed weak, to those among them who believed…﴾, and the verse continues.

(fa-idhā) is a sudden-occurrence particle (fujāʾiyya), and its governing element is implied, not (yakhtaṣimūn), in disagreement with Abū al-Baqāʾ, because (yakhtaṣimūn) is a qualifier of (fariqān), as he himself said, and the complement of a qualifier cannot precede the qualified noun. It has been said that this ruling applies where the complement is not an adverb of time or place. The pronoun in (yakhtaṣimūn) refers to the two factions collectively; he did not say (yakhtaṣimān) for the sake of the rhyme (fāṣila). The wording of some of them suggests that the clause is a second predicate, but that, as you see, is untenable.

(hum) refers back to Thamud, because it is the name of the tribe. It has also been said that it refers to those previously mentioned, so as to include Ṣāliḥ, peace be upon him. In that case the two factions are: one consisting of Ṣāliḥ alone, and the second, his people.

What motivates this interpretation, as Ibn ʿĀdil mentioned, is the conjunction by (fa-), for it indicates that they became two factions immediately after the sending, without any interval. Yet his people would not become two factions except after some time.

In response: this is contradicted by His words, Exalted is He, ﴿We have taken omen from you and from those who are with you﴾, and the reckoning of each thing is according to what suits it. Moreover, it is permissible for the (fa-) to indicate mere sequence.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 27, verse 46:

It may be that the majority of the disbelieving group were the ones addressed; for this reason he addressed them with His words: ﴿O my people﴾, as is related of him in His statement, exalted is He: ﴿He said, "O my people"﴾, because he was treated as though he were the whole (community). That is, he said, peace be upon him, to the disbelieving faction among them, after he had witnessed from them what he witnessed of extreme obstinacy and stubbornness, to the point that they went so far in their arrogance as to say to him, peace be upon him: ﴿O Salih, bring us what you threaten us with, if you are one of the messengers﴾, speaking to them gently: "O my people."

﴿Why do you seek to hasten the evil before the good?﴾ That is, the punishment that will harm you, ﴿before the good﴾, that is, repentance, so that you postpone it until the time of its descent. They, out of their ignorance and error, used to say: if his threat comes to pass, then we will repent at that time; otherwise we will remain as we are. ﴿Why do you not seek forgiveness from Allah?﴾ That is, why do you not seek forgiveness from Him, exalted is He, before its descent, ﴿that you may be shown mercy﴾ by its acceptance; for the custom of Allah, exalted is He, is that repentance is not accepted at the time of the descent (of punishment).

He, peace be upon him, addressed them according to their own conjecture and their ignorance in this matter, that what they conjectured of repentance at that time would be corrupt, and that their haste in this was beyond reason.

The contrast between evil and good, in the sense you have heard, arises from one of them being good and the other evil. It has also been said that by "evil" is meant their denial of him, peace be upon him, and their disbelief in him, and by "good" is meant their affirmation and faith. The meaning of His words "Why do you seek to hasten" ... and so on is their reproach for hastening to deny him and disbelieve in him, and their urging to repent of that by abandoning denial and adopting faith. The sum of it is their reproach for committing denial at the time of the call rather than affirmation, and their urging to make amends for that.

That the wording might imply the absence of blame for committing denial after affirmation is something hardly worth turning to; and it is not hidden, after setting aside dispute over what has been mentioned, that the more fitting meaning, given what Allah, exalted is He, related of the people in Surah al-A'raf and what has come in the narrations, is the first meaning.

From here, what has been related from Mujahid, interpreting "the good" as the mercy of Allah, exalted is He, so that it corresponds to "the evil" interpreted as His punishment, exalted and majestic is He, and so that the meaning of their seeking punishment before mercy is their seeking it and not mercy, has been deemed weak. So reflect.

﴿They said, "We have taken omen."﴾ Its original form is تَطَيَّرْنا (*tatayyarna*), which is also recited in that form. The taʾ was assimilated into the ṭāʾ (*idgham*, assimilation of consonants), and a hamzat al-wasl (connecting hamza, a hamza pronounced only when beginning speech) was added so that the word could be pronounced at the beginning. *Taṭayyur* (taking omens from birds) means *tashāʾum* (considering something an ill omen). It is expressed by this term because, when they set out on journeys and passed by a bird, they would drive it away. If it passed *sānih* (from right to left, which they took as auspicious), they considered themselves blessed. If it passed *bārih* (from left to right, which they took as inauspicious), they considered themselves ill-starred. This is because one who passes by it in that manner cannot throw at it without turning aside. When they attributed good and evil to the bird, the term was borrowed for what was the cause of both from the decree and ordainment of Allah, exalted and majestic, or from the deed of the servant, which is the cause of mercy and blessing. That is, ﴿We have considered you and those with you as an ill omen﴾ in your religion, since hardships followed one another upon us, and they had been afflicted with drought, and we have not ceased to be in disagreement and division since you invented your religion. Their considering it an ill omen may be attributed to the whole group, or to each of the two parties joined together.

Page 212

﴿He said, "Your omen is with Allah"﴾: that is, your cause, from which there befalls you what befalls you of evil, is ﴿with Allah﴾, and that is His decree, glorified be He, or your deed recorded with Him, mighty and majestic. ﴿Rather, you are a people being tested﴾: this is a *iḍrāb* (a shift in discourse) from explaining the source of their omen, which is the beginning of what befalls them, to mentioning what calls them to it. That is: rather, you are a people who are being tested by the alternation of ease and hardship, or being punished, or Satan tempts you by his whispering to you the taking of omens. The verb ﴿tuftanūna﴾ comes with the second-person *tāʾ* (taʾ of address) in consideration of ﴿antum﴾ (you), which is common in the language of the Arabs. In a construction like this, it is permissible to read it as *yuftanūna* with the third-person *yāʾ* (yāʾ of absence) in consideration of the word ﴿qawm﴾ (a people), though that is rare in their language.

**Al-Alusi's commentary (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 27, verse 48:**

﴿And there were in the city﴾, that is, the city of Thamud and their town, which is al-Hijr, ﴿nine men of a group﴾. Rahṭ is a collective noun (ism jam', a noun that denotes a plural without being its regular plural form) applied to a band of people fewer than ten, as al-Raghib said. In al-Kashshaf it is said that it applies to three or to seven through ten. It has also been said that it applies up to forty, but this is not acceptable. Its origin, according to what is reported from al-Kirmani, is from al-tarhib, which means magnifying the mouthfuls and intensifying eating. The number has been made an attribute (idafa) to it.

There is disagreement about whether it is permissible to attach a number to a collective noun. Al-Akhfash held that it is not analogous (yanqas), and whatever is reported of such attachment is by way of rarity. Sibawayh explicitly stated that one does not say thalāth ghanam (three sheep).

Some held that it is permissible and analogous, though it is still rare. Others distinguished between a collective noun that denotes a small number, such as rahṭ, nafar and dawd, in which case it is permissible to attach the number to it, treating it as the plural of paucity (jam' qilla); and one that denotes a large number, or one used for both, in which case attaching the number to it is not permissible. Rather, when one wishes to specify it, it is brought with min (from), as in "five from the people." And the Almighty said: ﴿So take four of the birds﴾. This is the view of al-Mazini.

Several scholars chose that the attachment of nine to rahṭ here is based on the consideration that rahṭ, being a collective noun for a small number, is in the position of ashkhāṣ (persons) and similar plurals of paucity, to which numbers are attached, as in "nine persons" and "nine souls." This is what they mean when they say that the placement of rahṭ as the specification of nine is by way of meaning: it is as if it were said "nine persons." It has also been said: that is, "nine souls." The number is feminine because the word mentioned in the noble text is rahṭ, which is masculine. That is not one of the non-eloquent usages, like his saying: "thalāthat anfus wa thalāth dhawd" (three souls and three she-camels). Indeed, the estimation of what preceded is safer from objection. As for what has been said, that it means "nine men," it involves the oversight of what we have pointed out.

Furthermore, it is not meant that rahṭ means "person" or "soul." Rather, the nine among persons or souls are the rahṭ. So what is counted as nine is not what the rahṭ indicates of a group, such that there would be nine groups rather than nine individuals.

The Imam said: "The closer view is that the intended meaning is nine in a plural sense, since the apparent meaning of rahṭ is a group. It is then possible that they were tribes, and it is possible that they came under the number because of differences in their attributes and conditions, not differences in lineage." End of quote.

It has also been said: these nine were chieftains, and each of them had a rahṭ with him, and for this reason it was said "nine men of a group." Their names, according to Wahb, were: al-Hudhayl ibn Abd Rabb, Ghanm ibn Ghanm, Dibab ibn Mihrij, Umayr ibn Kurdiya, Asim ibn Makhzama, Subayt ibn Sadaqa, Sam'an ibn Safi, Qidar ibn Salif, and they were the ones who strove to slaughter the she-camel. They were the most arrogant of the people of Salih and among the sons of their nobles.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Abbas that their names were: Dam'i, Du'aym, Haramiyy, HurayM, Dawab, Sawab, Diyab, Mis'tah, and Qidar, who is the one who slaughtered the she-camel.

﴿They spread corruption in the land﴾, not in the city only, a pure corruption with no admixture of any righteousness, as His saying the Exalted clearly indicates: ﴿and do not reform﴾, that is, they do not do anything of reform, or they do not reform any of things. The meaning is that their continuous habit was that corruption, as the present tense indicates. The clause is in the position of an attribute of rahṭ or of "nine."

[Page 213]

﴿They said﴾ is a resumptive clause (istinaf) explaining some of the corruption they committed. That is, some of them said to others during the consultation about the matter of the righteous man, peace be upon him. According to what is related from Ibn 'Abbas, this was after they had hamstrung the she-camel, when he warned them of the punishment. As for his saying ﴿Enjoy yourselves in your homes for three days﴾ and so on: ﴿Swear to one another by God﴾ is an imperative from the verb "taqasama" (to swear mutually), meaning to make a pact by oath. It is in the position of the content of the speech (maqul al-qawl), and this is the view of the majority.

It has also been permitted that it be a past-tense verb, substituting for (they said) or a circumstantial clause (hal) from its subject, with or without the particle "qad." That is: they said, swearing mutually, and the content of the speech is ﴿We will certainly attack him and his family by night﴾ and so on. Abu Hayyan, on this view, permitted that (by God) be part of the content of the speech.

Al-bayat means surprising an enemy and attacking him by night while he is heedless. They intended to kill him, peace be upon him, and his family by night while they were heedless. It is related from Alexander (al-Iskandar) that he was advised to attack by night, and he said: "It is not the custom of kings to steal victory."

Ibn Abi Layla read "taqassamu" without an alif and with a shadda on the sin, and the meaning is as in the reading of the majority. Al-Hasan, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "latubayyitannahu" with the ta' as an address from some of them to others. Mujahid, Ibn Wathhab, Talhah and al-A'mash read "layubayyitannahu" with the ya' of the third person, and in this reading "taqasamu" can only be correct as a report (khabar), unlike the first two readings, which may be either a report or an imperative. The reason is that the imperative is an address, and if the sworn matter that follows is viewed as an address, the ta' of address is required; if it is viewed as the form of their words at the oath, the nun is required. As for the ya' of the absent third person, there is no basis for it. If it is taken as a report, then it is in the third person, as you say: "He swore he would certainly do it."

﴿Then we will certainly say to his heir﴾, that is, to the heir of Salih. By this is meant the one who seeks vengeance for his blood among his kinsmen if he is killed. He read "lataqulannahu" with the ta' by one who read "latubayyitannahu" in that way, and he read "layaqulannahu" with the ya' of the third person by one who read it so earlier. Humayd ibn Qays read the first with the ya' of the third person, and this one with the nun.

It has been said: the meaning according to this is, they swore to one another by God that a group among us would attack him by night, then all of us would say to his heir: ﴿We did not witness the destruction of his people﴾. That is, we were not present at their destruction. Here (mahlik) is either a verbal noun like (marji'), or the place of their destruction, taking it as a noun of place, or the time of their destruction, taking it as a noun of time.

What is meant is the negation of witnessing the destruction that took place in it. They chose to deny witnessing the destruction of his people rather than denying killing them, for the sake of emphasis, as if they said: we did not witness that, let alone that we undertook their destruction.

From this it is known that the killing of Salih, peace be upon him, is also negated, for one who did not kill his followers, how would he kill him? It has also been said that there is an ellipsis in the speech, that is: we did not witness the destruction of his people or his destruction. Abu Hayyan preferred this and then said: The omission of such a conjoined element is permissible in eloquent speech, as in the saying of God Most High: ﴿Garments that protect you from the heat﴾, meaning and from the cold. And the poet said:

*So there was not between the good, had he come back safe, Abu Hujr, except a few nights.*

That is: between the good and me. End of quotation. In it is what is not hidden.

It has also been said: the pronoun in (his people) refers to the heir, and by the people of the heir is meant Salih and his people. It was objected that if the people of the heir were meant, it would have said: "your people" or "his people." This was answered by saying that this is not necessary, since it has been read: ﴿Say to those who disbelieve: you will be overcome﴾ with address and with the third person. The reasoning for this is clear. Yes, the return of the pronoun to the heir is contrary to the apparent sense, as is not hidden. The majority read "muhlak" with a damma on the mim and a fatha on the lam, from (ahlaka), and in it are the three possibilities. Abu Bakr read "mahlak" with fatha on both, taking it as a verbal noun.

﴿And indeed we are truthful﴾ is coordinated with (we did not witness), as Al-Zajjaj held, and the meaning is: and we swear that we are truthful. It has also been permitted that the waw be circumstantial, that is: while the situation is that we are truthful in what we have mentioned. The difficulty has been raised about their claim to truthfulness in this, when they are rational people who shun lying as much as possible. It was answered that being present at a matter is not the same as directly performing it in common usage, since one does not say of someone who killed a man that he was present at his killing, even though presence is necessarily implied by performing it. So they swore according to the customary meaning, as is the habit in oaths, and they gave the adversary the impression that they meant its linguistic meaning. Thus they are truthful and not oath-breakers. And that they are among the people of common usage does not harm the matter; rather it yields a complete benefit. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is as if they believed that if they attacked Salih and attacked his family, combining the two attacks, and then they said: we did not witness the destruction of his people, mentioning one of them, they would be truthful, because they did both attacks together, not one of them.

It has been objected that one who did two things and denied one of them has no ambiguity in his lie. The ruse is only complete if they had done one thing and it was alleged against them that they did two things, and they denied the whole. For this reason the scholars did not differ that one who swore "I will not strike Zayd," and then struck Zayd and 'Amr, was an oath-breaker. But one who swore "I will not strike Zayd and 'Amr," or "I will not eat two loaves," and then ate one of them, is a point of scholarly disagreement regarding whether he breaks the oath. The truth is that acquitting them of lying in what was mentioned is not necessary, so that one would have to strain to justify it. They are the ones who lied against God Most High and His Messenger, peace be upon him, and committed what is worse than lying in what was mentioned. Al-Zamakhshari's aim was to support what he and his people claim, the doctrine of the goodness and ugliness of acts by reason, by the agreement of the people of Salih with it, and this can hardly be achieved for him.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 27, verses 50–51:**

﴿And they schemed a scheme﴾ by this agreement. ﴿And We schemed a scheme while they were not perceiving﴾. That is: We destroyed them with a destruction unlike any customary one, or We requited their scheme from where they did not expect. ﴿So see how was the end of their scheme﴾. This begins an explanation of what followed from the scheming they undertook. The apparent reading is that (how, *kayfa*) is the predicate (*khabar*) placed before (*kāna*, "was"), and ("the end," *ʿāqibah*) is its subject (*ism*). That is: the end of their scheme was an occurrence in a wondrous manner from which one should take warning. The clause is in the position of an accusative, as the object of (*unẓur*, "see"), and it is suspended (*muʿallaqah*) from the place of the interrogative. The intended meaning is: reflect on that.

God's words, ﴿that We destroyed them﴾, are in the sense of a verbal noun (*maṣdar*) that stands as a substitute (*badal*) for "the end of their scheme," or as the predicate of an omitted subject (*mubtadaʾ*), which is the pronoun referring to "the end." The clause clarifies the vagueness in "the end of their scheme." That is: it is the manner of Our destruction and annihilation of them. ﴿And their people﴾, those who were not among them in actually carrying out the night attack, ﴿all of them﴾, such that not one of them escaped. Or it is with a governed preposition understood: for Our destruction of them, or with Our destruction of them. This would be a reason for what is indicated by the command to look at the manner of the end of their affair, of terror and horror.

Some have permitted it to be a substitute for (*kayfa*). Others said: this is not permitted, because a substitute for an interrogative requires repeating its particle, as in your saying: "How is Zayd, healthy or sick?"

It is also permitted that it be the predicate of (*kāna*), and then (*kayfa*) would be a circumstantial accusative (*ḥāl*). Its governing element would be (*kāna*) or what the speech indicates of the meaning of a verb. It is also permitted that (*kāna*) be complete, with (*kayfa*) being a circumstantial accusative only. The permissible possibilities regarding ﴿that We destroyed them﴾ are not hidden.

Most readers read (*innā*) with a kasra on the hamzah, so (*kayfa*) is the predicate of (*kāna*), and ("the end") is its subject. The clause ("indeed We destroyed them") is a resumptive clause (*istiʾnāf*) explaining the end, and it is permitted that it be the predicate of an omitted subject.

Al-Khafaji said: The apparent reading is that it is the affair (*shaʾn*) or its pronoun, and not anything else that requires a returning pronoun, so that it might be objected to for lacking a returning pronoun. It is not an objection that many grammarians prohibited omitting the pronoun of the affair in the nominative, for that is not accepted. It is permitted that (*kāna*) be complete and (*kayfa*) be a circumstantial accusative, as has preceded. The majority did not permit it to be incomplete with the predicate being the clause ("that We destroyed them"), because of the lack of a linking element.

It was said: it is permitted, and it suffices for the link that there be something that refers back to the related element of the subject, since its returning to itself is not necessary, and this is a strained view. It only holds according to the school of al-Akhfash, who said: when part of a clause takes the place of a genitive construct (*muḍāf*) whose complement refers back, it suffices with that. Other grammarians reject this. Abu Hayyan permitted, on both readings, that (*kāna*) be superfluous (*zāʾidah*), with ("the end") as the subject (*mubtadaʾ*), and (*kayfa*) as its fronted predicate.

Page 215.
