Ubayy read ﴿that We destroyed them﴾ with (*an*), the particle which by its nature puts the imperfect verb into the subjunctive. The previously mentioned possibilities for the verbal noun apply to it, as in the reading "*innā*" with a fatha on the hamzah.

Furthermore, there is disagreement about the manner of the destruction. It is related that Salih, peace be upon him, had a place of prayer in al-Hijr, in a ravine where he would pray. They said: Salih claims that he will be rid of us after three days, so we will rid ourselves of him and his family before the three days. So they went out to the ravine and said: when he comes to pray, we will kill him. Then we will return to his family and kill them. So God sent a rock from the mountain opposite them, and they hastened away, and it closed over the mouth of the ravine upon them. Their people did not know where they were, and they did not know what had been done to their people. God punished each of them in his place and saved Salih and those with him. It was also said that they came at night with their swords drawn.

God had sent angels to fill the house of Salih, peace be upon him, and they pelted them with stones. They saw the stones but did not see the one throwing them. The rest of the people perished by the Cry. It was also said that they resolved to ambush him, peace be upon him, and his family. God informed Salih of this, and he went out from among them. Then God destroyed them by the Cry, and that was on Sunday.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 27, verse 52:

﴿So those are their houses﴾ is a sentence confirming what precedes it. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿ruined﴾ means empty, or fallen and collapsed, its upper parts over its lower parts, as related from Ibn 'Abbas. ﴿Because of what they did wrong﴾ means because of their wrongdoing mentioned above. It is a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to "their houses," and the operative element in it is the sense of the demonstrative (al-ishara).

'Isa ibn 'Umar recited "ruined" (khawiyah) in the nominative, on the basis that it is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "they are ruined"; or a second predicate of "those" (tilka); or the predicate of it, with "their houses" in apposition (badal).

Their houses here are those about which the Prophet (ﷺ) said to his companions in the year of Tabuk: "Do not enter upon these punished people unless you are weeping," and the hadith continues. They are in Wadi al-Qura, between Madinah and Syria.

﴿Indeed in that﴾ means in what has been mentioned of the astonishing destruction because of their wrongdoing ﴿is a sign﴾, a great lesson ﴿for a people who know﴾. That is, [it is] of the kind of things that can be known; or for a people characterised by knowledge. It has been said: "for a people who know this story," but this is not correct. In this verse, according to what has been said, there is an indication that wrongdoing can be a cause for the ruin of dwellings.

It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "I find in the Book of Allah, exalted is He, that wrongdoing ruins houses," and he recited this verse. And in the Torah: "Son of Adam, do not wrong, lest your house be ruined." It has been said that this is an allusion to the destruction of the wrongdoer, since the ruin of his house follows his destruction. It is not hidden that wrongdoing, in the sense of oppression and transgression against the servants of Allah, exalted is He, being a cause of the ruin of dwellings is something widely observed in these eras; but that it means disbelief is not so. Yes, it is not far-fetched that there will come a day for the disbelievers when their houses will be ruined, God willing, exalted is He.

And We saved those who believed, [namely Salih] and those with him among the believers, ﴿and who had been pious﴾, [keeping away] from disbelief and sins with a constant piety; therefore they were singled out for deliverance. It is related that those who believed in him (peace be upon him) numbered four thousand. Salih set out with them to Hadramawt, and when he entered it he died there; for this reason it was named by this name. The believers built in it a city called Hadhura (Hadurā), and the discussion of that has already preceded, so recall it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on Surah 27, verse 54:

﴿And Lut﴾ is in the accusative (*mansub*) by an implied verb coordinated with "We sent" at the beginning of the story of Salih, peace be upon him, and it falls under the scope of the oath together with it. That is: "And We sent Lut, ﴿when he said to his people﴾." The phrase "when" (*idh*) is an adverbial complement to the sending, on the basis that what is meant is an extended period during which the sending took place, along with what passed between him and his people of circumstances and statements.

It has been permitted that it be accusative by the implied verb "mention" (*udhkur*), coordinated with what came before, as the coordination of one story upon another, with "when" (*idh*) being a substitute for it, a substitute of inclusion (*badal ishtimal*). But this is not the right view.

It has been said that it is coordinated with "Salihan" (Salih). This was objected to on the grounds that it is not sound, because "Salihan" is either a substitute or an explicative apposition (*'atf bayan*) for "akhahum" (their brother), and it has been restricted by a qualifier placed before it, namely "to Thamud." So if [Lut] were coordinated with it, he would be restricted by that qualifier, which is not valid, because Lut, peace be upon him, was not sent to Thamud. The restriction is binding when the qualifier comes first, unlike when it comes later.

It has been said: the binding of this is not accepted, since it is permissible to coordinate it with the whole of the qualifier and the qualified together. However, this goes against what is customary in rhetorical discourse (*khitabiyyat*), and committing the like of it is a forced reading that is not fitting. It has also been permitted that it be coordinated with "those who believed."

Page 216

It was objected that this does not suit the methods of narrating stories, by coordinating one of the two stories with the other, rather than with the continuation and appendix of the first, as is not hidden.

﴿Do you commit the abomination﴾: that is, do you perform the deed most extreme in ugliness and foulness? The interrogation is one of denunciation (*istifham inkari*). His words, exalted is He, ﴿while you see﴾, form a circumstantial clause (*jumla haliyya*) from the subject of (*ta'tun*, "you commit"), serving to emphasize the denunciation, for indulging in what is ugly while knowing its ugliness is more reprehensible and more shameful. (*Tubsirun*, "you see") is from the sight of the heart. That is: do you do it while you know with certain knowledge that it is as such?

It is also permissible that it be from the sight of the eye, meaning: while you see and witness that it is an abomination, by treating that as manifest, placing it in the position of what is perceived by the senses. It has been said that the object of (*tubsirun*) is, in its literal sense, among perceptible things, meaning: while you see the traces of the sinners before you; or: while some of you look at one another without concealing themselves or refraining from displaying it, due to your lack of concern for it. The way in which the clause, on both possibilities, also serves to emphasize the denunciation is clear.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 27, verse 55:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, you approach men lustfully⁠—﴾ is a repetition of the denunciation, and an explanation of what they were committing of the abomination by way of explicit statement after ambiguity. Emphasizing the sentence with the two particles of emphasis (inna and the lam of emphasis) serves to signal that its content is something no one would believe to have occurred, owing to its utter repulsiveness. The mention of the object by the title of manhood (rujuliyyah) rather than maleness (dhukuriyyah) serves to express disapproval and to show that it is specific to the sons of Adam. The stating of the reason for the approach as lust (shahwah) is a disapproval upon a disapproval, since they are not in its proper place; and in this there is an indication that they are mistaken in its proper place in action.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿instead of women﴾, meaning: going beyond the women who are the loci of desire, it is an indication that they are mistaken in it by abandonment. From what we have mentioned it is known that (shahwah, "lust") is an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu) for "approach," and it has been permitted that it be a circumstantial accusative (hal).

﴿Nay, you are a people who are ignorant﴾, meaning: you act as the ignorant act regarding the ugliness of that; or they do not know the consequence; or "ignorance" here carries the sense of foolishness and wantonness, meaning: rather, you are a people who are foolish and licentious. So said al-Kashshaf. And whatever the case, it does not contradict His saying, exalted is He: (while you see). Al-Tibi did not accept that and claimed that the word of retraction (bal) rejects it, and he explained the verse by saying: when He, exalted is He, denounced their act in general terms, calling it an abomination, and restricted it by the circumstance that establishes the basis of the problem, to complete the denunciation with His saying, exalted is He: (while you see), He wished to add further rebuke and denunciation, so He unveiled the reality of that abomination and indicated what He indicated; then He retracted from the whole with His saying, glorified is He: (Nay, you are) ... etc., meaning: how can it be said to one who commits this indecency while you know? So the retraction particle gave the pronoun (you) priority and made them an ignorant people, and he turned (you are ignorant) into an address of rebuke and reproach. End of quote; and there is scrutiny in it.

The view that there is a shift (iltifat) here has been stated by others too: it is a shift from the third person in (a people) to the second person in (you are ignorant). Al-Fadil al-Salkuti criticized it, saying it is an error, since the intended "people" is not the people of Lot, such that what is referred to in both expressions would be one, as is the condition of a shift; rather it is a universal meaning applied to the people of Lot, peace be upon him.

Some eminent scholars said: the address in it, despite it being an attribute of (a people) which is an apparent noun, is of the type of the absent for the sake of the meaning, since it is united with (you) by being interpreted as referring to it. Others, numerous, considered it of what has the address predominating (taghlib); and it was objected that in predominance there is a figurative usage (tajawwuz), and there is no figurative usage here.

It was answered that forms like (you are ignorant) are set for address with a group not mentioned by a third-person expression, and here it is not so; so how could there not be figurative usage in it? It was also said: their saying that in predominance there is figurative usage is an exit that goes out as the general case. Al-Fadil al-Salkuti said: His saying, exalted is He: (Nay, you are) ... etc. is of metaphor with regard to what was: the addressee in (you are ignorant) is with regard to the people being addressed in the expression (you), so there is no objection that the word was not used in other than what it was set for, nor the compositional structure, and the verb was not ascribed to other than what it belongs to, so there is no metaphor there. Understand.

(End of the nineteenth part of Ruh al-Ma'ani. Following it, God willing, is the twentieth part, whose beginning is: "So was not the answer of his people...")

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 27, verse 56:

Page 2

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿So the answer of his people was only that they said: "Expel the family of Lut from your town; indeed they are people who keep themselves pure."﴾ That is, whoever follows his religion. The expulsion of him (peace be upon him) is understood a fortiori (min bab awla). Some of the verifying scholars (al-muhaqqiqun) said: what is meant by "the family of Lut" is Lut (peace be upon him) and those who follow his religion, just as what is meant by "the children of Adam" is Adam and his descendants. In either case, his wife (peace be upon him) is not included among them. His, exalted be He, saying "illa" (except) and so on is a restrictive exception (istithna' mufarragh) occupying the position of the subject of kana (the ism of kana). Al-Hasan and Ibn Abi Ishaq read "jawabu" in the nominative, so that it occupies the position of the predicate (khabar). The detailed analysis of such a construction has already been discussed. And in His, exalted be He, saying "from your town," the attribution of the town to "kum" (you) serves to diminish the matter of the expulsion. His, majestic and exalted, saying "indeed they are people who keep themselves pure" is a justification for the command in a manner that carries mockery; that is, they are people who claim purity and cleanliness from our deeds, or from filth, and consider our action filthy, while they are pretending to display what is not in them. The apparent meaning is that this answer came from them at the final stage of his (peace be upon him) admonitions through command and prohibition, and not that no other speech came from them besides it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 27, verse 57:

﴿So We saved him and his family﴾, i.e., after the destruction of the people. The fa' here is fasihah (the fa' that indicates an implied condition). ﴿Except his wife; We had decreed her﴾, i.e., We had decreed her existence ﴿to be among those who remained behind﴾, i.e., those who remained in the punishment. The noun (the existence of "her") has been supplied because decree relates to the act and not to the essence itself. Another verse supports this, namely His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We decreed that she was among those who remained behind﴾.

Abu Bakr read "qadarnaha" with the dal lightened (qadarnaha, pronounced with a short dal).

And We rained upon them a rain (غَيْرَ مَعْهُودٍ, unlike any ordinary rain) ﴿And We rained upon them a rain, so evil was the rain of those who were warned﴾. That is, "how wretched was the rain of those who were warned, their rain." This has already passed, so return to what we mentioned there.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 27, verse 59:**

﴿Say: Praise be to God, and peace be upon His servants whom He has chosen.﴾ This comes after Allah, exalted is He, related to His Messenger (ﷺ) the stories of the aforementioned prophets and their accounts, which speak to the perfection of His power, the greatness of His majesty, and what He granted them of overpowering signs and dazzling miracles, which indicate the nobility of their rank and the soundness of their reports. Through their tongues He made clear the soundness of Islam and monotheism, the falsehood of disbelief and associating partners with God, and that whoever follows them is guided, while whoever turns away from them has fallen into the pits of destruction. He also expanded the noble breast of the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, with the various kinds of divine knowledge contained within those stories, and illuminated his heart with the lights of the sacred dispositions flowing from the world of holiness. Through this he confirmed the meaning of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed, you receive the Qur'an from One who is All-Wise, All-Knowing.﴾

He (ﷺ) was commanded to praise Him in the most complete manner for those blessings, and to send peace upon all the prophets, peace be upon them, among whom are those whose stories have been related and whose traces have been explained, in acknowledgment of their virtue and in fulfilment of the right of their precedence and their striving in the religion. Therefore, the "chosen servants" here refers to the prophets, peace be upon them, by the indication of the context, and by His saying, exalted is He, in another verse: ﴿And peace upon the messengers.﴾ It has also been said that this is a command to him (ﷺ) to praise God for the destruction of the destroyers among the disbelieving nations, and to send peace upon the prophets and their followers who were saved, may Allah's blessings be upon them. Sending peace upon non-prophets is permissible when it is not done independently, a matter on which there is no disagreement regarding its permissibility. Perhaps the fair-minded person will not doubt its permissibility upon the believing servants of Allah in general. It has also been said: it is a command to him, upon him be prayers and peace, to praise Him for what Allah, majestic and exalted is He, singled him out with, namely the lifting of the punishment of annihilation from his community, and their difference from those before them among the nations whose stories are related, who were wiped out by punishment; and to send peace upon the prophets who endured the hardships of the message.

Therefore, the "chosen ones" here refers to the prophets exclusively. Abd ibn Humayd, al-Bazzar, Ibn Jarir, and others related from Ibn Abbas that he said regarding them:

"They are the companions of Muhammad (ﷺ), whom Allah chose for His Prophet, upon him be prayers and peace."

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir also related from Sufyan al-Thawri that he said regarding ﴿And peace﴾ etc.: "It was revealed concerning the companions of Muhammad (ﷺ) exclusively." This clearly indicates the permissibility of sending peace upon non-prophets independently, as is the view of the Hanbalis and others. The discussion of all these opinions is connected to what precedes it. Al-Zamakhshari, however, considered it to be of the type of *iqtida'* (an abrupt beginning), as if it were a fresh sermon, saying: He commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to recite these verses, which speak through proofs of His oneness, His power over everything, and His wisdom, namely His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Is it God…?﴾ etc., and to begin by praising Him and sending peace upon His prophets and the chosen servants. In this there is a fine instruction and a guidance to a beautiful etiquette, and an incitement to seek blessing from the two mentions (God's praise and peace upon the prophets), and to seek support from their standing for the acceptance of what is conveyed to the listeners, their attentiveness to it, and the placing in their hearts of the station that the hearer desires. The scholars, preachers, and admonishers have indeed inherited this etiquette from generation to generation: they praise God and send blessings upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) before every beneficial knowledge, before every admonition and reminder, and at the beginning of every sermon. Those who correspond in writing followed them, placing it at the beginning of their books concerning conquests, congratulations, and other events of significance. End of quotation. Perhaps making this a transition (*takhallus*) from the stories of the prophets, peace be upon them, to what happened to him (ﷺ) with the polytheists is more fitting. The most remote of the opinions is that it is connected to what precedes it, and that this is a command to Lut, peace be upon him, to praise God for destroying the disbelievers of his people, and to send peace upon the one whom He chose with protection from indecencies and deliverance from destruction. This is because it does not fit with what follows it and requires an assumed clause ("and We said to him"). Ibn Atiyyah attributed this opinion to al-Farra', and said: "This is a barbarism from al-Farra'."

The apparent reading is that *salamun* (سَلامٌ) is the subject (*mubtada'*) and what follows it is its predicate (*khabar*), and the clause is conjoined to ﴿Praise be to God﴾, falling within the scope of the speech.

Abu al-Samal read "al-hamdu lillahi" with a *fatha* on the lam (لِلَّهِ), and ﴿ā-llāhu﴾ with a long vowel, by converting the hamzah of interrogation into an *alif*; the original form is *a-allāhu* (أاللَّهُ).

﴿Is God better, or what they associate?﴾ The apparent reading is that *mā* (ما) is a relative pronoun, and its returning pronoun is omitted, meaning: "(Is God), whose great affairs you have mentioned, better, or that which they associate with Him of idols?" *Khayr* (خَيْرٌ) is an elative of preference (*af'al al-tafdil*). The purpose of this alternative is to rebuke the disbelievers from His side, exalted and majestic is He, and to belittle their feeble opinions and mock them. For it is clear that there is nothing good whatsoever in what they associate with Him, exalted is He, so that one could weigh it against Him who is pure good. It has also been said that *khayr* here is not for comparison, like in your saying: "Prayer is good," meaning "a good among goods." The preferred view is the first, and Abu Hayyan favoured it, saying: "This type of elative often occurs where it is known and established that there is no partnership there, and it is mentioned only as a means of binding the opponent and drawing his attention to the error. The interrogative in such cases intends to bind him to acknowledging that preference is restricted to one side and absent from the other." He also favoured that the intended goodness is goodness in essence. It has also been said: goodness is in what relates to them. In the statement there is an omission in two places, and the estimate is: "Is the worship of God, exalted is He, better, or the worship of what they associate?" It has also been said: *mā* is verbal-nominal (*maṣdariyya*), and the omission is in one place, and the estimate is: "Is the monotheism of God better, or their associating?" But there is no need for all of this. In any case, the pronoun of the third person refers to Quraysh and others like them among the polytheists. It has also been said that it refers to those destroyed, but this is not correct.

The majority read *tushrikūna* (تُشْرِكُونَ) with a *ta'* above, directing the address to those disbelievers we mentioned, and this is more fitting with what follows it of the context of the noble arrangement. Abu al-Baqa' made this sentence part of the statement commanded, and it was objected that this is contradicted by His saying: ﴿So We caused to grow…﴾ etc., for this clearly indicates that the rebuke comes from Him, exalted and majestic, directly. He interpreted it as a report from him, upon him be prayers and peace, of what he was commanded to say in worshipping Him, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves…﴾ This is a clear artificiality without any need for it.

In some reports it is stated: "When he (ﷺ) recited this verse, he would say: 'Rather, God is better, more enduring, more exalted, and more generous.'"

[Translation begins]

The *am* (or) in His saying, ﴿Or who created the heavens and the earth?﴾ is disjunctive (*munqati'ah*), not conjunctive (*muttasilah*) like the preceding one. The *bal* (rather) that is implied according to the first reading, which is the reading of al-Hasan, Qatadah, 'Asim and Abu 'Amr, is for *al-idrab* (a turning away from one point to another) and *al-intiqal* (a transition) from rebuke (*tabkit*), by way of allusion, to explicit statement, in direct address, in a manner more manifest than it, for greater emphasis and intensification. As for the second reading, the *bal* is for repeating the rebuke and reiterating the obligation, like its similar instances that follow. The interrogative *hamzah* (the question particle) is for compelling them to affirm the truth, which no one with even minimal discernment can avoid affirming. The *min* (who) is a subject (*mubtada'*) whose predicate is omitted, together with *am* the coordinating particle that balances the *hamzah*, relying on what preceded in the first interrogation. Except for ﴿that you associate⁠﴾, which is implied here with the second-person *ta'* of address according to both readings together, and likewise in the four instances that follow. The meaning is: or who created the two regions of the physical world and the origins of the benefits that lie between them? ﴿And sent down for you⁠﴾ is a shift (*iltifat*) to address the disbelievers according to the first reading, to intensify the rebuke and obligation. The *lam* is causal, i.e., and sent down for your sake and benefit. ﴿from the sky water⁠﴾, i.e., a kind of it, which is rain. ﴿and We caused to grow thereby⁠﴾ according to the requirement of wisdom, not that growth is dependent upon it by necessity of reason. It was said: i.e., We caused to grow at its presence. ﴿gardens⁠﴾, plural of *hadiqah*, which, as in al-Bahr (*al-Bahr al-Muhit*), is an orchard, whether or not it is enclosed by a wall. This is the apparent sense of the unrestricted statement of Ibn 'Abbas, where he explained *al-hada'iq* to Ibn al-Azraq as "gardens" without restriction. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is an orchard surrounded by a wall, from *al-ihdaq*, which is encompassing. This is also transmitted from al-Dahhak. Al-Raghib said: it is a piece of land possessing water, named *hadiqah* by analogy with the pupil of the eye in its shape and in the presence of water within it. Perhaps the more evident is what is in al-Bahr. It seems that the reason an orchard is called *hadiqah* is that it is characteristic of it to encircle the walls or to turn the eyes toward it and to look at it. ﴿full of delight⁠﴾, i.e., possessing beauty and splendor by which the beholder is delighted and gladdened. ﴿It was not for you⁠﴾, i.e., it was not proper for you, nor within your power, ﴿to cause to grow their trees⁠﴾, let alone creating their fruit and all their wondrous attributes. ﴿Is there a god with Allah?⁠﴾ Is the predicate omitted here: "is it better, or what you associate?" This is what al-Zamakhshari chose, and others followed him.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the predicate is supplied as "he disbelieves in His blessing and associates others with Him," and similar in meaning. Abu al-Fadl al-Razi said in his book *al-Lawami'*: there must be an implied counterpart (*mu'adil*), and that implied element is like the stated one, because of the indication of the context (*dalalat al-fahwa*). The estimate is: or who created the heavens and the earth as one who did not create? Likewise it is estimated in its counterparts. He made explicit in another place what is implied here, as in His saying: ﴿Is then He who creates like one who does not create?⁠﴾ End. Perhaps the better is what the Neighbor of Allah (al-Zamakhshari) chose, and the same is said of what follows.

Al-A'mash read *aman* with lightening (the single *hamzah*), so that the *hamzah* is interrogative and *man* is a substitute (*badal*) for the Majestic Name. The fronting of the two complements of the sending down before its object is for the reason repeatedly mentioned: arousing eagerness for what is deferred. And the shift to the first person plural with the "We" of majesty is to emphasize the exclusivity of the act to His Essence by way of the correspondence of the contrast, and to indicate that the producing of those various gardens, differing in kinds, attributes, colors, tastes, scents and forms, together with their brilliant beauty and marvelous splendor, from one water, is a great matter which only He, alone, mighty and majestic, is almost able to bring about. He gave a hint of this by His saying: ﴿It was not for you⁠﴾ and so on, whether it is an attribute of *hada'iq* or a circumstantial clause (*hal*) or a resumptive statement (*isti'nafan*). The singularity of its previously mentioned attribute, namely *dhat bahjah* (full of delight), is because the meaning is "a collection of gardens full of delight," and this is common in broken plurals, like His saying: (purified spouses). Likewise the situation regarding the pronoun in "their trees."

Ibn Abi 'Ablah read *dhawat* in the plural, *bahajah* with an open *ha'*.

﴿Is there a god with Allah?⁠﴾, i.e., is there another god existing with Allah, the One who mentioned some of His acts which no one but Him is almost able to perform, so that it might be imagined that He is made a partner with Him in worship? This is a rebuke to them by denying divinity of what they associate with Him, Mighty and Majestic, within a general negation, in the demonstrative manner, after rebuking them by denying superiority from Him through the alternative mentioned. For just as anyone with minimal discernment cannot deny the total absence of superiority from Him, he likewise almost cannot deny the absence of divinity from Him altogether, especially after noticing the absence of its rulings from anything other than Him, Mighty and Majestic. The situation is the same with the four instances that follow. It was said: the meaning is the negation that there be another god with Him in creation, and what is conjoined to it. However, the rebuke is not by that negation alone, for they do not deny it, as indicated by His saying: ﴿And if you asked them who created the heavens and the earth, they would surely say, "Allah."⁠﴾ Rather, the rebuke is by their associating with Him what they admit is not shared with Him in what is mentioned of the requirements of divinity. It is as if it were said: is there another god with Allah in the peculiar properties of divinity so that he is made a partner with Him in worship? It was also said: the meaning is, is there another one who is joined with Him and made a partner in worship while He alone, exalted is His majesty, is unique in creation and bringing into being? So the denial is for reproach and rebuke with the existence of what is denied, not the negation itself, as in the two previous readings. It was preferred because it is more evident and agrees with His saying: ﴿And there was not with Him any god⁠﴾, and is more fitting to the proper circumstance, because it conveys the negation of the existence of another god with Him altogether, not merely the negation of His being joined with Him in creation and its branches.

Hisham, on the authority of Ibn 'Amir, read *a-alah* with a prolonged vowel between the two *hamzahs* and the second rendered between-between (*bayna bayna*, an intermediate sound). Abu 'Amr, Nafi' and Ibn Kathir read *a-ilahan* with a fatha, on the basis of an implied verb suitable to the context, such as "do you make," or "do you claim," or "do you associate."

﴿Rather, they are a people who deviate⁠﴾. This is a turning away and a transition from rebuking them by way of direct address to explaining the evil of their state and reporting it to others. *Ya'dilun* is from *al-'udul*, meaning deviation, i.e., rather they are a people whose habit is to turn away from the path of truth altogether and to deviate from uprightness in every matter. Therefore they do what they do of turning away from the clear truth, which is monotheism, and clinging to manifest falsehood, which is associating partners. It was said: it is from *al-'adl*, meaning equivalence, i.e., they equate others with Him, Exalted, from among their gods. This was transmitted from Ibn Zayd. The first is more fitting to what precedes it. It was also said: the speech on this reading is devoid of benefit.

[Translation ends]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 27, verse 61:

﴿Is it not He Who made the earth a stable abode﴾ i.e., He made it such that humans and animals can settle upon it, by bringing forth some of it from the water, spreading it out (dahw) and leveling it, in accordance with what their benefits depend upon. "Qararan" (a stable abode) here means "mustaqirran" (stable, settled), not "qarrah ghayra mudtaraba" (a firm, non-agitated place) as al-Tabarsi claimed, for the benefit is more complete on this reading. If the verb "ja'ala" (made) is transitive in the sense of "making into," then the two accusatives are two objects; otherwise the second is a circumstantial accusative (hal muqaddarah). The clause "Is it not He Who made" etc. is, as has been said, a substitution (badal) for His words "Is it not He Who created the heavens" and the remaining three clauses that follow it, and the ruling for all of them is one. Some eminent scholars said: The more evident view is that each of them is a transition (idrab wa intiqal) from rebuking by what precedes to rebuking by another aspect, falling under the obligation (ilzam) from one direction or another. Abu Muslim (sic: the author of al-Kashshaf) adopted the substitution view, and we will quote, God willing, from the author of al-Kashf what clarifies its meaning. ﴿And made rivers within it﴾ i.e., between its midst (awsatuha), plural of "khalal," whose origin is a gap between two things. Thus it is an adverbial of place occupying the position of a circumstantial clause from His words ﴿rivers﴾, and this is permissible despite its being indefinite because the circumstantial or the second object of "ja'ala" is preceded; and "anhaaran" (rivers) is the first object. The intended meaning of "rivers" is what flows in them, not the channel, which is the cleft. That is, He made within them flowing rivers from which you benefit. ﴿And made for it﴾ i.e., for the good of its affairs ﴿firm mountains (rawasi)﴾ i.e., stable mountains, for they have a customary effect which wisdom requires, in keeping the inhabited parts exposed and preserving them from shaking with their inhabitants, and the waters that feed the rivers, which lead to their freshness, in their lowlands, among other things. Some have mentioned among the benefits of mountains the formation of minerals in them and the springing of wells from their lowlands, and did not address the benefit of their preventing the earth from movement and tilting. They justified not addressing it by saying that had this been the intention, it would have been mentioned right after "made the earth a stable abode." Whoever is fair sees that the mountains' preventing the earth from movement and tilting, which would remove the earth from the realm of benefit and make its existence like its non-existence, is among the most important things mentioned here, since it is part of what the good of its affairs and the elevation of its status depend upon. The mention of "for it" rather than "in it" or "upon it" clearly indicates that what is intended is this kind of benefit, so reflect.

And returning the pronoun in "for it" to the rivers, so that the meaning would be "and made for their feeding firm mountains from whose lowlands water springs and feeds them," is not without its problems. ﴿And made between the two seas﴾ i.e., the sweet and the salt, according to al-Dahhak; or the seas of Persia and Rome, according to al-Hasan; or the seas of Iraq and Syria, according to al-Suddi; or the two seas of heaven and earth, according to Mujahid; ﴿a barrier﴾ a separator that prevents mixing. The discussion of the verification of this has already passed, so recall it. ﴿Is there a god with Allah?﴾ in existence, or in the origination of these wonders, as has passed. ﴿Nay, most of them do not know﴾ i.e., not any thing of worth; and for this reason they do not comprehend the falsity of the polytheism they hold, despite its complete evidentness.

[p. 7 marker follows]

﴿Is He who answers the one in distress when he calls upon Him?﴾ The one in distress (al-muḍṭarr) is one whom a hardship has driven to need, and whom a calamity has compelled to seek refuge and to plead humbly before Allah, Mighty and Majestic. It is the passive participle (ism mafʿūl) of al-idṭirār, which is a reflexive form (iftiʿāl) from ḍarūrah (necessity). To this meaning goes Ibn ʿAbbas's explanation of it as "the one who is exhausted" (al-majhūd), and al-Suddi's explanation as "the one who has no power or strength." It has also been said that what is meant is the sinner when he seeks forgiveness. The definite article in it, according to what has been said, is generic (li-l-jins, denoting the category) and not comprehensive (li-l-istighrāq, denoting every individual), so that it would not follow that every person in distress is answered, for how many a person in distress is not answered.

Some have permitted taking it in the comprehensive sense, but the answering is restricted by the Will (al-mashīʾah), as occurs in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿so He removes that for which you call upon Him, if He wills﴾. Despite this, the Prophet (ﷺ) disliked that a person should say, "O Allah, forgive me if You will."

He (ﷺ) also said: "Indeed, He, glorified is He, has no one who compels Him." Some of the Muʿtazilah (a rationalist theological school) restrict it to knowledge of what is in the interest (maṣlaḥah), because they make it obligatory for Him, exalted is He, to safeguard the interests of His creatures. The author of al-Farāʾid (Ṣāḥib al-Farāʾid) said: No one in distress calls upon Him without being answered, and the benefit of his supplication returns to him, either in this world or in the Hereafter. That is because supplication is the seeking of something. If he is not given that very thing, he is given something better than it; or if he is not given it at this time, he is given it afterward. End of quotation.

Its apparent meaning is to take it in the comprehensive sense without restriction on the answering. It is not hidden that if answering is interpreted as giving the petitioner what he asked for in the manner he asked, and not as ending his request, whether by the aforementioned giving or by something else, then what he mentioned does not hold. Al-ʿAllamah al-Ṭībī said: The definite article is for a specific reference (li-l-ʿahd), because the context of the discourse concerns the polytheists, and this is indicated by the address in His saying: ﴿and makes you successors﴾. The purpose is to alert that when they were in distress during the calamities of time and the afflictions of the age, they would turn to Allah, Exalted is He, and not to the partners and idols. What indicates this alerting is His saying: ﴿Is there a god with Allah? Little do you remember.﴾ The author of al-Miftāḥ (Ṣāḥib al-Miftāḥ) said: When a matter afflicted them, they would call upon Allah, Exalted is He, and not their idols. So the meaning is: when a matter or a blow of the calamities of time afflicts you, to the point that you despair of life, who will answer you in removing it and make you, after that, disposing of the lands like successors? ﴿Is there a god with Allah?﴾ Thus the one in distress is not general, nor is the supplication, for it is specific to a case like that of the ship. They were answered in it in His saying: ﴿until, when you are in the ship and they sail with them…﴾, the verse. End of quotation.

And you know that this is extremely far-fetched. Perhaps the preferable reading is the generic sense with restriction by the Will, and He, glorified is He, wills only what wisdom requires, and supplication for something is among the ordinary causes for it. So understand.

﴿and removes the evil﴾, that is, He lifts from the human being what befalls him of the matter that afflicts him. It has been said that removal (kashf) is more general than repelling (daf') and lifting (raf'), and the conjunction of this clause to what precedes it is in the category of conjoining the general to the specific (ʿaṭf al-ʿāmm ʿalā al-khāṣṣ). It has also been said that the meaning is "and removes his evil," that is, the one in distress's evil, or "and removes the evil from him," and the conjunction is in the category of explanatory conjunction (ʿaṭf al-tafsīr), for answering the one in distress is the removal of the evil from him, by reason of which he became in distress. And this, as you see, is [far-fetched].

﴿and makes you successors of the earth﴾, that is, successors of those before you among the nations in the earth, by making you inheritors of its dwelling and of disposing of it after them. It has been said that by succession is meant dominion and authority. Al-Ḥasan read "and We make you" with the plural of majesty (nūn al-ʿaẓamah). ﴿Is there a god with Allah?﴾, who has these affairs and blessings of His, Exalted is He. ﴿Little do you remember.﴾ That is, a little remembrance, or a little time you remember. The word "little" (qalīlan) is in the accusative either as a verbal noun (maṣdar) or as an adverb of time (ẓarf), because it is an adjective of a verbal noun or of an implied adverb of time. The particle "mā" is superfluous on both assessments, to emphasize the meaning of paucity, which is intended to mean nonexistence, or what resembles it in worthlessness and uselessness. The object of "remember" is omitted for the sake of the verse-ending (fāṣilah). It has been said that the implied object is "you remember His blessings"; it has been said that it is "you remember the content of what has been mentioned in the discourse"; and it has been said that it is "you remember what has passed for you of trials and joys." Perhaps the preferable reading is "His blessings" as mentioned. And to announce that the one who remembers is in the utmost clarity, such that he needs only to turn his attention to it, the closing is with the negation of remembrance. Al-Ḥasan, al-Aʿmash and Abu ʿAmr read "yadhakkarūn" with the third-person yāʾ, and Abu Ḥaywah read "tatadhakkarūn" with two tāʾs.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 27, verse 63:

﴿Is He who guides you in the darknesses of the land and the sea?﴾ That is, He guides you in the darknesses of the nights, on land and at sea, by the stars and other signs. The idafa (genitive construction) of "darknesses" to "land and sea" is for association, meaning that the darknesses are in them. It is also permissible that "darknesses" refers metaphorically to the roads, which are likened to darknesses in that they cause bewilderment.

﴿And who sends the winds as good tidings before His mercy?﴾ The explanation of the like of this clause has already passed. ﴿Is there a god with Allah?﴾ This is a negation that there should be with Him, glory be to Him, another god. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Exalted is Allah above what they associate with Him﴾ is an affirmation and confirmation of this. The explicit mention of the Majestic Name in place of the pronoun is to indicate the cause of the ruling, that is: exalted and sanctified is He by His essence, which is singular in divinity, entailing all the attributes of perfection and the qualities of majesty and beauty, which necessitate that all created things are subdued under His power. ﴿Above what they associate﴾ means: above the existence of what they associate with Him, glory be to Him, under the title of being a god and a partner to Him, exalted is He. Or: Allah is exalted above a partnership or a comparison of what they associate with Him, glory be to Him. It is permissible that "ma" be a verbal-noun particle, meaning: Allah is exalted above their associating. It was also read as "ta'mushrikun" (what you associate) with the second-person address.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 27, verse 64:**

﴿Is He who originates creation﴾, meaning He brings it into existence as a beginning, ﴿then repeats it﴾, meaning He repeats its bringing into existence and returns it as it was. This is after its destruction, since repetition cannot be conceived except after destruction. The apparent meaning is that this refers to the re-creation through resurrection after death. Accordingly, the *alif-lam* (ال, the definite article) in *al-khalq* (الخلق, "creation") is not for comprehensiveness (*istighraq*, meaning all instances without exception), because by scholarly consensus (*ijma'*, the agreement of the scholars) some creation is not re-created, and regarding the re-creation of some other creation there is disagreement among the Muslims. Its details belong in their proper place.

It has been objected that interpreting the verse as referring to resurrection is problematic, since the address is to the polytheists, most of whom deny it, so how can the speech be directed at them and addressed to them as though they acknowledged it? The answer is that, because the proofs for that re-creation are clear, they were treated as though they acknowledged it, since they were capable of knowing it; so they have no excuse for denying it. It was also said that some of them acknowledged it, and the speech is with respect to him, but this is not the case. As for the permissibility of the *alif-lam* being for the genus (*lil-jins*, referring to the category as a whole), and that the intended meaning of "beginning" and "repetition" is what is observed in the world of generation and corruption, namely the bringing into existence of some things and their destruction, followed by the bringing into existence of their like, this is something the polytheists who deny re-creation after death do not deny. Therefore it is nothing at all, as is not hidden.

﴿And who provides for you from the heaven and the earth﴾, meaning by heavenly and earthly causes which He has arranged in a wonderful order required by the wisdom upon which He built the matter of creation. ﴿Is there a god﴾ other ﴿with God﴾, existing, so that He would be made a partner to Him, glorified is He, in worship? His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: Bring your proof﴾, is a command to him, upon him be prayers and peace, to rebuke them following a rebuke, meaning: bring a proof, rational or transmitted, indicating that with Him, mighty and majestic, there is a god. It was also said: meaning, bring a proof that other than Him, exalted is He, is able to do anything of what has been mentioned of His acts, mighty and majestic. This was criticized on the ground that the polytheists do not claim this explicitly, nor do they hold that it is a necessary consequence of divinity, even though in reality it is part of it; so demanding proof for it, rather than for their explicit claim, has no basis. In attributing the proof to their pronoun (*burhanakum*, "your proof") there is a mockery of them, because it implies that they have a proof, and how could they have one? It was also said that the attribution is for increased rebuke, as if it were said: we are content with what you, O adversaries, consider a proof showing this, even though we and no one of sound intellect consider it so; and despite this you are incapable of bringing it. ﴿If you are truthful﴾, meaning in that claim. It was cited as evidence that a claim is not accepted unless it is illuminated by proof.

This, and in *al-Kashf* (the commentary of al-Tibi): the basis of these verses is ascent (*taraqqi*, progression from lesser to greater), because the discourse is about establishing that there is no good in the idols, while every good comes from Him, blessed and exalted. So He first summarized by mentioning His comprehensive name, glorified is He, in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah﴾. Then He proceeded to the detailed, making the creation of the heavens and the earth a preparation for sending down water and producing gardens, or rather for the latter, which is indicated by the shift (*iltifat*, change of grammatical person) there and the emphasis (*ta'kid*) in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It was not for you to grow its trees﴾. It is as though He, glorified is He, mentions the many benefits in it in colour, taste, fragrance, and the enjoyment of shade.

When He established that this is His specific act, He denied that He has any partner, and made them deviants from the path of correctness, or made them equate to Him, glorified is He, what does not deserve it. The first is more apparent. Then He ascended from this to what is of greater benefit to them and more evident in its usefulness, namely the making of the earth a place of settlement and what follows from it. So He mentioned, mighty and exalted is He, what the mentioned growth cannot be completed without, together with benefits before which the benefit of growth becomes insignificant. He followed this with their utter ignorance, which yields the mentioned deviation, and something worse than it and worse still. Then He pushed the ascent further and mentioned what is closest to them without intermediary, of repelling or of benefit, so He singled out their answering when they are in distress, and generalized with the removal of evil and harms. This concerns repelling what is feared and establishing them as vicegerents (*khulafa'*, plural of *khalifa*) on the earth, benefiting from it and from what is in it as they wish. This is more complete than the first two, more comprehensive, of greater standing, and of greater importance. For this reason it was separated by "little do you remember," and in it those exaggerations were carried to the utmost. As for the mention of guidance in the darkness of land and sea and the mention of sending the winds as bearers of glad tidings, these are digressions (*istitrad*, incidental remarks) because of the connection of the discussion of the winds with guidance at sea. So these are among the completions of the vicegerency, answering the distressed, and removing evil, so understand.

He drew attention to this by separating it with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Exalted is Allah above what they associate﴾. Then He concluded all of that with a turning away from this method, by reminding of the two blessings of origination and re-creation, since every blessing other than these two depends on them, the worldly and otherworldly blessings alike. He followed this with a summary that comprises all that He enumerated first and more, namely their provision from the heaven and the earth. He incorporated in its delay that it is inferior to the two blessings. For this reason He rebuked them by demanding proof concerning what is not... and He recorded their lying as an indication of its connection to all of it, and that this conclusion is a musk-scented seal, and whoever turns away from its fragrant breezes is himself musk-scented. From this explanation the aspect of the substitution (*badal*, the grammatical substitution in the verse) became manifest, its veil unveiled. Praise be to God, the Bestower, the Beneficent. (End of quote.)

(p. 9)

In *Ghurrat al-Tanzil* by al-Raghib (al-Isfahani) there is something that supports this, and al-Tibi summarized it in his commentary on *al-Kashshaf* (of al-Zamakhshari). And God knows best the secrets of His Book.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 27, verse 65 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Say: None in the heavens and the earth knows the unseen except Allah.﴾ After it had been established that He, exalted is He, alone is God, by showing that He alone possesses complete and perfect power and all-encompassing, active mercy, He followed this with a mention of what is inseparable from that, namely His exclusive knowledge of the unseen. This completes what came before and prepares for what follows concerning the resurrection. In al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit) it is said: The disbelievers asked the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, about the time of the Hour which he had promised them, and they pressed him insistently, so the verse ﴿Say: None knows…﴾ was revealed. On this view, its connection with what precedes it, His saying ﴿Is not He who originates creation and then repeats it…﴾, is the most complete connection.

The apparent and immediately understood reading is that "man" (من) is the subject of "knows" (يَعْلَمُ), being either a relative pronoun (موصول) or a qualifying noun (موصوف), that "the unseen" (الغيب) is its object, and that the noble Name (Allah) is in the nominative as a substitute (بدل) for "man" (من). The exception (الاستثناء), as some have said, is disconnected in reality (منقطع تحقيقًا) but connected in interpretation (متصل تأويلًا), following the pattern in the verse of the rajaz poet:

*And a town in which there is no companion, except the oryx and except the camels.*

This is based on including the oryx among "companions" by a kind of interpretation. The sentence then conveys emphasis in negating knowledge of the unseen from those in the heavens and the earth, by linking their knowledge to something whose impossibility is obvious, namely that Allah, exalted is He, should be one of them. It is as if it were said: If Allah is among those in the heavens and the earth, then among them there is one who knows the unseen. That is, the impossibility of their knowing the unseen is like the impossibility of Allah being one of them. A parallel to this, which has no exception in it, is his saying:

*Their greeting among them is a painful blow.*

Some have said that it is disconnected (منقطع) in the manner of the exception in his saying:

*On the day when spears cannot defend their position, nor arrows, except the keen, well-forged sword.*

That is, it belongs to the type where one of two dissimilar things is followed by the other, like "Zayd did not come to me except 'Amr," and "Your brothers did not help him except his brothers." Sibawayh mentioned both of these examples. Ibn Malik mentioned that their original form is: "No one came to me except 'Amr," and "No one helped him except his brothers." So in place of "no one" (أحد) some of its referents were put, namely Zayd and your brothers. Had they not mentioned those who are excluded from the negation of coming and helping, but mentioned them for emphasis, to specify their share of the negation, to repel the addressee's supposition that the speaker had not thought of what was emphasised, then the verse would, on this view, originally read: "No one among those in the heavens and the earth knows the unseen except Allah," so "no one" (أحد) is omitted and in its place some of its referents are put, namely those in the heavens and the earth, while the other part is those who are not in them. It suffices for something to be one of its referents that it truly applies to it, and its existence in external reality is not required. Scholars have stated that among universal terms there are some of which some or all individuals cannot exist externally. Moreover, some of the leading Muslim scholars have said that there exists something other than Allah, mighty and majestic, which is neither in the heavens nor on the earth, namely the Spirit of Command (الروح الأمرية), for according to them it has no place, similar to the immaterial intellects (العقول المجردة) of the philosophers.

He also said: The condition for this type of "following" (الاتباع) is that it must be correct to omit the thing excluded from and to dispense with it by means of the thing excluded. If this condition is not met, then the accusative (النصب) is required according to al-Tamimi, while al-Hijazi (uses the following) as in the verse of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿There is no protector today from the command of Allah, except for him upon whom He has mercy﴾. For in this case, dispensing with what precedes by means of the excluded thing is impossible without artificial effort. Al-Mazini claimed that the following of a disconnected exception is due to the prevalence of the rational (العاقل) over the non-rational. It follows from this that it would be restricted to one who is rational or similar, and this is false, as Ibn Kharuf said, because what is substituted from in this category is other than what was mentioned, and is more than can be counted.

End of quotation.

Al-Zamakhshari's speech, at its beginning, gives the impression that the exception here is of the same kind as the exception in the two examples mentioned by Sibawayh, and in the verse I mentioned just before them. Its ending implies that it is of the kind of exception in the earlier rajaz verse, and that what prompted the choice of the al-Tamimi position is the subtle point of emphasis you have heard. Scholars have stated that this subtle point can only be achieved if the exception is taken as disconnected in reality but connected in interpretation. Perhaps the truth is that if the intention is to indicate the strength of the negation, the exception must be of the type found in his saying: "And a town…" [p. 10] etc. And if the intention is to indicate the generality of the negation, it must be of the type found in their saying: "Your brothers did not help him except his brothers." So reflect on this.

It is also permitted that the exception be connected, as is the original case for exceptions, with "those in the heavens and the earth" meaning those who have knowledge of them in the manner of one present in them, by a metonymy (مجاز مرسل) or a metaphor (استعارة). Whichever it is, it is a general figurative meaning applicable to Him, exalted is His glory, and to the rational beings among His creation. This avoids the necessity of combining the literal and the figurative in one expression, a practice whose validity is disputed, as some who hold the connected view have done. It has also been said that on this reading the prepositional phrase is attached to a verb that mentions acts attributed literally both to Allah, exalted is He, and to created beings, not to a verb such as "to be located" (استقر), which cannot literally be attributed to Him, glory be to Him. The meaning would be: None of those mentioned in the heavens and the earth knows the unseen except Allah. It is also permitted to attach it to "to be located" (استقر), but it is made to be predicated of an omitted genitive construct, and the noun in the genitive takes its place: meaning, "None whose mention is established in the heavens and the earth knows the unseen except Allah." So the verb and the construct noun are omitted and the pronoun is concealed because it is in the nominative. This and what precedes it, as you see, are [weak].

The connected reading has been objected to on the ground that it entails equating Him, exalted is He, with others in applying one word, which is a blameworthy matter. Mus­lim, Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i reported from Adi ibn Hatim that a man gave a sermon in the presence of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, saying: "Whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger has been rightly guided, and whoever disobeys them has gone astray." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Evil is the orator of the people. Rather say: 'Whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger.'"

It is answered that this is blameworthy when it issues from a human being, but when it issues from Him, exalted is He, it is not blameworthy. Moreover, that it is blameworthy when issued by a human being in every case is not granted. For al-Bukhari, Muslim, al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasa'i reported from Anas, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Whoever has three qualities will find the sweetness of faith: that Allah and His Messenger are dearer to him than anything else," and so on in the hadith. Perhaps the basis of praise and blame is whether the wording contains a subtle point or not. It has been said regarding the hadith of Anas: the point of using the dual pronoun is to indicate that what is considered is the combined whole of the two loves. The point of using the singular in the hadith of Adi is to indicate that each of the two disobediences independently entails misguidance. The discussion of this topic has already passed, so recall it.

It is also permitted that "man" (من) be parsed as the object of "knows," and "the unseen" (الغيب) as a substitute of inclusion (بدل اشتمال) from it, with the noble Name as the subject of "knows," making it an exception with the excluded element omitted (استثناء مفرغ): meaning, "None knows the unseen of those in the heavens and the earth except Allah." Its distance from the apparent sense is not hidden.

Al-Ghayb (the unseen) is originally a verbal noun from "the sun and other things disappeared" when they were concealed from sight. It has come to be used for a hidden thing for which no sign has been set up. That this is unseen is relative to people and the like, not to Allah, mighty and majestic, for nothing is hidden from Him, exalted is He. However, it is not permissible to say that He, exalted and high is He, does not know the unseen, intending that there is no unseen relative to Him, so that one could say He knows it. Shaykh Ahmad al-Faruqi al-Sirhindi, famous as al-Imam al-Rabbani, in his Maktubat, severely criticised whoever said this with that intention, as is his habit, may Allah reward him with good, against anyone who has not adhered to the manners of the noble Shari'ah.

The apparent meaning is the generality of "the unseen." It has been said that what is meant is the Hour. It has been said that it is what the inhabitants of the heavens and the earth conceal in their hearts. It has also been said that what is meant is the genus of the unseen. Negating knowledge of the genus from anyone other than Allah, mighty and majestic, entails negating knowledge of each individual of it from that other. It does no harm to this view that the verse does not then indicate that He, mighty and majestic, knows every unseen thing; rather, the most it indicates is that knowledge of the genus of the unseen belongs to Him, glory be to Him, because that is what is explicitly negated from the excluded element. The affirmation of knowledge of this genus does not entail affirmation of knowledge of each individual of it, for the verse was not brought to prove that. And how many rational and transmitted proofs indicate it! It was objected that the unseen, insofar as it is unseen, does not vary, so whenever knowledge of some individuals of it is established, knowledge of all of them is established, to avoid the necessity of preference without a preponderant cause. So reflect.

[p. 11]

Some have chosen the comprehensive reading (الاستغراق), meaning: None of those in the heavens and the earth knows every unseen thing except Allah, for He, glory be to Him, knows every unseen thing, because this is more suited to the context. It was objected that this entails that among the inhabitants of the heavens and the earth there would be someone who knows some of the unseen, and the apparent statement of many of the great scholars rejects that. This is supported by what al-Shaykhan, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, Ahmad and a group of hadith scholars reported from Masruq, from Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, that she said: Whoever claims that Muhammad ﷺ informs people of what will happen tomorrow, and in some reports "knows what is in tomorrow," has greatly slandered Allah, while Allah says: ﴿Say: None in the heavens and the earth knows the unseen except Allah﴾.

Some have permitted that among them there may be someone who knows some of the unseen. In Bayan Qawati' al-Islam, the scholar Ibn Hajar, after refuting the one who declares disbelief on someone who is asked, "Do you know the unseen?" and answers "Yes," because what he said contradicts the explicit text, which is His saying: ﴿And with Him are the keys of the unseen; none knows them but He﴾, and His saying: ﴿Knower of the unseen, He does not reveal His unseen to anyone, except to a messenger whom He has approved﴾, wrote the following text: In any case, the special individuals (الخواص) may know the unseen in one matter or several matters, as has occurred for many of them and become well known. What is exclusive to Allah, exalted is He, is knowledge of all of it and knowledge of the keys of the unseen, referred to by His saying: ﴿And with Him are the keys of the unseen﴾, and so on. It follows from this statement that whoever claims knowledge of the unseen in one matter or several matters does not commit disbelief, and this is what is meant by what is in al-Rawda. Whoever claims knowledge of it in all matters commits disbelief, and this is what is meant by what is in its original (al-Asl). However, since his expression was unrestricted, covering this and other things, al-Nawawi was entitled to object to it. So if it is taken absolutely, it means nothing. Therefore the more correct view is what al-Nawawi's words imply, namely that there is no disbelief. End of quotation.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 27, verse 65 (part 2 of 2):

The sound view is that the knowledge of the unseen (al-ghayb) that is denied to anyone other than Allah, exalted is He, is that which belongs to a being essentially, that is, without an intermediary in its establishment for him. This cannot be conceived for anyone among the inhabitants of the heavens and the earth, because of the contingency (al-imkan) that applies to them in essence and in attribute, and contingency rejects that anything be established for them without an intermediary. Perhaps the expression "those in the heavens and the earth" in describing the excepted party points to the reason for the ruling. What befalls the elect (al-khawass) is not, by necessity, of this denied knowledge at all, since it is bestowed by the Necessary Being, exalted and mighty, upon them by one of the ways of bestowal. So it is not said that they know the unseen in that sense, and whoever says so has undoubtedly disbelieved. Rather, it is said that they were "shown" (undhiru) or "informed" (utli'u), in the passive voice, about the unseen or something similar, which conveys an intermediary in the establishment of knowledge for them. What supports what has been mentioned is that the Noble Qur'an never attributes knowledge of the unseen to anyone other than Allah, exalted is He, at all. Disclosure of the unseen is attributed to whichever messenger He has chosen, glorified is He.

It is not said: "It is permissible by this reasoning to say: so-and-so was informed of the unseen, in the passive voice, meaning that Allah, exalted is He, informed him and made him aware of it by one of the means of informing and making known. And if this is permissible, then it is permissible to say: so-and-so knows the unseen, intending to attribute to him the knowledge that came to him from being informed." We respond: there is no dispute about the permissibility of "u'lima" in the passive voice. The dispute concerns your statement, "and if this is permissible, then it is permissible to say," and so on. We say: if by "permissible" in the consequent of the conditional is meant permissibility in meaning (i.e., validity in terms of meaning), then this is granted. But not everything that is permissible in meaning in this sense is permissible in terms of the Shari'ah to use. If, however, what is meant is permissibility under the Shari'ah in the sense of not being prohibited from using it, then this is denied, because of what it contains of misleading implication and conflict with the apparent meanings of verses, such as the verse: ﴿Say: None in the heavens and the earth knows the unseen except Allah﴾, and others. I have heard from the Divine Imam, may Allah sanctify his luminous secret, that he sharply censured whoever says that Allah, glorified is He, said, "He knows not the unseen," interpreting it in the manner mentioned above, because of its conflict with the Qur'anic texts and others. There is in that much of the impropriety that it contains. They also denounced whoever says: "I hate the truth, love the trial, and flee from mercy," intending by "the truth" death, by "the trial" wealth or children, and by "mercy" rain, because of the shocking and offensive character that this apparently has, which is obvious.

Indeed, the one who says that does not disbelieve by that intention, but he is liable to discretionary punishment (ta'zir) so that he does not return to such speech.

Then, the knowledge of what is other than the unseen, of sensible and intelligible things, although it is not established for any contingent thing without an intermediary in its establishment either, nevertheless, in attributing it to any of them, only the attribute itself is taken into account, not restricted by the negation of that intermediary. This is because it was not intended to restrict that knowledge to Him, mighty and exalted, nor to deny it of anyone else, exalted is He. Rather, He explicitly stated in more places than can be counted that it is attributed to others besides Him, glorified is He. Even if what was stated about the knowledge of the unseen had been stated about it, the same condition would apply to it. According to what you have established, the knowledge of intellects of events that have not yet occurred, as the philosophers claim, is not knowledge of the unseen. Rather, even if it were granted that it is knowledge they obtained from the Overflowing Giver, exalted is His majesty, by one of the ways that wisdom requires, it should not be said of them that they "know the unseen." Whoever says it is either a disbeliever or a sinful Muslim.

The same applies to the knowledge of some ascetics (al-murtadin) among the Muslim Sufis and the disbelieving Jogis (al-jawkiyyah, Hindu yogis). Everything that comes to them of that is only by way of emanation (al-fayd). Its levels and states are uncountable. The aptitude for it may be innate, or it may be acquired, and the means of acquiring it are so diverse that they can hardly be exhausted. The bestowal of it upon disbelieving ascetics, although its bestowal resembles its bestowal upon the believing pious, nevertheless there is a great difference between the two according to the verifiers (al-muhaqqiqun). Some Sufis have mentioned that there is no truth except that a falsehood has been made to resemble it, because the abode is an abode of trial, and most of what is in it is affliction.

To the knowledge of the Jogi ascetics there is joined the knowledge of some Sufis who are ascribed to Islam but neglect most of its obligatory rulings and plunge into committing prohibited acts by day and night. It should not be believed that this is a karamah (miraculous favor), but rather it is a calamity leading to regret and remorse.

As for the knowledge of the astrologer (al-nujumi) of events in the cosmos, as he claims, it is not of this category, because those events that he reports are not of the unseen in the sense we have mentioned. Although they are hidden from us, they are, in his claim, things for which he has appointed a sign from the celestial configurations and astral relations, such as conjunction, trine, sextile, opposition, and the like. His knowledge of the indication of the signs that he claims arises from experience and from what the natures of the stars and zodiacal signs require, which he takes as indicated by the variation of effects in the world of generation and corruption. I do not see his knowledge of these as anything but the knowledge of a skilled physician who, seeing a man with excess yellow bile, for example, knows the degree of his temperament, and verifies that when he eats a certain amount of honey, after an hour or two such and such pain will afflict him. Applying the term "knowledge of the unseen" to that has its own problems. If you insist on calling that "unseen," then knowledge of it, because it comes through the means of causes, is not in any way of the knowledge of the unseen denied of others than Him, exalted is He. Likewise, every knowledge of a hidden matter obtained through some cause, such as our knowledge of Allah, exalted is He, and His sublime attributes, and our knowledge of Paradise and Hell and the like.

Moreover, if you are fair, you will know that what the astrologer and others like him possess is not true knowledge, but only conjecture and guesswork built upon something weaker than a spider's web. We will verify that, with what cannot be surpassed, in its proper place, if Allah, exalted is He, wills.

The strongest thing he has is knowledge of the times of solar and lunar eclipses and the times when specific relations among the planets occur. These arise from knowing the magnitudes of the motions of the planets and the universal and particular spheres. These are sensible matters, perceived through observation and instruments made for that purpose.

In sum, the knowledge of the unseen, directly, whether wholly or partly, is specific to Allah, exalted is He, and no one among creatures knows it at all. If the absolute negation of intermediaries is taken into account, it necessarily becomes one of the requirements of the Essence, so there is no differentiation within it between one unseen and another. There is no harm, then, in taking the definite article in "al-ghayb" as generic. If it is taken as comprehensive (al-istighraq), then it is fitting not to consider in the verse the negation of universality, but rather to consider the universality of the negation. And he is committed to the principle that the rule is a generality of the most part. The same applies to the negation and universality on the side of the agent. So reflect. This is what I have, and perhaps what you have is better than it. And Allah, exalted is He, knows best.

[Page 13]

﴿And they do not perceive when they will be raised up﴾, that is, when they will rise from the graves, although it is something they must face and among the most important matters for them. Here "ayyana" is an interrogative particle concerning time. For this reason it has been said that its origin is "ayya aana," meaning "what time," although the commonly known view is otherwise. It is governed by "yub'athun" (they will be raised), and the clause is in the place of the accusative (nasb) with "yash'urun" (they perceive). "Yash'urun" is suspended (u'allaqat) because of the interrogative. The plural pronoun refers to the disbelievers, although the lack of awareness of what was mentioned is general, so as to avoid breaking the connection between it and the pronouns mentioned afterward that are specific to them with certainty. It has been said that the pronoun is for everyone. Attributing the specific features of the disbelievers to all of them is of the type "the sons of so-and-so did such-and-such," where the doer is only some of them. There is discussion about this.

And al-Sulami read "iyyana" with a kasrah on the hamzah, and this is the dialect of the Banu Sulaym.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 27, verse 66:

﴿Nay, their knowledge has come to an end concerning the Hereafter.﴾ This is an idiomatic turn (idrab, a transition from what preceded) in a manner that serves to affirm and establish it. The original form of ﴿ādāraka﴾ is tadāraka, and the ta' was assimilated into the dal, so it became sakin and the hamzat al-wasl (the connecting hamza) was brought in. It derives from tadāraka banū fulān, when they followed one another into destruction. This is what those who explained tadārak here as "perishing and annihilation" intended; otherwise the root meaning of tadārak is succession and consecutiveness in general. (Concerning the Hereafter) is connected to "their knowledge." Knowledge (al-'ilm) may take fi as well as the ba' as its complement, and in that case fi carries the meaning of ba', as stated by al-Farra', Ibn 'Atiyya and others. The meaning is: their knowledge has followed on, one after another, concerning the matter of the Hereafter, which is the resurrection that was mentioned, and its states, until it ceased and was extinguished, and they no longer had any knowledge of anything that would occur in it, with certainty, even though its causes were abundantly available. Thus it is a progression from describing them with gross ignorance to describing them with a more gross ignorance. The assimilation (tadārak) of their knowledge in this sense does not mean that they had genuine knowledge of it which then gradually disappeared; rather, it is by way of metaphor, by treating the causes and beginnings of knowledge, namely the rational and transmitted proofs, as if they were its essence, and by treating the falling away of these from the level of their consideration, whenever they noticed them, as the course of their successive cessation until it ended.

It is also permitted that the speech is according to an implied omission (taqdir mudaf), i.e. ﴿ādāraka﴾ (their causes of knowledge followed on one another and ceased), with tadārak used metaphorically for the falling away mentioned. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Nay, they are in doubt about it﴾ is an idrab and a transition from their lack of knowledge of it to what is more gross than that, in the manner mentioned above, namely their bewilderment in that matter; i.e., nay, they are in great doubt about the Hereafter itself and its reality, like one who is bewildered in a matter for which he finds no proof, let alone the events that will occur in it. His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Nay, they are blind to it﴾ is an idrab and a transition from describing them as doubters to describing them with what is more dreadful than that, namely that they are blind, their insight utterly confused, such that they can scarcely perceive the path to knowledge of it, which is the proofs indicating that it is bound to happen. So the meaning is "blind to its proofs," or "blind to everything that would lead them to the truth and into which its proofs enter at the first level." (From it) is connected to "blind," and was placed before it for the sake of the rhyme (ri'ayat al-fawasil). Perhaps the reason it is construed with min rather than 'an is to make the Hereafter the starting point and source of their blindness. Disbelief in the consequence and the recompense leaves a person absorbed in securing the benefits of his belly and his private parts, not reflecting or seeing clearly in anything beyond that.

It is also permitted that ﴿ādāraka﴾ means "became firmly established and perfected," and that He describes them with the firm establishment and perfection of their knowledge of that as a form of mockery directed at them, just as you say to the most ignorant of people, "How knowledgeable you are!" in derision. The outcome of this mockery is the negation of their knowledge of that, as in the earlier aspect, but in a more emphatic form. The two idrabs are by way of progression from describing them with the dreadful to describing them with the more dreadful, as before, and this is a good aspect. The words of some of the verifiers (muhaqqiqun) seem to favour this over what we mentioned first.

It is also permitted that the intended meaning of al-idrak is firm establishment, but with the meaning: the causes of their knowledge that the Resurrection is bound to occur became firmly established, through decisive signs and clear proofs, and they attained knowledge to the utmost degree, yet they were ignorant in that. In this there is an
صفحة 14
observation: that the indication of the noble composition (al-nazm al-karim) for the intention "and they are ignorant" is not clear.

Al-Kirmani said: tadārak means succession, and the intended meaning of "knowledge" here is judgement and speech. The meaning: from them there followed one after another speech and judgement concerning the Hereafter, and much discussion of it occurred among them; some of them denied it, some of them doubted it, and some of them considered it far-fetched. And in this there is what there is.

It has been said: "concerning the Hereafter" is connected to ﴿ādāraka﴾. This was the view of al-Zajjaj and al-Tabarsi, and it is what some reports transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, imply. The meaning on this view, according to some, is: nay, their knowledge in the Hereafter became firmly established of what they had been ignorant of in this world, since they saw it with their own eyes. The apparent form would have been yudārik in the present/future form, but it was expressed in the past form to indicate the certainty of its occurrence.
