It has also been said: tadārak here is from "tadāraktu amr fulān," when you remedied his affair, and its object is omitted here: i.e., nay, in the Hereafter they remedied what they had been ignorant of in this world, i.e., they made it good. The essential meaning is: nay, they came to know that in the Hereafter, when knowledge no longer benefited them. The expression in the past form is as you know. It is not hidden that there is obscurity in the order of the three idrabs as they appear in the noble composition according to these two aspects, so reflect.

Abu 'Amr... [reading] Ubayy read ﴿am tadārak﴾ in the original form and made ﴿am﴾ replace ﴿bal﴾. Sulayman ibn Yasar read ﴿bal adraka﴾, transferring the vowel of the hamza to the lam and doubling the dal according to the pattern ifta'ala, so that the dal, which is the first radical of the word, was assimilated into the ta' after it was changed into a dal; thus there is inversion of the second letter with the first, as in their saying: "ithrid" (from ithtarid), derived from al-thard. The elided hamza whose vowel was transferred to the lam is the hamzat al-istifham, which was added to the hamzat al-wasl; the hamzat al-wasl was then elided, then the hamza itself was elided and its vowel placed on the lam of "bal." Abu Raja', al-A'raj, Shayba, Talha and Tawba al-'Anbari read likewise, except that they gave the lam of "bali" a kasra. This is narrated from Ibn 'Ayyash, 'Asim and al-A'mash.

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Abu Ja'far and the people of Mecca read ﴿bal adraka﴾ on the pattern af'ala in the sense of tafa'ala. It is also narrated from Abu Bakr, from 'Asim. 'Abdullah in one narration, and Ibn 'Abbas in the narration of Abu Haywa and others from him, and al-Hasan, Qatada and Ibn Muhaysin read ﴿bali ādraka﴾ with a long vowel after the hamzat al-istifham; its original form is a'addaraka, and the second hamza was changed into an alif to lighten it, since two hamzas together are disliked. Abu Bakr ibn Abi al-'Ala' rejected this reading, and Abu Hatim said: it is not permissible to use the interrogative after "bal," because "bal" is for affirmation, and the interrogative in this place is a denial in the sense of "did not happen," as in His saying: ﴿Did they witness their creation?﴾, i.e., they did not witness their creation; so the two cannot occur together, because of the contradiction between affirmation and denial, end of quote.

Some later scholars, as Abu Hayyan said, permitted the interrogative after "bal," comparing it to the saying of one who says: "Did you eat bread, nay, did you drink water?" by leaving the first speech and taking up the second. Mujahid read ﴿am adraka﴾, making "am" replace "bal" and "adraka" on the pattern af'ala. Ibn 'Abbas also read, in one narration, ﴿bal a-tadārak﴾ with a hamza entering upon ﴿tadārak﴾, so that the hamzat al-wasl introduced for the sake of the assimilation and the pronunciation of the sakin is dropped. Ibn Mas'ud also read ﴿bal a'addaraka﴾ with two hamzas, the hamzat al-istifham and the hamza of af'ala. Al-Hasan also, and al-A'raj, read ﴿bal adara­ka﴾ with a hamza and assimilation of the dal, the first radical of the word, into the dal of ifta'ala after the ta' became a dal. Warsh, in one narration, read ﴿bal iddaraka﴾ with the hamza of adraka dropped and its vowel transferred to the lam. Ibn 'Abbas also read ﴿bala adraka﴾ with the particle of affirmation by which the questioner affirms a negated statement. And he read ﴿bal (a'ādāraka)﴾ with an alif between the two hamzas. These are several readings; whichever of them contains an explicit or implicit interrogative is a denial and negation. As for the one containing "bala," Abu Hatim said of it: if it comes as an answer to a preceding statement, it is permissible to begin a new statement after it, as if a people had denied what was said before about power, and it was said to them: "Bala," an affirmation of what they denied; then the interrogative was resumed after it, and it was balanced by His saying: ﴿Nay, they are in doubt about it﴾, meaning "or are they in doubt about it?", because the particles of conjunction may alternate; and He withheld from the two sentences with His saying: ﴿Nay, they are blind to it﴾, end of quote. He means that the meaning is: "Has their knowledge of the Hereafter been attained, or did they doubt?" So "bal" in the sense of "am" is balanced by the hamza. Al-Bahr criticised this by making "bal" mean "am," and its balancing with the interrogative hamza is very weak. Some verifiers said: what contains "bala" is an affirmation of their awareness and an explanation of it as an attainment, in the manner of mockery, which is the most eloquent form of negation and denial; and what follows it, His saying: ﴿Nay, they are in doubt about it﴾ and so on, is a turning away from the explanation, for the sake of emphasis in negation and to indicate that their awareness of it is that they doubt it; rather, they are blind to it. It is on the pattern of: "Their greeting among them is a painful blow." Or it is a rejection and denial of their awareness, and the idrab is nullifying, so understand.

And His saying, exalted be He: ﴿And those who disbelieved said, "When we have become dust, and our fathers, shall we really be brought forth?"﴾ serves as an explanation of their ignorance of the Hereafter and of their state in it. Placing the relative pronoun (alladhina) in place of their pronoun serves to censure them through what lies within the scope of its clause (sila), and to indicate the cause of their false judgment, which is contained in the content of the saying. ["Idha" (when)] is an adverb for an omitted verb indicated by "mukhrajun" (brought forth). That is: "Shall we be brought forth when we have become dust?" It is not permissible for it to be an adverb for "mukhrajun" itself, because each of the hamza (interrogative particle), inna (indeed), and the lam (emphatic particle), according to what is said, prevents what follows from governing what precedes it, so how much more so when they are combined. Some did not consider the lam to be preventive, based on what is established in grammar regarding the permissibility of placing the complement of the predicate of inna, when it is accompanied by the lam, before it, as in inna Zaydan ta'amaka la-akilun (Indeed Zayd is one who will eat your food). Two preventers then suffice. I think that whoever said that adverbs are given more latitude than other elements does not hold that the ruling applies consistently in such a position. Their meaning by "bringing forth" is bringing out from the graves. It is permissible that the bringing forth is from the state of annihilation to life, but the first is the apparent meaning. The restriction of the bringing forth to the time when they are dust is not meant to limit the denial to bringing forth at that time only, for they deny resurrection after death absolutely, even if the body remains in its condition. Rather, it is meant to strengthen the denial by directing it at bringing forth in a state that, by their claim, is contrary to it. His saying, glorified be He: ﴿and our fathers﴾ is conjoined to the subject of kana (was), and he dispensed with separating the two by a pronoun through separation by the predicate, rather than by an emphatic pronoun. The repetition of the hamza in "a-inna" is for emphasis and intensification of the denial. The adorning of the sentence with inna and the lam is to emphasize the denial, not to deny the emphasis, as the apparent wording of the noble text may suggest, since the fronting of the hamza is due to its original place at the head of the sentence. The pronoun in "a-inna" refers to them and to their fathers, because being dust has encompassed them and their fathers.

Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read "a-idha" and "a-inna" with two interrogative particles combined, changing the second hamza into a ya'. Abu 'Amr separated the two with an alif.

Nafi' read "idha" with a single broken hamza (kasra). The interrogative hamza is then presumed along with the presumed verb, because the meaning is not that of a statement. He read "a-yyinna" with the interrogative hamza, changing the second hamza into a ya' with a mad (elongation) between them. Others read "a-idha" with an elongated interrogative and "annana" with two nuns, without an interrogative particle.

﴿Indeed, we have been promised this﴾, i.e., the bringing forth mentioned, ﴿we and our fathers before⁠﴾, i.e., before the promise of Muhammad (ﷺ). The placing of the promised object before "we" here serves to indicate that it is the one about which the speech was deliberately made and intended, to the extent that everything else seems discarded and a mere addition to it. This is indicated by the mention of what came from them, themselves, emphasized, established, and repeated. Its being placed after it in the verse of Surat al-Mu'minun is for preserving the original order. There is no reason for a change there, since nothing is mentioned there except their following their forefathers in disbelief and their denial of resurrection, without censuring them for it. The sentence is an *istinaf* (resumptive, a new independent sentence) brought to establish the denial, and beginning it with the oath is for greater emphasis. His statement, exalted is He, ﴿This is nothing but the fables of the ancients⁠﴾, is an establishment following an establishment.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 27, verse 69:

﴿Say: Travel through the earth and see what was the end of the criminals.﴾ This is because of their denial of the Messengers, upon them be blessings and peace, in what they called them to of belief in Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, alone, and in the Last Day, which you deny. For in witnessing their end there is sufficiency for those endowed with insight (ulu al-absar). And in expressing the deniers as "the criminals," which is more general than that by way of implication, there is a kindness to the believers in abandoning crimes, because it guides them to the understanding that sin in general is hateful to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 27, verse 70:

﴿And do not grieve over them﴾ because of their persistence in disbelief and denial. ﴿And do not be in distress﴾, i.e., in constriction of the breast, ﴿because of what they plot﴾, i.e., because of their scheming, for Allah the Exalted will protect you from the people.

Ibn Kathir read ﴿ḍīqin﴾ with a kasra on the ḍād, and this is also a verbal noun (maṣdar). It is also permissible that it be with a fatha on the ḍād and lightened (mukhaffaf) from ḍayqin, and it has indeed been read thus, i.e., "do not be in a matter of distress." Abu 'Ali (al-Farisi) disliked that this be a lightened form of what was mentioned, because it requires the deletion of the modified noun (al-mawsuf) and placing the adjective (al-sifah) in its position, and it is not among the adjectives that stand in for the modified noun regularly; and there is discussion in this.

﴿They say, "When will this promise be fulfilled?"﴾ That is, the imminent punishment that was promised. It seems they understood their being threatened with punishment from the command to travel and to observe the fate of those who denied before them. From this a point is also known about the expression ﴿يَقُولُونَ﴾ (yaqūlūna, "they say"), and about its not following the pattern of what precedes it, namely ﴿وقالَ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا﴾ (wa qāla alladhīna kafarū, "and those who disbelieved said"). Their question about the time of the coming of this punishment was in the manner of mockery and denial. For this reason they said:

﴿If you are truthful﴾ عانِينَ إنْ كُنْتُمْ صادِقِينَ, "if you are truthful in your report of its coming, then tell us its time." The plural is used in view of the believers sharing in the report of this.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 27, verse 72:**

﴿Say: Perhaps some of what you are hastening for has drawn near to you.﴾ The original meaning of ﴿radifa﴾ (رَدِفَ) is "followed," but what is intended here is "reached" and "arrived at." It is among the verbs that take their object directly and also with the particle *lam* (لام, "to"), like *nasiha* (نَصِحَ, "to advise").

It has been said that the *lam* is superfluous (مَزِيدَة), serving to emphasize that the verb reaches its direct object (المفعول به, "direct object"), just as the *ba'* (باء, "with") is added for the same purpose in His saying, ﴿and do not throw yourselves with your own hands into destruction﴾.

It has also been said that the *lam* is there because ﴿radifa﴾ is used in the sense of ﴿dana﴾ (دَنا, "drew near"), which takes *lam* just as it takes *min* (مِن, "from") and *ila* (إلى, "to"), as stated in *al-Asas* (الأساس, "The Foundation," a lexicon by al-Zamakhshari). Because of this implied sense, it is construed with *min* in the verse:

*"When we drew near to ʿUmayr and his companions, they turned and fled swiftly, while death was being driven on."*

It has further been said that the *lam* introduces the object of purpose (المفعول لأجله, "object of purpose"), and that the direct object, to which the verb reaches without a particle, is omitted, meaning: "he followed the people for your sake." The weakness of this view is not hidden.

It has also been said that the speech is complete at ﴿radifa﴾, with its subject being a pronoun referring to the promise, and then it resumes with His saying, ﴿for you is some of what you are hastening for﴾, where *ba'd* (بعض, "some") is the subject (مبتدأ, "subject of a nominal sentence"), and *lakum* (لَكم, "for you") is attached to an omitted element that serves as its predicate (خبرًا, "predicate"). What this involves of breaking up the sentence and departing from its apparent sense without any verbal or semantic reason is not hidden.

The meaning is: "Say: perhaps there has reached you and arrived at you some of what you are hastening for, its coming, which you seek time after time." What is intended by this part is the punishment of the Day of Badr. It has been said that it is the punishment of the grave, but this is not correct. The attribution of hastening this to them is based on what their denial and mockery require, for otherwise there is no actual hastening on their part. The expectation (التَّرَجِّي, "hope") understood from *ʿasa* (عسى, "perhaps") has been said to refer to the servants.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "Indeed, *ʿasa* (عسى), *laʿalla* (لعل, "perhaps"), and *sawfa* (سوف, "will") in the promises and threats of kings indicate the seriousness and certainty of the matter, leaving no room for doubt after them. They only mean by this to show their dignity, and that they do not hasten to take revenge, out of confidence in their power and victory, and their certainty that their enemy will not escape them, and that a mere gesture toward their aims is sufficient on their part. Upon this, the promise and threat of God Most High proceeded, glory be to Him." End of quotation.

Upon this, there is an allegorical metaphor (استعارة تمثيلية, "metaphorical analogy") in the speech. The excellence of this is not hidden, and the choice of what the noble arrangement has over saying "perhaps it will follow you," etc., is because it is more indicative of the certainty of the promise.

Ibn Hurmuz (ابن هرمز) read ﴿radafa﴾ (رَدَفَ) with a *fatha* on the *dal*, and this is a dialectal variant (لغة, "dialect") of the word.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 27, verse 73:

﴿Indeed, your Lord is full of bounty toward mankind﴾, that is, He is truly abounding in great bounty and favor toward all people. And among the sum of His bounty, Mighty and Majestic is He, and His exalted favor, is His deferring the punishment of these people for the sins they commit. ﴿But most of them do not give thanks﴾, that is, they do not give thanks to Him, glorified and exalted is He, for His bounty toward them, and among them are these people. It was also said: they do not know the true extent of His bounty toward them, expressing the absence of their knowledge of that by the absence of what follows from it of gratitude.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 27, verse 74:

﴿And indeed your Lord knows what their breasts conceal﴾, i.e., what they hide of secrets, among which is their enmity toward you, ﴿and what they reveal﴾, i.e., what they make manifest of statements and deeds, among which is what has been related about them. So the delay of their punishment is not because their condition is hidden from Him, glorified is He, or [it is so that] He may requite them for that. The act of the heart, when it is like love, hatred, affirmation, denial, and a resolute determination toward obedience or disobedience, is among what one is requited for. In the verse there is an indication that they have ugly deeds other than what has been related of them. The placing of concealment first is to make clear the intended meaning, that the hidden and the apparent are equal in His knowledge, exalted is He and high is He; or because what the breasts harbor is the cause of what appears upon the limbs. And to hint at the corruption of their breasts, which are the origin of all their other deeds, the noble composition has been preferred over saying: "Indeed your Lord knows what they conceal and what they reveal."

And Ibn Muhaysin, Humayd, and Ibn as-Sumayfa' read «تَكُنَّ» (takunna) with a fatha on the ta' and a damma on the kaf, from kanna ash-shay'a, meaning he concealed it and hid it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 27, verse 75:

﴿And there is not a hidden thing in the heaven and the earth﴾, i.e., a thing hidden and firmly concealed in them. The word ﴿gha'ibah﴾ is an adjective that has become predominant in this meaning, so that it is very common for it not to be applied to a noun it modifies, and for it to indicate permanence, even though it has not been transferred into a noun, like mu'min (believer) and kafir (disbeliever). Its ta' is therefore not a marker of feminine gender, since no modified noun is considered for which it would be applied, as in al-rawiyah (the one who narrates much) said of a man who narrates much; it is then the ta' of intensification (ta' al-mubalaghah). It is also permissible that it be an adjective transferred into a noun, used as a name for that which is absent and hidden, and the ta' in it is for transfer, as in al-Fatihah. The difference between the predominant (al-mughallab) and the transferred (al-manqul), according to what al-Khafaji said, is that the former may be applied to a masculine modified noun, unlike the latter.

The apparent meaning is the generality of ﴿al-ghaibah﴾, i.e., there is no hidden thing, whatever it may be, ﴿except that it is in a clear Book﴾, i.e., a clear book, or one that makes clear what is in it for whoever reads and examines it from among the angels, peace be upon them, and it is the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz). Its containing all of that, if it is finite, presents no problem; but if it is infinite, there is an obvious problem, given the existence of proof for the finitude of dimensions and the impossibility of the existence of what is infinite. Perhaps the existence of infinite things in the knowledge of God the Exalted in the Preserved Tablet is in the manner of what they claim concerning the existence of events in the al-Jafr al-Jami' (the comprehensive book of divination), although that is not exactly the same.

It has been said: the intended meaning of "the Clear Book" is His Exalted, eternal knowledge, which is the origin of the manifestation of things through will and power. It has also been said: it is His, glory be to Him, eternal decree, and applying the term "Book" to what has been mentioned is a metaphor, and what is in that is not hidden.

It has been said: the intended meaning of it is the Qur'an, and its containing every hidden thing is in the manner we have mentioned regarding the Preserved Tablet's containing it. It has been mentioned that some of the knowers extracted from al-Fatihah the names of the Ottoman sultans and the durations of their sultanates, up to the last of those who will rule among them, may God the Exalted perpetuate their dominion until the Day of Religion and grant them success in what is good for the Muslims. Some of them mentioned in this view that it is suitable for what follows concerning the description of the Qur'an, and in it is what is in it. 

Al-Hasan said: the "hidden thing" is the Day of Resurrection and its terrors. Sahib al-Ghaniyyan said: the events and calamities. It has been said: the deeds of the servants. It has been said: what is hidden of the punishment of the heaven and the earth. The generality is preferable, and this was transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, for Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him that he said regarding the verse: He, glory be to Him, says: there is no thing in the heaven and the earth, secret or public, except that God, glory be to Him and exalted, knows it. Some of them drew from this the interpretation of the Book as the eternal knowledge, and there is consideration in this, since it is possible that the being of that in a clear Book has been made a metaphor for His, Exalted's, knowledge of it.

Abu Hayyan went to the view that he, may God be pleased with him, considered in the verse the omission of one of the two opposites, being content with the other. His words, may God be pleased with him, admit of this. It is also possible that he mentioned "the public" in explaining the meaning because whoever knows the secret knows the public a fortiori. It is also possible that this is because there is no public matter except that it is hidden with respect to some persons; so he, may God be pleased with him, by explaining the meaning and mentioning the secret and the public in it, has indicated that the intended meaning of "hidden thing" in the verse is what includes both, namely what is characterized by being hidden, more general than whether it is absolute or relative. Thus it has been said; so reflect.

﴿Indeed, this Qur'an relates to the Children of Israel most of that over which they differ.﴾

When the Exalted (subhanahu) mentioned what pertains to the *mabda'* (the origin, i.e., the Creator and divine attributes) and the *ma'ad* (the return, i.e., resurrection and the afterlife), He, may He be exalted, then mentioned what pertains to *nubuwwah* (prophethood), for the Qur'an is the greatest proof by which the prophethood of our Prophet (ﷺ) is established. He, majestic and exalted, mentioned that it relates to the Children of Israel. By them is meant, as related from Qatadah, the Jews and the Christians. Their differences are the most persistent and continual in their nature, and the Qur'an clarifies for them the true reality of these matters. This would necessitate their acceptance of Islam if they had reflected and been fair, but they did not do so, and they were obstinate, just as you, O polytheists, are obstinate.

Among the matters on which they differed is the affair of the Messiah ('Isa, peace be upon him). Some say he is Allah, the Exalted; some say he is the son of Allah, glorified be He; some say he is the third of three; some say he is a prophet like the other prophets, peace be upon them; and some say he (far be it from him) is a liar in his claim to prophethood, and they attribute to Maryam (Mary) regarding him what she is free of, may Allah be pleased with her. These are the Jews, who denied him.

Also among them is the affair of the Prophet foretold in the Torah. Some say he is Yushu' (Joshua, peace be upon him); some say he is 'Isa (peace be upon him); and some say that he has not yet come and will come at the end of time.

Also among the matters on which they differed is the affair of the pig. The Jews said: its eating is forbidden; the Christians said: it is permissible; and so on with other differences.

Qur'an 27:77: ﴿And indeed it is guidance and mercy for the believers﴾ without restriction, so those among the Children of Israel who believed enter among them first and foremost. Restricting "the believers" to them, as some have done, is contrary to the apparent meaning. As for specifying "the believers" in the mention, although it is a mercy to the worlds (al-'alamin), it is because they are the ones who benefit from it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 27, verse 78:

﴿Indeed your Lord will judge between them﴾, that is, between the Children of Israel who differed, or between the believers and the people in general. ﴿With His judgment﴾. It was said: that is, with His wisdom, exalted is His majesty. This is supported by the reading of Janah ibn Hubaysh, *bi-hikamihi* (with a kasra on the *ha* and a fatha on the *kaf*), the plural of *hikmah* (wisdom), construed with a pronoun referring to Him, exalted is He. It was also said: what is meant by *al-hukm* (judgment) is *al-mahkum bihi* (the thing judged), using the verbal noun (*masdar*) in the sense of the passive participle. What is meant by the thing judged is the truth and justice. On both interpretations, it no longer retains the verbal-noun meaning. The motive for this is that *yaqdi* means *yahkum* (judges). For if *hukm* retained its verbal-noun sense, the sentence would be like your saying: "Zayd strikes with his striking," and this is not said in Arabic speech.

An objection was raised to this: it is valid to say that in the sense of "he is struck with his well-known striking, which is known for its severity," for example. So the meaning here is: He judges with His judgment, known for being associated with truth, or He judges with His own judgment, exalted is He, not with the judgment of another, such as humans.

It was replied to this: the obstacle to the validity of such a statement is not the verbal noun being construed with a pronoun of the agent, for there is no dispute about its validity, just as its being construed with a pronoun of the object in ﴿sa'a laha sa'yaha﴾. Rather, the obstacle is the entry of the *ba'* (the preposition "with") upon the emphatic verbal noun (*masdar mu'akkid*). Furthermore, the first meaning gives the impression that He, glory be to Him, has a judgment that is not known with association with truth, and the second only becomes evident if He had placed *bi-hukmihi* first. And in this is that, according to what was mentioned, it is not an emphatic verbal noun. The non-permissibility regarding the specific-type verbal noun (*masdar nau'i*), especially when it is not from its own root, is not accepted. Also, it appears that the obstacle, in the view of the one who interprets it, is the necessity of redundancy (*laghw*) if it were not interpreted as mentioned; and it is preferable to keep it in its verbal-noun sense. Most of the annexation (*idafah*) is to a known referent. The meaning being as the objector said, "He judges with His judgment known for being associated with truth," the matter is a simple one (lit. "on the tip of the *thumam*," a trivial plant).

Whatever the case, the genitive pronoun refers to the Lord, glory be to Him. Its referring back to the Qur'an is also possible, on the basis that the meaning is: He judges by the ruling that the Qur'an contains and comprises, namely rewarding the one in the right and punishing the one in falsehood. In that case, it does not need much talk and argument. What is in it of talk and argument is not hidden from one who has the least discernment in the styles of speech.

﴿And He is the Mighty﴾, so His judgment, glory be to Him, and His decree, exalted is His majesty, are not repelled. ﴿The All-Knowing﴾ of all things, among which is that which He decides,

The particle fa' in His words, ﴿So put your trust in Allah﴾, is for the arrangement of the command upon what has been mentioned of His (glorified and exalted) attributes, for they necessitate trust in Him (exalted) and call for the command to it. Mentioning Him by the all-encompassing Name (Allah) reinforces this; that is, "So put your trust in Allah, the One whose state is this, for it necessitates that everyone trust in Him and entrust all their affairs to Him, (exalted is He)."
* * *
His words, ﴿Indeed you are upon the manifest truth﴾, are a clear reason for trusting in Him (exalted), in that he (upon him be prayers and peace) is upon the clear truth, or the truth that separates it from falsehood, or that separates the one who is right from the one who is wrong. For his being (may Allah's prayers and peace be upon him) so is among the things that necessarily make one confident of His (exalted) protection, support and strengthening, without doubt.

His words (glorified is He), ﴿Indeed you cannot make the dead hear﴾, etc., are another reason for trust, which is an expression for devoting oneself to Allah (exalted), entrusting the matter to Him (glorified is He), and turning away from clinging to anything other than Him. He first gave a reason from His side that necessitates it, namely His (exalted and mighty) judgment with the truth, His might and His knowledge (blessed and exalted is He). Second, He gave a reason from the side of him (upon him be prayers and peace), in one of the two aspects: his being (may Allah's prayers and peace be upon him) upon the truth, and from His side in the other aspect, namely Allah's (exalted) help and support for the one who is right. Then He gave a third reason, which necessitates it not directly but through its necessitating turning away from clinging to anything other than Allah (exalted): for their being like the dead, the deaf and the blind necessitates cutting off all hope of their companionship and support, and calls for restricting reliance to Him (exalted), which is what is meant by trusting in Him (may His majesty be exalted).

It has also been allowed that His words (exalted), ﴿Indeed you cannot make hear﴾, etc., be an explanatory resumptive clause, answering a question arising from what precedes it, namely "Indeed you are upon the manifest truth." It is as if it were said: "What is the matter with them that they do not believe in one who is upon the manifest truth?" So it is said: ﴿Indeed you cannot make the dead hear﴾, etc.

It has been objected that the context rejects this. It has also been objected by denial: they were likened to the dead, according to what is said, because they are not affected by the thunderous warnings recited to them. The omission of the object of "hear" is to show that they hear nothing of what is heard. It has also been said: perhaps the intended meaning is the likening of their hearts to the dead in the aforementioned lack of awareness, for the heart is one of the faculties of perception, and its invalidity is indicated entirely. Then he explained the invalidity of the two faculties of the ear and the eye, as in His words: ﴿They have hearts with which they do not understand, and they have eyes with which they do not see, and they have ears with which they do not hear﴾. Otherwise, after likening their selves to the dead, there appears no added excellence in likening them to the deaf and the blind. It is perhaps for this reason that in al-Bahr it is said: that is, the dead of hearts; or they were likened to the dead because they do not benefit from what is recited to them, thus he put first the possibility of attributing death to their hearts.

It has been objected that what has been mentioned is a cold imagination, because the heart is described with understanding and comprehension, not hearing; and what was mentioned first, that they themselves were likened to the dead, is the apparent meaning. Its aspect is that it is by way of supposition and considering their states, as if it were said: "How can you make them hear the guidance to the path of truth while they are dead?" This is considering the beginning of the call. "Even if We had given them life, it would not benefit, for they are deaf, and they have turned back, retreating." This is considering their state after the eloquent delivery and their aversion from it. Then: "Even if We made them hear, they are blind, not guided to act upon what they hear." This is the final outcome of their affair. From this one knows the added excellence in this, free of artifice.

It has been allowed that the likening is for groups according to their degrees of misguidance: among them is one who is like the dead, and one who is like the deaf, and one who is like the blind. Although this is a lightly burdensome aspect, it is also contrary to the apparent meaning. ﴿Nor can you make the deaf hear the call﴾, that is, the call to some matter. The restriction of the negation by His words, ﴿when they turn away retreating﴾, serves to complete and emphasize the negation, for they, along with their deafness to the call to the truth, are turned away from the caller, turning on their backs. There is no doubt that the deaf one does not hear the call even when the caller is directly opposite his ear and close to him, so how much more when he is behind him and far from him. A similar example in completion is the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

They carried a Rudaynī spear whose tip was like a flash of flame not joined with smoke.

Ibn Kathir read: "the deaf do not hear the call" with the yā' (third person masculine) and an open mīm, and with the raising of the ḍamma (the subject being the deaf, in the nominative).

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 27, verse 81:**

﴿And you cannot guide the blind away from their error﴾. That is: you are not one who turns the blind away from their error by guiding them to a guidance that brings them to the goal, because the customary condition for being guided is absent, which is sight. (ʿan), "away from," is connected to the guidance, in view of its implying the meaning of turning away, as we have indicated. Abu al-Baqa' permitted that it be connected to "the blind," so that the meaning would be that their blindness arose from their error, but this is far-fetched. The use of the nominal sentence is for emphasis in negating guidance.

Yahya ibn al-Harith and Abu Haywah read *bi-hādin* with tanwin, and *al-ʿumyа* in the accusative. Al-A'mash, Talhah, Ibn Thabit, Ibn Ya'mur and Hamzah read *tahdī*, the present tense of *hadā*, with *al-ʿumyа* in the accusative. Ibn Mas'ud read *wa-mā an tahtadiya*, with *an* added after *mā*, as in the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

*I swore to her by God an oath of a sinner:*
*They slept, so there was no talk nor [any] speech.*

Here *tahtadī* is the present tense of *ihtadā*, and *al-ʿumy* is in the nominative. ﴿If you make hear﴾, that is: you do not make hear a hearing that benefits the hearer.

﴿Except those who believe in Our signs﴾, that is: it is in their nature to believe in them, and they are those who are neither dead, nor deaf, nor blind.

Some of the eminent scholars said: that is, except those who are, in the knowledge of God the Exalted, such. This was objected to on the grounds that the form of the future tense (*istiqbāl*), though valid in view of the connection of knowledge to what has not yet occurred, is not the appropriate form; the appropriate form is the past tense. The objector chose that the meaning is: except those who affirm that the Qur'an is the speech of God the Exalted, for then his prophethood (ﷺ) is established, so that his words are accepted and his making them hear benefits. It was responded that this would break the restriction to those who affirm in the future tense, if the form is for the present (*ḥāl*), and to those who affirm in the present, if the form is for the future (*istiqbāl*). When the objection of breaking the restriction is removed by making it cover both, it would require the use of a homonym in both its meanings at once, or the combining of the literal and the metaphorical. It was answered that the intended meaning is the present, and other times enter into it by the indication of the text without any constraint.

Some of the verifiers said: the present tense may be intended to mean the future in the broad sense that includes all times. For the future, as is established in the principles of jurisprudence, may be considered with regard to the time of the ruling and of the speaking, and may also be considered with regard to the knowledge of the speaker. Thus ﴿those who believe﴾ here includes those who believe in the present, as it includes those who will believe in the future. So there is no difficulty in the meaning that the objector chose from this aspect.

Yes, it has been said: there is in it a semblance of obtaining what has already been obtained (*taḥṣīl al-ḥāṣil*), because affirming the Qur'an is its beneficial hearing. Perhaps the one who deviated from this view deviated for that reason, and did not regard the difference between these two matters, which is evident after correct consideration. The truth is that what has been mentioned of the semblance of obtaining what has been obtained is very slight, because the difference is evident between the hearing intended in the verse and affirming that the Qur'an is the speech of God the Exalted, as is not hidden.

It may be permitted that by "the signs" are meant the miracles that God the Exalted manifested at his hand (upon him be blessings and peace), which include both the revealed signs and the created signs; and that by them are meant the created signs only. Believing in them is affirming that they are signs of God the Exalted and are not magic. If by the beneficial hearing in this case is meant the hearing of the revealed signs, so that they may act upon what they contain of beliefs and deeds, then the speech is further and further from having a semblance of obtaining what has been obtained, though this is not free of something.

In *Irshad al-ʿAql al-Salim* it is said that the mention of hearing in negation and affirmation, rather than guidance, though guidance is close to it (as in: "you do not guide except those who believe," and so on), is because the path of guidance is the hearing of the revealed signs; so understand.

As for His saying the Exalted: ﴿so they are submitting﴾, it has been said: it is a reason for their believing in them, as if it were said: for they are submitting to the truth at every time. And it has been said: they are sincere to God the Exalted, from His saying the Exalted: ﴿Yes, whoever submits his face to God﴾. And it has been said: it is a reason for what the speech indicates, that they hear a hearing beneficial to them. In the use of the singular pronoun at one time and the plural at another, there is consideration of the wording of *man* and its meaning.

It has been cited, by His saying the Glorified: ﴿Indeed you cannot make the dead hear﴾, as evidence that the dead do not hear the speech of people absolutely. The detailed discussion of this will come, God the Exalted willing, in surah al-Rum, in the most complete manner.

[p. 21]

﴿And when the word comes to pass against them﴾ is an explanation of what was alluded to by His saying, ﴿some of what you were hastening﴾, namely the rest of what they were hastening of the Hour and its precursors. By "the word" is meant what the noble verses declared about the coming of the Hour and the various kinds of terrors in it, which they were hastening. Its "coming to pass" means the establishment and occurrence of the Hour. He expressed it in this way to signal the severity of its impact and effect. Attributing it to the word is because the intent is to explain its occurrence insofar as it is the fulfilment of the declaration that announced its coming. "Coming to pass" is intended to mean its drawing near and approach, as in His saying, ﴿The command of Allah has come﴾. Thus there is a metaphorical usage of imminence, meaning: when the content of the aforementioned word, which they can hardly hear, and its fulfilment, draw near.

﴿We will bring forth for them a beast from the earth﴾. This is according to what Ibn Mardawayh narrated from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, raised to the Prophet (marfu'), and what a group narrated from Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, as a statement of his own (mawquf): "When enjoining good and forbidding evil is abandoned."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "Increase your circumambulation of the House before it is lifted up, and people forget its place. Increase your recitation of the Qur'an before it is lifted up." It was said: "How can what is in the breasts of men be lifted up?" He said: "It will be carried away by night, and they will wake up empty of it, and they will forget the saying 'There is no god but Allah', and they will fall into the saying and poetry of the Jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance). That is when the word comes to pass against them." This indicates that the emergence of the beast is when no good remains on the earth. This implies that it will be after the death of 'Isa (Jesus) and the Mahdi and their followers, peace be upon them. There will come, if Allah wills, from the reports what clearly states that it will emerge while 'Isa is circumambulating the House with the Muslims.

Nu'aym ibn Hammad narrated from Wahb ibn Munabbih, who said: "The first of the signs is the Romans, the second is the Dajjal, the third is Ya'juj and Ma'juj, the fourth is 'Isa, the fifth is the smoke, and the sixth is the beast." al-Saffarini preferred that it is before the smoke. The truth is that it will emerge while there are among the people both believer and disbeliever. Therefore, the report mentioned from Ibn Mas'ud is evidently not authentic.

[Page 22]

And what supports what we have mentioned of the truth is what Ahmad, al-Tayalisi, Nu'aym ibn Hammad, 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it as hasan, good), Ibn Majah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'The beast of the earth will emerge, and with it will be the staff of Musa and the ring of Sulayman, peace be upon them both. It will mark the face of the believer with the ring, and it will shatter the nose of the disbeliever with the staff, until people gather at the table, and the believer is recognised from the disbeliever.'"

The narrations concerning it have differed greatly. Abu Hayyan in al-Bahr and al-Damiri in Hayat al-Hayawan related a report that it will emerge in every town a beast of the kind that is dispersed in the earth, so it is not a single beast. Accordingly, "beast" is meant as a genus that is true of many. However, most of the narrations say it is a single beast, and this is the sound view. Therefore, the expression of it by the name of a genus, and the emphasis on its indefiniteness by tanwin (nunation) indicating magnification, indicates the strangeness of its affair and that its attributes exceed the scope of description, which is not hidden. And regarding its being a single beast, there is also disagreement. It was said: it is of mankind, and this is supported by what Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi narrated, who said: "'Ali, may Allah honour his face, was asked about the beast, and he said: 'Indeed, by Allah, it is not a beast that has a tail, but it has a beard.'" And in al-Mizan of al-Dhahabi, from Jabir al-Ju'fi, who was a liar, Abu Hanifah said: "I did not meet anyone more lying than him. He used to say that it is of mankind, and that it is 'Ali himself, may Allah honour his face." Upon this, a group of his Shi'i brothers gathered, and they have narrations on this. Among them is what 'Ali ibn Ibrahim narrated in his tafsir from Abu 'Abd Allah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "A man said to 'Ammar ibn Yasir: 'O Abu al-Yaqzan, a verse in the Book of Allah has corrupted my heart.' 'Ammar said: 'And which verse is it?' He said: 'His saying, ﴿And when the word comes to pass against them﴾, the verse. So what beast is this?' 'Ammar said: 'By Allah, I will not sit, nor eat, nor drink until I show it to you.' Then 'Ammar came with the man to the Commander of the Faithful, 'Ali, may Allah honour his face, while he was eating dates and butter. He said: 'O Abu al-Yaqzan, come.' 'Ammar sat and ate with him. The man was astonished by this. When 'Ammar stood up, the man said: 'Subhan Allah! You swore that you would not sit, nor eat, nor drink until you showed it to me.' 'Ammar said: 'I have shown it to you, if you understand.'" Al-'Ayyashi narrated this same story from Abu Dharr as well. All that they narrate concerning this is clear falsehood, and in it is the doctrine of return (raj'ah), for which no evidence supports them.

There are in some reports what contradicts what has been mentioned. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Nazzal ibn Sabrah, who said: "It was said to 'Ali, may Allah honour his face: 'Indeed, some people claim that you are the beast of the earth.' He said: 'By Allah, the beast of the earth has feathers and down, and I have no feathers or down. It has a hoof, and I have no hoof. It emerges from the hoofprint of a noble horse three times, and not a third of it has emerged.'" And the well-known view, which is the truth, is that it is a beast that is not of the species of mankind. It was said: it is the serpent that was in the hollow of the Ka'bah, which was snatched by the eagle when the Quraysh wished to build the Sacred House, and it prevented them. The eagle that snatched it threw it at al-Hajun, and the earth swallowed it. al-Damiri mentioned this from Ibn 'Abbas. Most scholars, however, hold that it is other than this.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn al-Zubayr that he described the beast, saying: "Its head is the head of an ox, its eye is the eye of a pig, its ear is the ear of an elephant, its horn is the horn of a stag, its neck is the neck of an ostrich, its chest is the chest of a lion, its colour is the colour of a leopard, its flank is the flank of a cat, its tail is the tail of a ram, and its legs are the legs of a camel. Between each two joints are twelve cubits." Ibn Jarir added: "by the cubit of Adam, peace be upon him."

al-Saffarini transmitted from Ka'b that he said: "Its voice is the voice of a donkey." Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "The beast is composed, having down and feathers, and in it are the colours of all beasts, and in it are the marks of every nation. Its mark from this nation is that it speaks

[Page 23]

in a clear Arabic tongue." And from Abu Hurayrah that he said: "In it are of every colour, and the distance between its two horns is a farsakh for a rider." In another narration from Ibn 'Abbas, its neck is raised so that whoever is in the east can see it just as whoever is in the west can see it. It has a face like the face of a man and a beak like the beak of a bird, having fur and down. From Wahb: its face is the face of a man, and the rest of its form is like the form of a bird. Some narrations explicitly state that it has two wings. Some have mentioned that its length is sixty cubits.

It has been differed regarding the place of its emergence. It was said: the Sacred Mosque, because of what Ibn Jarir narrated from Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) mentioned the beast, and Hudhayfah said: 'O Messenger of Allah, from where will it emerge?' He said: 'From the greatest of the mosques in sanctity with Allah, while 'Isa, peace be upon him, is circumambulating the House with the Muslims. Then the earth will shake beneath them, moving the lamp, and al-Safa will split from the side facing the mosque, and the beast will emerge from al-Safa. The first thing that appears is its head, glistening, having fur and feathers. No seeker will overtake it, and no fleeing one will escape it. It will mark people, believer and disbeliever. As for the believer, it will make his face appear as if it were a shining star, and it will write between his eyes "believer." As for the disbeliever, it will strike between his eyes a black spot, and write "disbeliever."'"

Ibn Abi Shaybah and al-Khatib in Ta'li al-Talkhis narrated from Ibn 'Umar, who said: "The beast will emerge from the mountain of Jiyad in the days of tashriq, while the people are at Mina."

Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'The beast of the earth will emerge from Jiyad, and its chest will reach the Corner (of the Ka'bah), and its tail will not yet have emerged. It is a beast with fur and legs.'"

al-Bukhari in his Tarikh, Ibn Majah, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Buraydah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) took me to a place in the desert near Makkah, and behold, there was dry land around which was sand. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'The beast will emerge from this place, and it will be a span by a span.'"

It has come in some narrations that it will emerge from the farthest part of the desert, and in some from the city of the people of Lut. And in some that it has three emergences in the course of time: it will emerge in the first emergence in the farthest part of Yemen, its mention spreading in the desert, and its mention will not enter the town, meaning Makkah. Then it will emerge in another emergence, and its mention will rise in the desert and enter the town. Then, while people are in the greatest of the mosques in sanctity, they will not be startled except by it being in the side of the mosque, near the Black Stone and the Gate of the Banu Makhzum. People will scatter from it in every direction, and a band of Muslims who know that they will not be able to escape Allah will remain steadfast. It will shake the dust off its head, and it will clear their faces until they appear like shining stars.

It has also been differed as to whether it will be created on the day it emerges or is already created now. It was said: it will be created on the day it emerges. And it was said: it is already created, but it has not been commanded to emerge.

It has been cited, based on what was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, that he struck al-Safa with his staff while he was in a state of ihram (pilgrim consecration), and said: "Indeed the beast hears the striking of this staff of mine." Upon this, some say it is the serpent, and some say it is the Jassasah (the spy), which spies on news for the Dajjal, as is narrated from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As. Some claimed that it was created in the time of the earlier prophets, peace be upon them. Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Hasan that "Musa, peace be upon him, asked his Lord, glorified is He, to show him the beast, and it emerged for three days and nights, going into the sky, and no one could see either of its ends. He, peace be upon him, saw a dreadful sight and said: 'O Lord, return it,' and He returned it."

It has come in a hadith narrated by Nu'aym ibn Hammad in al-Fitan and al-Hakim in al-Mustadrak from Ibn Mas'ud that when it emerges it will kill Iblis, may the curse of Allah be upon him, while he is prostrating, and that will be after the sun rises from its west, and his destruction will be certain to him. The reports concerning this beast are many.

[Page 24]

In al-Bahr: they differed regarding its nature and shape, its place of emergence, the number of its emergences, the amount that emerges from it, what it does to people, and with what it emerges. They differed in a confused manner, some contradicting others. So we have set aside mentioning it, because transmitting it is blackening paper with what is not authentic and wasting the time of its transmission. End of quote. This is a true statement. I have only transmitted some of that to satisfy the desire of one who loves to be informed of some of its reports, whether true or false. al-Saffarini, in his book al-Buhur al-Zakhirah, undertook to reconcile some of these conflicting reports, but I do not think he brought anything.

Then, among the reports mentioned, the one that al-Tirmidhi graded as good is closest to acceptance. Among the reports on this subject is what al-Hakim declared authentic, but his authentication is judged among the scholars of hadith as not to be relied upon. The most I will say concerning this beast is that it is a great beast with legs, not of the species of mankind at all, which Allah, exalted is He, will bring forth from the earth at the end of time. In restricting its emergence with His saying, glorified is He, ﴿from the earth﴾, there is a kind of indication, as has been said, that its creation is not by way of reproduction, but by way of spontaneous generation, similar to the creation of insects.

And it has been said: it is an indication of its formation within the depths of the earth. So the bringing forth of it from the earth is a symbol of what will happen at the Hour, when it comes out before the Hour, through the splitting of the earth and the emergence of people from its depths alive, with their creation complete. This, and what precedes it, implies that ﴿from the earth﴾ is connected to ﴿We shall bring forth﴾. This is the apparent reading, and it is the one to rely upon, rather than taking it as connected to a deleted element that serves as a description of "a beast" (dābbah), meaning a beast existing from the earth.

﴿And it will speak to them that the people were not certain of Our signs﴾. That is, it will speak to them, telling them that they were not certain of the signs of Allah, the Exalted, which declare the coming of the Hour and its precursors, or of all His signs, of which those signs are a part. It has been said: of His signs, of which its emergence before the Hour is a part, but this is not the correct view. The attribution of the signs to the plural "We" (nun al-‘aẓamah, the "royal we" of majesty) is because it is a narration from Him, the Exalted, of the meaning of its words, not of the exact wording of its speech. It has been said: it is because it is a narration from it of the words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. It has also been said: it is because of its particular connection to Him, the Exalted, and its high standing with Him, glorified be He, just as some of the close companions of a king say "our horses" and "our lands," when in truth the horses and lands belong to their master. It has also been said: there is an elided genitive, meaning "the signs of our Lord."

The apparent view is that the plural pronoun in ﴿it will speak to them﴾ refers to the disbelievers who deny resurrection in general, not to the disbelievers spoken of earlier in particular, since those people are not present at the emergence of the beast so that it could speak to them. Its speaking to them, while they are dead, is far-fetched or unintelligible. The return (al-raj‘ah) that the Shi‘ah believe in is not something we believe in, and the following verse does not indicate it, as they claim. What makes this easier is that the subject of the discourse about them is nothing other than their state of polytheism, disbelief in the signs, and denial of resurrection, and this is found both in them and in the disbelievers present at the emergence of the beast. The same applies to the pronouns ﴿upon them﴾ and ﴿for them﴾. By "the people" is meant the disbelievers of the past in general, not only the polytheists of Mecca. The purpose of its informing them of this is to express regret over what they missed of certainty about what is near to occur, and the clarification of the falsehood of what they believed about it, and their being held accountable for denying it with the strictest accountability. In this there is an appeal to their likes to abandon what they are upon, namely the denial and rejection of resurrection in which they shared with those (earlier) people. It is also permitted that by "the people" is meant the polytheists of Mecca, with the matter of informing remaining as it is.

It has been said: the pronouns may refer to people in general, not only to the disbelievers among them. By "the people" may then be meant either the disbelievers who deny resurrection, and the purpose of the informing is to create aversion to what they were upon of denial, so that the believer may be steadied and the disbeliever restrained; or the polytheists of Mecca, and the purpose of the informing is that.

It has been said: the purpose is to disgrace them before their friends and enemies alike. It speaks in the tongue of the beast so that it will be more eloquent, because of what it contains of the manifestation of their error before something one would not expect to perceive, let alone speak, and to proclaim it in the manner of disgrace. It occurs before the Hour so that it may be followed, without much interval, by something resembling it: the testimony of the limbs against them, which is further in occurrence, together with the disgrace of the beast. Its occurrence after this resembles a progression from the great to the greater. It has been supported that the pronouns refer to people in general, and that by "the people" mentioned in the noble text are the people of Mecca, by what is related from Wahb, that the beast will inform everyone who sees it that the people of Mecca were not certain of Muhammad (ﷺ) and the Qur'an. It has been said: the pronouns ﴿upon them﴾ and ﴿for them﴾ refer to the polytheists of Mecca spoken of earlier, and the meaning of ﴿for them﴾ is "to blame them" or something similar, and the pronoun in ﴿it will speak to them﴾ refers to the people present at the emergence, or to the disbelievers in the same way, and by "the people" mentioned in the noble text are those polytheists. It has been said: other than that. Nothing is hidden from you, with the slightest reflection, as to which of these statements is the more preferable and apparent in the verse. Whichever it is, describing the people as not certain of the signs, while they were in fact rejecting them, is to indicate that it was their duty to be certain of them and to affirm their truth, and they had instead embraced the opposite of that. That the speaking is by way of speech (al-kalam) is the apparent meaning, and it is supported by the recitation of Ubayy: "tunabbi'uhum" (it will inform them), and the recitation of Yahya ibn Sallam: "tuhaddithuhum" (it will tell them).

It has been said: it is from al-kalm, meaning wounding, and the form (taf‘il) indicates intensification. This is supported by the recitation of Ibn ‘Abbas, Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr, Abu Zur‘ah, al-Jahdari, Abu Haywah and Ibn Abi ‘Ablah: "takla‘uhum" (it will wound them), with a fatḥah on the tā', a sukūn on the kāf and a lightened lām; and the recitation of some who read "tajrahuhum" (it will wound them) in place of "tukallimuhum." It seems that by wounding is meant what is the opposite of praising, and this returns to the meaning of disgrace. The pronouns referring to the disbelievers spoken of earlier is unobjectionable. The words of the Exalted, ﴿that the people﴾ and so on, are in the sense of ﴿that the people﴾ (bi-anna al-nās), and the meaning is that it disgraces them by this speech, and by "the people" in it is meant those disgraced people. The apparent reading of the verse is that it occurs in its speech in this wording. Perhaps the listeners understood that the intended people were the polytheists of Mecca at the time of the disgrace, by the aid of a context indicating this at that time. It is possible that what occurs in it in place of this is "the polytheists of Mecca" or something similar, but it came in the narration with the word "the people." The point in this, it has been said, is to hint at their great number.

It has been said: the purpose is to signal the extreme ugliness of their lack of certainty. From what has been mentioned, the reason for shifting from "that they" to ﴿that the people﴾ is known. It is permitted that it be in the sense of a particle of causation, meaning "because the people," and this is a causal statement from Him, the Exalted, for its wounding of them. In it there is the placing of a noun in place of the returning pronoun, as with the earlier pronouns referring to the polytheists of Mecca. It is also permitted that the preposition (bā’) be understood as indicating cause. It is also permitted that by "the speech" (al-kalm) is meant wounding in the sense of branding,

for it has been related that it brands the forehead of the disbeliever. In another report, it smashes his nose with the staff of Moses, peace be upon him, which is with it. Some have preferred that what is meant is this, on account of a ḥadīth narrated by Nu‘aym ibn Ḥammād and Ibn Mardawayh from ‘Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "It is not a speech nor a word, but a mark that marks those whom Allah, the Exalted, commands it to." Abu al-Hawra’ asked Ibn ‘Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, whether the reading in the verse is "tukallimuhum" or "tukalmuhum." He said: "It does all of that: it speaks to the believer, and it wounds the disbeliever." The apparent reading is that, on the assumption that the meaning of the speech is wounding and branding, the pronouns refer to the disbelievers in general, not to those spoken of earlier, since there is no sense in its branding them. It is necessary that by "the people" are meant those disbelievers to whom the pronouns refer. Perhaps the meaning is that it brands them because they were, in Our knowledge of Our signs, not certain. The recitation of Ibn Mas‘ud is "bi-an" (with an), and this is taken as supporting the speech reading, which is based on the apparent meaning; otherwise the bā’ may indicate causation, which accords with the reading as wounding. Some of the seven readers recited "in" (with a kasrah on the hamzah), and this is explained either by supposing an implied "saying," or by treating speaking as speech in that respect, or by taking the statement as a new sentence coming from Him, glorified be He, as a causal explanation. So reflect.

[Page 26]

﴿And on the Day We gather from every nation a company of those who deny Our signs﴾: a general statement of the state of the deniers at the onset of the Hour, after the mention of some of its preliminary signs. ﴿And the Day﴾ is in the accusative, governed by a verb understood, addressed to our Prophet (ﷺ): that is, "Remember the Day." The directing of the command to remember a time, although the intended purpose is to remind of the events that occur in it, has been explained more than once. The gathering meant here is the gathering for rebuke and punishment, following the general gathering that encompasses all of creation, which is mentioned afterwards in the words of the Exalted: ﴿And the Day the Trumpet is blown﴾ to the end of the verse. Perhaps the reason for placing what includes this before what includes that, and not the reverse, although the chronological order requires the reverse, is to indicate that each of the states included in this and that is a great calamity and a dreadful disaster, truly deserving of being remembered on its own. Had the chronological order been observed, it might have been supposed that all of it is one single calamity whose remembrance was commanded, as was mentioned in Surat al-Baqarah. Moreover, the more fitting arrangement, given that the statement ﴿they do not believe in the signs﴾ is meant as "they deny them," would be to mention after it what includes the rebuke by the Exalted and the punishment for that denial. The second ﴿min﴾ is explanatory (bayaniyyah), brought to clarify ﴿a company﴾. The first ﴿min﴾ is partitive (tab'iyyah), because every nation is divided into one who affirms and one who denies. That is: "And on the Day We gather from every nation, from the nations of the Prophets (peace be upon them), or from the people of every age among the ages, a large group who deny Our signs." ﴿Then they are driven on﴾: that is, the first of them is held back until the last of them, so that they catch up with one another and assemble at the place of rebuke and questioning. In this there is an indication of the vastness of their number and the spread of their extremities, which is not hidden. It has been said that the second ﴿min﴾ is partitive like the first, and that the ﴿company﴾ means a group of the leaders who were followed by the disbelievers. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that Abu Jahl, al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah and Shaybah ibn Rabi'ah will be driven before the people of Makkah, and likewise the leaders of all the other nations will be gathered before them to the Fire. This verse is among the most prominent verses cited by the Imamiyyah (Twelver Shi'is) as evidence for the raj'ah (the return of the dead to this world before the Resurrection).

Al-Tabarsi said in his tafsir Majma' al-Bayan: "Whoever among the Imamiyyah holds this view has used this verse as proof for the validity of the raj'ah, saying: The presence of ﴿min﴾ in the sentence necessitates partiality, and this indicates that a group will be gathered and not another. That is not the characteristic of the Day of Resurrection, concerning which the Glorified says: ﴿And We gathered them and left none of them behind﴾. The reports from the Imams of guidance from the family of Muhammad (ﷺ) have been widely transmitted that God, the Exalted, will restore at the rising of the Mahdi a group of those whose death came earlier, from among His friends and partisans, so that they may attain the reward of his victory and assistance and rejoice in the manifestation of his dominion; and He will also restore a group of his enemies, so that He may take vengeance upon them and they may receive some of the punishment they deserve, by being killed at the hands of his partisans, or by humiliation and disgrace through witnessing the exaltation of his word."

No sensible person doubts that this is within God's power and not impossible in itself. God, the Exalted, has done this with the earlier nations, and the Qur'an speaks of it in several places, such as the story of 'Uzayr and others (peace be upon them). It is also authentically reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "There will occur among my community everything that occurred among the Children of Israel, step by step and exactly alike, so that even if one of them had entered a lizard's burrow, you would enter it too."

A group among the Imamiyyah interpreted what has been transmitted in the reports concerning the raj'ah as meaning the return of the state, the command and the prohibition, and not the return of individuals and the reviving of the dead. They interpreted the reports on this matter because they thought that the raj'ah contradicts the obligation of religious duty (taklif). It does not, because there is nothing in it that compels the performance of obligatory acts and the abstention from what is ugly, and religious duty remains valid along with it, just as it remains valid alongside the manifestation of dazzling miracles and overpowering signs, such as the splitting of the sea, the transformation of a staff into a serpent, and things similar to that.

And because the raj'ah has not been established by the apparent meanings of the transmitted reports, so that interpretation could be applied to them. What is relied upon in this matter is only the ijma' (consensus) of the Imamiyyah Shi'ah, although the reports support and corroborate it. End of quotation.

Now I say: The first to speak of the raj'ah was 'Abd Allah ibn Saba', but he restricted it to the Prophet (ﷺ). He was followed by Jabir al-Ju'fi at the beginning of the second century, who spoke of the return of the Commander of the Faithful, may God honour his face, as well, but did not fix a time for it. When the third century came, its people among the Imamiyyah established the return of all the Imams and their enemies, and they specified the time of the manifestation of the Mahdi for it. They based this on what they had transmitted from the Imams of the People of the House. The Zaydiyyah, as a whole, reject this claim with strong rejection, and they have refuted it in their books in a comprehensive manner, with reports from the Imams of the People of the House as well, which contradict the reports of the Imamiyyah. The verses mentioned here do not indicate the raj'ah as they allege, and I do not think any of them claims that they indicate it. At most, what they say is that they indicate the return of the deniers or their leaders, and so they would indicate the basic principle of the raj'ah and its validity, but not the raj'ah in the manner they describe. There is something in al-Tabarsi's words that points to this.

You know that it is hardly valid to intend by the verse a return to the world, because it indicates that the gathering mentioned is for the rebuke and reproach of the deniers from the side of the Mighty and Majestic. Rather, what follows indicates that He, the Exalted, Himself rebukes and reproaches them for their denial of His signs, the Glorified. The known usage of such verses for this is the Day of Resurrection. Moreover, they also indicate the infliction of punishment upon them and their being occupied with it so that they cannot answer, but they do not indicate their death and return to something far more severe and more lasting, which is the punishment of the Hereafter, which the magnitude of their crime requires. Thus the apparent meaning is the continuation of their life and their punishment after this gathering, and that is not possible except if it is the gathering of the Day of Resurrection. Perhaps it is also said, as something that prevents taking the mentioned gathering to be the raj'ah, that there is in it a certain relief for them, since by it they escape the punishment of the barzakh (the intermediate state) in which the deniers are, in whatever form it may be, which is more severe than the punishment of this world. In that there is neglect of what the magnitude of the crime requires. Also, how can the raj'ah be intended from it when the verses contain what contradicts it? Among them is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿He will say, "My Lord, send me back, that I may do righteousness in what I left behind." No! It is only a word he is saying, and behind them is a barrier until the Day they are resurrected.﴾ The end of the verse clearly indicates the absence of any raj'ah whatsoever. That the revival after death and the return to the world are among the matters within the power of the Mighty and Majestic is something on which no two rams butt heads. The question, however, is whether it occurs, and Ahl al-Sunnah and those who agree with them do not hold that it occurs, and they reject intending it from the verse, relying on many verses for that. As for the reports which the Imamiyyah transmitted on this subject, the Zaydiyyah have spared us the burden of refuting them. Moreover, al-Tabarsi indicated that they are not proofs and that reliance is not placed upon them, and that the proof is only the ijma' of the Imamiyyah, and reliance is placed on nothing but that.

You know that the basis of the authority of ijma' according to them (the Imamiyyah) is the attainment of certainty of the agreement of the infallible one (al-ma'sum). This certainty has not been attained by the Sunni from their consensus, so it does not stand as proof against him. Moreover, he has a consensus that contradicts it, namely the consensus of his own people on the absence of the raj'ah, which reveals what the master of the infallibles (ﷺ) held. Whatever the Imamiyyah say about this consensus, the Sunni says the same about their consensus. As for what was mentioned of the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "There will occur among my community..." the hadith, we do not know its authenticity with this wording. Rather, the apparent meaning is that it is not authentic, for among the Children of Israel there occurred things that no one has mentioned would occur in the like manner in this community, such as the lifting of the mountain over them when they refused to accept what God, the Exalted, had given them of the Book, and their remaining in the wilderness (al-tih) for forty years when they said to Musa (peace be upon him): ﴿So go, you and your Lord, and fight; indeed, we are sitting right here.﴾ And the descent of manna and quails upon them in it, and other things besides.

[Page 28]

In sum, the claim of the raj'ah as the Imamiyyah allege is something for which no proof stands. How many a verse of the Noble Qur'an rejects it, not admitting of interpretation! It seems that the darkness of their hatred for the Companions, may God be pleased with them, prevented them from comprehending those verses, so they fell into the errors into which they fell.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 27, verse 84:

﴿Until, when they come﴾ to the place of questioning, answering, debate, and reckoning, ﴿He says﴾, that is, Allah, mighty and majestic, rebuking them for their denial, not asking as one seeking information, glory be to Him, since that is impossible for Him, mighty and majestic. The absence of questioning about the sin on the Day of Resurrection by anyone other than Him, such as the angels, peace be upon them, is not because it is impossible, as His saying indicates: ﴿No human or jinn will be asked about his sin﴾, according to one of the two interpretations. The shift (iltifat) from the third person to the first is to cultivate awe. ﴿Did you deny My signs﴾, which speak of the meeting of this your day? His saying, ﴿and you did not encompass them in knowledge﴾, is a circumstantial clause (jumla haliyya) serving to increase the heinousness of the denial and its extreme ugliness, and it reinforces the disapproval and rebuke. That is: Did you deny them at first glance, without examining them in a way that would lead to knowledge of their reality and to the certainty that they deserve belief? According to what has been said, this clearly shows that what is meant by "signs" earlier is the revealed signs (al-ayat al-tanziliyya), because they contain the proofs of soundness and their evidences, which they did not encompass in knowledge, even though it was obligatory for them to reflect and ponder upon them, not the Hour itself and what is in it.

Some eminent scholars said: The denial, by its apparent sense, rejects that the "signs" meant are the cosmic signs (al-ayat al-takwiniyya), such as miracles and the like, since there is no relation in them to which that denial could attach. Intending the more general meaning requires considering a figurative extension (taghlib) and taking the denial to mean denying that they indicate what is meant by them, like confirming the Prophet ﷺ regarding the miracles and similar in the signs of the self and the horizons, which goes against the apparent meaning. So it is better to keep it on its apparent meaning and to take the signs as the revealed signs. It has also been said that it is coordinated (ma'tuf) with "you denied", and the hamza is for denying the combination and rebuking for it, as if it were said:

Did you combine denial of My signs with failure to reflect upon them?

﴿Or what was it that you used to do?﴾, that is, or what was it that you used to do with them? The intention is rebuke, and that they did nothing except denial. This is one of two interpretations mentioned by al-Zamakhshari, and he established it in al-Kashf by saying: "Am" is connected (muttasila), and the original is "Did you deny My signs, or did you believe?" The equation is between the two verbs concerning the signs, but the first was brought in a known and established form, and the second not in that manner, to indicate its negation, as if it were said: Is it what was known of denial, or has some new event occurred? The point of evidence is that he made the counterpart indeterminate within it, so he did not place affirmation in the same position as denial in asking about their state. Rather, he only doubted the existence of a counterpart to denial, because His saying, ﴿Or what was it that you used to do?﴾ includes the denial mentioned first and its true counterpart. This is evidence that the question was not asked from ignorance of the situation, but only intended as rebuke and binding argument, in the sense of: "Tell me, woe to you, if some other matter occurred," stating definitively that nothing contrary to the first had occurred, and indicating that if he were asked about what he did, he would answer only with what he had mentioned first. Then he said: This is a clear interpretation. The use of "am" before the interrogative "ma" is permissible for this subtle point, since it has left the reality of the question toward a definitive judgment, not toward an equivalent, but toward the first. The second is that the meaning is: You had no deed in the world except disbelief and denial of the signs of Allah, ﴿Or what was it that you used to do?﴾ other than that. He also established it in al-Kashf by saying that "am" is connected, but the equation is between denial and every other deed related to the signs first, and the presentation in the form of a question is for the aforementioned point. This shows that they had no deed except denial and disbelief, as if they had not been created except for that, so for its sake they did no other deed, and he made the rest of their deeds, for the continuation of disbelief in them, the very disbelief or no deed at all. Then he said: This is a fitting and forceful interpretation. From this it became clear that the entry of "am" upon interrogative nouns is not objectionable when it has left the reality of the question, and this is measured in meaning, even if observing the form of the question is also measured in terms of wording. But they give preference in such cases to the side of meaning and do not give heed to the wording. End of quotation.

Abu Hayyan chose that "am" is disconnected (munqati'a), so it is rendered as "bal" alone, and it is for transition from one rebuke to another. There is no trace in that of an interrogative entering upon an interrogative, and what preceded is less far-reaching in meaning. The phrase "ma dha" may be, as a whole, an interrogative in the accusative position as the predicate of "kana", which is ﴿ta'malun﴾ (you do). Or it may be in the nominative as a subject, with the clause after it as its predicate and the resumptive pronoun omitted, that is, "you do it." It may also be that "ma" there is interrogative and "dha" is a relative noun meaning "alladhi" (which). They are then subject and predicate, and the clause after the relative clause, with its returning pronoun omitted.

Abu Haywa read «amadha» with the mim lightened, and in it there is the entry of an interrogative upon an interrogative, and I have already explained its rationale.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 27, verse 85:

﴿And the word will come into effect against them﴾ — the punishment has descended upon them, and it is what the spoken word signifies by its descent, namely their being thrown into the Fire. ﴿Because of what they wronged﴾ — that is, because of their wrongdoing, which is their denial of the signs of Allah the Exalted. ﴿So they will not speak﴾ — with any proof, since proof has been entirely cut off from them, and they are afflicted with the painful punishment that has descended upon them. It is also said: He will seal their mouths, so they will not be able to speak anything at all.

In al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit by Abu Hayyan) it is stated that the negation of their speech may occur at one of the stations of the Resurrection, or it may apply to a particular group of people, because the Noble Qur'an explicitly states that they will speak at some stations, offering excuses and what they hope will bring them salvation from the Fire.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 27, verse 86:
