﴿Have they not seen that We made the night for them to rest in it﴾ The seeing (al-ru'yah) here is of the heart (qalbiyyah), not of the eye (basariyyah), because the very nature of night and day, although they are among the things that are seen, their being made as mentioned belongs to the category of things known by the intellect. That is: Have they not known that We made the night, with the darkness that is in it, so that they might rest in it through stillness and sleep? Some of the rajaz poets said:

Sleep is the rest of the sensory faculties from movements, and of the psychic faculties.

﴿And the day as something to see by﴾: that is, so that they might see, by the light that is in it, the paths of turning about in the affairs of their livelihood. It is hyperbolic (fa-buligha) in that it made seeing, which is a state of people, a state belonging to the day, and an attribute of its attributes with which it was made, in such a way that it never separates from it. It did not take this same course with the night, because the effect of the darkness of night on stillness is not equivalent to the effect of the light of day on seeing. It is well known that in the verse there is the figure of speech called ihtibak, and the estimate is: We made the night dark so that they might rest in it, and the day something to see by so that they might spread out in it. ﴿Surely in that﴾: that is, in Our making them as they have been described; and the word for "that" (dhalika) carries the meaning of distance, to indicate the great distance of its rank in excellence. ﴿are signs﴾, great ones, ﴿for a people who believe﴾. For it indicates tawhid (the oneness of God), the possibility of resurrection (hashr), and the sending of the messengers, peace be upon them, because the alternation of light and darkness in a particular manner, not determined by their own essence, can only occur by an overpowering power, which is not that which the polytheists associated with Him. And whoever is able to replace darkness with light within a single substance is able to replace death with life in the substances of bodies. And whoever made night and day two causes for their benefits and interests, perhaps He will not neglect that which is the criterion of all their interests in their livelihood and their hereafter, which is the sending of the messengers, peace be upon them.

Page 30

In Irshad al-Aql al-Salim: "[They are] great signs, many, for a people who believe", indicating clearly the soundness of resurrection and the truthfulness of the verses that speak of it. How not, since whoever reflects on the alternation of night and day and their differing in wondrous aspects, founded on delicate wisdoms in whose understanding intellects are bewildered and which only the knowledge of God, majestic and exalted, encompasses; and who witnesses in the horizons the change of the darkness of night, which resembles death, into the light of day, which resembles life; and who observes in himself the change of sleep, which is the brother of death, into waking, which is like life, judges that the Hour is coming, there is no doubt in it, and that God, exalted, will raise those in the graves, with a perfected decree; and he is certain that God, exalted, has made this a model and a proof by which its occurrence may be inferred, and that the verses which speak of it, and of the condition of night and day being a proof for it, and all the other verses, are entirely true, descended from God, exalted. End.

Perhaps the first is preferable, especially when there is added to the inference for the permissibility of resurrection the resemblance of sleep and waking to death and life, because of the obscurity of the indication in this (second view). And the specification of the believers by mention is because they are the ones who benefit from the signs. The connection of this verse to what precedes it is that it serves as a proof for the soundness of what the preceding verses contained of resurrection.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 27, verse 87 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And [mention] the Day when the trumpet is blown﴾. It is either conjoined (ma'tuf) to ﴿the Day We gather﴾ and governed by the same governing verb, or it is governed by a implied verb conjoined to that governing verb. The trumpet (al-ṣūr), according to what is in al-Tadhkira, is a horn of light. al-Bukhari reported from Mujahid that it is like a horn (buq).

al-Tirmidhi reported from Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As, who said: "A Bedouin came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: 'What is the ṣūr?' He said: 'A horn into which it is blown.'" The well-known view is that the holder of the trumpet is Israfil, peace be upon him.

al-Qurtubi mentioned that the nation agrees on this, and that it is created today. al-Tirmidhi, who graded it as good (hasan), reported from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, from the Prophet ﷺ, that he said: "How can I be at ease when the holder of the trumpet has put the horn to his mouth, listening for the command, waiting for when he will be ordered to blow?" It seemed heavy upon the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, so he, peace and blessings be upon him, said to them: "Say: 'Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Guardian.'"

It is also related from Abu Hurayra, as a marfu' (traced to the Prophet ﷺ) report: "The holder of the trumpet has not lowered his gaze since he was entrusted with it, standing ready beside the Throne, fearing that he will be ordered to blast the cry before his glance returns, as though his eyes were two shining stars."

It also came from Abu Hurayra through a marfu' hadith: "The greatest circle in it is like the breadth of the heavens and the earth."

This is among the matters one believes in, and one leaves its modality (kayfiyya) to the Knower of the unseen. It has been said that al-Ṣūr (with a sukun on the waw) means the same as al-Ṣuwar (with a damma on the ṣad and a fatha on the waw), the plural of ṣūra (form), and Abu Ubayda held this view. According to both readings, the speech is on its literal meaning.

It has also been said that there is an allegorical metaphor (isti'ara tamthiliyya) in the speech: it likens the manner in which the dead rise from their graves to the place of gathering, when they are called to stand, to the manner of an army that is blown for with the well-known wind instrument (mizmar), and their marching to a place appointed for them. The first view is that of most scholars, and it is what is relied upon, because the words of the Exalted, ﴿Then it is blown a second time﴾, clearly indicate that al-Ṣūr (ṣūr, with the pronoun "fīhi", "in it" [masculine singular]) is not the plural of ṣūra, for otherwise He would have said "fīhā" (in them) instead of "fīhi". Resorting to interpretation by making the speech a matter of figurative representation clearly denies that there is literally a trumpet there, and that contradicts what the sound hadiths state. Abu al-Haytham, as quoted from him by al-Qurtubi in his tafsir, said: "Whoever denies that the ṣūr is a horn is like one who denies the Throne, the Bridge (al-Sirat), and the Scale, and seeks interpretations for them."

As for this blowing, it has been said that the intended blowing is the second blast. Sahib al-Ghaniyan adopted this view, and al-Allama Abu al-Su'ud chose it and said: "What the context and the sequence of this noble arrangement require is that the fear mentioned in the words of the Exalted, ﴿So whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth is seized with terror﴾, is the dread and awe that overcome all at the Resurrection and the Raising, the two necessary and innate sorts of fear, caused by witnessing the terrifying matters which break the habits, in the souls and in the horizons." Then he said: "It has also been said that the intended blowing is the first blast, and the fear is that which entails death because of the extreme intensity of the terror, as in the words of the Exalted, ﴿And the trumpet is blown, and whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth swoons﴾. Its effect thus applies only to those who are alive when it occurs, not to those of the nations who died before that."

It has also been said that the intended blast here is the blast of fear which comes before the blast of swooning, which is meant by the words of the Exalted, ﴿They await but a single cry, with no pause﴾. He condemned both views with what is mentioned in his tafsir.

al-Allama al-Tibi said: "The truth is that the intended meaning of the words of the Exalted, ﴿It is blown in the trumpet, so whoever is in the heavens is seized with terror﴾, is the first blast, and the words of the Exalted that come later, ﴿And all﴾ etc., refer to the second blast. Know that they differed about the number of blasts. It has been said there are three: the blast of swooning, mentioned in the words of the Exalted, ﴿And the trumpet is blown, and whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth swoons﴾; the blast of raising, mentioned in the words of the Exalted, ﴿And the trumpet is blown, and behold, they come out from the graves to their Lord, hastening﴾; and the blast of fear, mentioned in the verse mentioned here. This is the view chosen by Ibn al-Arabi."

It has been said there are two: the blast of fear is the blast of swooning, because the two matters, fear (fazaʿ, meaning dread) and swooning (ṣaʿq, meaning death), have no separate time for each. al-Qurtubi said: "The Sunna supports this, as in the hadith of Muslim from Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As, which is long, here with some omission: 'Then the trumpet is blown, and the first to hear it will be a man who is repairing his water-trough, and he will swoon, then the people will swoon, then it will be blown a second time, and behold, they will be standing, looking.' This indicates that the blasts are two, not three, and this is the correct view. The blast of fear is the very blast of swooning, because the exception in the two verses is the same." It was objected in the treatise called Sharh al-'Ashr fi Ma'shar al-Hashr, attributed to Ibn al-Kamal, that the hadith contains no indication that there is no third blast. At most, it and the other hadiths of the same kind are silent about it, and that does not necessitate its non-existence. Likewise, the sameness of the exception in the two verses does not indicate that what is mentioned in them is one blast, and this is clear. Then he said: "The view I hold as correct is what was said in the first opinion, that the blast of fear is other than the blast of swooning. For the hadith of the two Sahihs, 'Do not prefer me over the prophets, for the people will swoon on the Day of Resurrection, and I will be the first to regain consciousness, and behold, I will find Musa, peace be upon him, holding onto one of the legs of the Throne, and I do not know whether he regained consciousness before me or was recompensed with the swoon of Mount Sinai,' is explicit that the swooning on the Day of Resurrection is not a death. It is a fear without death. So whoever says there are three blasts: the blast of fear, then the blast of swooning, which is death, then the blast of raising, has indeed been right in distinguishing between the blast of fear and the blast of swooning, but he was not right in his claim that the blast of fear comes before the blast of swooning. How so, when the hadith of the two Sahihs mentioned above indicates the general applicability of the ruling of the blast of fear to the prophets, peace be upon them, who died before the blast of swooning, that is, death?"

al-Qadi Iyad said: "The blast of fear is after the raising, when the heavens and the earth are split. So it becomes clear that the blasts are three, or indeed four: a blast by which Allah the Exalted causes all creation to die, as came in the hadith, and at that time He calls out: 'To whom belongs the Kingdom today?' The words of the Exalted, ﴿Everything perishes except His Face﴾, support this call. Then the blast of raising, as the words of the Exalted express: ﴿And the trumpet is blown, and behold, they come out from the graves to their Lord, hastening﴾. Then the blast of swooning, which is the very blast of fear, and you have heard their two verses. And a blast for returning to consciousness, as the Exalted said after mentioning the blast of swooning: ﴿Then it is blown a second time, and behold, they are standing, looking﴾. You have learned the flaw in the claim that the blast of swooning is the very blast of fear, so reflect." The end.

Someone else objected to this: it would then follow, on the view that the blast of fear differs from the blast of swooning, that the blasts are five. No one we have heard has said that. Furthermore, this view says that the blast of swooning comes after the blast of raising, and the words of the Prophet ﷺ contradict this: "I am the first whom the earth splits open for, and I raise my head, and behold, Musa is holding onto one of the legs of the Throne. I do not know whether he regained consciousness before me or was among those whom Allah the Exalted excepted."

For the splitting of the earth for him ﷺ comes after the blast of raising, without doubt. So when the raising of his head follows it, and the sudden sight of Musa, peace be upon him, holding onto one of the legs of the Throne, then where is the blast of swooning?

It is not hidden that the blasts being five, which has not been heard of, is what is most probable in opinion, and the acceptance of what he mentioned second depends on the soundness of the report he cited. Perhaps the one who held the view mentioned earlier has an answer to this objection.

It has been said: "The most apparent view is that the blasts are three. The first is the blast of swooning, in the sense of death, as it is one of its two meanings, indicated by the words of the Exalted, ﴿It is blown in the trumpet, so whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth swoons﴾. The second is the blast of raising, indicated by the words of the Exalted, ﴿Then it is blown a second time, and behold, they are standing, looking﴾, and the words of the Exalted, ﴿It is blown in the trumpet, and behold, they come out from the graves to their Lord, hastening﴾. The third is the blast of fear, indicated by what is here, and it is, as you have heard from al-Qadi Iyad, after the raising, when the heavens and the earth are split."

Its root meaning, as al-Raghib said, is a contraction and a recoiling that befalls a person from a frightening thing. What is meant is intense terror. Perhaps the swooning mentioned in the hadith of the two Sahihs is a loss of consciousness that results directly from the terror, and also from the blast by means of it. Al-Asas explicitly stated this meaning for it. He said: "One says ṣaʿiqa al-rajul (the man swooned) when he falls unconscious from a crash or a loud sound that he hears." What indicates that it means unconsciousness is the words of the Prophet ﷺ: "I will be the first to regain consciousness (yufiq)," because regaining consciousness happens only after unconsciousness, not after death.

Here he did not express it with the word ṣaʿq intending the unconsciousness mentioned in the hadith, lest it be imagined that death is intended by it, since there is no indicator here like the one in the hadith and it is not accompanied by what suits that meaning.

Some have chosen the view that is well-known, that the blasts are two, and they answer what suggests an extra blast. The first blast is the blast of swooning in the sense of death, with a terrifying state, by which those alive in the heavens and the earth die shortly before it, except whom Allah the Exalted wills. The words of the Exalted, ﴿and it is blown in the trumpet and so-and-so swoons﴾ etc., indicate this. The second blast is the blast of raising, indicated by the verse ﴿Then it is blown a second time, and behold, they are standing, looking﴾. In the well-known view, the interval between them is forty years. In the two Sahihs, from Abu Hurayra as a marfu' report, "forty," without mention of the unit. It was said: "Forty days." Abu Hurayra said: "I refuse." It was said: "Forty months." He said: "I refuse." It was said: "Forty years." He said: "I refuse."

The blast of fear, in the sense of terror and dread, is this very blast. The reason is that the trumpet is blown for raising, so creation is raised and they rise. When they become certain on the Day of Resurrection and witness the signs of the greatness of Allah the Exalted, they are frightened and terrified, except whom Allah the Exalted wills. The fear is linked to the blowing with the particle fa (then), to indicate that the time between them is short, due to the speed of their certainty and their witnessing of what was mentioned.

The genitive construction in our saying "the blast of raising" and our saying "the blast of fear" is the attribution of a cause to its effect, except that the blast's causation of the raising is direct, while its causation of the fear is indirect. The hadith of the two Sahihs, "Do not prefer me over the prophets, for the people will swoon on the Day of Resurrection," etc., contains nothing except the affirmation of swooning in the sense of unconsciousness, as the mention of the people regaining consciousness on the Day of Resurrection suggests, and it does not address a blast that causes it. Yes, expressing it with ṣaʿq, according to what they mentioned about its meaning, requires that there be a crash or a loud sound that whoever hears it swoons from. However, it does not specify the blast, because that could be a sound arising from the splitting of the heavens, which occurs

[p. 33]

after the raising and the fear on the Day of Resurrection, and what they witness of its terrors.

Some denied that it necessarily entails that, since it may mean swooning due to some great event of the Day of Resurrection other than the blast. It was also said: it is among the branches of the blast of raising, because the trumpet is blown, so the creatures are raised, and they realize what they realize and witness what they witness, and they are frightened, and they swoon, except whom Allah the Exalted wills. The hadith of the two Sahihs does not reject this, and the need for regaining consciousness to require another blast is within the scope of denial. It was said:

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 27, verse 87 (part 2 of 2):

Concerning the explanation of the unity of the Trumpet of Resurrection and the Trumpet of Terror: the intended meaning of "terror" is responding and hastening to stand before the Lord of the worlds. The verses have indeed made clear that people hasten at the Resurrection. Thus He, exalted is He, says: ﴿And the Trumpet will be blown, and behold, they will rush forth from the graves to their Lord﴾, and He, glorified is He, says: ﴿They will come forth from the graves swiftly, as though they were rushing toward a shrine, hastening﴾. Its remoteness is not hidden, and the explanation of the exception, which has become difficult, requires an artificial justification. So it is better to construe the unity by what has preceded, so consider this carefully. The use of the past tense form, although the conjoined verb, namely yunfakh (will be blown), is in the present tense, is to indicate the certainty of occurrence, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So He led them into the Fire﴾ after His saying: ﴿He will precede his people﴾. As for the reason for delaying the explanation of the states occurring at the beginning of this blast until after the explanation of what happens afterward, namely the gathering of the deniers, the discussion of it has already passed, so recall it.

﴿Except whom Allah wills﴾: this is a connected exception, as is apparent from "man" (whom). The object of the will is omitted, i.e., except whom Allah, exalted is He, wills not to be terrified. What is meant by this, as has been said, is one who brought a good deed, based on His saying concerning them: ﴿and they will be secure from terror that Day﴾. It has been objected that the terror in that verse is other than the terror intended by His saying, glorified is He: ﴿and [they] will be terrified (fazi'a)﴾, etc., and we will mention that, if Allah, exalted is He, wills.

Those who took the blowing here to refer to the first blast, which is for the swoon (sa'q), i.e., death, differed about their identity. It was said they are Jibril, Mika'il, Israfil and Izra'il, and this was narrated from Muqatil and al-Suddi.

Al-Dahhak said: they are the youths (wildan), the large-eyed houris (hur 'in), the guardians of Paradise, and the bearers of the Throne. Some have related these two opinions regarding the identity of those excepted, on the supposition that by the blowing is meant the second blast and by the terror is meant fear and dread. It was objected against both of them that the bearers of the Throne are not among the inhabitants of the heavens and the earth, because the heavens are within the Kursi, and their relation to it is like the relation of a ring in a desert, and the relation of the Kursi to the Throne is likewise this same relation; how then could its bearers be in the heavens? Likewise the youths, the houris and the guardians of Paradise, because all of these are in Paradise, and all the Gardens are above the heavens and below the Throne, as made clear by the saying of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace: "The ceiling of Paradise is the Throne of the Merciful." So those in it of youths, houris and guardians cannot validly be excepted from those in the heavens and the earth. As for Jibril and those with him of the angels brought near, peace be upon them, they are among the ranks who stand in glorification around the Throne, and if the Throne is above the heavens, the standing in ranks around it cannot be in the heavens. It is answered that it is permissible for "the heavens" to mean what includes the Throne, the Kursi and other celestial bodies, for this is most fitting to the context, and the use of "whoever is in the heavens and the earth" is widespread when the intention is comprehensiveness and totality.

It has been said: there is no obstacle to taking "the heavens" to mean the seven heavens, and to maintaining that the exception on the two aforementioned opinions is disjunctive (munqati'). What is in this is not hidden. Some counted Musa, peace be upon him, among those excepted, and you know that this hardly holds unless by the terror is meant the swoon on the Day of Resurrection after the second blast; as for if by it is meant what occurs in this world at the first blast, then it does not hold. Moreover, his, peace be upon him, being counted among those who are not swooned on the Day of Resurrection, after the saying of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in the Sahihayn hadith mentioned earlier, "So I do not know whether he regained consciousness before me or was recompensed with the swoon of Mount Sinai," requires a sound report that comes after this.

Abu Hurayrah narrated from the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, that "they are the martyrs with their Lord, who are provided for." Al-Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi authenticated it, as al-Qurtubi said, and with this a refutation is made of one who claims that no sound report has come concerning their identity. Ibn Jubayr adopted this view, and his wording is: they are the martyrs, bearing swords around the Throne. Likewise al-Halimi held this view and said: it is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. He then weakened the other opinions. Many of the exegetes have mentioned it, except that some mentioned it in the explanation of "whom Allah wills" in the verse of the swoon, and others mentioned it in its explanation in the verse of terror, so reflect.

﴿And each﴾, i.e., each one of those terrified who are raised at the blast, ﴿came to Him﴾, i.e., they attended the place of standing before the Lord of Might, may His majesty be exalted, for questioning, answering, debate and reckoning. It was said: i.e., they returned to His command and submitted. The plural pronoun is in consideration of the meaning of "each" (kull). Qatadah read atahu as a past-tense verb with its subject the pronoun of "each" according to its wording.

Most of the Seven read atawhu as an active participle, ﴿humbled﴾, i.e., abased. Al-Hasan and al-A'mash read dakhirin without an alif, and in both readings it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) from the pronoun of "each" (kull).

**[Page 34 continues from the previous section]**

His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And you see the mountains﴾ is coordinated with "it is blown" (*yunfakhu*) and falls under the same ruling of reminder. "You see" is from sight with the eye. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿you think them solid﴾ means fixed in their places, not moving. It is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) referring either to the subject of "you see" or to its object. It is also permitted that it be a substitute (*badal*) for the preceding word. His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿while they pass by like the passing of clouds﴾ is a circumstantial clause referring to the pronoun of "the mountains" in "you think them." It is also permitted that it be a circumstantial clause referring to the pronoun in "solid," but Abu al-Baqa' prohibited this because it would imply that they are both solid and passing at the same time. The meaning is: you see the mountains with the sight of the eye, still, while in fact they pass through the air like clouds driven by the winds at a rapid pace. This is because bodies that are gathered together, numerous, and tightly joined, when they move in one direction, hardly show their movement. On this is the saying of al-Nabigha al-Ja'di describing an army:

*With a host like a mountain, you think they are standing still for pilgrims, while the riding-beasts trot briskly.*

It has been said that he likened their passing to the passing of clouds in that they move at a moderate pace, as al-A'sha said:

*As if their gait, from the house of their neighbour, is the passing of clouds, neither slow nor hasty.*

The well-known point of resemblance is speed. The cause of the aforementioned supposition is what you have heard. It has also been said that the observer's supposing them solid while they pass is due to the terror of that day, so there is no firm mental attention in the thought that would establish that they are solid. But this is not the case. In the aforementioned comparison there is also an embedded comparison of the state of the mountains with the state of clouds in the loosening of their parts and their scattering, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the mountains will be like tufts of wool, fluffed﴾.

There is disagreement about the time of this. In *Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim* it is said that it is among the things that occur after the second blast, like the terror mentioned at the gathering of creation. Allah, exalted is His majesty, will change the earth into another earth, alter its form, and move the mountains from their places in the awe-inspiring form described, which the people of the gathering will witness. Although they will be crushed and split at the first blast, their movement and the leveling of the earth will occur only after the second blast, as His saying, exalted is He, declares:

﴿They ask you about the mountains. Say: My Lord will scatter them as dust.﴾ ﴿Then He will leave it a level plain.﴾ ﴿You will not see therein any crookedness or unevenness.﴾ ﴿On that day they will follow the Caller.﴾

And His saying, glorified is He: ﴿On the day the earth will be changed into other than the earth, and the heavens too, and they will come forth before Allah, the One, the Subduer.﴾ The following of the Caller, who is Israfil, and the emergence of creation before Allah, exalted is He, can only occur after the second blast. They have said, in explaining His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the day We set the mountains in motion, and you see the earth as bare, and We gather them﴾, that the past tense used in the coordinated clause, while the coordinating clause is in the future, is to indicate that the gathering precedes the setting in motion and the seeing, as if it were said: "And We gathered them before that." End of quotation.

Another said that it occurs at the first blast. This is because the earth and the mountains will quake, then the mountains will separate from the earth and move through the air, then fall and become a heap of sand poured out, then scattered dust. What indicates that this transformation does not follow the quaking immediately and without interval is the coordination with "and" rather than "then" in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿On the day the earth and the mountains quake, and the mountains will be a heap of sand poured out.﴾ The use of the past tense in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And you see the earth as bare, and We gather them﴾ is to affirm that the occurrence is certain, as mentioned just before. The word "day" in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They ask you about the mountains﴾ and so on, and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿On the day the earth is changed﴾ etc., may be taken as a name for the broad time in which occur what happens at the first blast, namely scattering and transformation, and what happens at the second blast, namely following the Caller and emerging before Allah, exalted is He, the One, the Subduer. The day has also been understood to extend over what occurs at both blasts, in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then when one blast is blown on the Trumpet﴾ ﴿and the earth and the mountains are lifted and crushed with one crushing﴾ ﴿then on that day the Event will occur﴾ ﴿on that day you will be presented.﴾ This is like saying: "I came to him in such a year," while your coming was in one of its times.

Many scholars have held that the change of the earth, like the emergence, occurs after the second blast, because of what is in *Sahih Muslim* from Aisha: "I said: O Messenger of Allah, tell me about the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿On the day the earth is changed into other than the earth﴾, where will the people be? He said: On the Bridge (al-Sirat)."

In other reports there is what indicates that it is before the first blast. The author of *al-Ifsah* reconciled the reports by saying that the change occurs twice: once before the first blast and once after the second blast. Al-Bahr relates that the first of the states is its trembling, then its becoming like tufts of wool fluffed, then like dust, by being broken into pieces after having been like wool, then its being blown away by the winds sent upon it, then its being carried through the air like dust, then its becoming a mirage. All of this, according to what the statement of al-Saffarini implies, occurs before the second blast. Whoever follows the reports will find them manifest in this. The verse here admits that the mentioned seeing might be before the second blast and might be after it, so reflect.

﴿The handiwork of Allah﴾. It is apparent that this is an emphatic infinitive (*maṣdar mu'akkid*, an absolute object used to stress the meaning of the preceding clause), and the clause of the circumstance it governs, which is indicated by the fact that all of this is from His handiwork, exalted is He. It is as if it were said: "Allah, exalted is He, has done that as a work." This is like saying: "He owes me a thousand, truly." In their terminology this is called the infinitive that emphasizes itself. Al-Zajjaj and Abu al-Baqa' went to this view.

Some of the verifying scholars said: It emphasizes the meaning of what precedes it, on the basis that it refers to all that has been mentioned of the blowing in the Trumpet and what follows from it. It is intended to draw attention to the greatness of those acts and the awesomeness of their matter, and to inform that they are not a way of disrupting the order of the world and corrupting the conditions of beings entirely without wisdom. Rather, they are among the wonders of Allah's handiwork, founded on wisdom, leading to beautiful ends for which the preliminaries of creation and the beginnings of origination were arranged in a firm way and a sound method, as His saying, exalted is He, indicates: ﴿Who perfected everything He created﴾, that is, perfected its creation and shaped it according to what wisdom requires. End of quotation. Its goodness is evident.

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is one of the emphatic infinitives, except that what it emphasizes is omitted, and it is the governing verb of "the day the trumpet is blown." The meaning is: "On the day the trumpet is blown, such and such happens; Allah, exalted is He, rewards the good-doers and punishes the wrongdoers." Then He, glorified is He, said: ﴿the handiwork of Allah﴾, intending by it—mighty and majestic is He—the reward and the punishment, and so on to the end of what he said. This indicates that he took the day as extending and encompassing the times of both blasts and what is after them, and he made the infinitive an emphasis for this omitted element, which is indicated by the detail in His later saying: "whoever comes, and whoever comes," and by the summoning of "the day the trumpet is blown" as the governing word, and he drew consequences from it. Abu Hayyan criticized him: an infinitive emphasizing the meaning of a clause cannot have its clause omitted, because it is governed by a verb of its own root, so the omission of the governing verb and the omission of the clause whose meaning it emphasizes would combine, and that is a heavy and disruptive omission. Whoever follows the course of these infinitives that emphasize the meaning of a clause finds the clauses stated explicitly, and no omission was intended in any of them, since the principle is that the emphasizing element should not be omitted, for omission contradicts emphasis: insofar as it emphasizes, it is important, and insofar as it is omitted, it is not important. It seems that what led him to depart from the apparent meaning, as is said, is that the perfected handiwork does not seem to suit the setting of mountains in motion. But you know that this is at the edge of a thumbnail. Yes, the better view is to take it as emphasizing the meaning of what was mentioned of the blowing in the Trumpet and what follows, and it was brought to draw attention to the greatness of those acts, as you have heard from some of the verifying scholars.

It has been said that it is in the accusative as an incitement, meaning: "Look at the handiwork of Allah." But this, as you see, is weak.

The verse has been cited as evidence for permitting the application of the word "creator" (*ṣāni'*) to Allah, mighty and majestic is He. This is based on the view of those who hold that the occurrence of the verb is sufficient.

Some have cited, for this permissibility, the sound report: "Indeed Allah is the Creator of every creator and his craft."

This was objected to, on the ground that the condition is that the expression should not occur in the manner of contrast, such as His saying: ﴿Do you cause it to grow, or are We the Growers?﴾ This is in contrast to al-Halimi, according to what his statement requires: "It is recommended for one who casts a seed into the earth to say: Allah is the Sower, the Grower, the Bringer to Maturity." And what is in this hadith is of this kind. Also, what is in the report is with an annexation (*iḍāfa*), so it does not indicate the permissibility of the unannexed form. Do you not see that when the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: "O Companion of every secret conversation, You are the Companion on the journey," they did not derive from it that "the Companion" without qualification is one of Allah's names, so likewise, it is not derived from it that "the Creator" without qualification is one of His names. So reflect on this. Similar to this is the argument from Muslim's report: "Let him be resolute in supplication, for Allah, exalted is He, is the Creator of whatever He wills; no one can compel Him."

Since what is in it is of the kind of the annexed or the qualified, the better argument is what is authentic in the report of al-Tabarani and al-Hakim: "Fear Allah, exalted is He, for Allah, exalted is He, is the Opener for you and the Creator." There is no difference, according to the jurists, between the definite and the indefinite, because the definiteness of an indefinite does not change its meaning. For this reason they permit in the opening takbir: "Allah is the Greatest" (*Allahu al-Akbar*).

Qadi Abd al-Jabbar argued from the generality of His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Who perfected everything﴾ that the evil deeds of the servant are not of His creation, glorified is He. Otherwise, they would have to be described as perfected. Consensus prevents this. It was answered that the verse is specified to exclude accidents, because perfection means firm construction, which is a quality of compounds. And even if it is granted, to describe all accidents with it is disputed, for there is no general statement that has not been specified. And even if it is granted, the stated consensus is disputed; rather, they are also perfected in the sense that wisdom requires them.

His saying: ﴿Indeed, He is Aware of what you do﴾. Some of the verifying scholars made this a reason for the statement that what was mentioned of the blowing in the Trumpet and what follows is a handiwork firmly established by Him, exalted is He. It shows that His knowledge, exalted is He, of the outward acts of the responsible persons and their inward aspects necessitates their manifestation and the explanation of their modes as they are, in goodness and evil, and the arrangement of the recompense upon them after their resurrection and gathering and the moving of the mountains, as the revelation has declared.

*[Page 36 — end of this passage]*

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 27, verse 89:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Whoever comes with a good deed will have better than it﴾, is an explanation of what was alluded to by His, Exalted is He, comprehensive knowledge of their deeds, through the arrangement of its being better as a consequence of them. The Allamah al-Tibi said: His saying, Exalted is He, "Indeed Allah..." etc., is a resumptive statement (isti'naf) that came as an answer to the saying of one who asks: "What will happen after these calamities?" So it was said: "Indeed Allah is Aware of what the doers do," and He will recompense them for their deeds, and He detailed that with His saying, Glorified is He: "Whoever comes..." etc.

The address in ﴿they do﴾ is to all the responsible (mukallafun). Al-'Arabiyyan (Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub... [as in the source: the two Arab readers, i.e., Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub]) and Ibn Kathir read «yaf'alun» with the third-person ya' of absence. The meaning of "the good deed," as narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud, Mujahid, al-Hasan
صفحة 37
al-Nakha'i, Abu Salih, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, 'Ata', and Qatadah, is the testimony that there is no god but Allah. 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Hurayrah, and Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Daylami from Ka'b ibn 'Ujrah, that the Prophet (ﷺ) explained it thus. The meaning of this testimony is accepted monotheism (al-tawhid al-maqbul). It was also said: the meaning of "the good deed" is whatever is realized by what was mentioned and other good deeds, and this is the apparent meaning, considering that the definite article (al-) is genuinely for the category.

Some of them said: the first is the apparent meaning, because the apparent is to take the unrestricted (mutlaq) as the complete (kamil), and the most complete category of good deed is monotheism. And had generality been intended, the apparent would have been to use the indefinite noun. Sufficient for preferring the first is the view of most of the early scholars (al-salaf) toward it, and when the hadith about it is sound, one hardly deviates from it.

Al-Nakha'i used to swear to this without adding an exception (istithna'). The apparent is that "khayr" is comparative, and the excess of the recompense over the good deed is whatever its quantity.

It was said: this is with regard to multiplication or with regard to permanence. Some claimed that the statement has an implied genitive (taqdir mudaf), meaning "better than its measure," and that is, as you see, [weak]. Some eminent scholars said: the reward of theoretical knowledge (al-ma'rifah al-nazariyyah) and of monotheism attained in this world is the necessary knowledge (al-ma'rifah al-darurriyyah) in the most perfect manner in the Hereafter, and the gazing upon His Noble Face, glorified is His majesty, and that is the most noble of felicities. It was also said: "khayr" is not comparative, and "min" is for the beginning of the limit, meaning "then for him is a good from the goods whose origin and source is from it," i.e., from the direction of the good deed. This was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatadah, Mujahid, Ibn Jurayj, and 'Ikrimah.

﴿And they﴾, i.e., those who came with the good deed, ﴿are safe from terror﴾, i.e., a great, terrifying terror whose extent cannot be measured, ﴿on that day﴾. The adverbial phrase "on that day" is in the accusative, governed by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿secure﴾. And "from terror" is also connected to it, and security is used with the preposition and without it, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Do they feel secure from the plan of Allah?﴾. It is permitted that the adverb be in the accusative governed by "terror," and that it be in the accusative governed by an omitted word that functions as an attribute of it, i.e., "terror occurring at that time."

Al-'Arabiyyan (the two readers Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub), Ibn Kathir, and Isma'il ibn Ja'far from Nafi' read «faza'in yawma'idhin», with the "fazaʿ" construct-annexed to "yawm" and the mim of "yawm" kasra. Nafi' in narrations other than that of Isma'il read likewise, except that he pronounced the mim with fatha, a fatha of indeclinability, because "yawm" is annexed to an indeclinable word. The tanwin of "idh" is for compensation for a sentence omitted. The better view, according to al-Bahr, is that the omitted sentence that "idh" compensates for is what is near the adverb, i.e., "the day when he came with the good deed." It is also permitted that the estimate is "the day when the trumpet is blown into," especially if by that blowing is meant the second blast. Shaykh al-Islam limited himself to this and explained the terror as the terror arising from witnessing the punishment after the completion of the reckoning and the manifestation of good and bad deeds, which is the one in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The greatest terror will not grieve them﴾. It is related from al-Hasan that this occurs when the servant is ordered to the Fire, and from Ibn Jurayj that it is when death is slaughtered and it is proclaimed: "O people of Paradise, eternity, no death! O people of the Fire, eternity, no death!" That is the case in the reading with tanwin and the reading with annexation. In the second reading it is not meant to be all the terrors occurring on that day; the basis of the annexation is that this is the greatest and most extreme of terrors, as if whatever else is not terror in comparison with it. He said, following others: the terror indicated by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and he was terrified﴾ etc., is nothing but dread and awe arising at the beginning of perceiving a terrifying thing, and hardly anyone is free of it by natural disposition, even if one is safe from harm reaching him.

Abu 'Ali said: it is permitted that by "terror" in both readings is meant one single terror, and that by it is meant multiplicity, since it is a verbal noun. If multiplicity is meant, it includes every terror that occurs on the Day of Resurrection; and if the single one is meant, it is the one alluded to by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The greatest terror will not grieve them﴾. Its completion, God willing, will come shortly as a continuation of the discussion on the verse.

﴿Whoever brings an evil deed﴾, which is polytheism (*shirk*). Those who interpreted the "good deed" as the testimony that there is no god but Allah (*shahadat an la ilaha illa Allah*) also interpreted it this way, and you know who they are. It has also been said that the intended meaning includes polytheism and other evil deeds. ﴿Their faces will be thrown into the Fire﴾, meaning they will be cast into it face-down, overturned. The attribution of the casting (*kabb*) to the faces is therefore metaphorical (*majaz*), because it is said *kabbahu* and *akabbahu* when one overturns something.

[p. 38]

It has also been said that it is permissible to mean by "the faces" the selves (*anfus*), just as "the hands" are meant in His words, exalted is He: ﴿And do not throw yourselves with your own hands into destruction﴾. Thus the meaning is: ﴿their selves will be thrown into the Fire﴾. ﴿Are you recompensed except for what you used to do?﴾ This is either an *iltifat* (shift in grammatical person or address) for emphasis, or it is by supposing a verb of saying, meaning "it being said to them". In the latter case there is no *iltifat* in it, because it belongs to a different speech. Among the conditions of *iltifat* is that the two speeches be unified, as has been verified in the books of *ma'ani*.

Some of the Murji'ah, who hold that no sin harms one who has faith just as no obedience benefits one who has disbelief, cited His words, exalted is He: ﴿Whoever brings a good deed﴾ and so on, on the basis that the sinful believer is not punished on the Day of Resurrection; otherwise he would not be safe from the terror of witnessing the punishment on that day. This contradicts what the noble verse indicates. It was answered by denying that the sinful believer is included in the generality of the verse, because the intended "good deed" is the complete good deed, namely faith that has not been defiled by any sin, and this is not realized in him. Or because what is understood is coming with a good deed unmixed with an evil deed, and this too is not realized in him. Whoever realizes it is safe from that terror. Indeed, it is not far-fetched that he is safe from every terror of the terrors of the Day of Resurrection. And if his inclusion is granted, we say: the terror from which the one who brings a good deed is safe is what occurs when Death is slaughtered and the caller calls, "O people of Paradise, eternity, no death!" and "O people of the Fire, eternity, no death!", as I heard from Ibn Jurayj. Or it is when Hell closes over its people and they are terrified, as was narrated from al-Kalbi. This does not occur except after the people of Paradise have completely entered Paradise. The punishment that some sinful believers undergo is before that, and the verse does not indicate its negation in any way whatsoever.

Some answered that it is possible for the sinful believer to be safe from the terror of witnessing the punishment, even if he is punished, because he knows that he will not dwell eternally; thus his punishment is counted like the hardships that a lover endures on the path to union with the Beloved. This is extremely weak, as is not hidden.

Some of the Mu'tazilah cited His words, exalted is He: "Whoever brings an evil deed" and so on, to show there is no difference between the punishment of the disbeliever and the punishment of the sinful believer, because "whoever brings an evil deed" includes both, and the casting on the faces into the Fire has been attributed to them. Thus, since that is for the disbeliever in the manner of eternity, it is likewise for the sinful believer. It was answered that the intended "evil deed" is polytheism, as was narrated from most of the early community (*salaf*) who interpreted it thus. So the sinful believer does not enter among "whoever brings an evil deed". Even if his inclusion is granted on the basis of the view that "evil deed" is general, we do not accept that the verse indicates his eternal dwelling in the Fire. That the casting into the Fire is, for the disbeliever, in the manner of eternity does not necessitate that it be so for him. Often a judgment is passed on a group with a general ruling, while what is established for some of them is one type and for others another type of it. This is beyond doubt. Furthermore, the verse belongs to the category of threat (*wa'id*), so on the supposition that the sinful believer is included in its generality, it is to be treated in the manner that the Ash'ariyyah have said regarding the verses of threat. So understand and reflect.

**[Ruh al-Ma'ani, al-Alusi, on Surah 27, verse 91]**

﴿Indeed, I have been commanded only to worship the Lord of this city, who has made it sacred﴾. This is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf, a new sentence that begins without a conjunction), with *qul* (say) understood before it. It is a command to the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, to say this to these disbelievers after he had explained to them the conditions of the origin and the return, and had described the conditions of the Resurrection, in order to stir their resolve in the most gentle manner, so that they would busy themselves with setting right their own affairs, obtaining what benefits them, and turning to reflect upon the wondrous signs that have reached their ears, which are sufficient for their guidance and a cure for their ailments.

The "city" is, according to what has been related from Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah and others, Makkah the Honoured. In *Tarikh Makkah* it is said that it is Mina. [The chain:] Yahya ibn Maysarah narrated to us, from Khallad ibn Yahya, from Sufyan, that he said: "The city is Mina, and the Arabs still call it 'the city' to this day."

Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from Abu al-'Aliyah an explanation of it in the same sense. Some of the eminent scholars mentioned that most of the exegetes hold the first view. Specifying it by the annexation (to the Lord) serves to magnify its status and to honour its place, and mentioning that Allah, exalted is He, has made it sacred is an honour upon an honour and an exaltation following an exaltation. Along with this, the phrase indicates the reason for the command and the necessity of obeying it, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So let them worship the Lord of this House, who has fed them against hunger and secured them against fear﴾ (Qur'an 106:3–4).

It also contains an allusion to the extreme ugliness of what they did in it. Do you not see that, although it is sacred, its sanctity was violated: its grass was cut, its trees were uprooted, its game was frightened, and they intended to commit sacrilege in it? Indeed, they persisted in committing the most heinous of sins and the most abominable of acts of impiety, for they abandoned the worship of its Lord, set up idols in it, and devoted themselves to worshipping them. May Allah fight them; how are they deluded!

There is no contradiction between what is in this verse, which attributes its sanctification to Allah, exalted is He, and what is in the saying of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him: "Indeed Ibrahim, peace be upon him, made Makkah sacred, and I have made Madinah sacred." The attribution there is to Ibrahim, peace be upon him, because in the verse the one who truly sanctifies is Allah, while in the hadith Ibrahim, peace be upon him, is the one who makes manifest His ruling, exalted is His majesty.

Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud read *allati* (the one which) as an attributive adjective to "the city". The reading of the majority is more eloquent in magnifying the matter. In *al-Kashf* it is said that applying a description to the Lord, exalted is His majesty, magnifies both the description itself and what the description relates to, and adds a further specification of that to whom the description is applied, by way of incidental inclusion (idmaj), and it makes that a matter taken as established and proven. This is not the case if the city were described by a description intended only for specification or praise.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and to Him belongs everything﴾, means by creation, ownership and disposal, without anything sharing with Him, glory be to Him, in any part of that. It is an affirmation of the truth and an alert that the singling out of Makkah by annexation is for the magnification and honour mentioned, along with the generality of Lordship over all existing things.

Some people have used this verse as evidence for the permissibility of what ignorant Sufis say: "*shay'un lillah*" (a thing for Allah). They argue that it means "everything is for Allah, exalted is His majesty," in the manner of the proverb "a date is better than a locust." But you know that they do not say it with that intention. Rather, they say, "*shay'un lillah*, O so-and-so," to some of the great ones among the dead, either meaning "give me something for the sake of Allah, O so-and-so," or meaning "you are a great thing among the signs of Allah's power." Whoever does not declare them disbelievers because of it has given it this interpretation, and that is the truth, though on the first of the two interpretations its outward meaning is asking something from one who has no power over anything. Yes, it is better to guard the tongue from such expressions.

﴿And I have been commanded to be among the Muslims﴾, that is: I remain steadfast in what I have been upon, being among those who stand firm upon the religion of Islam and monotheism, or among those who have submitted their faces wholly to Allah, exalted is He, drawn from His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And who is better in religion than one who submits his face to Allah﴾ (Qur'an 4:125).

﴿And that I should recite the Qur'an﴾, that is, that I should persist in reciting it to the people, by repeating the call and reiterating the guidance, since it is sufficient for guiding to the path of right direction. It was also said: that is, that I should persist in reciting it so that its exquisite truths stored within its folds may be revealed to me gradually, for persistence in reciting it is one of the means of opening the doors of divine outpourings and sacred secrets. It has been related that "he (ﷺ) stood one night praying, and he recited His words, exalted is He: ﴿If You punish them, they are Your servants﴾, and he kept repeating it, and there kept becoming apparent to him of its secrets what became apparent, until dawn broke."

It was also said: *atlu* means "to follow," from "talāhu" when one follows him, i.e., "and that I should follow the Qur'an." This is contrary to the apparent meaning. What supports the meaning we mentioned first is what is in the reading of Ubayy, as Abu 'Ubayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Harun: "*wa-tlu ʿalayhimu al-Qurʾān*" (and recite to them the Qur'an). And it is related from him in al-Bahr that he recited "*wa-tlu hādhā al-Qurʾān*" (and recite this Qur'an). But there is no support in this for what we have mentioned.

Abdullah (Ibn Mas'ud) read "*wa-ani tlu*" without the waw, as an imperative from *talā*. Thus *an* may be a verbal *an* (that) connected to the imperative, and it may be an explanatory *an*, with "I have been commanded" implied.

﴿So whoever is guided﴾, that is, by faith in the Qur'an and acting upon what it contains of laws and rulings. It was said: that is, by following in what was mentioned of worship and submission, and the recitation of the Qur'an or following it.

﴿then he is guided only for his own self﴾, that is, the benefits of his guidance return to him.

﴿And whoever goes astray﴾, by disbelieving in it and turning away from it. It was said: by opposing what was mentioned.

﴿Then say﴾, that is, to him.

﴿I am only one of the warners﴾, and I have discharged the obligation of warning, so there is upon me no burden of your misguidance; rather it is upon you alone. It is known from what we have mentioned that the response of the conditional is the clause of the saying and what is within its scope, and the linking pronoun required in such a case is omitted. Some have estimated it after "the warners," that is, "among the warners of him." Abu Hayyan allowed that the response is omitted, that is, "whoever goes astray, the burden of his misguidance is specific to him," and it was omitted because the response of its counterpart indicates it. Some allowed that the clause following is the response, and because it is an allusive, indirect expression of what Abu Hayyan estimated, it does not need a linking pronoun. Moreover, the apparent explicitness of "say" here requires that "whoever is guided," etc., be part of His speech, exalted and majestic is He, with which He follows up the command to His Messenger (ﷺ) to say to them what preceded it. And there is no remoteness in its being part of the saying estimated before His words, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed I have only been commanded﴾, as

[Page 40]

﴿Say: "Praise be to God"﴾, that is, for the bounties He has bestowed upon me, the greatest of which is the blessing of prophethood, which entails all kinds of religious and worldly blessings. He has also enabled me to bear its burdens and to convey its rulings through clear signs and luminous proofs. God's words, ﴿"He will show you His signs, and you will recognize them"﴾, are part of the speech commanded, meaning: say, "He will show you His signs, O Exalted One, and you will recognize them," that is, you will recognize that they are the signs of God, Exalted is He, at a time when such recognition will no longer benefit you. It has also been said that the meaning is: He will show them to you in this world. By "the signs" is meant the smoke and the chastisements of God that befell them, among which is counted the slaying on the Day of Badr and the admission of the slain to this, in deed, and the admission of others to it, in potential. It has also been said that the signs are the emergence of the beast and the other portents of the Hour. The address is to the whole of mankind, not only to those in the time of prophethood.

Ibn Abi Hatim and a group [of scholars] related from Mujahid that the signs are those within the souls and those on the horizons. The verse is then like His words, ﴿"We shall show them Our signs on the horizons and within themselves"﴾. It has also been said that the signs are the miracles of the Messenger (ﷺ), and their attribution to His pronoun is because they are His act, which He, Mighty and Majestic, manifested through the hand of His Messenger, peace be upon him, as a confirmation. By "recognition" is meant that which is compatible with denial. God's words, ﴿"Your Lord is not heedless of what you do"﴾, are a statement from Him, Glorified is He, delivered by way of tadhyil (a concluding appendage) that confirms what precedes it and includes both promise and threat, as is indicated by the attribution of "Lord" to his pronoun (ﷺ) and by the address being first specified to him, peace be upon him, and then generalized to the disbelievers by taghlib (prevalence of the masculine/collective form in address). The meaning is: ﴿"Your Lord is not heedless of what you do"﴾, meaning of the good deeds you (Prophet) do and of the evil deeds you disbelievers do, so He will recompense each of you for his deeds without fail. Most readers, however, recited ﴿ya'maluna﴾ with the third-person yā' (of absence), in which case it is a pure threat, and the meaning is: "Your Lord is not heedless of their deeds, so He will surely punish them. Let them not suppose that the delay of their punishment is due to God's heedlessness of the deeds that necessitate it." Whoever reflects upon these verses will find that this concluding statement is one that astonishes minds and bewilders understandings. How marvelous is the Revelation, and what could be said about the speech of the All-Knowing King?

* * *

Among the allusory (ishari) interpretations of the verses is what has been said: ﴿"And He sent down water from the sky"﴾, that is, from the sky of the heart, a water which is the water of the gaze of mercy. ﴿"And We caused to grow thereby gardens of delight"﴾ of knowledge, meanings, secrets and profound wisdoms. ﴿"You could not have caused their trees to grow"﴾, that is, their roots, because divine knowledge is not within one's choice. Rather, every knowledge is in itself not optional; otherwise it would follow that a thing precedes itself. Yes, it is optional with respect to its causes. ﴿"Or who made the earth"﴾, that is, the earth of the soul, a dwelling place in the body, ﴿"and placed within it rivers"﴾ of the impulses of humanity, ﴿"and placed for it firm mountains"﴾ of the powers of humanity and the senses, ﴿"and placed between the two seas"﴾, the sea of the spirit and the sea of the soul, ﴿"a barrier"﴾, which is the heart. ﴿"Or who answers the distressed one"﴾, who is the one predisposed to something of the things, ﴿"when he calls upon Him"﴾ with the tongue of predisposition, and seeks from Him, Exalted is He, what he is predisposed to. Some of them said: the distressed one is one immersed in the seas of His longing, Exalted is He. ﴿"And when the word is fulfilled against them, We shall bring forth for them a beast"﴾, which is the rational soul and the human spirit, ﴿"from the earth"﴾, that is, the earth of humanity. Along this pattern they have spoken concerning the rest of the verses. Al-Shaykh al-Akbar (Ibn 'Arabi), may his secret be sanctified, cited God's words, ﴿"And you see the mountains, thinking them fixed, while they pass away like the passing of clouds"﴾, as evidence for what he claims of the renewal of substances like accidents, according to al-Ash'ari, and their non-persistence for two moments of time. The basis of this, in his view, is the doctrine of wahdat al-wujud (the unity of being), and that He, Glorified is He, "every day is in a state [of glory]." The discussion of the soundness of this basis and of its implication of the claim is not hidden from the knower. As for citing this verse for this purpose, it is among the mother of wonders and the strangest of strange things. And God knows best.

[p. 41]
